Overall, the data reveal a fundamental shift in the country's energy supply. After modest gains to 25 TWh in 2005, output surged, outstripping both gas and coal by 2020 at 140 TWh and reaching 190 TWh in 2025.

The graph compares monthly visitor numbers to a seaside town in 2010 and 2020.

In both years, tourism was heavily concentrated in the summer, with August the peak month. The key difference, however, is that the seasonal pattern became much less pronounced over the decade: summer numbers fell substantially, while the quieter months attracted more visitors.

In 2010, the town received between 11,000 and 15,000 visitors a month during the first quarter. Numbers then rose steeply from April, reaching 90,000 in July and a peak of 96,000 in August, roughly nine times the February low. This was followed by an equally steep decline to 24,000 in October and just 13,000 in November.

By 2020, the summer surge had become far more modest. August remained the busiest month, but with only 65,000 visitors, while July saw 60,000, some 30,000 fewer than a decade earlier. Conversely, arrivals outside the peak season were consistently higher. January and February brought in 18,000 and 17,000 visitors respectively, and the figures for October and December, at 35,000 and 28,000, far exceeded their 2010 equivalents. Only in September were the two years broadly similar, at 50,000 and 48,000.

The charts compare the allocation of a city council's budget across six service areas in 2010 and 2025.

The standout development over the fifteen-year period was the rapid growth of social care, which overtook education to become the largest item of expenditure. This expansion was accompanied by a shrinking share for most other services, nearly all of which received a smaller proportion of the budget by 2025.

In 2010, education absorbed 34% of council spending, comfortably ahead of social care at 22%. Transport accounted for 15%, while housing and administration each took 10%, and parks and culture received the smallest share, at 9%.

By 2025, the share devoted to social care had climbed to 35%, an increase of 13 percentage points, whereas education had slipped to 30%. Transport and administration were both cut back, to 12% and 7% respectively, but the sharpest proportional reduction was in parks and culture, whose share almost halved to just 5%. Housing was the only other area to gain funding, and even then only marginally, rising by a single point to 11%. Taken together, education and social care accounted for almost two-thirds of the budget in 2025, compared with 56% in 2010.

The most notable change over the thirty years was that transport replaced energy supply as the principal source of emissions. More generally, the shares attributable to energy supply and industry contracted, while every other sector accounted for a larger proportion by 2020.

In 1990, energy supply was responsible for 36% of emissions, well ahead of industry (22%) and transport (16%). Buildings contributed 14%, and agriculture and waste were comparatively minor sources, at 9% and 3% respectively.

As a result, emissions were spread more evenly across the main sectors at the end of the period than at the beginning.

Overall, access to both services improved in every region over the twenty years, although safe water was consistently more widely available than sanitation. Europe had the highest levels of provision, whereas Sub-Saharan Africa lagged far behind the other regions.

Sub-Saharan Africa, however, only rose by ten points to 33%, meaning two thirds of people still lacked basic sanitation.

Overall, there was a clear generational divide. Younger people spent most of their media time on video streaming and social media, while older age groups favoured more traditional media, particularly broadcast TV.

Among 16- to 24-year-olds, video streaming was the most popular activity, at 185 minutes a day, closely followed by social media at 160 minutes. Time spent on these two media declined steadily with age, falling to just 20 and 15 minutes respectively for those aged 65 and over. These were also the main media for the 25–44 age group, at 120 and 95 minutes.

The opposite trend can be seen for broadcast TV, radio and newspapers. Viewing of broadcast TV rose dramatically from only 25 minutes among the youngest group to 270 minutes, or four and a half hours, among the over-65s. Similarly, time spent listening to radio or podcasts increased from 40 to 110 minutes across the age groups. Printed newspapers were the least used medium overall, although reading time grew from 2 minutes for the youngest to 42 minutes for the oldest.

Radio and podcasts follow the same upward trend, peaking at 110 minutes, as do printed newspapers, which occupy 42 minutes of the oldest group's day. In contrast, streaming and social media fall to just 20 and 15 minutes respectively for this group.

The table shows the average temperature, rainfall and sunshine hours for each month in a city called Port Sella.

Firstly, the temperature is lowest in January with 11°C and it goes up every month until July and August, when it reach 27°C. After that it goes down again to 20°C in October and 12°C in December.

Rainfall is very different. The wettest month is December with 110 mm, and January and November also have a lot of rain, 98 mm and 92 mm. From February the rain decrease, and in summer there is almost no rain, only 6 mm in June, 1 mm in July and 3 mm in August. Then it increases again in the autumn, for example 58 mm in October.

Sunshine is similar like the temperature. In December there is only 4.2 hours a day and in January 4.5 hours, but in July there is 11.8 hours, which is the most sunny month. June and August have 11.0 and 10.9 hours.

Overall, Port Sella has hot, dry and sunny summers and cool, wet winters with less sunshine.

The table gives the average monthly temperature, rainfall and daily hours of sunshine in Port Sella over the course of a year.

Overall, the city has warm, dry and sunny summers, while its winters are cooler, wetter and much less sunny. Rainfall generally moves in the opposite direction to temperature and sunshine.

Temperatures are lowest in January, at 11°C, and rise steadily through spring to reach a peak of 27°C in July and August. They then fall again in autumn, dropping to 20°C in October and 12°C by December. Sunshine follows a very similar pattern, increasing from around four and a half hours a day in winter to a maximum of 11.8 hours in July, before declining to 4.2 hours in December, the least sunny month.

Rainfall, by contrast, is heaviest in the winter months. December is the wettest month, with 110 mm, followed by January (98 mm) and November (92 mm). From February onwards, the amount of rain falls considerably, and the summer is extremely dry, with only 6 mm in June, 1 mm in July and 3 mm in August. The rain then returns in autumn, rising to 58 mm in October.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The table provides monthly averages for temperature, rainfall and daily sunshine in the city of Port Sella.

The data show a pronounced seasonal pattern, with hot, sunny and almost completely dry summers contrasting with mild, wet winters that receive considerably less sunshine. Temperature and sunshine rise and fall together, whereas rainfall follows the reverse pattern.

Temperatures climb gradually from a low of 11°C in January to a peak of 27°C in both July and August, a difference of 16 degrees, before falling back to 12°C in December. Hours of sunshine mirror this trend closely: the city receives only 4.5 hours a day in January and 4.2 in December, but almost three times as much in midsummer, when the figure reaches 11.8 hours in July.

Rainfall, in contrast, is concentrated in the cooler months. December is the wettest month, with 110 mm, and November and January are almost as wet, at 92 mm and 98 mm respectively. Precipitation then declines sharply through spring, to 22 mm in May, and virtually disappears in summer, with July recording just 1 mm. The rains return from September, when 18 mm falls, rising steeply to 58 mm in October.

the campus has been significantly expanded with new academic, residential and sports buildings, largely at the expense of parking space and green areas, although its central core has remained the same.

The main teaching building, the entrance road leading to it from the south, the lake in the north-east and the original student halls in the north-west were all unaffected. The library in the west, however, has been extended on both sides, and the trees which covered the north of the campus have been cleared to make way for new student halls.

The southern part of the campus has seen the greatest change. The large car park in the south-west has been replaced by a science and engineering building, with only a much smaller car park beside it, next to the entrance road. To the south-east, the sports field has been divided into a sports centre and a pitch.
In addition,
a cycle path now crosses the whole campus from west to east, just south of the teaching building, and a small café have opened on the eastern edge, south of the lake.

Finally, a cycle path has been laid across the campus, just south of the teaching building, and a café has been added on the eastern boundary.

The maps depict Seaview, a coastal town, in 1950 and 2020. Over this seventy-year period, the town evolved from a modest fishing community set among farmland and trees into a tourism-focused resort, with most of its open land developed, while its seafront and principal landmarks were largely retained.

The southern part of the town has kept its essential character. The beach, Coast Road, the hotel and the church are all still in place, but the fishermen's cottages in the west now house cafés and shops, and the pier no longer extends as far out to sea. In addition, a walkway has been laid along the full length of the seafront.

North of the coast road, the transformation has been far more dramatic. The railway that once crossed the town from west to east has been removed altogether, and the extensive farmland beyond it has been built over, with housing in the north-west and a large block of holiday apartments to its east. The woodland in the north-east has been cleared for a car park, and a new route, Hill Road, now runs northwards from Coast Road, separating the apartments from the car park.

The maps show Hollin Farm in 2005 and the same site in 2024, following its conversion into an eco-park. The essential shift has been from agriculture to recreation and conservation, with fields and farm buildings repurposed, although the framework of the site, namely the roads, farmhouse, stream and woodland, remains exactly as before.

The greatest changes are to the farmland itself. The western wheat field has been partly transformed into a wildflower meadow, with the remainder of the field given over to a pond overlooked by a bird hide. To the east, the grazing land has become a camping area. These areas are now framed by a nature trail, which descends the western side of the site, follows the stream and climbs back up the eastern side.

Firstly, people leave their empty bottles in bottle banks in the street. Then a lorry take the bottles to the recycling plant. Overall, the process starts with the collection of bottles and ends with the distribution of new bottles, and then it begin again from the collection stage, so it is a cycle. The most important part is at the recycling plant where the glass is sorted, cleaned, crushed and melted.

The diagram illustrates the way in which used glass bottles are recycled so that they can be turned into new ones.

Overall, the process is cyclical and consists of eight stages, beginning with the collection of empty bottles from street bottle banks and ending with the distribution of new bottles, after which the cycle starts again.

Finally, these bottles are sent to drinks factories and shops, and the whole process then begins again with the collection stage, meaning that the same glass can be used many times.

The diagram show how olive oil is produced. There are nine stages, from harvesting the olives to using the by-product.

First, olives are harvested between October and December. The olives are shaken from the trees and they fall onto a nets. Then the olives are washed for removing leaves and dirt. After that, the olives and the stones are crushed and they become a paste.

Next step is malaxation, the paste is stirred slowly for 30–40 minutes. Then a centrifuge separate the oil from water and solids. After this, the oil is left in steel tanks for 4–6 weeks to settle. Then it is filtered, so the particles which remain are removed. After filtering, the oil is sealed in dark glass bottles.

Finally, the pulp which is left over is dried and burned as a fuel. Overall, it is a linear process with many steps and some of them take long time, especially the settling in the tanks, and even the waste is used in the end.

The diagram illustrate the life cycle of the honeybee. It have six stages and it is a cycle.

At the beginning, the queen lays an egg in a wax cell. After 3 days the egg hatches and becomes a larva. The larva is fed royal jelly at first and then pollen and honey, and this stage is 6 days. Then the worker bees seal the cell with a wax.

After that the larva is a pupa. In this stage it develop legs, wings and eyes, and it takes about 12 days. On day 21 the adult bee chews through the wax cap and comes out of the cell.

Finally, the adult becomes a worker bee. The worker bee cleans, feeds larvae and later it collects nectar. It lives for 5–6 weeks. Then the cycle start again with a new egg from the queen.

Overall, the honeybee has six stages from egg to worker bee, and the development inside the cell take 21 days in total, which is much shorter than the life of the worker bee.

Broadly speaking, the process falls into three phases: the preparation of the raw wood, the chemical treatment of that wood to create pulp, and the mechanical formation of the paper itself. The sheet is then pressed between rollers and dried over a series of heated cylinders. In the last step, the finished paper is wound onto large reels and later cut into sheets of the required dimensions.

The diagram shows how a pumped-storage hydroelectric power station work. There are eight stages and they make a cycle, which happen every day and night.

At night, the demand for electricity is low, so the station takes the cheap surplus electricity from the grid. This electricity is used for pumping the water from the lower reservoir up to a tunnel. Then the water is stored in the upper reservoir on the top of the mountain.

During the day, the demand is high, so the valves are opened. After that the water is released and it flows down through the tunnel. Next, the falling water spin the turbines, which are connected to generators. Then the power is sent to the national grid.

Finally, the water is collected in the lower reservoir and it is ready to be pumped again at the next night. Overall, the station uses electricity at night and produces electricity in the day, and the same water is use again and again.

The diagram explains how a pumped-storage hydroelectric plant functions over a cycle of night and day, using the same body of water repeatedly.

In essence, the system consists of eight repeating stages and operates in two distinct modes: during periods of low demand at night it consumes electricity to move water uphill, whereas during periods of high demand in the daytime it releases that water to generate power.

At night, inexpensive surplus electricity is drawn from the grid and used to pump water from the lower reservoir up through a tunnel. The water is then held in an upper reservoir on the mountain top, where it waits until it is needed. Crucially, this pumping phase relies on electricity at a time when it is both cheap and plentiful.

Once demand rises during the day, valves are opened and the water is allowed to flow back down the tunnel. As it falls, it drives turbines linked to generators, and the electricity this produces is fed into the national grid. The water then collects in the lower reservoir, where it remains until it can be pumped up once more, at which point the entire cycle resumes.

The diagram shows the process of making hard cheese. There are eight stage, from collecting milk to packaging.

Firstly, fresh milk is delivered from dairy farms. Then the milk is pasteurised, it is heated to 72°C for 15 seconds and then cooled. After that, culture and rennet are added to the milk and it begin to set.

Next, the milk separate into solid curd and liquid whey. Then the curd is cut into cubes and heated, and the whey is drained off. After this, the curd is salted and it is pressed into the moulds.

In the ripening stage, the cheese is stored at 10°C for 3–24 months. This is the longest stage in the process. Finally, the cheese is cut, wrapped and labelled, so it can be sold in the shops.

Overall, making hard cheese is a linear process with many steps. The milk become cheese through heating, cutting, salting and a long time of ripening, and this is why it takes a lot of time.

The diagram shows the life cycle of the Atlantic salmon. There are seven stages and it is a cycle, because the adult salmon come back to the river where they was born.

Firstly, the eggs are laid in the gravel of the upper river and they hatch in spring. Then the baby fish are called alevin. They stay in the gravel and they feed on their yolk sac. After that, they become fry and they come out from the gravel to feed in the river.

Next stage is parr. The parr live in the river for 1–3 years. Then they become smolt, they turn silver and swim downstream to the sea. In the sea, the adult salmon feed and grow for 1–4 years, so they spend quite a long time there.

Finally, the salmon swim back up the same river to spawn, so the new eggs are laid and the cycle start again. Overall, the salmon spend some years in the river and some years in the sea, and in the end they return to the place where the cycle begin.

The diagram illustrates the life cycle of the Atlantic salmon, which is spent partly in a river and partly in the ocean.

Overall, the cycle consists of seven stages. The first four take place in the river, after which the fish migrate to the sea to mature before returning to the same river to spawn, so that the cycle begins again.

The eggs are laid in the gravel of the upper river and hatch in spring. The young fish, known as alevin, remain in the gravel at first and feed on their yolk sac. They then emerge as fry to feed in the river, and later develop into parr, which live in the river for between one and three years.

Finally, they make a return migration, swimming back up the same river in which they hatched in order to spawn, and new eggs are laid in the gravel of the upper river, which starts the whole cycle once again.

The diagram shows how cement is produced and how it is used for making concrete. There are eight stages in the process.

First, limestone and clay are extracted from a quarry. Then the raw materials are crushed and mixed together. After that, the mixture is grinded into a fine powder. Next, the powder is heated in a rotating kiln to 1,450°C and it form clinker.

In the fifth stage, the clinker is cooled and grinded with gypsum, and this make cement. Then the cement is packed in bags, so it is ready to use.

After that, the cement is used to make a concrete. The concrete is made from 15% cement, 10% water, 25% sand and 50% gravel, so the gravel is the biggest part of the mixture. Finally, the concrete is poured into moulds and it is left to harden.

Overall, the process has two parts, the first part is producing cement and the second part is making concrete. It is interesting that the cement is only a small part of the concrete, although most of the stages are for making it.

The diagram shows how ethanol fuel is produced from sugar cane. There are eight stages in this process, from growing sugar cane to deliver the fuel.

Firstly, the sugar cane is grown for 12–18 months. When it is ready, the cane is harvested and cut by a machine. Then it is crushed by rollers and the juice is extracted from it.

The waste from the crushing, which is called bagasse, is fibrous. This waste is burned and it gives the power to the factory, so the factory use its own waste. Meanwhile, yeast is added to the juice and the sugar turns into alcohol, this is fermentation.

After that, in distillation stage, the ethanol is separated from the water. Then the ethanol is mixed with petrol, it is called blending. Finally, the fuel is delivered to the filling stations, where people can buy it.

Overall, the process takes a long time because the sugar cane need more than one year to grow. The main product is ethanol fuel and also the waste bagasse is used to power the factory.

The diagram shows how the food waste from a household is changed into compost. There are seven stages and it is a cycle.

At first, vegetable peelings and food scraps are collected in a kitchen caddy. Then the waste is put in a compost bin in the garden, and leaves and cardboard is added too. After that, the waste is broken down by worms and bacterias, this is decomposition.

Next, the compost is mixed every 2–3 weeks for adding air. This is called turning. Then the compost is left for 6–12 months until it becomes dark and crumbly, so this stage takes the longest time.

When the compost is ready, it is spread on the soil in the garden. Finally, vegetables are grown in the soil and people eat them. The scraps from these vegetables go back to the kitchen caddy, and the cycle start again.

Overall, the process starts and finishes in the kitchen, and the food waste is not wasted because it helps to grow new vegetables which people can eat again.

The diagram shows the stages of producing black tea. There is eight stages, from plucking the leaves to packing and exporting.

Firstly, the top two leaves and a bud are picked by hand. Then the leaves are spread on racks for 12–18 hours, this is called withering. After that the leaves are rolled for breaking the cell walls.

Next, the leaves are left for oxidation. In this stage, the colour of leaves change to copper-brown and it takes 1–3 hours. Then the leaves are dried with hot air at 120°C, and this stops the oxidation.

In the sixth stage, the leaves are sieved and sorted by the size. After that, professional tasters check the samples of tea to see if it is good. Finally, the tea is packed in sacks which have foil inside and it is exported.

Overall, black tea production has many stages and some of them take a lot of hours, for example withering. The process starts with picking leaves by hand and ends with export to other countries.

The diagram shows the process of recycling plastic bottles to make polyester fibre for clothes. There are eight stages in the process.

First, the bottles are collected from homes. Then they are sorted, and the PET bottles are separated from another plastics. After that, the bottles are washed and the labels and caps is removed. At the end of this stage the bottles are clean.

Next, the bottles are shredded, it means they are cut into small flakes. So the bottles become small pieces of plastic. Then the flakes are melted at 260°C and become liquid. After this, the liquid is pushed through a very tiny holes and it forms threads. This is the extrusion stage.

In the seventh stage, the threads are stretched and they are spun into yarn. Finally, the fabric is made and it is sewed into jackets and T-shirts.

Overall, the process begin with old plastic bottles and ends with new clothes. Most of the stages are about changing the bottles into thread, and only the last stage is about making the clothes.

The diagram shows the stages of how coal is formed. There are eight stages, from the swamp forest to the mining of coal.

In the first stage, plants grow in warm wetlands, which is called swamp forest. Then the plants die and they fall into the water, but they do not decay fully. After that, the layers of dead plants build up and they are compressed, and this become peat.

Next, the peat is covered by sand and mud and this take millions of years. Then the heat and the pressure remove the water from it, so it change into lignite. After more compression, it becomes bituminous coal, which has more carbon than before.

In the seventh stage, the coal become anthracite. This is the hardest coal and it has about 90% of carbon. Finally, people extract the coal from underground seams by mining, so it can be used.

Overall, the process is very long and it starts with living plants and ends with hard coal which is mined from under the ground. The coal has more carbon in the later stages of the process.

The diagram illustrates how coal is formed over time, beginning with plants in swamp forests and ending with the extraction of coal from the ground.

Overall, there are eight stages in the process, which takes millions of years. As the material is buried and compressed, it gradually changes from peat into different types of coal, with the later types containing more carbon.

The diagram outlines the natural process by which coal is formed and the point at which it is finally extracted by humans for use.

It is clear that coal formation is an extremely slow, eight-stage process spanning millions of years, during which buried plant matter is progressively compressed into increasingly carbon-rich forms of coal, culminating in anthracite. Only the last stage involves human activity.

The sequence starts in warm, swampy wetlands, where plants flourish. When these plants die, they fall into the water and, crucially, fail to decompose fully, so that successive layers of debris accumulate and are compressed into peat. Over millions of years, this peat is buried beneath deposits of sand and mud.

Heat and pressure then drive out the water, converting the compressed peat into lignite, the first of the three types of coal shown. With further compression, lignite becomes bituminous coal, which has a higher carbon content, and ultimately anthracite, the hardest variety, containing approximately 90% carbon. At the final stage, this coal is extracted by mining underground seams, marking the shift from a natural process to a human one.

The diagram shows how a solar water heating system give hot water to a house. There are six stages and it is a cycle.

First, there is a solar panel on the roof of the house. The sunlight heats the fluid which is in the dark pipes of the panel. Then the hot fluid rises and it is carried to the storage cylinder.

In the storage cylinder there is a heat exchanger. It is a coil and it transfer the heat from the fluid to the water of the house. After that, the hot water is kept in a insulated cylinder, so the people in the house can use it later.

On cloudy days, there is not so much sun, so a backup boiler heats the water. Finally, the fluid which is cooled is returned to the solar panel by a pump, and then the cycle start again.

Overall, the system uses the sun to heat the water, but when the weather is cloudy it needs the boiler too. The fluid goes round and round between the panel and the cylinder, so it is used many times.

The system operates as a continuous six-stage loop in which a fluid circulates between a roof-mounted solar panel and a storage cylinder, collecting heat at one end and releasing it at the other, before being pumped back to begin again. A backup boiler supplements the system when the weather is cloudy.

The cycle begins on the roof, where sunlight heats a fluid flowing through the dark pipes of the solar panel. Once heated, the fluid rises and is carried to the storage cylinder, where a coil acting as a heat exchanger transfers its heat to the household water. This water is then retained in an insulated cylinder so that it stays hot until required.

On overcast days, a backup boiler is used to heat the water. Having given up its heat, the cooled fluid is pumped back up to the panel on the roof, where it is warmed once again by the sun, allowing the process to repeat without interruption.

The diagram shows how the raw wool from sheep is processed into yarn. There are eight stages in the process.

Firstly, the fleece is removed from the sheep in spring, this is called shearing. Then the dirty edges of the wool are removed and the wool is graded by its quality. After that, the wool is washed in warm soapy water for removing the grease. This stage is called scouring.

Next, the wool is dried by warm air. Then the fibres are combed so they are straight, and they make a soft web. This is carding. After that, the fibres are twisted and they become yarn, which is called spinning.

In the seventh stage, the yarn is dyed in large vats, so it have colour. Finally, the yarn is wound into balls or into cones.

Overall, the process start with the sheep and it ends with yarn which is ready to use. Most of stages are about cleaning the wool and making it into yarn, and the colour is added near the end of the process.

The diagram illustrates the stages through which raw sheep's wool passes before it becomes yarn.

Overall, the process is linear and consists of eight stages. The first half involves removing the wool from the sheep and cleaning it, while the second half focuses on turning the fibres into yarn, colouring it and winding it.

The process begins in spring, when the fleece is sheared from the sheep. During skirting and grading, the dirty edges are cut away and the wool is graded according to the quality. It is then scoured, meaning that it is washed in warm soapy water to remove grease, and afterwards it is dried using warm air.

In the carding stage, the fibres are combed straight to create a soft web, and these fibres are then twisted into yarn during spinning. Following this, the yarn is coloured in large vats in the dyeing stage, before finally being wound into balls or cones. This means that the colour is added only after the yarn has been made. At this point, the yarn is ready to be used, for example for knitting or weaving.

The diagram shows how the old smartphones are recycled. There are eight stages in this process.

First, people return their phones to the shops or send them by post. Then all the personal data on the phones is erased. After that, the phones are tested. If the phone is working, it is repaired and sold again to other people.

The faulty phones go to the next stage, it is dismantling. In this stage, the battery and the screen is removed. Then the battery is recycled and lithium and cobalt are recovered from it. The remaining parts of the phone are shredded into small pieces.

After the shredding, the metals like gold, silver and copper are extracted. Finally, all the materials are sold to manufacturers so they can use it again.

Overall, the process begins with the drop-off of old phones and ends with the reuse of materials. Some phones is repaired and sold again, but the others are broken into parts to get the metals and other materials from them.

The diagram illustrates the process by which old smartphones are recycled, either by being reused as phones or by being broken down for their materials.

Overall, the process has eight stages, beginning with phones being dropped off and ending with materials being sold to manufacturers. A key feature is that phones which still work are repaired and resold, whereas faulty ones are taken apart so that their materials can be recovered.

At the start, phones are returned either to shops or by post, and all personal data is erased from them. They are then tested, and those that are working are repaired and sold again, so they do not continue to the later stages. Faulty phones, however, are dismantled, with the battery and the screen being removed.

After that, the batteries are recycled so that lithium and cobalt can be recovered, while the remaining parts of the phones are shredded. From this shredded material, three metals, namely gold, silver and copper, is extracted. In the final stage, all of these recovered materials are sold to manufacturers, who can reuse them to make new products.

The diagram outlines how old smartphones are processed for recycling, from the moment they are handed in to the point at which their materials re-enter manufacturing.

Of the eight stages, testing is pivotal, since it determines which of two routes a phone will take: working devices are repaired and resold, while faulty ones are dismantled and broken down so that their constituent materials can be recovered and sold on.

Phones are first returned, either to shops or by post, after which all personal data stored on them is wiped. They are then tested, and those found to be in working order are repaired and put back on the market. Defective handsets, by contrast, are dismantled, with the battery and screen being removed. Notably, both routes begin only after the data-wiping stage, so no phone is tested while it still holds personal information.

The batteries are recycled to recover lithium and cobalt, whereas the remaining components are shredded. Gold, silver and copper are then extracted from this shredded material. Finally, all of the recovered materials are sold to manufacturers for reuse, which brings the process to an end.

Nowadays many parents and teachers are discussing about whether young children should get homework or not. Some people think that homework in primary schools must be stopped because children needs time to play and rest. I mostly agree with this idea, although I think a small amount of homework can still be useful.

Firstly, primary school children are very young and they already spend six or seven hours in the classroom every day. When they come home they are tired and they want to play with their friends or watch cartoons. If they have to do a lot of homework, they can feel stressed and they may start to hate school. Also, playing is important for children because they learn how to share, how to solve problems and how to be creative. For example, when children play football in the park they learn teamwork, which is not possible from a worksheet.

Secondly, homework can make problem in the family. Many parents work until late and they don't have time to help their children. As a result, the child cannot finish the task or the parent do it for him, so the homework is not useful. In my country, I have seen many parents who argue with their children every evening because of homework.

However, some homework can be good. For example, reading a short story with parents for ten minutes is enjoyable and it improve the child's reading skill. This kind of activity is not same as difficult exercises.

In conclusion, I agree that most homework should be abolished in primary schools because children need to play and rest after school. But short and easy tasks like reading can still be given, because they help children without making them tired.

It is often argued that primary school pupils should no longer be given homework, since young children need free time to play and recover after a long school day. While I accept that heavy workloads can be harmful at this age, I largely disagree with abolishing homework altogether, because short, well-designed tasks bring benefits that cannot easily be replaced.

There is certainly some truth in the argument for abolition. Young children have limited concentration, and after six hours of lessons many of them are simply too tired to learn effectively. Unstructured play is not a waste of time either; it helps children develop social skills, imagination and physical health. When homework takes up most of the evening, it can create anxiety and turn learning into a source of conflict between parents and children, which is clearly counterproductive.

However, the solution to excessive homework is to reduce it, not to remove it completely. A few minutes of daily reading or practising multiplication tables helps pupils to consolidate what they have learned in class, and a regular practice is particularly important for basic skills such as literacy and numeracy. Moreover, simple tasks teach children to organise their time and take responsibility for their own work, habits which will become essential at secondary school, where the workload increases sharply.

Homework can also strengthen the link between school and home. When parents see what their child is studying, they are better able to support them and to notice any difficulties at an early stage. A child who reads aloud to a parent each evening, for instance, is likely to gain confidence as well as fluency.

In conclusion, although young children certainly need time to play and rest, I do not believe homework should be abolished in primary schools. Instead, it should be limited to short, meaningful activities that support learning without taking over family life.

answers.text:
The question of whether primary school children should be set homework has become increasingly contentious, with critics arguing that young pupils need their evenings for play and rest. I agree with this view to a considerable extent: formal homework offers limited academic benefit at this age, and the time it consumes is better spent on activities that support children's broader development. Nevertheless, I would stop short of banning all learning outside school.

The strongest case for abolition rests on how young children actually learn. At primary level, understanding is built largely through exploration, conversation and play rather than through repetitive written exercises. A seven-year-old who spends an evening building something with friends or helping to cook a meal is practising language, problem-solving and cooperation in a way that a worksheet rarely replicates. Rest matters just as much: tired children struggle to concentrate, and a school day followed by an hour of compulsory tasks can leave little room for the sleep and relaxation they need.

Homework also tends to widen existing inequalities. Pupils whose parents have the time and confidence to help them tend to complete assignments to a high standard, whereas those from busier or less advantaged households may fall behind or become discouraged. Reading together for pleasure, for example, is widely regarded as valuable and places little strain on children. Schools could therefore replace compulsory assignments with optional, informal suggestions of this kind.

Overall, I largely support abolishing formal homework in primary schools, since young children gain more from play, rest and family life. Informal reading at home, however, should still be warmly encouraged.

answers.text:
With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, many students can now produce a well-written essay simply by typing a request into a chatbot. As a result, some argue that universities should stop assessing students through written assignments completed at home. I disagree with this view, as I believe such assignments remain valuable if they are redesigned rather than abandoned.

Admittedly, AI poses a serious challenge to traditional coursework. When a tool can generate a coherent essay in seconds, it becomes difficult for lecturers to know whether the submitted work reflects a student's own understanding. This undermines the fairness of grades and may discourage those who complete their assignments honestly. Supervised exams would obviously reduce this risk, which explain why the idea of abolishing take-home work is attractive to some institutions.

Nevertheless, relying only on timed exams would come at a considerable cost. Extended assignments teach skills that a two-hour exam cannot measure, such as researching independently, evaluating sources and developing an argument over several weeks. These abilities are exactly what graduates need in most professional roles, where reports are rarely written under exam conditions. Removing coursework would therefore make university assessment less relevant to working life.

A more sensible approach is to adapt assignments to the new technology. Universities could require students to submit drafts and notes showing how their ideas developed, or ask them to discuss their work in a short oral examination. Tasks could also be linked to local data, fieldwork or class discussions, which a general AI tool would struggle to reproduce convincingly. Some courses might even permit AI use openly and assess how critically students used it.

In conclusion, while AI has made cheating easier, it does not justify abandoning home-based written assignments. Universities should instead redesign these tasks so they continue to develop and assess the independent thinking that higher education is meant to encourage.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Generative AI has made it possible for almost anyone to produce a fluent essay in seconds, and this has led some commentators to argue that universities should abandon take-home written assignments altogether. I agree with this position only to a limited extent. While unsupervised essays can no longer be trusted as the sole measure of a student's ability, eliminating them entirely would sacrifice some of the most important aims of higher education.

It is undeniable that the traditional take-home essay has become vulnerable. Detection software is unreliable, and a student who submits machine-generated text with a few careful edits may be almost impossible to identify. When grades can be obtained without genuine learning, qualifications lose credibility, and conscientious students are effectively penalised for their honesty. For modules where assessment is heavily weighted towards a single essay, the case for introducing supervised elements is therefore compelling.

However, extended written work serves purposes that invigilated exams cannot. Producing a substantial piece of writing requires students to locate and evaluate sources, sustain an argument and revise their thinking over time. These are precisely the capabilities employers and researchers value, and they cannot be demonstrated in a two-hour sitting where memory and speed are rewarded above reflection. Replacing coursework wholesale with exams would, in effect, narrow what universities teach to what can be tested under pressure.

The more productive response is to rethink how assignments are designed and verified. Requiring annotated drafts, research logs or a brief viva in which students defend their arguments makes outsourcing far less attractive. Tasks grounded in personal fieldwork, recent seminar discussions or original data are also much harder to delegate to a general-purpose model.

In short, AI has exposed genuine weaknesses in take-home assessment, but the appropriate remedy is reform rather than abolition. Universities that adapt their assignments thoughtfully can protect academic integrity without abandoning the independent thinking that written work develops.

There is ongoing debate about who should carry the main burden of protecting the environment. Some people believe that large corporations bear the greatest responsibility, while ordinary consumers play only a minor role. I largely agree with this view, although I think consumers have an important part to play in pushing companies to change.

The most convincing reason for placing responsibility on large companies is the scale of their impact. Energy firms, manufacturers and major retailers are responsible for a large share of carbon emissions, waste and deforestation, often far more than any individual could produce in a lifetime. A single decision by a multinational to switch to renewable energy or reduce packaging can therefore have a greater effect than millions of individual efforts. Companies also possess the financial resources and technical expertise needed to develop cleaner processes, which most households simply do not have.

Furthermore, consumers' choices are shaped and limited by what companies offer. It is difficult for someone to live sustainably if affordable products are all packaged in plastic or if public transport is poorly developed. In this sense, blaming individuals can distract attention from the structural changes that are really needed, and some businesses may even encourage this focus to avoid stricter regulation.

Nevertheless, consumers are not powerless. Businesses respond to demand, so when large numbers of people buy second-hand clothes or avoid products linked to environmental damage, companies have a strong incentive to adapt. Individual behaviour, such as reducing food waste or flying less, also add up when it is widespread and can help to create social pressure for government action.

In conclusion, I agree that large companies should take the main responsibility for protecting the environment because of their enormous impact and resources. However, consumers still have a meaningful role, mainly by using their purchasing power to hold those companies accountable.

Whether environmental protection is chiefly the duty of large corporations or of individual consumers is a question that shapes how societies respond to climate change and pollution. In my view, the primary responsibility does lie with major companies, but framing the issue as a choice between the two risks overlooking how closely their behaviour is connected.

The case for holding corporations principally accountable is persuasive. Industrial production, energy generation and global supply chains account for a large share of emissions, and decisions taken in a handful of boardrooms determine how goods are made, transported and packaged for millions of people. When a major retailer eliminates single-use plastics or an airline invests in cleaner fuels, the environmental gain dwarfs anything a conscientious shopper could achieve alone. Companies also have the capital to fund research into cleaner technologies, and they are the ones that profit from environmentally harmful practices, which strengthens the moral argument for making them pay for the damage.

Moreover, emphasising personal responsibility can be misleading. Consumers can only choose from the options available to them, and sustainable alternatives are often more expensive or simply unavailable. A family living in a suburb without reliable public transport, for instance, has little choice but to drive. Urging such people to change their habits while leaving corporate practices largely untouched shifts the burden onto those with the least power to solve the problem.

This is not to say that individuals are irrelevant. Collective consumer behaviour sends signals that companies cannot ignore, and public pressure is often what persuades governments to regulate industry more strictly. The growth of demand for plant-based food and electric vehicles illustrates how shifting preferences can reshape entire markets.

Overall, I agree that large companies bear the greater responsibility, given their scale, resources and profits. Consumers, however, remain an important catalyst, since their choices and political pressure help to ensure that corporations actually meet that responsibility.

Traffic congestion is a serious problem in most big cities around the world. Some people believe that if public transport is completely free, more people will use it and the traffic will decrease. I agree with this idea for the most part.

The first reason is that money is important for many people when they choose how to travel. If a person have to pay for the bus every day, it can be expensive, especially for students and workers with low salary. So they prefer to use motorbike or car. But if buses and trains are free, many of them will leave their cars at home. This will make the roads less crowded and also reduce the air pollution, which is a big problem in cities like mine.

Another reason is that free transport is fair for everyone. Poor people can travel to their job, to hospital or to school without worrying about the cost. This can help them to find better jobs and improve their life. In addition, the city will save time because there is no need to sell tickets and check them.

However, there are some problems with this idea. The government need a lot of money to run the buses and trains, so it may have to increase the taxes. Also, if the service is not good, people will still use their cars even it is free. For example, if the bus is always late or very crowded, people don't want to use it.

In conclusion, I agree that making public transport free can reduce traffic congestion, because it encourages people to stop using private cars. However, the government must also improve the quality of the service, otherwise the plan will not be successful.

Many cities suffer from severe traffic congestion, and one proposed solution is to make public transport entirely free for passengers. Although this policy has some clear attractions, I largely disagree that it is the best way to tackle congestion, because cost is rarely the main factor that keeps drivers off buses and trains.

Supporters of free travel argue that removing fares would encourage people to switch from private cars. This may be true for some groups, such as students and low-income workers, for whom daily fares represent a significant expense. Free services would also make cities more inclusive, since everyone could reach jobs, schools and hospitals regardless of their income.

However, most car owners choose to drive because it is faster, more comfortable or more convenient, not because public transport is too expensive. If buses are overcrowded, unreliable or do not reach the suburbs where people live, abolishing fares will change very little. In fact, some cities that have introduced free transport found that many new passengers were people who previously walked or cycled, which does nothing to reduce the number of cars on the road.

Furthermore, fares provide an important source of funding. Without this income, transport authorities would depend entirely from taxation, and in times of budget pressure they might be forced to cut routes or delay improvements. This could make the service less attractive and eventually encourage more people to drive.

A more effective approach would be to invest in frequent, reliable services and combine this with measures that make driving less appealing, such as congestion charges or limited parking in city centres. Reduced fares for certain groups could also be offered.

In conclusion, while free public transport would benefit some residents, I do not believe it would significantly reduce congestion on its own. Improving service quality and discouraging car use are likely to be far more effective.

answers.text:
Abolishing fares on buses, trams and trains is sometimes presented as a simple remedy for urban traffic congestion. While I accept that free public transport has genuine social merits, I disagree that it is, by itself, an effective way of reducing congestion, and I believe the money it would require could be spent more productively.

The appeal of fare-free travel is easy to understand. It removes a cost that weighs most heavily on low-income households, simplifies journeys for occasional users and sends a strong public signal that the city values collective transport over private cars. For young people and those on modest wages, eliminating fares might well be the deciding factor that makes the bus a realistic alternative.

The difficulty is that motorists are generally less sensitive to price than to time and convenience. A commuter who drives does so because the car offers a direct, predictable journey; if the equivalent trip by public transport involves two changes and a long wait, making it free will rarely alter that calculation. Experience in several cities suggests that fare-free schemes tend to attract people who would otherwise have walked or cycled, which increases demand on the network without taking many cars off the road.

There is also the question of funding. Ticket revenue typically covers a substantial part of operating costs, and replacing it would place a permanent burden on public budgets. When finances tighten, it is service frequency and maintenance that usually suffer first, precisely the qualities that persuade drivers to switch.

Congestion is therefore better addressed through a combination of measures: sustained investment in faster, more frequent services, dedicated bus lanes, and policies such as road pricing that reflect the true cost of driving. Targeted discounts can protect those on the lowest incomes without sacrificing essential revenue.

In conclusion, free public transport may be socially desirable, but as a strategy for reducing congestion it promises more than it is likely to deliver.

Many cities have old centres with beautiful buildings and long history. Some people think the government should not allow any new buildings in these areas, even if it is bad for economy and housing. I agree with this opinion to a large extent.

Firstly, historic city centres are very important for a country's culture and identity. Old buildings like churches, markets and palaces show how people lived in the past and they are part of our heritage. If the government allow modern buildings there, the old character of the area will be destroyed and we can never get it back. For example, a tall glass tower next to an old castle looks very strange and it make the area less beautiful.

Secondly, historic centres attract a lot of tourists. Tourists come to see the old streets and traditional architecture, not modern offices. So protecting these areas can actually help the economy, because tourism creates many jobs in hotels, restaurants and shops. In this way, the economic loss from not building is not so big as people think.

On the other hand, I understand that cities need more houses because the population is growing. Young people cannot find apartments with cheap price in the centre. However, I think new houses can be built in other parts of city, such as suburbs, where there are more space and the land is cheaper. The government can also improve public transport so people can travel to the centre easily.

In conclusion, I believe the government should stop new construction in historic city centres because these areas are very valuable for culture and tourism. The need for housing and economic growth can be solved in other areas of the city.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
In many cities, there is tension between preserving historic centres and meeting the demand for economic development and new housing. Some argue that governments should ban all new construction in these areas, whatever the economic cost. I agree that historic centres deserve strong protection, but I believe a complete ban goes too far.

There are strong reasons to protect historic districts. Their architecture represents centuries of cultural history, and once an old building is demolished or overshadowed by a modern tower, the loss is permanent. These areas also give cities a distinctive identity, which is valued by residents and is a major attraction for the tourists. In many European and Asian cities, the old town is the main reason visitors come at all, so careless development could damage the local economy rather than help it.

However, an absolute ban would create serious problems. City centres are usually where jobs, transport and services are concentrated, and preventing all new building there would push housing further from workplaces, increasing commuting times and rents. It might also turn historic districts into museum-like spaces, full of tourists but empty of ordinary residents and local businesses. A living city needs schools, shops and homes, not only monuments.

A more balanced solution is strict but flexible regulation. Governments can limit the height and design of new buildings so that they fit the character of the area, protect the most important landmarks completely, and encourage the conversion of old, empty buildings into housing. Many cities have successfully added modern homes on vacant plots without harming their historic appearance.

In conclusion, while historic city centres should be carefully protected, I disagree with preventing all new construction. Carefully controlled development can preserve heritage while still allowing cities to meet the needs of the people who live in them.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Historic city centres are among the most visible expressions of a society's past, and the pressure to redevelop them is often intense. The proposal that governments should forbid all new construction in these districts, regardless of the economic and housing consequences, reflects a legitimate concern for heritage. However, I largely disagree with it, since a blanket prohibition would ultimately harm the very places it aims to preserve.

It is certainly true that insensitive development can do irreversible damage. A single oversized office block can dominate a skyline that has remained largely unchanged for centuries, and the demolition of a period building cannot be undone. Historic quarters also have considerable economic value in their own right, drawing visitors whose spending supports thousands of local businesses. For these reasons, protecting landmarks and the overall character of old districts should be a clear priority for planners.

Yet a complete ban confuses preservation with freezing a city in time. Historic centres have always evolved, with each generation adding buildings of its own era, and many admired streets are the result of such layering. More practically, prohibiting construction where land is most in demand drives up property prices, forces lower-income residents out and leaves the centre dominated by short-term lets and souvenir shops. The outcome is often a district that looks authentic but has lost the everyday life that once defined it.

A more sophisticated approach combines firm protection with carefully managed change. Listed buildings can be safeguarded absolutely, while strict design codes govern the height, materials and scale of anything new. Derelict sites and disused commercial buildings can be converted into homes, bringing residents back without compromising the streetscape. This allows cities to accommodate growth while keeping their historic identity intact.

In conclusion, historic centres deserve robust protection, but an outright ban on new building would sacrifice housing, vitality and affordability for the sake of a static appearance. Intelligent regulation, rather than prohibition, is the better course.

In the past, having a good degree or certificate was the most important thing for getting a job. Nowadays, some people say that in the future the ability to learn new skills quickly will be more important than qualifications. I agree with this statement.

The main reason is that technology is changing very fast. Many jobs that exist today will disappear, and new jobs will appear which we cannot imagine now. A person who studied a subject ten years ago may find that his knowledge is already old. For example, many office workers had to learn how to use new software and online tools during the last few years. The people who learned fast was able to keep their job, but others had difficulties. This shows that learning quickly is a very useful ability.

In addition, companies today want employees who can adapt. When a company starts a new project, it need workers who can understand new things without long training. A person with many certificates but who cannot learn is not so helpful for the company. Also, a lot of skills can now be learned online for free, so the qualification from university is not the only way to prove your knowledge.

However, I don't think qualifications will become useless. Some jobs, like doctors, engineers or lawyers, always need official degrees because they are very responsible jobs. Nobody want to be treated by a doctor without a qualification.

In conclusion, I agree that the ability to learn new skills quickly will be more important than qualifications in the future, because the world of work is changing very quickly. But for some professions, qualifications will still be necessary.

answers.text:
It is often claimed that, in the future, the capacity to acquire new skills rapidly will matter more than formal qualifications. I partly agree with this view: adaptability is becoming increasingly valuable in a changing job market, but qualifications will continue to play an essential role, particularly in certain professions.

On the one hand, the pace of technological change means that specific knowledge becomes outdated more quickly than before. Software, industries and even entire job categories can transform within a few years, so employees who can learn new tools and methods efficiently are likely to remain employable. Many employers now place greater emphasis on problem-solving and flexibility during interviews, recognising that a degree obtained years earlier says little about how well a person will cope with tomorrow's challenges. The growth of short online courses also allows workers to update their skills continuously without returning to university.

On the other hand, qualifications still serve important purposes. In fields such as medicine, law and engineering, formal training ensures that professionals meet agreed standards, and it would be dangerous to allow people to practise simply because they claim to learn quickly. Qualifications also provide employers with a reliable way to compare candidates, especially when hundreds of people apply for the same job. Moreover, completing a degree often demonstrate the very ability to learn that critics claim is more important.

In my view, the two are becoming complementary rather than competing. A qualification may open the door to a career, but the ability to keep learning will determine how far a person progresses once they are inside.

In conclusion, I agree that the ability to learn new skills quickly will grow in importance, but I do not think it will replace qualifications. Both will be necessary, with adaptability becoming the key to long-term success.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
As automation and digital technology reshape the labour market, many commentators predict that the ability to learn quickly will soon outweigh the value of formal qualifications. I agree with this prediction to a large extent, although I believe qualifications will remain important as a baseline, particularly in regulated professions.

The central argument concerns the shrinking shelf life of knowledge. A graduate entering the workforce today may find that much of what they studied is obsolete within a decade, as new tools, regulations and business models emerge. In such an environment, what distinguishes successful employees is not what they learnt at twenty-two but how effectively they can master unfamiliar tasks at forty. A marketing specialist who can quickly grasp a new analytics platform, for instance, is often more valuable to an employer than a colleague with a more prestigious degree who struggles to adapt.

Hiring practices already reflect this shift. A growing number of companies assess candidates through practical tasks and probation periods rather than relying solely on certificates, and some technology firms have dropped degree requirements for certain roles altogether. At the same time, the availability of online courses and workplace training means that skills can be acquired and demonstrated outside traditional education, weakening the monopoly that formal credentials once held.

Nevertheless, qualifications are unlikely to disappear. In professions where mistakes can endanger lives, such as surgery or civil engineering, society rightly insists on rigorous, standardised training that cannot be replaced by a talent for fast learning. Degrees also signal persistence and a foundation of knowledge on which further learning can be built.

On balance, I expect qualifications to become a starting point rather than a guarantee of career success. Adaptability and the capacity for continuous learning will increasingly determine who thrives, while formal credentials will remain indispensable only where public safety and professional standards demand them.

Nowadays children see advertisements everywhere, on television, on the internet and even in their games. Some people think that all advertising for children who are under twelve should be banned. I completely agree with this idea.

The first reason is that young children cannot understand the purpose of advertising. They believe what they see on the screen and they don't know that the company only want to sell products. For example, if a child see an advert for a new toy with happy children playing, he thinks that he will be very happy if he gets it. Adults can think critically but children are not able to do this, so it is not fair to target them.

The second reason is that advertising can be bad for children's health. Many adverts for children are about sweets, fast food and sugary drinks. These products are very attractive with bright colours and cartoon characters, and children ask their parents to buy them. If they eat this kind of food too much, they can become overweight and have health problems in the future.

In addition, adverts create pressure on the parents. Children always want the newest toys and they cry or become angry if parents say no. Many families don't have enough money to buy everything, so this cause arguments at home. Also children can feel sad when their friends have things that they don't have.

Some people say that companies need to advertise to sell their products. However, they can still advertise to parents, because parents are the one who pay for the products.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that advertising aimed at children under twelve should be banned, because children cannot understand it and it can harm their health and their family life.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Children today are exposed to a constant stream of advertisements on television, websites and mobile games. As a result, there have been calls for a complete ban on advertising directed at children under twelve. I strongly agree with this proposal, since young children are especially vulnerable to persuasive marketing.

The main reason for my view is that young children lack the ability to recognise advertising for what it is. Before a certain age, many children cannot clearly distinguish between entertainment and a commercial message, and they tend to accept claims at face value. When a cartoon character they love tells them that a particular cereal will make them stronger, they are likely to believe it. Targeting an audience that cannot critically evaluate information is, in my opinion, fundamentally unfair.

Secondly, much of the advertising aimed at children promotes products that are harmful or unnecessary. Sugary snacks, fast food and expensive toys dominate children's channels and apps, and their marketing often relies on bright colours, free gifts and celebrity endorsements. This contributes to unhealthy eating habits and encourages a materialistic attitude from an early age. It also puts a considerable pressure on parents, who may face tantrums or feel guilty when they cannot afford the latest products.

Opponents argue that a ban would harm businesses and restrict freedom of expression. However, companies would still be able to market their products to parents, who are ultimately the ones making purchasing decisions. Moreover, several countries already restrict advertising to children, which suggests that such regulation is both practical and effective.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that all advertising aimed at children under twelve should be banned. Protecting young children from manipulation and unhealthy influences is more important than the commercial interests of advertisers.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Advertisers spend vast sums targeting children, whose influence over family spending is considerable. The suggestion that all advertising aimed at under-twelves should be prohibited is therefore a significant one, and I agree with it to a large extent, while recognising that a ban would need to be carefully defined to be workable.

The most compelling argument concerns children's cognitive development. Younger children often struggle to recognise the persuasive intent behind an advertisement and are inclined to accept its claims uncritically. Marketing techniques that would barely register with an adult, such as a favourite cartoon character endorsing a snack or a toy shown in an exaggeratedly exciting setting, can be highly effective on a seven-year-old. Directing such messages at an audience that cannot defend itself against them is difficult to justify ethically.

The consequences extend beyond the individual child. Advertising to children is dominated by foods high in sugar and fat, and repeated exposure shapes preferences that may persist into adulthood, with obvious implications for public health. It also fuels what is often called "pester power", placing parents under pressure to buy products they cannot afford or would not otherwise choose, and encouraging children to measure their worth by what they own.

Critics of a ban raise two points: that it would unfairly restrict legitimate businesses, and that parents, not governments, should protect their children. Yet firms would remain free to advertise to adults, who make the actual purchasing decisions, and the sheer volume of online marketing, much of it embedded in games and videos, makes parental supervision alone unrealistic.

The main practical challenge lies in enforcement, particularly on digital platforms where age and intent are harder to define. Clear rules on content designed to appeal to children would be essential.

In conclusion, I strongly support banning advertising aimed at children under twelve. Their vulnerability to persuasion outweighs the commercial arguments against such a restriction.

In recent years, the number of people who are overweight has increased in many countries. Some people think the government should put a tax on unhealthy food like sugary drinks and fast food, as they do with cigarettes. I agree with this idea to some extent.

On the one hand, a tax can make people buy less unhealthy food. When the price of something goes up, people usually buy less of it. For example, many people stopped smoking or smoked less when cigarettes became very expensive. The same thing can happen with fizzy drinks and burgers. Also, the government can use the money from this tax for hospitals and for health education in schools, which will help the whole society.

On the other hand, unhealthy food is not exactly the same like tobacco. Cigarettes are always harmful, but eating a pizza or a chocolate sometimes is not dangerous. The problem is only when people eat too much of it. So it is not fair to punish everybody who enjoy fast food occasionally. Moreover, this tax can be a problem for poor families, because cheap fast food is sometimes the only thing they can afford after a long working day, and fresh food is often more expensive.

In my opinion, the government should tax the most unhealthy products, such as sugary drinks, but not all fast food. At the same time, they should make healthy food more cheaper and teach people about good diet.

In conclusion, I partly agree that unhealthy food should be taxed like tobacco. A tax can reduce consumption and give money to health services, but it must be used together with other actions so that poor people are not affected too much.

There are clear arguments in favour of taxing unhealthy food. Price has a strong influence on consumer behaviour, and higher prices usually lead to reduced consumption, as has happened with cigarettes in many countries. A tax on sugary drinks, in particular, could discourage people from consuming large amounts of sugar without any real nutritional benefit. The revenue could also be used to fund public health campaigns or subsidise fruit and vegetables, which would make healthier choices more accessible.

However, food is fundamentally different from tobacco. There is no safe level of smoking, but most foods that are considered unhealthy are only harmful when eaten regularly and in large quantities. Taxing them heavily would therefore penalise the many people who consume them occasionally and responsibly. In addition, defining what counts as "unhealthy" is much more complicated than identifying a tobacco product; a burger made at a restaurant and one prepared at home may be quite similar, yet only one could realistically be taxed.

Such taxes may also have a disproportionate affect on low-income households, who spend a larger share of their income on food and often rely on cheap, processed meals. Unless the money raised is used to make healthy food more affordable, the policy could increase inequality without improving diets.

In conclusion, I support moderate, targeted taxes on products such as sugary drinks, but I do not agree that unhealthy food in general should be taxed as heavily as tobacco. Education and support for healthier choices are equally important.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
With obesity and related conditions placing growing strain on health systems, some argue that governments should tax sugary drinks and fast food as they tax tobacco. I agree that fiscal measures have a role to play, particularly for sugar-sweetened beverages, but I believe equating unhealthy food with tobacco is both conceptually flawed and potentially counterproductive.

The case for taxation rests on sound principles. Consumers respond to price, and the dramatic decline in smoking in many countries owes much to sustained increases in tobacco duty. Sugary drinks are an especially suitable target: they provide calories with virtually no nutritional value, they are easy to define, and there is evidence that levies on them encourage manufacturers to reduce sugar content. Revenue raised in this way can be reinvested in school meals, sports facilities or subsidies for fresh produce, amplifying the health benefit.

Nevertheless, food differs from tobacco in crucial respects. Cigarettes are harmful in any quantity, whereas burgers, chips or chocolate are problematic only as part of an unbalanced diet. A tax modelled on tobacco would therefore treat moderate consumption as though it were inherently dangerous, which many people would reasonably regard as excessive state intervention. Moreover, "fast food" is a notoriously vague category, and drawing a line between a takeaway meal and a restaurant dish would invite both confusion and avoidance.

There is also the issue of fairness. Food taxes are regressive, weighing most heavily on households with the least disposable income, and in areas where fresh food is expensive or hard to obtain, higher prices may simply reduce families' budgets rather than change what they eat. Any such tax must therefore be paired with measures that make healthy alternatives genuinely affordable.

In conclusion, targeted taxes on clearly defined products like sugary drinks are justified, but applying a tobacco-style regime to unhealthy food in general would be neither fair nor effective.

Good behaviour and respect for other people are very important qualities for children. Some people think that parents, not teachers, should be mainly responsible for teaching these things. I agree with this statement.

Firstly, children spend most of their time with their family, especially in the first years of life. Before they start school, they already learn how to speak, how to eat and how to behave with other people from their parents. If parents teach them to say "please" and "thank you" and to share with others, these habits will stay with them for all their life. Also, children usually copy what their parents do. If a father is polite with his neighbours, his son will probably learn to be polite too.

Secondly, teachers have many students in one class, sometimes more than thirty. They don't have enough time to pay attention for the behaviour of every child. Their main job is to teach subjects like maths, science and languages. If the teacher must spend a lot of time to correct bad behaviour, the other students cannot learn well.

However, teachers also have some role. At school, children learn how to work in groups, how to follow rules and how to respect people from different backgrounds. Teachers can support what the parents teach at home. But if the parents don't teach good manners, it is very difficult for teachers to change a child's behaviour.

In conclusion, I believe that parents should be mainly responsible for teaching children good behaviour and respect because children spend more time with them and learn by copying them. Teachers can help, but the main responsibility belong to the family.

answers.text:
It is often debated whether parents or teachers should take the main responsibility for teaching children to behave well and respect others. Some people believe this is primarily the role of parents. I partly agree with this view, as I think parents should lay the foundations, but schools have a vital and distinctive contribution to make.

Parents clearly have the greatest influence during a child's early years. Long before children start school, they learn how to treat others by observing the adults around them, and values such as honesty, kindness and patience are absorbed through daily routines at home. A child whose parents speak respectfully to each other and to strangers is far more likely to adopt the same attitude. Moreover, parents can give individual attention and correct behaviour consistently, which is difficult for a teacher responsible for a whole class.

However, schools provide experiences that the family cannot. In the classroom, children must cooperate with peers from different backgrounds, follow shared rules and resolve conflicts without their parents' help. These situations teach respect in a wider social context and prepare children for adult life in a diverse community. Teachers can also reinforce good behaviour through clear expectations and by being positive role models, which is particularly important for children whose home environment are less supportive.

For these reasons, I believe the responsibility should be shared. Parents are best placed to instil basic values, while teachers help children to apply them in a broader setting. When the two work together and send consistent messages, children are much more likely to develop good behaviour that lasts.

In conclusion, although parents should play the leading role in teaching manners and respect, I do not think teachers' contribution should be seen as secondary. Effective moral education depends on cooperation between home and school.
