answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The question of who should teach children good behaviour and respect for others is often framed as a choice between home and school. I agree that parents should bear the primary responsibility, since the values children absorb in their earliest years are formed largely within the family. However, I would argue that teachers play an indispensable supporting role rather than a marginal one.

The strongest argument for parental responsibility lies in the timing and nature of early learning. Children's attitudes towards others begin to take shape long before they enter a classroom, and they are shaped less by explicit instruction than by imitation. A toddler who sees a parent listen patiently, apologise when wrong and treat service workers courteously internalises these patterns almost unconsciously. Parents also have a depth of knowledge about their own child and the continuity of contact over many years that no teacher, responsible for thirty pupils for a single year, can match.

There is also a question of accountability. If parents come to assume that manners and respect will be taught at school, they may neglect this aspect of upbringing, leaving teachers to address behavioural problems that divert time from learning. Recognising that the family is the first line of moral education places responsibility where it can be exercised most effectively.

That said, schools offer something that homes cannot: a structured community of peers. Learning to share resources, wait one's turn, work with classmates one did not choose and respect people from different cultures are lessons best learnt in a group setting. Teachers who model fairness and enforce consistent rules can reinforce good habits and, crucially, compensate for children who receive little guidance at home.

In conclusion, parents should be principally responsible for teaching good behaviour and respect, but this responsibility is most effectively fulfilled when schools reinforce and extend the values children first learn within the family.

When a person commits a crime, the court must decide what punishment to give. Some people think the court should only look at the crime and not at the background of the person who did it. I disagree with this opinion because I think the situation of the offender is also important.

Firstly, not all crimes happen for the same reason. For example, if a poor mother steal food from a shop because her children are hungry, it is different from a rich man who steals for fun. Both of them committed the same crime, but I believe the mother should get a lighter punishment because she had a serious reason. If the court ignore this, the punishment will not be fair.

Secondly, looking at the background can help to reduce crime in the future. If the judge knows that a young offender grew up in a difficult family or has problem with drugs, the judge can send him to a programme to help him instead of prison. In prison, young people often meet other criminals and they become more worse. But with the right help, they can change their life and not commit crimes again.

However, I understand why some people want the courts to consider only the crime. They think that everyone should be treated equal and that some criminals may use their difficult past as an excuse. This is true, and the judges must be careful. The background should not be used to avoid punishment totally for serious crimes like murder.

In conclusion, I disagree that courts should consider only the crime. The personal background of the offender should also be considered, because it makes the punishment more fair and can help people to stop committing crimes.

Some people argue that when courts decide on a sentence, they should focus solely on the crime itself and ignore the offender's personal background and circumstances. Although I understand the desire for consistency, I largely disagree with this view, as I believe justice requires courts to consider the individual as well as the offence.

Those who support this approach believe it guarantees equal treatment. If two people commit the same crime, they should receive the same punishment, regardless of their wealth, family history or social status. This principle is appealing because it prevents judges from showing favouritism and makes sentences more predictable. There is also a concern that offenders might exploit sympathetic stories about their past to avoid appropriate punishment.

However, identical acts can carry very different levels of blame. A teenager who commits a theft under pressure from an older gang member is not equally responsible as an adult who plans the same crime for profit. Similarly, factors such as mental illness, severe poverty or a history of abuse can affect a person's judgement, and ignoring them would produce sentences that feel harsh and unjust. A fair system should reflect not only what was done but why it was done.

Considering circumstances can also serve the wider purpose of reducing crime. If a court understands that an offender's behaviour is linked to addiction, it can impose a sentence that includes treatment, which is more likely to prevent reoffending than a short prison term. In this way, taking background into account benefits society as well as the individual.

In conclusion, while treating similar crimes consistently is important, I disagree that courts should ignore offenders' circumstances completely. Sentences should be based mainly on the seriousness of the crime, but adjusted where personal factors genuinely affect responsibility or the chance of rehabilitation.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Whether sentencing should be based purely on the offence, or should also take account of the offender's background, touches on a fundamental tension in criminal justice between consistency and individual fairness. I disagree with the view that courts should consider only the crime, although I accept that the weight given to personal circumstances must be carefully limited.

The argument for focusing exclusively on the offence has genuine merit. Equality before the law implies that similar acts should attract similar penalties, and sentencing that varies according to personal history risks appearing arbitrary. There is also a legitimate worry that well-resourced defendants, able to present their lives sympathetically through expensive legal representation, may secure more lenient treatment than those without such advantages.

However, a system that looks only at the act itself would disregard the degree of culpability, which is central to any meaningful notion of justice. An offence committed by someone acting under coercion, suffering from a serious mental illness or driven by desperate need is not morally equivalent to the same act committed out of greed or cruelty. Most legal systems already recognise this through concepts such as mitigating and aggravating factors, and removing them would make sentences blunter rather than fairer.

Circumstances are also relevant to the forward-looking purposes of punishment. A sentence is not merely retribution; it is intended to protect the public and reduce the likelihood of reoffending. Understanding that a young offender's behaviour is rooted in addiction or an unstable home allows a court to choose interventions, such as supervised treatment, that address the underlying cause rather than simply imposing a custodial term.

The key, therefore, is proportion. The seriousness of the offence should set the broad range of any sentence, while personal circumstances inform where within that range it falls. On this basis, I believe courts are right to consider both, rather than the crime alone.

News is very important in our life because it tells us what is happening in the world. Some people think that news organisations must report only facts and journalists should not give their own opinion. I agree with this idea to a large extent.

The main reason is that people need correct information to make decisions. For example, before an election, people read the news to know about the candidates. If the journalist write his personal opinion, the readers can be influenced and they may vote for the person the journalist like, not the person they really prefer. This is dangerous for democracy. News should help people to think by themselves.

Another reason is that nowadays there are too much fake news and many people do not trust the media. When news is full of opinions, it is difficult for the readers to know what is true and what is only the idea of the writer. If news organisations report only facts, people will trust them more.

On the other hand, sometimes opinion can be useful. Some topics, like economy or politics, are very difficult to understand, and an expert journalist can explain what the facts means. However, I think this should be in a separate part, for example an opinion column, and it must be clear to the readers that it is not the news.

In conclusion, I mostly agree that news organisations should report only facts and not the opinions of their journalists, because people need true information and trust in the media. If opinions are included, they should be clearly separated from the news reports.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
In an era of instant news and widespread misinformation, some people argue that news organisations should limit themselves strictly to reporting facts, without any personal opinion from journalists. While I agree that news reports should be as objective as possible, I disagree that opinion should never be included, as analysis plays an important role when it is clearly labelled.

There are good reasons to value factual reporting. Readers rely on the news to form their own views on political and social issues, and when a journalist's opinions are mixed into a report, the audience may be influenced without realising it. This is particularly concerning during elections or crises, when biased coverage can shape public opinion on a large scale. Strictly factual reporting also helps to rebuild trust in the media at a time when many people suspect that news outlets are pushing a particular agenda.

However, facts alone do not always tell the full story. A list of figures about inflation or a statement from a government minister may mean little to ordinary readers unless someone explains the context and possible consequences. Experienced journalists who have covered a subject for years is often well placed to offer this kind of insight. Removing all interpretation would leave audiences with information but little understanding.

The real problem, in my view, is not opinion itself but the failure to separate it clearly from news. Reputable newspapers usually distinguish between news articles and editorials or columns, allowing readers to know when they are reading an interpretation. Maintaining this distinction, and making it obvious on websites and social media, would address most of the concerns raised.

In conclusion, news reports should be based on facts, but I do not believe journalists' opinions should be banned entirely. Clearly labelled analysis and commentary help audiences to understand complex events and remain a valuable part of journalism.

Concerns about media bias and misinformation have prompted calls for news organisations to report nothing but verifiable facts, excluding the personal views of their journalists altogether. I agree that the core of news reporting should be factual and impartial, but I disagree that opinion should never appear, since informed commentary, when clearly identified, serves a valuable public function.

Citizens depend on the news to understand events and hold those in power to account, and they are entitled to form their own conclusions. When commentary is woven into ostensibly neutral reports, readers may absorb a journalist's perspective without recognising it as such. This subtle blurring is arguably more damaging than openly partisan coverage, because it erodes the audience's ability to distinguish evidence from interpretation, and with it their trust in the media as a whole.

Yet it is naive to suppose that facts can be presented without any judgement. Deciding which stories to cover, which sources to quote and what context to include already involves editorial choices. Moreover, many issues, from climate policy to interest rates, are so complex that raw data offers little insight to non-specialists. A correspondent with years of experience can explain why an event matters and what its likely implications are, which enriches public understanding rather than distorting it.

The more sensible standard, therefore, is transparency rather than prohibition. News reports should strive for accuracy and balance, while analysis and opinion should be explicitly labelled and presented separately, as is the practice in most respected publications. The challenge in the digital age is to preserve this distinction when articles are shared on social media, often stripped of the labels that signal their purpose.

In conclusion, factual reporting should remain the foundation of journalism, but clearly marked opinion has a legitimate place. The priority should be to keep the two distinct, not to eliminate commentary entirely.

In conclusion, I agree that social media companies should verify the real identity of users because it can reduce bullying and online crime. However, the companies must keep the personal information safe and they should not show the real names to everyone.

answers.text:
Online abuse, scams and fake accounts have become serious problems on social media, leading some people to argue that platforms should be required to verify the real identity of every user. Although I understand the reasons for this proposal, I largely disagree with it, since the risks to privacy and free expression outweigh the likely benefits.

Supporters of mandatory verification believe it would make users more accountable. When people know that their posts can be traced back to them, they may be less likely to harass others or spread deliberate misinformation. Verification could also make it harder for criminals to create multiple fake accounts for fraud, and it would help authorities to identify offenders more quickly.

However, the evidence that real names improve behaviour are limited. Many people already post offensive content under their own names, which suggests that anonymity is not the only cause of online abuse. At the same time, requiring every user to upload identity documents would create huge databases of sensitive information, which could be targeted by hackers or misused by the companies themselves. A single data breach could expose the personal details of millions of people.

Anonymity also protects vulnerable groups. Whistle-blowers, victims of domestic abuse and people who live under authoritarian governments often rely on pseudonyms to speak freely without putting themselves in danger. For them, compulsory verification could mean choosing between silence and serious risk, which would be a significant loss for public debate.

A better approach would be for platforms to invest in faster moderation, to verify accounts only in specific cases, such as those used for advertising or selling products, and to cooperate with police when a crime is reported.

In conclusion, while identity checks might reduce some harmful behaviour, I do not believe they should be applied to every user. Targeted measures would protect people more effectively without sacrificing privacy and freedom of speech.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
As concerns grow about online harassment, fraud and coordinated disinformation, the idea of obliging social media companies to verify the real identity of every user has gained considerable support. I agree that anonymity is sometimes abused, but I disagree with universal verification, which I believe would create serious new harms while doing relatively little to address the existing ones.

The appeal of the proposal is understandable. Anonymous accounts can be created in seconds, allowing individuals to harass others, operate networks of fake profiles or impersonate legitimate businesses with little fear of consequence. Linking every account to a verified person would, in theory, restore a degree of accountability and make it easier for victims and law enforcement to pursue those responsible.

In practice, however, the relationship between anonymity and misconduct is weaker than often assumed. A great deal of abusive content is posted openly under users' real names, indicating that social norms and platform design shape behaviour at least as much as identifiability does. Meanwhile, compelling billions of users to submit passports or identity cards would concentrate highly sensitive data in the hands of private companies, whose record in safeguarding personal information is far from reassuring. The consequences of a breach on that scale could be severe.

Equally significant is the value of anonymity to those with legitimate reasons to conceal their identity. Journalists' sources, employees exposing wrongdoing and political dissidents in repressive states often depend on pseudonyms to speak at all. For such users, mandatory verification would not merely be inconvenient; it could expose them to retaliation, with a chilling effect on precisely the kind of speech that open societies should protect.

More proportionate measures are available: verification for accounts that advertise, sell goods or reach very large audiences, stronger moderation, and swift cooperation with courts when unlawful conduct is reported.

In conclusion, universal identity checks would be a blunt instrument whose costs to privacy and freedom of expression outweigh its limited benefits.

answers.text:
Traditional arts and crafts, such as hand-weaving, woodcarving and folk music, are declining in many parts of the world as mass-produced goods and modern entertainment become dominant. Some argue that governments should fund these activities even if public demand is low. I agree with this view to a large extent, although I believe such support should be designed to encourage self-sufficiency.

The most important reason for state support is that traditional crafts represent a form of cultural heritage that cannot be easily replaced. The techniques involved are often passed down orally from one generation to the next, and when the last skilled practitioners retire without apprentices, the knowledge disappears permanently. Unlike buildings, which can sometimes be restored, a lost craft is extremely difficult to revive. Low demand today does not mean these skills have no value; it simply means the market fails to reflect their cultural importance.

Moreover, financial support can help traditional arts to find new audiences. With funding for training, exhibitions and online marketing, artisans can adapt their products for modern consumers or the tourist market, and some crafts have regained popularity in this way. Governments can also include traditional arts in school programmes, which increase awareness among young people.

On the other hand, public money is limited, and critics argue that it should be spent on essential services rather than on activities few people are interested in. This concern is reasonable, which is why funding should be targeted and relatively modest. Rather than paying artisans indefinitely, governments could offer grants that help them to become commercially viable over time.

In conclusion, I believe governments should support traditional arts and crafts even when demand is limited, because they are an irreplaceable part of cultural identity. However, this support should aim to help these traditions survive independently in the long term.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
As global markets fill with inexpensive, mass-produced goods, many traditional arts and crafts are struggling to survive. Whether governments should fund them despite limited public demand is a question of how societies value their cultural inheritance. I agree that such support is justified, provided it is aimed at preservation and renewal rather than indefinite subsidy.

The strongest case for public funding is that traditional crafts embody knowledge that the market cannot adequately value. Techniques such as natural dyeing, instrument-making or regional embroidery have often been refined over centuries and are transmitted through years of apprenticeship rather than written manuals. Once the last generation of practitioners disappears, that knowledge is effectively irretrievable. Low demand at a given moment therefore says little about a craft's long-term worth, in the same way that a museum's value is not measured by its ticket sales.

Traditional arts also contribute to a community's identity and cohesion in ways that are difficult to quantify. Festivals, local markets and workshops centred on these crafts give places a distinctive character, foster pride among residents and can form the basis of cultural tourism. Targeted funding can help artisans reach new audiences, whether through collaborations with contemporary designers or through online platforms that connect them with buyers worldwide.

Admittedly, public budgets face competing demands, and it would be difficult to justify spending heavily on crafts while essential services are underfunded. There is also a risk that permanent subsidies preserve traditions in a lifeless, artificial form. These objections argue not against support altogether, but for designing it wisely: documenting endangered techniques, funding apprenticeships and helping practitioners develop sustainable businesses.

In conclusion, I believe governments should provide financial support for traditional arts and crafts even when demand is weak, since their cultural value far exceeds their current market value. The aim, however, should be to give these traditions a viable future rather than to keep them artificially alive.

Tourism is a very big industry and many cities and islands are visited by millions of people every year. Some people think that famous tourist places should limit the number of tourists to protect the local people. I agree with this idea.

Secondly, a large number of tourist can damage the environment. They produce a lot of rubbish and use a lot of water and energy. Beautiful beaches and historical buildings can be destroyed if too many people visit them every day. If this happen, the place will not be attractive anymore, and in the future tourists will stop coming.

On the other hand, some people say that tourism bring money and jobs to the local people. This is true, but if the number is limited, the tourists can still come and spend money. The place can also increase the price of tickets so that it still earn enough money.

In conclusion, I agree that popular tourist destinations should limit the number of visitors every year. It will protect the local communities and the environment, and it will also help these places to stay beautiful for the future.

answers.text:
In recent years, several popular destinations have struggled with overcrowding, and some people believe that annual limits on visitor numbers are needed to protect local communities. I agree with this view to a large extent, although I think such limits should be applied flexibly and combined with other measures.

The main argument for limiting visitors is the impact of mass tourism on residents' daily lives. In many historic cities and small islands, streets, public transport and beaches become so crowded during peak season that locals can no longer use them normally. In addition, the growth of short-term holiday rentals has pushed up housing costs, forcing many families and young people to leave the neighbourhoods where they have always lived. Without controls, some destinations risk becoming places that exist only for tourists.

Excessive tourism also damages the natural and cultural assets that attract visitors in the first place. Fragile environments, such as coral reefs and mountain trails, can suffer long-term harm from heavy use, while ancient sites deteriorate when thousands of people walk through them each day. Setting a maximum number of visitors can help preserve these places for future generations.

Nonetheless, tourism is a vital source of income for many communities, and a strict cap could lead to job losses in hotels, restaurants and shops. For this reason, limits should be carefully planned. Destinations could introduce daily quotas for the most vulnerable sites, charge higher fees during the busiest months, and encourage visitors to travel in the off-season or visit less well-known areas nearby. By this way, the economic benefit is spread more evenly.

In conclusion, I believe popular destinations are justified in limiting visitor numbers to protect local residents and the environment. However, these limits should be part of a wider strategy which balances the needs of communities with the economic advantages of tourism.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Few issues illustrate the tension between economic opportunity and quality of life as sharply as mass tourism. Some argue that the most popular destinations should cap the number of visitors each year to protect local communities. I agree with this principle, but I believe that rigid annual limits are often less effective than more targeted forms of visitor management.

There is little doubt that unchecked tourism can seriously undermine residents' wellbeing. In some historic cities, the conversion of apartments into holiday lets has driven up rents to the point where long-standing residents are priced out, while local shops give way to souvenir outlets. Overcrowded streets, congested public transport and constant noise can make everyday life exhausting. When a community begins to feel like a stage set for visitors, the very authenticity that attracted tourists is lost.

The environmental case is equally compelling. Coastal ecosystems, mountain paths and archaeological sites can absorb only so much footfall before suffering lasting damage. For such places, limiting access is not merely desirable but essential if they are to survive in any recognisable form.

However, a single annual quota is a rather crude tool. Tourist pressure is usually concentrated in particular seasons, days and districts, so a yearly cap may do little to relieve overcrowding at peak times while needlessly turning visitors away in quieter periods. It could also harm the many residents whose livelihoods depend on tourism. More refined measures, such as timed entry to key sites, daily limits on cruise-ship arrivals, restrictions on short-term rentals and higher fees in peak season, can address the specific sources of pressure while preserving the income that tourism brings.

In conclusion, popular destinations are right to control visitor numbers in order to protect their residents and environment. Yet this is best achieved through flexible, carefully targeted management rather than a blunt annual ceiling.

Firstly, it is very difficult to know which research will be useful in the future. Many important inventions came from research that seemed to have no practical use at the beginning. For example, scientists studied electricity and light many years ago only because they were curious, but now we use this knowledge for computers, phones and medicine. If they only did research with clear benefit, we might not have this technology today.

Secondly, knowledge itself has value. Humans always want to understand the world, for example how the universe began or how the brain is working. This kind of research makes our life more rich and it inspires young people to study science. Also, pure research gives the base for practical research. Engineers and doctors use the discoveries of basic science to create new products and treatments.

However, I understand that the money for research is limited. When there are serious problems like diseases or climate change, it makes sense to give more money to research which can solve them quickly. People who pay taxes wants to see results from the money they give.

In conclusion, I disagree that scientific research should be funded only for practical benefits. Both kinds of research are important, and governments should give money to research that increase human knowledge as well, because in the future it can bring many benefits that we cannot imagine now.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
With limited public budgets, many people argue that scientific research should be funded according to its likely practical benefits rather than simply to expand human knowledge. While I accept that applied research deserves significant support, I disagree with making practical value the main criterion for funding decisions.

It is understandable why some prefer to focus on practical outcomes. Research is expensive, and governments must justify their spending to taxpayers who expect visible results, such as new medical treatments, cleaner energy or improved crops. When societies face urgent challenges like pandemics or climate change, directing money towards solving them seems both logical and responsible.

However, the history of science shows that the most transformative discoveries often come from research with no obvious application at the time. Scientists who investigated the structure of atoms or the behaviour of light were motivated largely by curiosity, yet their work eventually led to technologies ranging from medical imaging to the internet. Had funding been limited to projects with predictable benefits, many of these breakthroughs might never have happened. The problem is that practical value is extremely difficult to predict in advance.

Furthermore, basic research provides the foundation that applied science depends on. Engineers and medical researchers build on theories and data produced by scientists who were simply trying to understand how the natural world works. Reducing support for fundamental research would therefore weaken applied research in the long term, since there would be fewer new ideas to develop.

In my view, a balanced system is needed, in which a substantial part of funding goes to curiosity-driven research selected for its scientific quality, while specific programmes target pressing practical problems.

In conclusion, although practical benefits are important, I do not think they should determine all research funding. Supporting the expansion of knowledge for it's own sake is essential, as it is frequently the source of the most valuable practical advances.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Decisions about which scientific research to fund have become increasingly contested, with some arguing that public money should be directed primarily towards projects likely to yield practical benefits. I disagree with this position. Although applied research clearly merits substantial investment, making practical utility the principal test for funding would, paradoxically, reduce the practical returns of science over time.

The case for prioritising applied research is not without force. Governments are accountable to taxpayers, and when resources are scarce it seems reasonable to favour work that promises better treatments, more efficient energy or safer infrastructure. In the face of pressing problems such as antibiotic resistance, research with clear objectives offers a tangible sense of progress.

The central difficulty, however, is that the usefulness of knowledge can rarely be foreseen. Many of the technologies that define modern life emerged from inquiries pursued for their own sake: studies of quantum behaviour made possible the semiconductors in every smartphone, while research into obscure bacteria provided the tools behind modern gene editing. No funding committee assessing these projects at the outset could have predicted such outcomes. A system that rewards only anticipated benefits would systematically overlook the unexpected discoveries that often prove most valuable.

Fundamental research also sustains the wider scientific ecosystem. It trains highly skilled researchers, generates the theoretical frameworks on which applied work depends and keeps a country at the frontier of knowledge. Moreover, there is intrinsic worth in understanding the origins of the universe or the workings of the mind, questions that reflect a basic human aspiration and inspire future generations of scientists.

The most sensible approach is therefore a portfolio: dedicated funding for mission-driven research on urgent problems, alongside secure support for curiosity-driven work judged on its scientific merit.

In conclusion, while practical benefits matter, they should not be the dominant criterion for funding science, since the pursuit of knowledge itself remains the most reliable source of future innovation.

In recent years, the idea of a four-day working week has become very popular. Some people think that the law should make all employers to give their workers a four-day week with the same salary. I partly agree with this idea.

On the one hand, a four-day week has many advantages for workers. People today are very stressed because they work long hours and they don't have enough time for their family and hobbies. With an extra day off, they can rest, do sport and spend time with their children. As a result, they will be more happy and healthy. Also, some companies which tried this system found that their employees worked more efficient and made less mistakes, so the productivity did not go down.

On the other hand, I don't think this should be a law for every employer. Some businesses cannot close one day in the week. For example, hospitals, restaurants and shops need workers every day. If they must give a four-day week without reducing pay, they have to hire more staff, and this is very expensive. Small companies especially may not have enough money and some of them can go bankrupt. Then the workers will lose their jobs, which is worse than working five days.

In my opinion, the government should encourage the companies to try the four-day week, for example by giving them some help or tax reduction, but it should not force them. Each company know its own situation better than the government.

In conclusion, I believe a four-day week can be good for employees, but it should not be required by law for all employers, because some businesses cannot afford it.

answers.text:
The four-day working week has attracted growing interest, and some people now argue that employers should be legally obliged to offer it without any cut in pay. Although I believe shorter working weeks can bring real benefits, I disagree that they should be imposed on all employers by law.

There is no doubt that a four-day week could improve employees' wellbeing. Many workers suffer from stress and exhaustion, and an extra day off would give them more time to rest, look after their families and pursue personal interests. Several companies that have experimented with the model report that staff became more focused and motivated, and that productivity stayed the same or even improved. A healthier and more satisfied workforce may also mean fewer sick days and lower staff turnover.

However, making this a legal requirement would ignore the huge differences between sectors. In offices where work can be reorganised, a four-day week may be relatively easy to introduce. But in hospitals, care homes, factories and shops, where services must be provided every day, reducing hours without cutting pay would mean hiring extra staff at considerable cost. Small businesses, which often operate on narrow profit margins, could struggle to survive, and some might respond by cutting jobs or raising prices.

A more practical solution would be for governments to encourage rather than force the change. They could support pilot schemes, share results with employers and perhaps give staff a legal right to request shorter hours, while leaving each organisation to decide what are workable.

In conclusion, a four-day week without loss of pay has clear advantages for employees, but a universal legal requirement would place an unfair burden on many businesses. Voluntary adoption, supported by government, is a more realistic way forward.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Trials of the four-day week in various countries have produced encouraging results, prompting calls for employers to be legally required to offer it with no reduction in pay. While I am broadly sympathetic to the aims of this proposal, I disagree that it should be made compulsory, since a universal mandate would fail to account for the diversity of modern workplaces.

The potential benefits are considerable. Long working hours are associated with stress, burnout and poorer physical health, and an additional day of rest could allow employees to recover, care for relatives and engage more fully in family and community life. Many organisations that have adopted a shorter week report that staff concentrate more effectively, waste less time in unnecessary meetings and are less likely to leave, suggesting that output need not fall when hours do. For knowledge-based work in particular, time spent at a desk is a poor measure of productivity.

However, these results come largely from firms that chose to participate and were able to reorganise their work accordingly. The picture is very different in sectors where output is tied directly to hours, such as healthcare, retail, hospitality and manufacturing. A hospital cannot simply provide twenty per cent less care; to maintain services on full pay, it would need to recruit additional staff, often in areas already facing shortages. For small businesses with tight margins, the added cost could lead to redundancies or closure, ultimately harming the workers the policy is meant to help.

A more effective approach would be to promote the four-day week through incentives and evidence rather than compulsion. Governments could fund pilot programmes, publish their findings and give employees a statutory right to request flexible arrangements, which employers could refuse only on reasonable grounds.

In conclusion, a four-day week may well represent the future of work in many industries, but legislating it for every employer would be premature and potentially damaging.

Nowadays it is very difficult for young people to buy a house because the prices are very high. Some people think the government should improve rented housing instead of helping young people to buy their own homes. I agree with this opinion to some extent.

Firstly, many young people cannot buy a house even with help from the government. They have low salaries at the start of their career and they cannot save enough money for a deposit. If the government give them a small amount of money, the house prices will probably go up and the problem will not be solved. So it is more useful to make rented houses better, because many young people will rent for a long time anyway.

Secondly, the quality of rented houses in many cities is quite bad. Some apartments are old, cold and have problems like damp walls. Also, landlords can increase the rent or ask the tenants to leave with a short notice. This make people feel stressed and they cannot plan their life. If the government make rules to protect tenants and improve the condition of houses, the life of millions of people will become better.

However, owning a home is still a dream for many people. A house gives people security for the future and they don't have to pay rent when they are old. So I think the government should not stop helping completely, for example they can help people who buy their first home with low price.

In conclusion, I mostly agree that the government should focus on the quality and security of rented houses, because this help more people. But some help for young buyers is also necessary.

answers.text:
As property prices have risen faster than incomes in many countries, home ownership has become increasingly unattainable for young people. Some argue that governments should therefore concentrate on improving the quality and security of rented housing rather than on helping young people buy homes. I largely agree with this view.

One key reason is that schemes to help first-time buyers often fail to achieve their aims. Grants or subsidised loans increase the amount that buyers can spend, but if the supply of housing does not increase, the main effect is simply to push prices higher. Such schemes also tend to benefit those who were already close to affording a home, while doing little for young people on lower incomes, who may never be able to buy.

By contrast, improving the rental sector would benefit a much larger number of people. In many cities, a growing proportion of young adults rent for most of their twenties and thirties, yet they often live in poorly maintained properties and face sudden rent increases or eviction at short notice. Introducing minimum standards for housing quality, longer tenancy agreements and limits on excessive rent rises would give tenants the stability to settle, start families and plan for the future. In several European countries, where renting is secure and well regulated, it is considered a normal long-term option rather than a temporary stage.

That said, home ownership remains important for financial security, particularly in retirement, when people without property must continue paying rent on a reduced income. Governments should therefore not abandon support for buyers entirely, but it should focus on increasing the overall supply of affordable homes.

In conclusion, I agree that improving rented housing should be the priority, since it would help more young people more quickly and effectively. Support for home ownership should be a secondary goal, achieved mainly through building more homes.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In many countries, soaring property prices have put home ownership beyond the reach of a generation of young adults. One response is to argue that governments should prioritise making rented housing better and more secure, rather than trying to help young people onto the property ladder. I agree with this view to a considerable extent, although I believe the two goals are more connected than the statement suggests.

The weakness of many home-ownership schemes lies in their effect on prices. When governments offer deposit grants or subsidised mortgages without increasing the supply of homes, they largely add to demand, and much of the benefit is absorbed by higher prices. These policies also tend to favour those already on the verge of buying, offering little to young people on modest or insecure incomes, and they can be costly for the public purse.

Improving the rental sector, in contrast, would directly benefit the millions of young people who rent, many of them for far longer than previous generations did. Too often they face damp or poorly insulated homes, unpredictable rent increases and the constant possibility of being asked to leave. Enforceable quality standards, longer and more secure tenancies and protection against arbitrary eviction would allow tenants to put down roots, enrol children in local schools and plan their lives with confidence. Where renting is well regulated, as in parts of continental Europe, it is regarded as a respectable long-term choice rather than a precarious stopgap.

Ownership nonetheless matters, not least because retired people who rent must meet housing costs from a reduced income. The most effective way to support it, however, is not through demand-side subsidies but by building more homes, which would also ease pressure on rents.

In conclusion, governments should make secure, decent rented housing their immediate priority, while pursuing wider access to ownership through increasing housing supply rather than through subsidies for individual buyers.

Today countries trade with each other more than ever before, and food can be imported easily from all over the world. Some people believe that because of this, it is not necessary for each country to produce enough food for its own people. I disagree with this idea.

The main reason is that depending on other countries for food is risky. If there is a war, a natural disaster or a political problem, the imports can stop suddenly. For example, during the pandemic, many countries closed their borders and some food products became very expensive or difficult to find in the shops. If a country cannot produce its own food, its people can suffer from hunger in this kind of situation.

Another reason is that farming gives jobs to many people, especially in the countryside. If a country buy all its food from abroad, the farmers will lose their jobs and they will move to the cities to find work. This can make the cities more crowded and the villages will become empty. Also, the traditional way of life in rural areas will disappear.

On the other hand, it is true that some countries cannot produce all their food because they have a dry climate or not enough land. For them, import is necessary and it can be cheaper. But I think they should still try to produce the most important foods, such as rice or wheat, as much as possible.

In conclusion, I do not agree that it is no longer necessary for countries to produce enough food for their people. Although import is useful, every country should try to be independent in food so that they are safe in difficult times.

answers.text:
Global trade has made it possible for countries to import food from almost anywhere, leading some to argue that national self-sufficiency in food is no longer necessary. I partly agree with this view: complete self-sufficiency is unrealistic and often inefficient, but I believe every country should still maintain a significant capacity to feed its population.

It is true that international trade brings important benefits. Countries differ greatly in climate, soil and water resources, and it makes economic sense for each to specialise in what it can produce most efficiently. A desert nation that tried to grow all its own grain would waste enormous amounts of water and money, whereas importing it from countries with fertile land is far cheaper. Trade also gives consumers access to a wider variety of food throughout the year, and it can help stabilise supplies when one region experiences a poor harvest.

However, relying heavily on imports leaves a country vulnerable to events beyond its control. Wars, trade disputes and pandemics can disrupt supply chains suddenly, and in recent years export bans by major producers have caused sharp price rises for staple foods in many importing countries. Poorer nations are particularly exposed, as they may be unable to compete for limited supplies when global prices increases. In such situations, a strong domestic farming sector can act as essential insurance.

Furthermore, agriculture supports rural employment and communities, and abandoning it entirely could lead to economic decline in the countryside and the loss of valuable farming knowledge.

For these reasons, I believe the sensible approach is a balance: countries should trade for food where it is efficient, but ensure that they can produce enough of their basic staples, or hold sufficient reserves, to cope with a crisis.

In conclusion, although globalisation means that total self-sufficiency is no longer essential, I do not think countries can safely abandon domestic food production altogether.

answers.text:
The expansion of global trade has transformed how food reaches our tables, and some now argue that national food self-sufficiency has become an outdated goal. I agree that complete self-sufficiency is neither necessary nor, for many countries, achievable. However, I disagree with the broader implication that nations can safely neglect their capacity to feed themselves.

There is a strong economic logic to relying on trade. Agricultural conditions vary enormously, and forcing every country to grow all its own food would be highly inefficient. Arid or densely populated states would need to divert scarce water and land to crops that can be produced far more cheaply elsewhere, raising prices for their own citizens. Open markets allow resources to be used where they are most productive and can cushion the impact of a failed harvest in any one region by drawing on supplies from others.

Yet the assumption that global markets will always function smoothly is a dangerous one. Food supply chains are long and interdependent, and they have repeatedly proved fragile in the face of conflict, extreme weather and pandemics. When supplies tighten, exporting countries often prioritise their own populations by restricting sales abroad, precisely when importers need them most. Nations with weak domestic production and limited purchasing power are the first to suffer, and food shortages can quickly lead to social unrest.

Climate change is likely to heighten these risks, as droughts and floods disrupt harvests in major producing regions more frequently. In this context, maintaining a viable farming sector, diversifying import sources and holding strategic reserves are prudent forms of insurance rather than economic nationalism.

In conclusion, globalisation has made total self-sufficiency unnecessary, but it has not removed the need for food security. Each country should aim for sufficient domestic capacity and resilience to withstand disruption, even if it continues to rely on trade for much of what it consumes.

Nowadays people can find almost any information on the internet with their phones or computers. For this reason, some people think that public libraries are not necessary any more. I strongly disagree with this opinion.

Firstly, not everyone has access to the internet at home. Some families are poor and they cannot pay for a computer or a good internet connection. For these people, the library is the only place where they can use computers for free, search for jobs or do their homework. If libraries are closed, this people will have fewer chance to improve their life.

Secondly, libraries are not only a place for books. They are also a quiet place for students to study, especially for those who live in small houses with big families. In my city, the library is always full of university students during exam period, because they can concentrate there better than at home. Also, libraries organise many activities like reading clubs for children, language classes and events for old people. These activities help people to meet each other and feel part of the community.

Thirdly, not all information on the internet is reliable. There are many fake news and wrong information online. In the library, the books are chosen carefully and librarians can help people to find good sources for their research.

Some people say that libraries cost a lot of money for the government. But I think this money is a good investment because libraries give education and support to everyone.

In conclusion, I disagree that public libraries are no longer necessary. Even though a lot of information is online, libraries still provide free access, a place to study and community activities, so we should keep them.

With the vast amount of information now available online, some people claim that public libraries have become unnecessary. I strongly disagree with this view, as libraries provide important services that the internet cannot replace.

Firstly, libraries play a crucial role in providing equal access to information. Although internet use is widespread, a significant number of people still lack a reliable connection or a suitable device at home, particularly the elderly people and low-income families. For them, the local library offers free computers, printing and Wi-Fi, allowing them to apply for jobs, access government services and complete school assignments. Without libraries, the gap between those who are connected and those who are not would likely widen.

Secondly, the internet contains a great deal of information, but much of it is inaccurate or misleading. Librarians are trained to help people find reliable sources and to evaluate what they read, which is an increasingly valuable skill in the age of misinformation. Libraries also give free access to books, academic journals and databases that would otherwise be expensive, which benefits students and researchers alike.

In addition, libraries serve as community spaces. They offer a quiet environment for studying, host activities such as story sessions for young children and digital skills classes for older adults, and provide a safe, welcoming place for people to meet. In an era where many people feel isolated, these functions are arguably more important than ever.

Admittedly, libraries need to adapt to changing habits, for example by expanding their digital collections and offering more flexible opening hours. However, this is a reason to modernise them, not to close them.

In conclusion, I firmly believe that public libraries remain necessary despite the growth of online information. They ensure fair access to knowledge, support reliable research and strengthen local communities in ways the internet cannot.

answers.text:
The claim that public libraries have been rendered obsolete by the internet rests on the assumption that their sole purpose is to supply information. I disagree with this view. While the internet has undoubtedly changed how people find information, libraries continue to fulfil social, educational and democratic functions that online resources cannot replicate.

Perhaps the most important of these is ensuring equal access. It is easy to assume that everyone is online, yet many households still lack a reliable connection, an adequate device or the skills needed to use them effectively. As more essential services, from job applications to benefit claims, move online, a library's free computers and trained staff become a lifeline for those at risk of being left behind. Closing libraries would therefore deepen existing inequalities at the very moment when digital participation has become essential.

Libraries also address a problem the internet has intensified rather than solved: the difficulty of distinguishing reliable information from falsehood. Librarians guide users towards credible sources and help them develop the critical skills to evaluate what they read. Moreover, much high-quality content, including many academic journals and recent books, remains behind paywalls, and libraries make it freely available to anyone.

Beyond information, libraries function as some of the few remaining public spaces that are open to everyone and require no payment. Students without a quiet place to study at home, parents attending reading sessions with toddlers and older people seeking company all rely on them. In an increasingly fragmented society, such shared spaces help sustain a sense of community.

This is not to suggest that libraries should remain unchanged. They must continue to evolve, expanding digital lending and offering training in technology. But adaptation is an argument for investment, not closure.

In conclusion, public libraries remain necessary because their value extends far beyond information retrieval, encompassing equality of access, digital literacy and community life.

In modern society, many people buy more things than they really need, such as clothes, electronic devices and household items. Some people think that the government should do something to stop this behaviour. I agree with this idea to some extent.

On the one hand, buying too many goods is bad for the environment. Factories use a lot of energy and natural resources to make products, and they produce pollution. When people throw away things that they don't use, the rubbish goes to the landfill and it take many years to break down. For example, many people buy new clothes every month and wear them only few times. If the government reduce this, the environment will be more cleaner.

Also, overconsumption can cause problems for people themselves. Some people spend all their money on shopping and they have debts because of their credit cards. The government can help them by teaching about money management in schools or by controlling advertisements which make people want to buy more.

On the other hand, I think the government should not control people's life too much. People work hard and they have the right to decide how to spend their own money. Moreover, if people buy less, many shops and factories will have less customers and workers can lose their jobs. This can be bad for the economy of the country.

In my opinion, the government can encourage people to buy less by education and by making companies produce products that last longer, but it should not force people.

In conclusion, I partly agree that the government should discourage people from buying things they don't need. It can use soft methods like education, but people should still be free to make their own choices.

In many wealthy societies, people routinely buy clothes, gadgets and other goods that they rarely use, and some argue that governments should take steps to discourage this. I agree with this view to a large extent, as excessive consumption causes environmental and social problems that individuals alone are unlikely to solve.

The most serious consequence of overconsumption is its impact on the environment. Every product requires raw materials, energy and transport, and many items, such as cheap fashion and short-lived electronics, are thrown away after a short period. This contributes to pollution, the depletion of natural resources and overflowing landfill sites. Since these costs are not reflected in the price consumers pay, there is a strong case for government intervention to correct this.

Governments are also well placed to influence behaviour on a large scale. They could require manufacturers to make products that last longer and can be repaired, introduce taxes on goods with a high environmental impact, or restrict aggressive advertising techniques that create artificial needs. Supporting repair shops, second-hand markets and rental services would make it easier for people to consume less without feeling they are missing out.

Critics argue that such measures interfere with personal freedom and could harm economic growth, as many jobs depend on consumer spending. These concerns are valid, and governments should avoid telling people what they may or may not buy. However, encouraging more sustainable habits does not mean banning shopping; it means shifting the economy towards durable goods and services, which can also creates employment, for example in repair and recycling.

In conclusion, I believe governments should discourage people from buying more than they need, mainly by encouraging durability, reducing waste and regulating advertising. Such measures can protect the environment while still respecting individual choice.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Consumer culture in many prosperous countries encourages people to buy far more than they need, from fast fashion to frequently upgraded phones. The suggestion that governments should actively discourage this behaviour raises questions about both sustainability and personal freedom. On balance, I agree that intervention is justified, provided it targets the systems that drive overconsumption rather than policing individual purchases.

The environmental argument is compelling. The production, shipping and disposal of consumer goods account for a considerable share of resource use and emissions, and the problem is aggravated by products designed to be replaced rather than repaired. A garment worn a handful of times before being discarded, or a device abandoned because a single component has failed, represents a significant waste of materials and energy. Because these environmental costs are largely borne by society rather than by the buyer, the market alone has little incentive to correct them.

Governments possess tools that individuals do not. Legislation requiring durability, access to spare parts and a right to repair would extend the life of countless products. Tax policy could make repair and second-hand goods cheaper relative to new ones, while tighter rules on advertising, particularly the targeted online promotions that exploit impulse buying, would reduce the constant pressure to acquire more. Measures of this kind reshape the choices available without dictating what anyone must buy.

The main objections are that such policies infringe personal liberty and threaten economic growth. The first is less persuasive when intervention focuses on product standards and marketing rather than consumer decisions. The second deserves more attention, since many jobs depend on retail spending, but a shift towards repair, refurbishment and services can generate employment of its own.

In conclusion, governments are right to discourage excessive consumption, though the most effective and legitimate way to do so is by changing how goods are made and marketed, rather than by restricting what people are allowed to buy.

Nowadays, learning a foreign language is very important in the modern world. Some people think children should start to learn it in primary school, while other people believe secondary school is a better time. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, there are some reasons why starting at secondary school can be better. Firstly, older students are more mature and they can understand grammar rules more easier. For example, a twelve years old student can study by himself and use a dictionary. Secondly, young children already have many subjects to learn, like maths and their mother language, so adding another language can make them confused. Also, many primary schools do not have enough qualified teachers, so the lessons may be not good quality.

On the other hand, many people think that primary school is the best time. Young children can learn new sounds very quickly and they are not shy to speak. That is why children who learn English early usually have a better pronunciation than adults. In addition, if they start early, they will have more years to practise, and by the time they finish school they can speak fluently. Learning language can also be fun for children because teachers use songs and games.

In my opinion, I believe that it is better to start at primary school. Although older students understand grammar better, the advantage of young age is more important, especially for speaking and listening. However, the government should make sure there is enough good teachers.

In conclusion, both views have some good points. Older students can learn grammar easily, but young children learn speaking more naturally. I think children should begin a foreign language in primary school if the teaching is good.

answers.text:
There is ongoing debate about the ideal age at which children should start studying a foreign language. While some argue that secondary school is the more appropriate stage, I believe that introducing languages in primary school brings greater long-term benefits, provided it is done well.

Those who favour a later start point to the cognitive maturity of older pupils. Teenagers are able to grasp abstract grammatical concepts, use learning strategies such as keeping vocabulary notebooks, and take responsibility for their own progress. As a result, they can often cover in two or three years what younger learners take much longer to achieve. There is also a practical argument: primary timetables are already crowded with literacy and numeracy, and some educators worry that a second language might distract young children from mastering their mother tongue.

However, advocates of an early start emphasise the natural advantages of youth. Young children tend to imitate sounds effortlessly and are far less self-conscious about making mistakes, which means they are more willing to speak. A child who hears and repeats a language from the age of six or seven is likely to develop more accurate pronunciation and greater confidence than someone who begins at thirteen. Furthermore, an early start gives learners many more years of exposure, which is arguably the most important factor in achieving fluency.

In my view, the benefits of starting in primary school outweigh the drawbacks. The concern about overloading children can be addressed by keeping lessons short, playful and focused on listening and speaking, with formal grammar introduced later. The real challenge is the shortage of well-trained teachers, and this is something that governments needs to invest in.

In conclusion, although older learners have certain analytical advantages, I am convinced that children should begin learning a foreign language at primary school, as long as the teaching suits their age.

answers.text:
Few educational questions generate as much debate as when a child should first encounter a foreign language. Some maintain that it should be introduced in primary school, whereas others contend that it is more sensible to wait until secondary level. Having weighed both positions, I would argue that an early start is preferable, although its success depends on how it is implemented.

The case for delaying language study rests largely on the capabilities of older learners. By the age of eleven or twelve, pupils have developed the analytical skills needed to understand how a language is structured, and they can apply techniques such as comparing its grammar with that of their first language. This allows them to make rapid, systematic progress. Moreover, deferring a second language gives younger children time to consolidate reading and writing in their mother tongue, a foundation on which all later learning depends. From this perspective, early lessons may consume valuable classroom time without producing meaningful results.

Nevertheless, there are compelling reasons to begin sooner. Young children acquire language largely through imitation and play, and they are generally uninhibited about experimenting with unfamiliar sounds. Consequently, those who start early often develop more natural pronunciation and a more intuitive feel for the language than learners who begin in adolescence, when embarrassment can hold them back. An early start also provides more years of exposure, and sustained contact over a long period is what ultimately produces confident, fluent speakers.

On balance, I find the second argument more persuasive. The concerns raised about primary-level teaching are genuine, but they relate to poor delivery rather than to the principle itself. If lessons are brief, oral and enjoyable, and are led by properly trained teachers, they complement rather than compete with literacy in the first language.

In conclusion, while older pupils learn grammar more efficiently, the advantages of early exposure are difficult to replicate later in life. Children should therefore begin a foreign language in primary school, with formal study left to secondary level.

In today's society, many students go to university. Some people say that the main aim of university is to prepare students for a job, but others think it should be a place where people can learn knowledge for its own sake. This essay will discuss both opinions.

Firstly, people who think university is for employment have strong reasons. University education is very expensive and many students take a loan to pay the fees. So they expect to find a good job with high salary after graduation. Also, companies need workers who has practical skills, for example in engineering, medicine or computer science. If universities only teach theory, the graduates will not be ready for work and the economy will suffer.

Secondly, other people believe that university should be a place for learning any subject which students are interested in. Subjects like history, philosophy or literature does not lead directly to a job, but they help people to think critically and understand the world. In addition, many important discoveries in science was made by researchers who were only curious and did not think about money. If universities focus only on jobs, this kind of research may disappear.

In my opinion, I think both purposes are important, but preparing for employment should be the main purpose. Most of students go to university because they want a better career, and it is fair that universities help them. However, universities should still keep some space for pure knowledge and research.

In conclusion, some people think universities are for jobs, and others think they are for knowledge. Although both views have advantage, I believe employment is the main purpose, but knowledge for its own sake should not be forgotten.

Universities today face competing expectations. Many people see them primarily as training grounds for the workforce, while others insist that their true value lies in the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake. Although I accept that employability matters, I believe universities should not be reduced to vocational institutions.

Supporters of the employment-focused view make a reasonable case. Higher education has become costly, and students who graduate with considerable debt understandably want courses that lead to secure, well-paid work. Employers, too, frequently complain that graduates lack practical skills such as teamwork, project management or familiarity with industry software. From this perspective, a university that ignores the job market is failing both its students and the wider economy.

On the other hand, there are strong arguments for protecting learning that has no immediate practical purpose. Disciplines such as philosophy, history and pure mathematics develop the ability to analyse complex problems, question assumptions and communicate ideas clearly, qualities that are valued in almost any career. Moreover, much of the research that has transformed modern life began as curiosity-driven enquiry, with no commercial application in mind at the time. If funding and teaching are directed only towards what is currently profitable, society risks losing the foundations of future innovation.

In my opinion, the two goals are less opposed than they first appear. A literature student can still gain transferable skills through internships and careers guidance, while an engineering student benefits from exploring the ethical and historical context of their field. Universities should therefore offer practical preparation without abandoning there commitment to independent thought.

To conclude, while preparing graduates for employment is an important function of universities, I believe it should not be the main or only one, since the pursuit of knowledge itself brings long-term benefits to individuals and to society.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The role of higher education has become increasingly contested as tuition costs rise and labour markets change. One camp holds that a university exists chiefly to equip students for employment; another maintains that it should be a place where knowledge is pursued for its own sake. In my view, a university that sacrifices the latter in favour of the former undermines what makes it distinctive.

It is easy to see why the employment argument resonates. For most undergraduates, a degree represents a substantial financial commitment, and it is reasonable for them to expect that it will improve their career prospects. Governments that subsidise higher education likewise want a return on that investment in the form of skilled professionals, whether doctors, engineers or data analysts. Seen in this light, courses detached from the needs of the economy can appear to be an expensive luxury.

However, this view rests on a narrow conception of usefulness. Many of the capabilities employers prize most, such as the capacity to evaluate evidence, construct an argument and adapt to unfamiliar problems, are cultivated precisely through open-ended academic study rather than job-specific training. Furthermore, skills tailored to today's labour market may be obsolete within a decade, whereas a deep understanding of a discipline endures. At the level of society, fundamental research undertaken without any commercial aim has repeatedly laid the groundwork for later technological breakthroughs.

For these reasons, I believe the pursuit of knowledge should remain at the heart of a university's mission, with employability treated as a valuable by-product rather than the overriding objective. This does not mean ignoring students' career needs; work placements and professional guidance can sit comfortably alongside rigorous academic study. What should be resisted is the notion that a subject is worthwhile only if it leads directly to a particular job.

In conclusion, although universities clearly have a role in preparing people for work, their deeper and more enduring purpose is to advance and share knowledge, which ultimately serves both individuals and the economy better.

Deciding when a child should receive their first smartphone has become a common dilemma for modern parents. Some argue that phones should be given as soon as children start school, while others feel they should be delayed until the teenage years. In my view, the latter approach is wiser, although a basic phone may be useful earlier.

Those who favour giving smartphones at a young age usually stress safety and convenience. A phone allows parents to contact their children at any time and, with location-sharing apps, to know exactly where they are. This can be particularly reassuring for working parents whose children travel to school or activities independently. Supporters also point out that many educational apps make learning interactive and enjoyable, and that children who grow up with technology will be better prepared for a digital world.

Nevertheless, there are serious concerns about young children owning such devices. Smartphones are designed to hold attention, and a six-year-old has limited ability to control how long they spend on games or videos. Excessive screen time is widely linked to poor sleep, reduced physical activity and difficulty concentrating. In addition, young children are poorly equipped to recognise online risks, such as inappropriate content or contact from strangers, and parental controls are rarely fool proof.

In my opinion, the risks for young children clearly outweigh the benefits. The safety argument is valid, but it can be met with a simple phone that only makes calls and sends texts. By the early teenage years, children are more mature, and parents can gradually introduce a smartphone with clear rules and open conversations about responsible use.

In conclusion, while early smartphone ownership offers some practical advantages, I believe children should generally wait until they are teenagers, using a basic phone in the meantime if they needs to stay in contact with their parents.

answers.text:
The age at which children should be given a smartphone is a question that divides parents and educators. One view is that a child should have their own device from the first day of school; the opposing view is that ownership should be postponed until adolescence. While both positions reflect genuine concern for children's welfare, I believe that delaying full smartphone access is the more responsible course.

Advocates of early ownership frame the issue in terms of security and preparation. A smartphone enables parents to stay in touch with their children throughout the day and to track their location, which offers considerable peace of mind. There is also an argument that digital literacy is now as fundamental as reading, and that children who become familiar with technology early will navigate it more competently later. Finally, some parents fear that a child without a phone will be socially isolated if most classmates already own one.

Those who favour waiting, however, raise concerns that are harder to dismiss. Young children lack the self-discipline to limit their own screen time, and devices engineered to maximise engagement can easily displace sleep, outdoor play and face-to-face interaction, all of which are vital for healthy development. Equally worrying is children's vulnerability online: a seven-year-old is unlikely to recognise manipulative content or the risks of communicating with strangers, and even well-configured parental controls can be circumvented.

Weighing these arguments, I am persuaded that the risks of early ownership outweigh its advantages. The legitimate need for contact can be met by a basic handset without internet access, and digital skills can be taught under supervision at school or at home. Once children reach their early teens, a smartphone can be introduced gradually, with agreed limits that are relaxed as they demonstrate responsibility.

In conclusion, although giving young children smartphones offers reassurance and convenience, these benefits can be achieved in safer ways. Postponing ownership until the teenage years allows children to develop the maturity they need to use such devices wisely.

Nowadays many companies use technology in recruitment. Some people think artificial intelligence should decide which job applicants to hire because it is more objective than humans. However, others believe people should always make this decision. This essay will discuss both views.

On the one hand, AI has some advantages in choosing employees. Human managers sometimes have bias, for example they may prefer a candidate who is from same city or university as them. A computer program does not have feelings, so it can judge all applicants by the same rules. In addition, AI can read thousands of CVs in few minutes, which save a lot of time and money for big companies.

On the other hand, there are many reasons why humans should make the final decision. Firstly, AI learns from old data, and if the old data was unfair, the AI will also be unfair. For instance, if a company hired mostly men in the past, the system may choose men again. Secondly, a computer cannot understand personality or motivation very well. A good employee need skills like communication and teamwork, and it is difficult for a machine to measure these things. Also, applicants may feel it is not fair to be rejected by a machine without explanation.

In my opinion, I think AI can be useful but people should make the final decision. Companies can use AI to check CVs quickly, and then managers can interview the best candidates and choose.

In conclusion, AI is fast and can be more objective in some ways, but it has also problems. Therefore, I believe that decisions about employing people should be made by humans, with help from technology.
