answers.text:
As artificial intelligence becomes more sophisticated, some companies have begun using it to screen and select job applicants. Supporters claim that software is more impartial than human recruiters, while critics insist that hiring decisions must remain in human hands. I believe AI can play a useful supporting role, but the final decision should be made by people.

The argument for AI-led recruitment is based largely on the problem of human bias. Interviewers are often influenced, even unconsciously, by factors such as an applicant's appearance, accent or background, which have little to do with their ability to do the job. An algorithm, by contrast, can be programmed to assess every candidate against identical criteria. It can also process huge numbers of applications quickly and consistently, which is a clear advantage for large organisations.

However, the claim that AI is objective is questionable. These systems are trained on past hiring data, so if a company has historically favoured certain groups, the software may simply learn to reproduce that pattern on a larger scale. Moreover, many of the qualities that make someone a good colleague, such as integrity, adaptability and the ability to work in a team, are difficult to measure through data alone. There is also the question of accountability: when a qualified candidate is rejected by an algorithm, it is often unclear who is responsible or how the decision was reached.

In my view, the most sensible approach is to combine both. AI tools could be used to organise applications and highlight relevant experience, but trained managers should conduct interviews and make the final choice, while regularly checking the software for signs of bias.

In conclusion, although artificial intelligence can make recruitment faster and reduce some form of human prejudice, it is not truly neutral, and decisions that affect people's livelihoods should ultimately be taken by people.

answers.text:
The use of artificial intelligence in recruitment has prompted a lively debate. Proponents argue that algorithms can assess candidates more objectively than human interviewers, whereas opponents maintain that decisions of such consequence should always rest with people. Although AI has a legitimate role in the hiring process, I would argue that handing it the final say would be a mistake.

The appeal of automated selection lies in its apparent neutrality. Human judgement is notoriously susceptible to prejudice: recruiters may warm to candidates who resemble themselves, or be swayed by first impressions that bear no relation to competence. A well-designed system, by contrast, applies the same criteria to every application without fatigue or favouritism. For organisations that receive thousands of applications, this consistency, combined with the speed of automated screening, is highly attractive.

Yet the promise of objectivity is, in practice, difficult to fulfil. Algorithms learn from historical data, and if past recruitment favoured particular genders, ethnic groups or educational backgrounds, the software is likely to absorb and even amplify those preferences while giving them a veneer of scientific authority. Furthermore, the qualities that often distinguish an outstanding employee, such as judgement, resilience and the capacity to collaborate, are precisely those that resist quantification. Finally, automated rejection raises a serious problem of accountability, since applicants are rarely able to learn why they were turned down or to challenge the outcome.

For these reasons, I believe AI should inform rather than determine hiring decisions. It can usefully handle routine tasks such as sorting applications or flagging relevant qualifications, but the assessment of a person's suitability requires human insight, and those making the decision must be answerable for it.

In conclusion, while artificial intelligence can reduce certain inconsistencies in recruitment, it is neither as impartial nor as perceptive as its advocates suggest. The responsibility for choosing who to employ should therefore remain firmly with people.

The appeal of automated selection lies in its apparent neutrality. Human judgement is notoriously susceptible to prejudice: recruiters may warm to candidates who resemble themselves, or be swayed by first impressions that bear no relation to competence. A well-designed system, by contrast, applies the same criteria to every application without fatigue or favouritism. For organisations that receive thousands of applications, this consistency, combined with the speed of automated screening, is highly attractive.

Yet the promise of objectivity is, in practice, difficult to fulfil. Algorithms learn from historical data, and if past recruitment favoured particular genders, ethnic groups or educational backgrounds, the software is likely to absorb and even amplify those preferences while giving them a veneer of scientific authority.
Furthermore,
the qualities that often distinguish an outstanding employee, such as judgement, resilience and the capacity to collaborate, are precisely those that resist quantification.
Finally,
automated rejection raises a serious problem of accountability, since applicants are rarely able to learn why they were turned down or to challenge the outcome.
For these reasons,
I believe

AI should inform rather than determine hiring decisions. It can usefully handle routine tasks such as sorting applications or flagging relevant qualifications, but the assessment of a person's suitability requires human insight, and those making the decision must be answerable for it.
In conclusion,

while artificial intelligence can reduce certain inconsistencies in recruitment, it is neither as impartial nor as perceptive as its advocates suggest. The responsibility for choosing who to employ should therefore remain firmly with people.

How humanity should respond to environmental damage is one of the defining questions of our time. Some are confident that technological innovation will provide the answers, whereas others argue that nothing less than a change in how people live will be effective. In my view, technology is essential but insufficient on its own.

Those who place their faith in technology can point to impressive progress. The cost of renewable energy such as solar and wind power has fallen dramatically, electric vehicles are becoming mainstream, and researchers are developing methods to capture carbon and produce food more efficiently. The attraction of this approach is that it does not require billions of people to give up comforts they value. Instead, it allows economies to keep growing while their environmental impact declines.

On the other hand, critics argue that relying on future inventions is a risky strategy. Many promising technologies are still expensive or years away from large-scale use, while the damage to ecosystems is happening now. Moreover, efficiency gains are often cancelled out by rising consumption: cars have become cleaner, for instance, but there are far more of them on the roads. Unless people reduce waste, buy fewer disposable products and rethink habits such as frequent flying, even the cleanest technology may simply allow us to consume more.

I believe the most realistic solution combines both approaches. Governments should invest heavily in green technology, but they also need to encourage lifestyle changes through measures such as better public transport and incentives for repairing rather than replacing goods. Technology can make sustainable choices easier, but people must still be willing to make it.

In conclusion, while new technology will undoubtedly play a major role in solving environmental problems, lasting change also depends on individuals adapting the way they live.

answers.text:
Faced with mounting evidence of environmental decline, societies are divided over where the solution lies. Some believe that technological progress will eventually resolve the crisis, while others insist that meaningful change can only come from altering the way people live. Although both perspectives contain important truths, I would argue that neither is adequate without the other.

The optimism surrounding technology is not without foundation. In recent decades, renewable energy has become cheaper and more widely available, battery technology has improved considerably, and innovations in areas such as building insulation and precision farming have reduced waste. Crucially, technological solutions do not depend on persuading billions of individuals to sacrifice their comfort, which makes them politically and socially more achievable than widespread behavioural change. From this perspective, human ingenuity offers the most practical route to a sustainable future.

However, relying solely on innovation carries significant risks. Many of the most ambitious technologies remain unproven at scale, and waiting for them to mature may squander time that the planet does not have. There is also a well-documented tendency for efficiency gains to be offset by increased consumption: as products become cheaper and cleaner to run, people often simply use more of them. Without a shift in attitudes towards consumption, waste and travel, technology risks treating the symptoms of environmental damage rather than its underlying causes.

In my view, the two approaches are mutually reinforcing. Technology is most effective when it makes sustainable behaviour convenient, as affordable public transport or efficient home heating does, and lifestyle changes are easier to sustain when practical alternatives exist. Policy should therefore pursue both, funding research while also using regulation and incentives to discourage wasteful habits.

In conclusion, while technological advances are indispensable in tackling environmental problems, they cannot succeed in isolation. A genuine solution requires people to reconsider how they live, supported by innovations that make greener choices easier.

Tackling climate change will require enormous investment, and there is disagreement over how this burden should be distributed. Some believe that wealthy nations should cover most of the cost, while others argue that every country should contribute equally. In my opinion, richer countries should pay the larger share, although all nations must play some part.

The case for wealthy countries paying more rests on both history and capacity. Industrialised nations have been burning fossil fuels for over two centuries, so they are responsible for a large proportion of the greenhouse gases already in the atmosphere. They have also benefited economically from this development. Furthermore, they have the financial resources and technical expertise to fund clean energy projects, whereas many poorer countries are struggling to provide basic services such as healthcare and electricity for their citizens.

Those who support equal contributions, however, raise valid points. Several fast-growing economies are now among the largest emitters, and if they are not required to pay, there may be little incentive for them to limit their emissions. Some also argue that since climate change threatens everyone, every country has an equal interest in solving it and should therefore carry an equal responsibility. There is a concern too that citizens in rich countries may be unwilling to support policies which appear to place the whole burden on them.

On balance, I believe that an equal split would be unfair and unrealistic. Asking a low-income country to pay the same as a wealthy one ignores huge differences in wealth and historical responsibility. A better system would be based on a combination of past emissions and current income, so that each country contributes in proportion to it's ability and impact.

In conclusion, although all nations share the consequences of climate change, the costs of tackling it should fall mainly on wealthy countries, with developing countries contributing according to their means.

As the costs of addressing climate change mount, so does the question of who should bear them. One view holds that wealthy nations should shoulder most of the financial burden; another insists that the costs should be divided equally among all countries. I believe that a fair arrangement must reflect differences in both responsibility and capacity, which means that richer countries should pay considerably more.

The argument for placing the main burden on wealthy countries is rooted in historical responsibility. The nations that industrialised first have emitted the bulk of the carbon dioxide that has accumulated in the atmosphere, and their current prosperity was built, in large part, on that fossil-fuel-driven growth. It therefore seems just that they should now fund a substantial share of the transition. They are also far better placed to do so, possessing the capital, infrastructure and research capacity that many developing countries lack.

Advocates of equal contributions nevertheless make a case that deserves serious consideration. Emissions are no longer concentrated in the traditional industrial powers; several rapidly developing economies now produce a significant proportion of global emissions. Exempting them from financial responsibility could weaken their commitment to decarbonisation and breed resentment among taxpayers in wealthier states. Moreover, since climate change threatens every country, some would argue that a shared problem demands an equally shared solution.

In my view, however, treating unequal nations equally would itself be inequitable. Requiring a country where much of the population lacks reliable electricity to contribute as much as one of the world's richest economies would hinder its development while doing little for the climate. A more defensible approach would scale contributions according to historical emissions, current emissions and national income, ensuring that every country participates while the heaviest costs fall on those most able to bear them.

In conclusion, although all nations have a stake in combating climate change, fairness requires that wealthy countries fund the greater part of the effort, with others contributing in proportion to their means.

In my opinion, governments should spend most of the money on public transport. It is good for environment and it helps more people, including those who cannot afford a car. However, roads in rural areas still need to be repaired and improve.

In conclusion, more roads can help traffic in short term, but public transport is a better long-term solution. Therefore, I believe the money should mainly go to railways and buses.

Traffic congestion has become a serious issue in many growing cities, and governments must decide how best to address it. Some argue that building additional roads is the answer, while others believe investment in railways and public transport would be more effective. I am of the opinion that the second approach offers greater long-term benefits.

Supporters of road building make several reasonable points. New or wider roads can relieve bottlenecks and reduce journey times, at least in the short term. They are also essential for freight, as most goods are still delivered by lorry, and delays cost businesses a considerable amount of money. Furthermore, in rural areas where public transport is limited or non-existent, people depend on cars, and good roads are the only realistic way to connect these communities.

However, building roads rarely solves congestion permanently. When road capacity increases, driving becomes more attractive, and the extra space is often filled with new traffic within a few years. Public transport, by contrast, moves large numbers of people using much less space. A single train can replace hundreds of cars, reducing both congestion and air pollution. In cities which have invested in reliable metro or tram networks, commuters are often happy to leave their cars at home, which benefit the whole population.

In my view, the most effective strategy is to prioritise public transport in urban areas while maintaining the existing road network. Money should be directed towards frequent, affordable services that give people a genuine alternative to driving, and new roads should only be built where there are no practical alternatives.

In conclusion, although more roads can provide quick relief and remain important in rural regions, investing in railways and public transport is a more sustainable way of tackling traffic problems.

answers.text:
Congested roads impose significant costs on economies and on the quality of urban life, and governments face a choice about how to respond. One view is that expanding the road network is the most direct solution; another is that the same funds would achieve more if spent on railways and other forms of public transport. While road investment has its place, I believe that public transport represents the better use of money in most circumstances.

The argument for building roads is intuitive. If traffic is heavy, providing more lanes should, in principle, allow vehicles to move more freely and reduce journey times. Roads are also indispensable for the movement of goods, emergency services and residents of rural areas, where population densities are too low to support frequent bus or rail services. For these communities, well-maintained roads are not a luxury but a lifeline.

Nevertheless, the benefits of road expansion in cities tend to be short-lived. Additional capacity makes driving more convenient, which encourages more people to drive and gradually recreates the original congestion, a phenomenon often described as induced demand. Public transport, by contrast, is inherently more space-efficient: a single rail line can carry far more passengers than a lane of private cars. Well-designed networks also bring wider advantages, including cleaner air, lower carbon emissions and greater mobility for those who cannot afford to drive or are unable to.

In my view, therefore, governments should concentrate urban transport spending on rail, trams and buses, while reserving road construction for areas where no viable alternative exists and for essential maintenance. The key is to make public transport sufficiently frequent, reliable and affordable that it becomes the natural choice rather than a last resort.

In conclusion, although building roads can offer temporary relief and remains vital in rural areas, investment in public transport provides a more lasting and equitable solution to traffic problems.

I believe

However,
the government should make sure that every new area has at least a small park, so residents have somewhere to go.
In conclusion,
parks improve health and environment, while housing and business help people to live and work.

cities need a balance, but homes should be the first priority.

As urban populations grow, the question of how to use limited city land has become increasingly important. Some people believe it should be devoted mainly to parks and green spaces, while others think housing and commercial development should take priority. In my view, both are essential, but green space should not be sacrificed simply to meet short-term demand for buildings.

Those who favour housing and businesses make a practical argument. In many large cities, property prices have risen so sharply that ordinary workers, such as nurses and teachers, can no longer afford to live near their jobs. Building more homes on available land would help to ease this shortage. In addition, businesses need space for offices and shops, which generate employment and tax revenue. From this perspective, leaving valuable land undeveloped could seem like a luxury that crowded cities can't afford.

On the other hand, supporters of green space argue that parks are not a luxury but a necessity. They provide opportunities for exercise and relaxation, which contributes to both physical and mental health. Trees and plants also improve air quality, reduce flooding by absorbing rainwater, and help to lower temperatures during heatwaves. Once a park is built on, it is almost never restored, so losing green space is effectively permanent.

I believe the solution lies in smarter planning rather than choosing one use over the other. Cities can increase housing by building upwards and redeveloping disused industrial sites, rather than using existing parks. At the same time, new developments should be required to include green areas, so that residents benefit from nature on their doorstep.

In conclusion, while the need for housing and businesses is urgent, I believe cities should protect and expand their green spaces, since they are vital for the long-term wellbeing of residents.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Land in cities is a scarce and valuable resource, and how it is allocated shapes the lives of millions of residents. Some argue that it should be used predominantly for parks and other green spaces, whereas others believe that housing and commercial premises should take precedence. In my view, although the demand for homes is pressing, green space must be treated as essential infrastructure rather than as a dispensable amenity.

The case for prioritising housing and business is compelling in many cities. Chronic shortages of affordable accommodation force workers to endure long commutes or to leave urban areas altogether, which harms both their quality of life and the local economy. Commercial development, meanwhile, generates employment, attracts investment and provides the tax revenue that funds public services. Seen from this angle, reserving large areas for parks might appear to be an indulgence that a growing city can ill afford.

However, this reasoning underestimates the tangible value of green space. Parks offer residents, particularly those living in flats without gardens, a place to exercise, socialise and escape the pressures of urban life, with well-documented benefits for physical and mental health. They also perform important environmental functions: vegetation absorbs rainwater, mitigating the risk of flooding, and helps to counteract the heat that builds up in densely built areas. Crucially, once green space is developed, it is rarely, if ever, recovered.

Rather than framing the issue as a stark choice, I believe cities should pursue housing growth in ways that preserve and even enhance green areas. Building at higher densities, redeveloping former industrial land and converting underused offices into homes can all increase supply without encroaching on parks. New developments, in turn, can be required to incorporate gardens, tree-lined streets and shared open spaces.

In conclusion, while the need for homes and businesses is undeniable, green space is too important to be treated as expendable. Careful planning allows cities to meet both needs, but existing parks should be protected rather than sacrificed.

In the past, most people worked for one company for all their life, but now many people change their job often. Some people think it is better to stay with the same employer, while others believe changing jobs brings more benefits. I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

There are several advantages of staying in one company for a long time. Firstly, employees can get job security, which means they do not need to worry about losing their income. Secondly, if a worker stay for many years, the company trust him and he can get promotion to a higher position. For example, a person who start as a junior staff can become a manager after ten years. Moreover, they can build strong relationship with their colleagues.

On the other hand, changing jobs frequently also have many benefits. When people move to a new company, they usually get a higher salary than before. They also learn new skills and experience different ways of working, which make their CV more attractive. In addition, if someone is not happy in their job, it is better to leave and find a job they enjoy instead of feeling bored for many years.

In my opinion, changing jobs is better for young people, but staying with one employer is better later in life. When people are young, they should try different jobs to find what they are good at. After that, they can stay with a good company and build their career there.

In conclusion, both staying and changing jobs have advantages. I think people should change jobs when they are young and then stay with one employer when they find the right place.

answers.text:
Attitudes to careers have changed considerably, and people now debate whether loyalty to one employer or regular job changes is the better path. While each approach has its merits, I believe that changing jobs periodically, rather than constantly, offers the greatest benefits for most people.

Remaining with the same organisation for many years can be highly rewarding. Long-serving employees develop an in-depth understanding of how their company works, which often makes them strong candidates for promotion to senior roles. They also tend to enjoy greater job security and build strong, trusting relationships with colleagues and managers. In addition, stability of this kind can make it easier to plan major life decisions, such as buying a home or starting a family.

On the other hand, people who change jobs more frequently often progress faster in terms of salary and responsibility. Moving to a new employer is frequently the quickest way to negotiate a significant pay rise, and each new role exposes the worker to different systems, technologies and working cultures. This variety helps them to develop a broad set of skills and a wider professional network, both of which is increasingly important in a fast-changing job market. Staying in one place for too long, by contrast, can lead to complacency and outdated skills.

In my opinion, the ideal lies somewhere between these extremes. Changing jobs every few months can suggest a lack of commitment, but remaining in the same position for decades may limit personal growth. Spending a few years in each role, long enough to make a real contribution, allows people to gain both depth and breadth of experience.

In conclusion, although long-term loyalty brings security and recognition, I believe that moving between employers at sensible intervals generally offers greater opportunities for development and advancement.

answers.text:
Whereas a single lifelong employer was once the norm, many workers today move between organisations several times during their careers. This has sparked debate over whether long-term loyalty or frequent change is more advantageous. Having considered both sides, I would argue that the answer depends partly on career stage, but that a willingness to move is generally more beneficial.

There is much to be said for staying with one employer. Over time, an employee accumulates detailed knowledge of the organisation's systems, clients and culture, which can make them indispensable and position them well for internal promotion. Long tenure also tends to bring stability, both financial and emotional, together with close working relationships that can make the workplace more fulfilling. Employers, for their part, often reward such commitment with additional benefits and greater trust.

Nevertheless, frequent job changes carry advantages that are difficult to ignore. Moving to a new organisation is often the most effective way to secure a substantial increase in salary, since external candidates can negotiate from a stronger position than existing staff. Each move also exposes the employee to unfamiliar challenges, methods and colleagues, accelerating the acquisition of skills and broadening their professional network. In a labour market where entire industries can be transformed within a decade, such adaptability is arguably a greater form of security than loyalty to a single firm.

On balance, I believe that moving between employers is more beneficial, particularly in the early and middle stages of a career, when breadth of experience matters most. That said, changing jobs too often can undermine credibility and prevent people from seeing projects through to completion. The most rewarding pattern is perhaps to stay long enough in each role to achieve something meaningful before moving on.

In conclusion, while long service offers stability and recognition, periodic job changes generally provide faster growth, higher earnings and greater resilience in an uncertain economy.

Businesses play a big role in our society. Some people think a company only exist to make money for its owners, while others believe businesses should also help society. This essay will discuss both views, and I think businesses should do both.

People who believe profit is the main purpose have some good reasons. A business is not a charity, and the owners invest their money because they want to earn more. If a company does not make profit, it will close and all the workers will lose their job. Also, when companies are successful, they pay tax to the government, and the government can use this money for schools and hospitals. So making profit is already helping society in an indirect way.

However, other people argue that companies have a bigger responsibility. Big companies use a lot of natural resources and sometimes they pollute rivers and air. Some also pay very low salaries or sell unhealthy products to people. Because they have so much power, they should think about the effect on society, for example by protecting the environment, treating workers fairly and support local communities. Many customers today prefer to buy from companies who are responsible.

In my view, making profit is important, but it should not be the only goal. A company can be successful and also be good for society at the same time. For example, a factory can use clean energy and still earn money.

In conclusion, although profit is necessary for any business to survive, I believe businesses also has a responsibility to society. The best companies are the ones which can balance both of these things.

The role of business in modern society is often debated. Some people argue that a company's primary purpose is to generate profits for its owners and shareholders, whereas others believe businesses have wider obligations to the communities in which they operate. In my opinion, profit is essential, but it should be pursued in a socially responsible way.

Those who emphasise profit argue that this is simply what businesses are designed to do. Investors risk their capital in the expectation of a return, and managers have a duty to use that money efficiently. Moreover, profitable companies already benefit society indirectly by creating jobs, paying taxes and developing products that people want. Some also suggest that social problems are better handled by governments and charities, which are directly accountable to the public.

On the other hand, many people believe that large companies have too much influence to ignore their wider impact. Business activities can damage the environment, exploit low-paid workers or harm consumers' health, and these costs are often paid by society rather than by the company itself. For this reason, it seems reasonable to expect businesses to reduce pollution, pay fair wages and behave ethically. Such behaviour can also be good for profits, since customers and employees increasingly prefer to be associated with responsible brands.

I believe these two goals are not necessarily in conflict. A company that treats its staff well tends to retain talented employees, and one that respect the environment avoids costly fines and reputational damage. Therefore, social responsibility should be seen as part of long-term business success rather than as an optional extra.

In conclusion, while making a profit is the fundamental aim of any business, I believe companies also have a clear responsibility to benefit society, and the most successful ones will be those that manage to achieve both.

answers.text:
The question of what businesses are ultimately for has become more pressing as corporations grow in size and influence. One school of thought maintains that the sole purpose of a business is to maximise returns for its owners; another holds that companies bear a broader responsibility to society. While I accept that profitability is indispensable, I would argue that a narrow focus on shareholder returns is neither ethically defensible nor, in the long run, commercially wise.

Advocates of the profit-centred view make a coherent case. Owners and shareholders provide the capital that allows a company to exist, and they do so on the understanding that it will be managed in their financial interest. A profitable enterprise also contributes to society as a matter of course, by employing people, paying taxes and supplying goods and services that meet genuine demand. On this view, asking companies to pursue social goals risks diluting their efficiency and allowing unelected executives to make decisions that properly belong to governments.

However, this argument overlooks the extent to which business activity affects people who have no say in it. Pollution, unsafe working conditions and misleading marketing all impose costs on communities, workers and consumers, often while the company itself profits. Given the power that large firms wield, it is reasonable to expect them to take responsibility for these consequences. Moreover, responsible conduct increasingly aligns with self-interest: firms with strong ethical reputations tend to attract loyal customers and talented staff, and are better protected against regulatory and reputational risks.

In my view, then, profit and social responsibility should be seen as complementary rather than competing aims. A business must be financially sound to survive, but its legitimacy ultimately depends on the trust of the society in which it operates, and that trust must be earned.

In conclusion, although generating profit is a fundamental objective, businesses have a duty to consider their wider impact, and those that embrace this duty are likely to prove more successful and sustainable over time.

Nowadays, many people suffer from health problems such as obesity and heart disease. Some people believe that everyone should take care of their own health, but others think the government should play an important role to encourage healthy lifestyle. In my opinion, both individuals and governments has responsibility, but the government role is very important.

On the one hand, it is true that people should be responsible for their own health. Adults can decide what they eat, how much they exercise and whether they smoke or not. Nobody can force another person to go to the gym or eat vegetables. If someone chooses an unhealthy lifestyle, it is their own decision and they should accept the results. Also, some people do not like when the government tells them how to live.

On the other hand, the government can help people a lot. Many people do not know enough about healthy food, so government can run campaigns on TV and in schools to educate them. In addition, the government can put higher taxes on cigarettes and sugary drinks, which make these products less attractive. It can also build parks and sports centres so people have more chance to do exercise. When people are healthier, the country spend less money on hospitals.

In my view, individuals must make the final choice, but government should make the healthy choice easier. For example, if fruit and vegetables are cheap and there are safe places for cycling, more people will live healthily.

To conclude, personal responsibility is important, but governments also need to play a major role. Working together, they can help people to live longer and more healthy lives.

Rising rates of lifestyle-related illnesses such as diabetes and heart disease have raised the question of who should be responsible for people's health. Some believe this is a matter of personal choice, while others argue that governments should take an active role in promoting healthy living. I believe that although individuals must take responsibility for their choices, governments have an important part to play in shaping those choices.

Those who emphasise individual responsibility argue that adults have the right to decide how they live. Eating habits, exercise and smoking are personal decisions, and many people resent being told what to do by the state. In addition, when people take ownership of their health, they are more likely to maintain positive habits over time than if they are simply following official advice. From this perspective, government campaigns can seem patronising and a waste of public money.

However, there are strong reasons for governments to intervene. Individual choices are heavily influenced by the environment people live in. Unhealthy food is often cheaper and more heavily advertised than healthier options, and many neighbourhoods lack safe spaces for walking or cycling. Governments can address these issues through measures such as taxes on sugary drinks, clear food labelling and investment in parks and sports facilities. Moreover, since poor health places enormous pressure on public healthcare systems, the state has a legitimate interest in prevention.

answers.text:
Few would dispute that good health depends heavily on everyday behaviour, yet there is considerable disagreement about who should take responsibility for it. Some maintain that health is essentially a personal matter, whereas others believe governments should actively encourage citizens to lead healthier lives. In my view, individual responsibility and state involvement are not mutually exclusive, and the latter is often necessary for the former to be meaningful.

The argument for personal responsibility rests on the principle of autonomy. Adults are entitled to make decisions about their own diet, activity levels and habits, even when those decisions carry risks, and government intervention in such matters can easily become paternalistic. There is also a practical point: lasting change in behaviour tends to come from personal motivation rather than external pressure, so public campaigns may achieve little if people are not genuinely committed to improving their health.

Nevertheless, this view underestimates how strongly circumstances shape behaviour. People on low incomes may find nutritious food less affordable and less accessible than processed alternatives, while those living in areas without parks or safe streets have fewer opportunities to exercise. Commercial pressures, such as the aggressive marketing of high-sugar products to children, further tilt the balance towards unhealthy choices. Governments are uniquely placed to counteract these influences through regulation, taxation, urban planning and education. Furthermore, because the cost of treating preventable illness is largely borne by taxpayers, the state has a clear interest in reducing it.

For these reasons, I believe governments should play a major role, not by dictating how people live, but by creating conditions in which healthy choices are realistic for everyone. Individuals would still be responsible for their decisions, but they would make them in an environment that supports rather than undermines their wellbeing.

In conclusion, while personal responsibility remains important, it cannot be exercised equally when circumstances differ so widely. Active government involvement is therefore essential to enabling people to lead healthier lives.

In democratic countries, important decisions are usually made by the government. However, some people think that the public should decide important national issues directly by voting in referendums, while others believe politicians and experts should make these decisions. I will discuss both side in this essay.

Some people support referendums because they are the most democratic way to decide. In a referendum, every citizen can vote, so the result shows what the majority of people really want. This can make people feel more involved in politics and trust the government more. Also, politicians sometimes do not keep their promises, so a referendum give ordinary people more power to control important decisions.

However, there are also problems with referendums. Many national issues are very complicated, for example economy or international agreements, and most people do not have enough knowledge to understand them. As a result, people may vote because of emotions or false information on social media. In contrast, experts have studied these topics for many years and politicians have advisers to help them, so they can make more better decisions. Moreover, organising a referendum is very expensive and take a long time.

In my opinion, most decisions should be made by elected politicians with the help of experts. This is why we vote for politicians, because we trust them to make difficult decisions for us. However, for some very important issues, such as changing the constitution, a referendum can be useful.

In conclusion, referendums are democratic but they have some risks. I believe that elected politicians and experts should make most national decisions, but people can vote directly for a few very important issues.

answers.text:
In most democracies, citizens elect representatives who then make decisions on their behalf. However, some people argue that major national issues should be decided directly by the public through referendums, while others maintain that such decisions are better left to politicians and experts. In my view, representative decision-making should remain the norm, with referendums used only in exceptional cases.

Supporters of referendums see them as the purest form of democracy. When citizens vote directly on an issue, the outcome clearly reflects the will of the majority, which gives the decision strong legitimacy. Referendums can also increase public engagement in politics, as people are encouraged to research and discuss the issues at stake. In addition, they offer a way to settle questions on which politicians are deeply divided or seem out of touch with voters.

On the other hand, there are significant drawbacks. Many national decisions, such as trade agreements or economic reforms, are highly complex and involve consequences that are difficult to predict. Most voters do not have the time or expertise to study these in detail, so campaigns are often dominated by simplified slogans or even misinformation. Furthermore, a referendum reduces a complicated issue to a simple yes-or-no choice, which leaves little room for compromise. Elected politicians, by contrast, can consult experts, negotiate and adjust policies over time, and they can be removed at the next election if the public are dissatisfied.

In my opinion, the advantages of representative democracy outweighs those of direct voting for most decisions. Referendums may be appropriate for fundamental constitutional questions, but even then the public should be given clear, balanced information before they vote.

In conclusion, although referendums give citizens a direct voice, I believe important national decisions are generally better made by elected politicians guided by expert advice, as they are better placed to deal with complexity and to be held accountable.

answers.text:
The question of how far ordinary citizens should be directly involved in national decision-making goes to the heart of what democracy means. Some believe that major issues should be settled by referendum, giving the public the final word, whereas others argue that such matters are better entrusted to elected representatives and specialists. While referendums have a place in a healthy democracy, I believe they are poorly suited to most important decisions.

The appeal of direct democracy is easy to understand. A referendum allows every voter to express a view on a specific question, producing a result that carries considerable moral authority. It can also re-engage citizens who feel alienated from mainstream politics, and it provides a means of resolving contentious issues that parliaments have been unable or unwilling to settle. From this perspective, entrusting decisions to politicians risks allowing a narrow political class to disregard public opinion.

However, the practical limitations of referendums are considerable. Many national questions involve intricate trade-offs, uncertain long-term consequences and technical detail that few voters have the time or background to evaluate thoroughly. In such circumstances, campaigns tend to reward emotive messaging over careful analysis, and misleading claims can prove decisive. Moreover, the binary format of a referendum forces a nuanced issue into a simple choice, leaving no scope for amendment or compromise, and the result can be extremely difficult to reverse. Representative institutions, by contrast, allow policies to be scrutinised, refined and revisited, while voters retain the power to remove politicians who fail them.

On balance, I believe that elected representatives, informed by expert advice, should make most important national decisions. Referendums can be justified for questions of fundamental constitutional significance, provided that voters have access to impartial information, but they should remain the exception rather than the rule.

In conclusion, although referendums offer a direct expression of the popular will, representative democracy is generally better equipped to handle complex decisions responsibly and accountably.

Deciding on a career is a major step for any young person, and families often disagree about how much influence parents should have. While some argue that parents should steer their children towards a specific profession, others believe young people must be free to follow their own path. In my view, parents should offer guidance, but the final choice should rest with their children.

There are understandable reasons why parents want to direct their children's careers. Having experienced the world of work themselves, they often have a realistic understanding of which professions offer financial stability and long-term prospects. Teenagers, by contrast, may base their decisions on limited information or on idealised images of certain jobs. Parents who have invested heavily in their children's education may also feel they have a right to ensure that this investment leads to a secure future.

However, pushing a young person into a career they have not chosen can have serious consequences. People tend to perform best in work that matches their interests and abilities, and someone who studies engineering to please their parents may lack the motivation needed to succeed. They may even abandon the career later, having wasted years of training. Furthermore, the job market is changing rapidly, and the professions that parents regard as safe may not offer the same security in the future, while new fields are emerging that parents might know little about.

I believe the most constructive role for parents is that of an adviser rather than decision-maker. They can help their children explore options, arrange work experience and discuss the realities of different jobs, while respecting that it is the young person who will live with the consequences.

In conclusion, although parental guidance can prevent unrealistic choices, I believe young people should ultimately be free to choose their own careers, since genuine interest is the strongest basis for long-term success and satisfaction.

answers.text:
The extent to which parents should influence their children's choice of career is a question on which cultures and families differ considerably. Some believe that parents, with their greater experience, should direct their children towards a particular profession, while others hold that young people must be free to make this decision for themselves. My own view is that parental guidance is valuable, but only when it informs rather than overrides a young person's choice.

The argument for parental direction is not without merit. Parents generally have a clearer picture than teenagers of the practical realities of working life, including the stability, income and progression that different fields offer. Young people, meanwhile, may be drawn to glamorous but precarious occupations, or may simply lack the information to make a well-founded decision. Parents who have made sacrifices to fund their children's education can therefore feel both entitled and obliged to ensure that it leads somewhere secure.

Nevertheless, the costs of directing a child into an unwanted career can be considerable. Motivation is a powerful determinant of success, and a person who has chosen their field is far more likely to persevere through the demanding early years of a career than one who is fulfilling someone else's ambitions. Moreover, parents' knowledge of the job market is often rooted in the past; occupations that once seemed secure may be vulnerable to automation, while entirely new fields are opening up. A choice imposed on the basis of outdated assumptions may prove neither fulfilling nor safe.

Weighing these considerations, I believe parents should act as well-informed advisers. By encouraging their children to explore different options, seek work experience and think realistically about their strengths, they can help them make a sound decision without taking it out of their hands.

In conclusion, while parental experience can be a valuable resource, young people should ultimately be free to choose their own careers, since a career that is genuinely chosen is more likely to be both successful and satisfying.

Crime is a serious problem in every society, and prisons are one way to deal with it. Some people believe prisons should mainly punish criminals, while others think they should help prisoners to become good citizens again. In this essay I will discuss both views.

People who support punishment believe that criminals must pay for what they did. If someone hurts another person or steal their property, it is fair that they lose their freedom. Also, hard punishment can stop other people from committing crimes because they are afraid of going to prison. Victims and their families may also feel that justice is done when the criminal is punished strictly.

On the other hand, many people think that rehabilitation is more important. Most prisoners will return to society one day, so if they learn nothing in prison, they may commit crime again after they are released. If prisons give them education and job training, they can find a work and live normal life. For example, a prisoner who learn to be a mechanic or a cook has a better chance to get a job. This is also cheaper for government, because keeping people in prison costs a lot of money.

In my opinion, prisons should focus more on helping prisoners to change. Punishment is necessary, but it is not enough to solve the problem of crime. However, for very dangerous criminals, protecting the public should be the first priority.

In conclusion, although punishment is important, I believe that prisons should mainly help offenders return to society, because this reduce crime in the long term.

Societies differ in how they view the purpose of prison. Some people believe that its main function is to punish those who break the law, while others argue that prisons should concentrate on rehabilitating offenders so that they can return to society as law-abiding citizens. I believe that while punishment has its place, rehabilitation should be the primary goal.

Those who see punishment as the main purpose argue that justice requires offenders to suffer consequences in proportion to the harm they have caused. Victims often feel that a harsh sentence acknowledges their suffering, and the public expects serious crimes to be treated seriously. In addition, supporters of this view claim that the threat of an unpleasant prison experience deters potential criminals. If prisons are seen as too comfortable, they argue, this deterrent effect may be lost.

On the other hand, advocates of rehabilitation point out that the vast majority of prisoners are eventually released. If they leave prison with no qualifications, no job prospects and the same attitudes that led them to crime, there is a high risk that they will reoffend. Education, vocational training and counselling can give former prisoners the skills and confidence to build a new life, which ultimately protects the public more effectively than punishment alone. There is also a financial argument, as reducing reoffending lowers the enormous cost of repeatedly imprisoning the same people.

In my view, the loss of freedom is itself a significant punishment, and time in prison should be used constructively. Although some dangerous offenders must be kept away from society for long periods, even they should be given opportunity to change.

In conclusion, while punishment is a necessary element of any justice system, I believe prisons should focus mainly on rehabilitation, since this is the most effective way to reduce crime and make communities safer.

How a society treats those it imprisons reveals a great deal about its values. One view holds that the principal purpose of prison is to punish offenders for their crimes; another maintains that prisons should prioritise preparing inmates to return to society as law-abiding citizens. Although punishment is an unavoidable element of imprisonment, I would argue that rehabilitation should be its central aim.

The case for punishment rests on principles of justice and deterrence. Many people feel that those who inflict harm on others deserve consequences proportionate to their actions, and that a sentence perceived as lenient fails to respect victims. It is also argued that the prospect of a harsh prison regime discourages potential offenders, and that prioritising prisoners' welfare sends the wrong message about the seriousness of crime.

However, this approach has significant limitations. Since the great majority of prisoners are eventually released, the question is not whether they will rejoin society but in what condition. An offender who leaves prison without skills or support, and with stronger links to criminal networks, is highly likely to reoffend, creating new victims and returning to custody at great public expense. Rehabilitation programmes, by contrast, address the underlying causes of offending, whether a lack of education, unemployment or addiction, and thereby offer more lasting protection for the public. Moreover, the deterrent value of harsh conditions is questionable, as many crimes are committed impulsively or by people who do not expect to be caught.

For these reasons, I believe that the deprivation of liberty should be regarded as the punishment itself, and that time spent in prison should be used to reduce the likelihood of future offending. This does not mean ignoring the need to protect the public from genuinely dangerous individuals, but even in such cases the goal of reform should not be abandoned.

In conclusion, while punishment has a legitimate role, prisons best serve society when they focus on rehabilitation, as this ultimately leads to fewer crimes and fewer victims.

Today, celebrities such as singers, actors and sports players are very popular, especially among young people. Some people think famous people must be role models, while others believe they should be free to live how they want. I will discuss both views and give my own opinion.

On one hand, many people believe that celebrities have a responsibility to behave well. Young people follow them on social media every day and often copy their clothes, their language and their behaviour. If a famous footballer takes drugs or a singer drink too much alcohol, teenagers may think that it is cool to do the same. Also, celebrities earn a lot of money because of their fans, so they should give something back by being a good example.

On the other hand, some people argue that celebrities are normal human who make mistakes like everyone else. They did not choose to be role models, they only wanted to be a good actor or athlete. It is not fair that their private life is always in the newspapers. Furthermore, parents and teachers should be the main role models for children, not people on the television.

In my opinion, celebrities should try to behave responsibly in public, because they have big influence on young people. However, they also deserve some privacy in their personal life. The media should not report every small mistake they make.

In conclusion, both views have some points. I believe that famous people have some responsibility to be a good role model, but they should also have freedom in their private life, and parents should teach children not to copy celebrities blindly.

In an age of social media, celebrities have more influence over young people than ever before. Some believe that this influence brings a responsibility to act as a positive role model, while others argue that famous people should be free to live as they choose. In my opinion, celebrities do have some responsibility, but it should be limited to their public behaviour.

Those who expect celebrities to set a good example point to the powerful effect they have on young fans. Teenagers frequently imitate the appearance, attitudes and lifestyles of the stars they admire, and a famous person who glamorises reckless behaviour, such as dangerous driving or excessive drinking, may encourage others to copy them. Moreover, celebrities benefit enormously from public attention, earning fame and wealth through the support of their fans. It therefore seems reasonable that they should accept certain obligations in return.

On the other hand, many argue that it is unfair to impose such expectations. Most celebrities became famous because of a particular talent, such as acting, singing or playing sport, not because they wanted to guide young people's moral development. They are ordinary human beings who inevitably make mistakes, and constant media scrutiny of their private lives can cause them considerable stress. Critics of the role-model idea also suggest that responsibility for young people's values lie primarily with parents, teachers and communities.

I believe a balanced position is most appropriate. Celebrities should be aware of their influence and avoid promoting harmful behaviour in their public statements, performances and social media posts. However, their private lives should be respected, and it is unrealistic to expect them to be perfect.

In conclusion, although celebrities should not be forced to act as moral guides in every aspect of their lives, I believe they have a responsibility to use their public platform in a way that does not harm the young people who admire them.

The influence of celebrities on young people has grown enormously with the rise of social media, prompting debate about what, if anything, famous people owe their audiences. Some argue that celebrity brings with it a duty to act as a role model, whereas others contend that public figures are entitled to live as they please. In my view, celebrities have a genuine but limited responsibility, one that applies to their public conduct rather than to every aspect of their lives.

Those who believe celebrities should be role models emphasise the scale of their influence. Young people often identify closely with the stars they follow, adopting their styles, opinions and habits, and when a well-known figure normalises behaviour such as heavy drinking or casual cruelty online, the effects can ripple through a large and impressionable audience. Furthermore, celebrities derive their wealth and status from public admiration, so it seems fair to expect them to recognise the obligations that accompany such privilege.

On the other hand, there are strong grounds for resisting this expectation. Fame is frequently a by-product of talent in a particular field, and a gifted athlete or musician has not necessarily chosen, or trained, to serve as a moral example. Demanding flawless conduct from them is not only unrealistic but can also justify intrusive media coverage of their private lives. Moreover, placing the burden of guiding young people on celebrities risks diverting attention from those who should bear it primarily, namely parents, educators and communities.

Balancing these arguments, I believe celebrities should be expected to exercise care in how they use their public platforms, avoiding the promotion of harmful behaviour, while their private lives should largely remain their own. At the same time, young people should be taught to admire achievement without uncritically imitating the individuals behind it.

In conclusion, although celebrities cannot reasonably be required to be perfect, their considerable influence carries a responsibility to act with care in public, even as they retain the right to a private life.

Nowadays, many people move to live and work in another country. Some people think that immigrants should follow the customs and lifestyle of their new country, while others believe they should keep their own traditions. This essay will discuss both sides before giving my opinion.

On the one hand, there are reasons why immigrants should adapt to the new culture. If they learn the local language and customs, it is more easy for them to find a job and make friends with local people. It also help them to feel part of the community. In addition, local people may be more welcoming if newcomers respect the rules and traditions of the country. If immigrants live in separate groups and do not mix with others, it can cause misunderstanding and conflicts.

On the other hand, many people believe immigrants should keep their own culture. Traditions such as language, food, festivals and religion are part of a person's identity, and it is very difficult to forget them. Also, children of immigrants can learn two cultures and two languages, which is a big advantage for them. Moreover, when different cultures live together, the society become more interesting and diverse. For example, in many big cities people can enjoy food and music from all over the world.

In my opinion, immigrants should do both. They should respect the laws and learn the language of the new country, but they can also keep their traditions at home and in their community. I think this is the best way for everyone to live together peacefully.

In conclusion, adapting to a new culture and keeping traditions are both important. I believe immigrants should find a balance between them.

International migration has made many societies multicultural, raising questions about how newcomers should relate to the culture of their adopted country. Some believe immigrants should embrace local customs, while others think they should preserve their own traditions. In my view, the most successful approach involves a combination of both.

Those who argue for adopting local customs emphasise the importance of integration. Immigrants who learn the language and understand social norms are likely to find employment more easily, build relationships with their neighbours and participate fully in public life. In contrast, communities that remain isolated may face misunderstanding and even hostility from the wider population. From this perspective, adapting to the new way of life is not only practical but also a sign of respect towards the host society.

On the other hand, many people believe that expecting immigrants to abandon their heritage is both unfair and unrealistic. Cultural traditions, including language, religion, cuisine and family customs, are a central part of personal identity, and giving them up can lead to a painful sense of loss. Moreover, the diversity that immigrants bring can enrich the host country, introducing new ideas, foods and festivals. Many of the world's most dynamic cities owe much of their character to generations of migrants who kept their traditions alive.

I believe integration does not require assimilation. Newcomers should respect the laws and core values of their new home and make a real effort to learn the language, as these are essential for living together harmoniously. However, they should also feel free to maintain the traditions that are meaningful to them, and host society should see this diversity as a strength instead of a threat.

In conclusion, although adapting to the local way of life is important for immigrants' success, I believe they should not have to give up their own cultural traditions, and a balance between the two benefits everyone.

answers.text:
As migration reshapes societies around the world, the question of how newcomers should relate to the culture of their adopted country has become increasingly prominent. Some maintain that immigrants ought to adopt the customs and way of life of their new home, while others believe they should retain their own cultural traditions. In my view, this is a false choice: successful integration involves adapting in some respects while preserving one's heritage in others.

The argument for adopting local customs centres on social cohesion and personal opportunity. Newcomers who master the language and understand prevailing norms are far better placed to secure employment, access public services and form friendships beyond their own community. Where migrant groups remain largely separate, mutual suspicion can develop on both sides, fuelling prejudice and limiting social mobility. Adapting to the host culture can therefore be seen as both a practical necessity and a gesture of goodwill.

Those who favour preserving cultural traditions, however, raise equally important points. A person's language, faith, cuisine and customs are deeply bound up with their sense of self, and pressure to abandon them can be alienating, particularly for older migrants. Moreover, cultural diversity is a source of vitality for host societies, enriching their food, arts and ideas; many of the world's most vibrant cities are defined precisely by the traditions that successive waves of migrants have brought with them.

For these reasons, I believe a distinction should be drawn between shared civic foundations and private cultural life. Immigrants should respect the law, embrace fundamental values such as equality, and make a genuine effort to learn the local language, since these form the basis of a common public life. Beyond this, they should be free to maintain the traditions that give their lives meaning, and host societies should welcome rather than merely tolerate them.

In conclusion, rather than choosing between assimilation and separation, immigrants and their new communities benefit most from a balance in which shared civic values coexist with a diversity of cultural traditions.

Since the pandemic, many companies allow their staff to work from home. Some people think this is better for employees, but others believe working in an office with colleagues is more effective. This essay will discuss both views and give my opinion.

There are many advantages of working from home. Firstly, employees do not need to travel to work every day, so they save time and money. For example, a person who spend two hours in traffic every day can use this time to sleep more or spend with his family. Secondly, people can organise their own schedule and work in a quiet place without interruption from colleagues. Many workers also say they feel less stress at home.

However, working in an office also has important benefits. When people work together in the same place, it is easier to communicate and solve problems quickly. New employees can learn from experienced colleagues by watching them and asking questions. In addition, some people feel lonely when they work at home alone for a long time, and they miss the chance to make friend at work. It can be also difficult to separate work and private life, because the office is in the living room.

In my opinion, the best solution is to mix both ways. Employees can work from home two or three days a week and go to the office on other days for meetings and teamwork. This give workers flexibility and also keep good communication in the company.

In conclusion, working from home and working in an office both have advantages. I believe that a combination of the two is the most effective way for employees and companies.

answers.text:
Remote working has become far more common in recent years, and opinions differ on whether it is a positive development. Some people believe working from home benefits employees, while others argue that an office environment is more productive. In my view, both arrangements have clear strengths, and a flexible combination is the most effective option.

Supporters of home working highlight the improvement it brings to employees' quality of life. Without a daily commute, workers save considerable time and money, which they can spend on rest, exercise or family commitments. Many people also find they can concentrate better at home, away from the noise and constant interruptions of an open-plan office. Furthermore, remote work allows people to live further from expensive city centres, and it makes employment more accessible for parents and those with disabilities.

On the other hand, there are important advantages to working alongside colleagues. Face-to-face contact makes communication quicker and more natural, and informal conversations often lead to new ideas that would never come up in scheduled video calls. Office working is particularly valuable for younger employees, who learn a great deal simply by observing more experienced staff. In addition, some people struggle with isolation at home and find it difficult to switch off when their workplace is also their living space.

In my opinion, the question is not which option is better, but how to combine them effectively. A hybrid model, in which employees spend part of the week at home for focused tasks and come into the office for collaboration and training, offers most of the benefits of each approach while reducing their drawbacks.

In conclusion, although working from home offers greater freedom and comfort, the office remains important for teamwork and learning, and I believe a hybrid arrangement serve both employees and employers best.

answers.text:
The widespread adoption of remote working has prompted a reassessment of where work is best done. Some believe that working from home is clearly preferable for employees, while others maintain that an office shared with colleagues is more effective. In my view, each setting suits different kinds of work, and the most productive arrangement is one that combines them deliberately.

The case for home working rests largely on autonomy and wellbeing. Eliminating the commute gives employees back hours each week and reduces both travel costs and stress. Many find that a quiet home environment enables sustained concentration that is difficult to achieve amid the distractions of a busy office. Remote work also widens access to employment, allowing people with caring responsibilities, health conditions or homes far from urban centres to participate more fully in the workforce.

Nevertheless, the office offers benefits that are not easily replicated online. Collaboration is often more fluid in person, where questions can be resolved in moments and chance conversations can spark ideas that would never surface in a scheduled video call. For those early in their careers, proximity to experienced colleagues is an invaluable, if informal, form of training. There is also a social dimension: prolonged remote working can leave people isolated, and the blurring of boundaries between home and work can make it hard to switch off.

Framing the issue as a choice between the two is therefore unhelpful. Tasks requiring deep concentration are often best carried out at home, whereas teamwork, mentoring and relationship-building benefit from shared physical space. Organisations should adopt hybrid arrangements designed around the nature of the work rather than habit, giving employees flexibility while preserving the collaborative culture that offices foster.

In conclusion, while working from home offers clear advantages for employees' comfort and focus, the office remains essential for collaboration and learning. A thoughtfully designed combination of the two is likely to serve both employees and organisations best.

Collaboration is often more fluid in person, where questions can be resolved in moments and chance conversations can spark ideas that would never surface in a scheduled video call. For those early in their careers, proximity to experienced colleagues is an invaluable, if informal, form of training. There is also a social dimension: prolonged remote working can leave people isolated, and the blurring of boundaries between home and work can make it hard to switch off.

Framing the issue as a choice between the two is therefore unhelpful. Tasks requiring deep concentration are often best carried out at home, whereas teamwork, mentoring and relationship-building benefit from shared physical space. Organisations should adopt hybrid arrangements designed around the nature of the work rather than habit, giving employees flexibility while preserving the collaborative culture that offices foster.
In conclusion,

while working from home offers clear advantages for employees' comfort and focus, the office remains essential for collaboration and learning. A thoughtfully designed combination of the two is likely to serve both employees and organisations best.

In many countries, the number of old people is increasing and there are fewer young workers. To pay for the pensions and health care of older people, some people think the government should raise the retirement age, while others believe young workers should pay more taxes. This essay will discuss both views.

On the one hand, raising the retirement age has some benefits. Today people live longer and are healthier than in the past, so many of them can continue working until 67 or 70. If they work longer, they continue to pay taxes and the government pay pensions for a shorter time. Also, older workers have a lot of experience and knowledge which is useful for companies.

On the other hand, some people think that younger people should pay higher taxes. Not all old people are able to work longer, especially people who have physical jobs like builders or farmers. It is unfair to make them to work until they are very old. Moreover, older people have worked hard for many years and paid taxes, so they deserve to rest. If young workers pay a little more tax, the government can take care of the elderly properly.

In my opinion, raising the retirement age is a better solution, but it should be flexible. Young people already have many financial problems, such as expensive housing and student loan, so higher taxes would make their life more harder. However, people with difficult physical jobs should be allowed to retire earlier.

In conclusion, both ideas have advantages and disadvantages. I believe that increasing the retirement age is more fairer for society, but the government must think about workers in different situations.

As life expectancy rises and birth rates fall, many countries face the challenge of supporting a growing number of retired people. Some argue that the best solution is to raise the retirement age, while others believe younger workers should pay higher taxes instead. In my opinion, gradually raising the retirement age is the fairer and more sustainable option, provided that exceptions are made for certain groups.

Supporters of higher taxes on younger workers argue that older people have earned the right to retire. Many have spent decades contributing to the economy and paying into the pension system, and they planned their lives around a particular retirement age. Moreover, not everyone is able to work into their late sixties. Those in physically demanding occupations, such as construction or nursing, may suffer from health problems that make continued employment unrealistic. For these people, a later retirement age could cause real hardship.

On the other hand, there are strong arguments for asking people to work longer. Retirement ages in many countries were set when people typically lived only a few years after leaving work, whereas today many enjoy retirements lasting two decades or more. Keeping experienced people in the workforce for longer increases tax revenue and reduces pension costs at the same time. In contrast, placing the entire burden on younger workers, who often already struggle with high housing costs and student debt, risk creating resentment between generations.

In my view, a gradual increase in the retirement age is the more balanced approach. However, it should be accompanied by flexible options, such as part-time work for older employees and earlier retirement for those whose jobs have damaged their health.

In conclusion, while higher taxes on younger people would protect current retirement plans, I believe raising the retirement age shares the cost of an ageing population more fairly across generations.

answers.text:
Demographic change is placing growing pressure on pension and healthcare systems, as the proportion of older people rises relative to those of working age. Some believe the most effective response is to raise the retirement age, whereas others argue that younger workers should instead pay higher taxes. In my view, a gradual rise in the retirement age is the more equitable solution, although it must be implemented with sensitivity to differences between occupations.

The argument for increasing taxes on the working population rests on fairness to those approaching retirement. Many older people have contributed to the system throughout their working lives in the reasonable expectation of retiring at a particular age, and changing the rules late in their careers can seem like a breach of trust. Moreover, the capacity to keep working is unevenly distributed: an office worker may comfortably remain employed until seventy, but someone who has spent decades in manual labour may simply be physically unable to do so.

Nevertheless, relying on higher taxes carries significant drawbacks. Younger generations in many countries already face high housing costs and considerable educational debt, and increasing their tax burden further could reduce their disposable income, discourage them from starting families and deepen intergenerational resentment. Furthermore, retirement ages were often fixed when life expectancy was considerably lower; linking them to current longevity simply restores the original balance between working life and retirement. Keeping healthy, experienced people in employment for longer also benefits the economy by retaining valuable skills.

On balance, I believe that raising the retirement age gradually, with plenty of notice, distributes the cost more fairly. Crucially, such a policy should include provisions for earlier retirement in physically demanding jobs and encourage flexible arrangements such as phased or part-time retirement.

In conclusion, although asking younger workers to pay more would spare older people from working longer, a carefully managed increase in the retirement age offers a fairer and more sustainable means of supporting an ageing population.
