Social media is used by billions of people every day, and some of the content on it is harmful, such as fake news or hate speech. Some people think social media companies should be responsible for this content, while others believe the users who post it should be responsible. I will discuss both views in this essay.

On the one hand, there are reasons to blame social media companies. These companies earn a huge amount of money from advertisements, and they design their platforms to keep people online as long as possible. Sometimes shocking or false posts get more attention, so the companies do not have strong reason to remove them. Also, they have the technology and money to check content and delete harmful posts quickly. If they are responsible by law, they will work harder to protect users, especially children.

On the other hand, many people think the users should be responsible. The person who write a post decides what to say, so it is their fault if the post is harmful or untrue. Every day millions of posts are uploaded, and it is impossible for companies to check all of them. In addition, if companies have to delete many posts, they may also delete normal opinions, and this can reduce the freedom of speech.

In my opinion, both the companies and the users should have responsibility. Users must think carefully before they post something and they should be punished if they break the law. However, companies must also remove dangerous content fastly when people report it.

In conclusion, there are good arguments on both sides. I believe that the responsibility should be shared between social media companies and the users, because both of them can make internet safer.

The spread of harmful material online, from false information to abusive messages, has raised the question of who should be held accountable. Some argue that social media companies should be responsible for everything that appears on their platforms, while others believe the responsibility lies with the individuals who post it. In my view, both share responsibility, but companies should be held to a higher standard than they currently are.

Those who blame individual users make a straightforward argument. The person who writes a post chooses its content, so they should face the consequences if it is defamatory, threatening or illegal. It is also argued that the sheer volume of material uploaded every minute makes it impossible for any company to review everything. Furthermore, if platforms were legally liable for all content, they might remove anything controversial to protect themselves, which could seriously limit freedom of expression.

However, there are strong reasons to place significant responsibility on the companies themselves. Social media platforms are not neutral spaces; their algorithms decide which posts are promoted, and content that provokes strong emotions is often spread most widely because it generates more engagement and advertising revenue. In addition, these firms are extremely wealthy and have the technical ability to detect and remove harmful material far more effectively than they do at present. Many users also post anonymously, so holding individuals accountable are often difficult in practice.

I believe the responsibility should be shared. Users who break the law online should face the same penalties as they would offline, but companies should be required to act quickly when harmful content is reported and to be transparent about how their algorithms work.

In conclusion, while individual users remain responsible for what they post, social media companies profit from and amplify this content, and therefore they should also be held accountable for it.

answers.text:
As social media has become a primary source of news and communication for many people, concern about harmful content, including misinformation, harassment and extremist material, has intensified. Some argue that the companies operating these platforms should be held responsible for what appears on them, while others insist that accountability lies with the individuals who post it. In my view, responsibility must be shared, but the role of the platforms has been significantly underestimated.

The case for holding users responsible rests on a basic principle of personal accountability. Each post is written by an individual who chooses its content, and it would seem perverse to excuse someone who spreads defamatory or threatening material simply because they did so online. There are also practical objections to placing the burden on companies. The volume of content uploaded every day is so vast that comprehensive monitoring is impossible, and platforms facing legal liability might respond by removing anything remotely contentious, with damaging consequences for free expression.

However, this view overlooks the active role that platforms play. They are not passive noticeboards: their recommendation systems determine what users see, and because provocative content tends to generate engagement, it is often amplified far beyond its original audience. Since these companies profit directly from this engagement, it is difficult to argue that they bear no responsibility for its effects. They also possess resources and technical expertise that no individual user could match, and anonymity frequently makes it impossible to identify the original author at all.

For these reasons, I believe a system of shared accountability is most appropriate. Individuals should face legal consequences for unlawful content, just as they would offline, while platforms should be obliged to respond promptly to reported material, limit the promotion of harmful posts and be transparent about how their algorithms operate.

In conclusion, although users are responsible for the content they create, social media companies shape and profit from its distribution, and they should therefore be held accountable for the part they play.

People today have many choices about how to spend their money. Some people believe it is better to spend money on experiences like travelling and concerts, while others think buying things that last for a long time is wiser. In this essay I will discuss both views and give my opinion.

On the one hand, spending money on experiences has many advantages. When people travel to other countries, they can learn about different cultures, try new food and meet new people. These memories stays with them for their whole life. For example, most of people still remember a family holiday from their childhood, but they have forgotten the toys they had. Also, sharing experiences with friends and family can make the relationship stronger.

On the other hand, buying possessions also has benefits. Things like a house, a car or good furniture can be used for many years and make daily life more comfortable. Some possessions, such as property or gold, can even increase in value, so they are a kind of investment for the future. In contrast, a holiday finishes after one or two weeks and the money is gone. For people who do not have much money, it is more sensible to buy useful things than spending on expensive trips.

In my opinion, experiences are more valuable than possessions, as long as people do not waste money they need for basic things. After buying the necessary items, people should spend their extra money for experiences which make them happy and help them learn.

In conclusion, both experiences and possessions have advantages. I believe experiences give more happiness in the long term, but people should first make sure they have what they need in their daily life.

How people choose to spend their disposable income reflects their priorities in life. Some believe that experiences such as travel, concerts and meals out offer the best value, while others argue that it is more sensible to invest in lasting possessions. In my view, experiences generally bring greater long-term satisfaction, although certain durable goods are clearly worthwhile.

Those who favour possessions emphasise their practical and financial value. Items such as a reliable car, quality furniture or a home can be used every day for many years, improving comfort and convenience long after the purchase. Some possessions, particularly property, may even increase in value and provide financial security in the future. By comparison, the money spent on a weekend away or an expensive concert is gone within days, leaving nothing tangible behind.

On the other hand, supporters of experiences argue that their benefits last longer than they first appear. Memories of travelling to a new country, learning a skill or celebrating with friends can bring pleasure for decades, and they often become part of a person's identity. Material goods, by contrast, tend to lose their appeal quickly as people become used to them or replace them with newer model. Experiences are also frequently shared, which strengthens relationships, whereas possessions can encourage comparison and competition with others.

In my opinion, the wisest approach is to buy durable items that genuinely improve daily life, and then to prioritise experiences with any remaining money. Spending on unnecessary luxury goods, which quickly become old-fashioned, is less rewarding than investing in activities that broaden one's horizons.

In conclusion, while lasting possessions provide comfort and security, I believe experiences such as travel and entertainment usually offer more lasting happiness, and they deserve a significant share of people's spending.

This avoids accumulating possessions that bring little lasting joy, while still providing the stability that essential goods offer.

In conclusion, although possessions that last can deliver comfort and security, experiences tend to provide richer and longer-lasting fulfilment, and they therefore represent the wiser use of money beyond life's necessities.

Nowadays, many young people decide to take a year off after they finish school and before they start university. In my opinion, the advantages of this gap year are more than the disadvantages, although there are some problems too.

On the one hand, a gap year have several benefits. Firstly, students can work and save money for their studies. University is very expensive in many countries, so if a student work for one year, he can pay some of his fees and he will not need to borrow so much money. Secondly, a year off give them time to think about what they really want to study. Many students choose a subject quickly and later they regret about it. Also, travelling to other countries can make young people more independent and confident.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. The main problem is that some students lose their motivation to study. After one year of working or travelling, it can be difficult to go back to books and exams, and some of them never go to university at all. In addition, travelling abroad is costly, so only students from rich family can enjoy this kind of gap year. Another problem is that they will finish their degree one year later than their friends.

In conclusion, I believe that taking a year off between school and university is more positive than negative. Although some students may lose interest in studying, most of them can gain money, experience and a clearer idea about their future. Therefore, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages if the student plan the year carefully.

It has become increasingly common for school leavers to spend a year working, volunteering or travelling before they begin a university degree. While this break can create certain risks, I would argue that its benefits are considerably greater, provided that the year is used purposefully.

Admittedly, a year out of education has some clear drawbacks. Some students find it hard to return to academic study after a long break, since the habits of revision and concentration they built at school may fade. Others treat the year simply as an extended holiday, which achieves little beyond delaying their education and their entry into work. There is also a financial aspect: travelling abroad can be expensive, and students from less wealthy families may not be able to afford the kind of gap year that is often promoted in the media.

Despite this, the advantages are more significant. The most important is that a gap year allows young people to make a more informed choice about their future. At eighteen, many students select a course simply because of their exam results or pressure from parents, and some later drop out when they realise the subject does not suit them. Spending time in the workplace or doing voluntary work gives them a clearer picture about their strengths and interests. Moreover, experiences such as living away from home or managing a budget help them develop the maturity and independence that university life demands. A student who works locally for part of the year, for instance, can save money and gain useful experience without losing contact with learning.

In conclusion, although a gap year may reduce motivation for some and is not equally accessible to everyone, the chance to mature and choose a degree more carefully outweighs these disadvantages. The key is that the year should have a clear purpose rather than being time simply spent waiting.

answers.text:
The practice of postponing university for a year, once associated mainly with affluent students travelling overseas, has become a mainstream option for school leavers. In my view, when the year is structured rather than aimless, the benefits it offers clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

Perhaps the strongest argument in favour of a gap year is that it leads to better-informed decisions about higher education. Students who move straight from school to university often commit to a three- or four-year course on the basis of limited self-knowledge, and a poor match between student and subject is a common reason for dropping out. A year spent in employment or volunteering exposes young people to the realities of working life, allowing them to test their interests before investing heavily in a degree. Equally valuable is the personal growth that comes from handling responsibilities outside the protective environment of school: someone who has held down a job, paid rent or organised their own travel is likely to arrive at university more self-reliant and more focused.

That said, the disadvantages should not be dismissed. A break of twelve months can erode study habits, and a minority of students never return to education at all, particularly if a job offers an immediate income that seems more attractive than further study. The year also postpones graduation and entry into a career, which carries a real cost in lost earnings. Furthermore, the more glamorous forms of gap year, such as extended travel abroad, remain out of reach for many families, which means the experience can reinforce existing inequalities.

On balance, however, most of these risks stem from poor planning rather than from the gap year itself. Where students set clear goals, combining paid work with volunteering or skills development, they tend to return to education with greater purpose.

Overall, therefore, I believe the advantages of a well-planned gap year outweigh its disadvantages, since the maturity and clarity it provides can shape the rest of a student's academic and professional life.

These days, a lot of universities are using online courses instead of the traditional classes in a classroom. This trend has both advantages and disadvantages, and I will discuss them in this essay.

The first advantage is that online courses are very flexible. Students can watch the lectures at any time and in any place, so they can study and work at the same time. This is very helpful for students who has a part-time job or a family to look after. Another advantage is the cost. Students do not need to pay for transport or rent a room near the university, so they can save a lot of money. Also, universities can teach more students because they do not need big lecture halls.

However, there are also some disadvantages of online learning. Firstly, students do not have much contact with their teachers and classmates. In a classroom, they can ask questions immediately and discuss about ideas with other students, but online it is more difficult. As a result, some students feel lonely and lose their motivation. Secondly, not every students have a good computer or a fast internet connection, especially in the countryside. This means that some students cannot follow the lessons properly. Finally, some subjects like medicine or engineering need practical work in a laboratory, and this is not possible on a screen.

In conclusion, online courses are flexible and cheap, and they help many people to study who could not go to university before. But they also reduce the communication between students and teachers and they are not suitable for all subject. I think universities should use a mix of both online and classroom teaching.

answers.text:
Across the world, a growing number of universities are moving their teaching from lecture theatres to digital platforms. This shift brings real benefits in terms of access and flexibility, but it also raises concerns about the quality of learning and the student experience.

One major advantage of online courses is that they make higher education available to people who would otherwise be excluded. Mature students with full-time jobs, parents with young children and those living far from a campus can all follow lectures at a time and place that suits them. In addition, recorded lessons allows learners to pause, replay and review difficult material at their own pace, which can be particularly helpful for those studying in a second language. From the institution's point of view, digital delivery reduces the need for expensive buildings, and these savings could be passed on to students through lower fees.

On the other hand, replacing classrooms entirely has significant drawbacks. Face-to-face teaching allows lecturers to notice when students are confused and adapt their explanations immediately, while online, many learners simply stop engaging without anyone realising. The social side of university is also lost: discussions with classmates, study groups and informal conversations with tutors all contribute to both learning and wellbeing, and these are hard to reproduce through a screen. Furthermore, practical subjects such as nursing, chemistry or architecture depend on hands-on work that cannot be done remotely.

A further problem is that online study demands a high level of self-discipline. Younger students who have just left school often struggle to organise their time without the structure of regular classes, and they may fall behind as a result.

In conclusion, online courses widen access and offer valuable flexibility, but they weaken interaction and are unsuitable for practical disciplines. For this reason, a blended approach is likely to serve most students better than a complete move away from the classroom.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The steady replacement of lecture halls with virtual classrooms is one of the most visible changes in higher education in recent years. Although this trend has made university study more accessible and adaptable, it also risks diluting some of the most valuable aspects of a traditional education.

The principal benefit of online provision is its capacity to widen participation. Because lectures can be accessed from anywhere, students in remote regions, those with disabilities that make travel difficult and adults balancing study with employment are no longer disadvantaged by geography or rigid timetables. Digital materials are also more flexible as learning tools: a recorded lecture can be revisited before an examination, subtitled or slowed down, giving learners greater control over how they absorb information. For universities, meanwhile, online delivery allows a single course to reach thousands of students without a corresponding increase in staff or facilities.

Yet these gains come at a cost. Learning at university is not merely the transfer of information; it is also shaped by debate, questioning and collaboration, which tend to flourish in shared physical spaces. In a live seminar, a tutor can challenge a weak argument or draw a quiet student into the discussion, whereas in an online forum such interaction is often delayed, superficial or absent altogether. Isolation is a related concern, as students who rarely meet their peers may feel less connected to their institution and more likely to abandon their studies. There are practical limitations too: laboratory work, clinical training and studio-based design cannot be meaningfully replicated at a distance.

Equally important is the issue of unequal access to technology. A course delivered entirely online assumes a reliable device and a stable internet connection, which not every student can take for granted.

In summary, online courses offer flexibility, reach and efficiency, but at the expense of interaction, community and practical training. The most effective universities are likely to be those that combine digital tools with meaningful face-to-face teaching rather than abandoning the classroom altogether.

Today in many countries, doctors are using artificial intelligence to find out what illness a patient have. I believe that this technology has more advantages than disadvantages, but we should be careful how we use it.

The main advantage is that AI can be very accurate. A computer program can look at thousands of X-rays and scans and it can learn to notice small problems which a human doctor might miss. For example, it can find early signs of cancer, and this can save many lifes. Another benefit is speed. Doctors in busy hospitals do not have enough time for every patient, but AI can check the results in a few seconds, so patients get their diagnosis more faster. This is also useful in poor areas where there is not many doctors.

However, there are some disadvantages. First, AI is not perfect and sometimes it makes mistakes. If the doctor trust the computer too much, the patient can get the wrong treatment. Second, patients' medical information is very private, and if it is stored in computer systems, it can be stolen by hackers. Moreover, many people prefer to talk with a real doctor, because a machine cannot understand their feelings or explain things in a kind way.

In conclusion, I think using artificial intelligence to help doctors is a good idea because it makes the diagnosis quicker and more accurate. The problems like mistakes and privacy are important, but they can be reduced if doctors always check the results of AI. So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages in my opinion.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being introduced into hospitals and clinics to support doctors in diagnosing disease. Although this development raises understandable concerns, I believe that its benefits are greater, as long as the final decision remains in human hands.

Admittedly, relying on AI in medicine involves several risks. No system is completely reliable, and an error in diagnosis could have serious consequences for a patient. There is also a danger that doctors become too dependent to software and gradually lose some of their own diagnostic skills. In addition, these systems need huge amounts of patient data to be trained, which creates concerns about privacy and about who controls such sensitive information. Finally, some patients may feel uneasy if they believe a machine rather than a person is responsible for their care.

Despite these issues, the advantages are more significant. AI tools are able to analyse medical images, such as scans and X-rays, extremely quickly and can often detect subtle patterns that even experienced specialists overlook. This means that serious conditions like cancer or heart disease may be identified at an earlier stage, when treatment is more likely to succeed. Furthermore, AI can reduce the heavy workload of doctors, allowing them to spend more time talking to patients and planning treatment. In regions where specialists are in short supply, a diagnostic tool on a computer or phone could provide an expert first opinion that would otherwise not be available at all.

Most of the disadvantages can also be managed. If AI is used as an assistant rather than a replacement, doctors can check its suggestions, and strict laws on data protection can reduce the risk to privacy.

In conclusion, while artificial intelligence in diagnosis brings risks of error, over-reliance and loss of privacy, its ability to detect illness faster and more accurately makes it a valuable tool. On balance, therefore, the advantages clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

answers.text:
The use of artificial intelligence to assist in diagnosing illness has moved rapidly from experimental research to everyday clinical practice in many countries. While the technology is not without its hazards, I am convinced that, used responsibly, it offers benefits that far outweigh its drawbacks.

The most compelling case for diagnostic AI lies in its accuracy and consistency. Algorithms trained on vast collections of medical images can identify minute abnormalities in scans that might escape a tired or inexperienced clinician, and unlike humans, they do not become less attentive at the end of a long shift. Earlier detection of conditions such as tumours can transform a patient's prognosis, turning a potentially fatal illness into a treatable one. AI also addresses a practical problem faced by health systems almost everywhere: a shortage of specialists. By screening routine cases, it frees doctors to concentrate on complex diagnoses and on the human side of medicine, and it can extend a degree of specialist expertise to rural clinics that have no radiologist on site.

The concerns, nevertheless, are real. Diagnostic systems are only as good as the data used to build them, so a tool developed mainly with records from one population may perform poorly for others, potentially widening existing inequalities in care. There is also the question of accountability: when an algorithm contributes to a misdiagnosis, it is unclear whether responsibility lies with the doctor, the hospital or the software developer. Moreover, the large-scale collection of health records required to train these systems inevitably raises questions of confidentiality.

Crucially, though, none of these problems is inherent to the technology. They can be mitigated through rigorous testing on diverse patient groups, clear legal frameworks and the principle that AI supports, rather than replaces, clinical judgement.

In conclusion, the risks associated with AI in diagnosis demand careful regulation, but they are outweighed by its potential to detect disease earlier, ease pressure on doctors and bring expert assessment to those who currently lack it.

In many cities today, more people are living in tall apartment buildings. There are some good points and bad points about this type of housing, but I think the advantages are bigger than the disadvantages.

The first reason is that high-rise buildings use land very efficient. Cities have a lot of people but not much space, so building upwards means that many families can live on a small piece of land. This can help to reduce the housing problem and keep the price of flats lower. Also, people who live in these buildings are usually close to the city centre, so they can go to work, school and shops easily and they do not need to drive a long distance every day. Many modern apartment blocks also have facilities like a gym, a swimming pool and security guards, which makes life more comfortable.

On the other hand, living in a high-rise building have some problems. For example, there is often no garden or green space, so children do not have a safe place to play outside. In addition, people in big buildings often do not know their neighbours, and some of them feel lonely and isolated. Another problem is safety. If there is a fire or the lift stop working, it can be very dangerous and difficult for old people to get out.

In conclusion, although high-rise apartments have some disadvantages such as the lack of green space and loneliness, I believe they are necessary for modern cities because they save land and are convenient. So in my opinion, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, especially if the government make sure the buildings are safe.

As urban populations continue to grow, high-rise apartment blocks have become the most common form of housing in many cities. Although this way of living has certain drawbacks, I believe the advantages are greater overall.

The main benefit of tall residential buildings is that they make efficient use of limited land. By housing hundreds of families on a single plot, they reduce the pressure to build on surrounding countryside and help to keep housing more affordable than it would otherwise be. Moreover, because high-rise blocks are usually located in central districts, residents can live close to their workplaces, schools and public transport. This not only saves time on commuting but also reduces the number of cars on the roads, which is better for environment. Many newer developments also provide shared facilities such as gyms, playgrounds and security staff that individual houses rarely have.

However, apartment living also has disadvantages. The most frequently mentioned is a weaker sense of community: residents may share a lift with dozens of people every day and yet hardly know any of them. Families with young children often complain about the lack of private outdoor space, while elderly residents can find themselves trapped if lifts break down. There are also concerns about safety in the event of fire, as evacuating a tall building is more difficult than leaving a house.

Nevertheless, most of these problems can be reduced through good design and regulation. Communal gardens, shared rooftop areas and strict fire-safety standards can make high-rise living both more sociable and more secure.

In conclusion, while tall apartment buildings can feel impersonal and present particular safety challenges, their efficient use of land and convenient locations make them an essential solution for crowded cities. For these reasons, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

answers.text:
Across the world's major cities, the skyline is increasingly dominated by residential towers, and a growing share of urban households now live many floors above the street. Although vertical living has undeniable shortcomings, I would argue that, in densely populated cities, its advantages prevail.

The strongest case for high-rise housing is a practical one. Land in city centres is scarce and expensive, and building upwards allows far more homes to be created on the same footprint than low-rise development ever could. This density has wider benefits: it limits urban sprawl into farmland and green belts, and it makes public transport, shops and services economically viable because enough people live within walking distance of them. For residents, the result is often a shorter commute and easier access to employment, education and leisure, which can significantly improve quality of life.

The drawbacks, however, are genuine. Tall buildings can be socially isolating, since the anonymity of long corridors and shared lifts rarely encourages the casual encounters that build neighbourly relationships. Families may struggle without private gardens, and older or disabled residents are particularly vulnerable when lifts fail. Safety is a further concern: evacuating hundreds of people from upper floors during a fire is inherently more complex than escaping from a house, and poorly maintained towers can become hazardous.

Yet these issues largely reflect how such buildings are designed and managed rather than the concept itself. Well-planned developments incorporate communal green spaces, community rooms and robust fire-safety systems, demonstrating that high-density living can be both safe and socially vibrant.

In conclusion, high-rise apartments may compromise privacy, outdoor space and, at times, community spirit, but these costs can be mitigated through thoughtful design. Given their efficient use of land and the accessibility they offer, I believe their advantages clearly outweigh their disadvantages.

Nowadays, many big international companies are building factories and offices in developing countries. This has both advantages and disadvantages for the local people. In my opinion, the advantages are more important.

The biggest advantage is jobs. When a foreign company open a factory, it needs hundreds of workers, so many people who was unemployed can get a job and earn a regular salary. This helps families to pay for food, education and health care. Also, international companies often pay higher wages than local companies. Another advantage is that workers can learn new skills and technology. For example, if an employee works in a car factory, he can learn how to use modern machines, and later he can use this knowledge in other jobs. Moreover, the government gets more money from taxes, which it can spend on roads and schools.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Some companies pay very low salary and the working conditions are bad, for example people work for long hours without enough rest. In addition, the factories can cause pollution to the rivers and air, and this is harmful for the people's health who live nearby. Finally, the most of the profit goes back to the company's home country, so the developing country does not get all the benefit.

In conclusion, international companies bring both good and bad effects to developing countries. They create jobs and teach new skills, but they can also cause pollution and pay low wages. I believe that the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but the government should make strict rules to protect workers and the environment.

answers.text:
In recent decades, multinational corporations have moved a growing share of their manufacturing and service operations to developing nations. While this trend can create problems for local communities, I believe that, overall, the benefits for ordinary people in these countries are greater than the costs.

The most obvious advantage is employment. Foreign firms often create thousands of jobs in regions where work is scarce, giving people a steady income and the chance to escape poverty. These jobs frequently pay more than local alternatives, and they may come with training that local employers cannot afford to provide. Over time, employees gain technical and managerial skills which they can take to other companies or use to start their own businesses. In addition, the presence of large international firms tends to improve local infrastructure, as roads, ports and power supplies are upgraded to serve them.

On the other hand, there are serious disadvantages. Some corporations are attracted mainly by cheap labour and weak regulations, and as a result workers may face long hours, low pay and unsafe conditions. Environmental damage is another concern, since factories can pollute rivers and air in countries where laws are poorly enforced. Furthermore, large foreign companies can drive small local businesses out of the market, and a significant part of the profits is sent back abroad rather than reinvested locally.

However, these negative effects are not unavoidable. When governments set and enforce minimum standards for wages, safety and pollution, foreign investment can bring benefits without the worst forms of exploitation.

In conclusion, although multinational companies can exploit workers and damage the environment, the jobs, skills and infrastructure they bring represent a major opportunity for people in developing countries. For this reason, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that effective regulation are in place.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The relocation of factories and offices by multinational corporations to lower-income countries is one of the defining features of the global economy. Its impact on local populations is mixed, but I would contend that, where host governments regulate effectively, the advantages for ordinary citizens outweigh the disadvantages.

The most immediate gain is employment. In economies with high levels of informal or subsistence work, a job with a foreign firm often provides the first regular wage a household has received, together with a degree of stability that enables families to plan, save and invest in their children's education. Beyond income, these positions frequently involve formal training, exposing workers to modern production methods, management practices and quality standards. Such knowledge rarely stays within one company; it spreads as employees move on or establish suppliers of their own, gradually raising the productivity of the wider economy. Foreign investment can also stimulate improvements in transport and energy that benefit the whole population.

The costs, however, can be severe. Some corporations deliberately seek out countries with lax labour and environmental laws, and the consequences can include excessive working hours, dangerous workplaces and serious contamination of land and water. There is also the risk of dependency: an economy built around foreign-owned plants is vulnerable if a company decides to relocate again in search of even cheaper costs, leaving entire towns without work. Moreover, much of the value generated flows back to shareholders overseas rather than being reinvested locally.

Importantly, these harms are largely a function of governance rather than of foreign investment itself. Countries that enforce labour rights, require environmental safeguards and encourage links with domestic suppliers tend to capture far more of the benefits.

In conclusion, multinational investment carries real risks of exploitation and instability, yet the jobs, skills and infrastructure it brings can transform living standards. On balance, and with sound regulation, its advantages for local people outweigh its disadvantages.

Nowadays many companies prefer to give workers short-term contracts instead of permanent jobs. This situation has some advantages but also many disadvantages for the workers, which I will discuss in this essay.

On the one hand, short-term contracts can be good for some workers. First of all, they give people more freedom. If a worker does not like the job or the company, he can simply leave when the contract finish and look for something better. Also, young people can try different jobs and get experience in many areas before they decide their career. For example, a graduate can work six months in marketing and then six months in sales. Moreover, some contracts pay a higher salary per hour because the company do not need to pay for holidays or pension.

On the other hand, the disadvantages are serious. The biggest problem is that there is no job security. Workers do not know if they will have a job next year, so it is difficult for them to plan the future, for example to buy a house or start a family. Banks also do not like to give loan to people without permanent job. In addition, temporary workers often do not receive the same benefits like sick pay, training or promotion. As a result, they may feel stressed and not part of the company.

In conclusion, short-term contracts give workers flexibility and the chance to gain different experiences, but they also create insecurity and fewer benefits. In my opinion, they are suitable for young people at the start of their career, but for most workers a permanent job is better.

answers.text:
It is becoming increasingly common for employers to hire staff on fixed-term contracts instead of offering them permanent positions. For workers, this arrangement brings some genuine benefits, but in my view these are outweighed by the insecurity it creates for most people.

There are some advantages to short-term employment. Firstly, it offers flexibility, which suits certain groups such as students, parents returning to work or people who want to travel between contracts. Secondly, it allows workers to gain experience across a range of organisations and industries in a relatively short time, which can make their CV more attractive and help them discover what kind of work suits them best. In some sectors, such as information technology, skilled contractors are also able to charge higher rates than permanent staff because employers value their specialist knowledge.

However, for the majority of employees, the disadvantages are more significant. The lack of job security is the most serious issue, as workers cannot be sure whether their contract will be renewed. This uncertainty makes it difficult to make long-term commitments, such as taking out a mortgage or starting a family, and it can cause considerable stress. In addition, temporary staff are often excluded from benefits like paid holidays, sick leave and pension schemes, and they rarely receive the training or promotion opportunities which is offered to permanent colleagues. Because they know they may soon leave, they may also feel less loyal to the company and less valued by their managers.

In conclusion, short-term contracts can be attractive for highly skilled professionals and for people who want flexibility at a particular stage of life. For most workers, though, the loss of security, benefits and career development makes this type of employment a less desirable option than a permanent job.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The shift away from permanent employment towards fixed-term and project-based contracts has reshaped working life in many economies. For employees, this change offers a certain degree of freedom, but it also transfers much of the risk that employers once carried onto individual workers.

On the positive side, short-term contracts can suit people whose priorities do not fit a conventional career path. A recent graduate, for example, may use a series of placements to sample different industries before committing to one, while a parent may value the ability to work intensively for several months and then take time off. For those with scarce, in-demand skills, contract work can be financially rewarding, as employers are often willing to pay a premium for expertise they need only temporarily. Moving between organisations also broadens professional networks and exposes workers to a variety of practices, which can make them more adaptable.

The drawbacks, however, fall most heavily on those with the least bargaining power. Without the assurance of continued employment, workers find it hard to plan ahead: securing a mortgage, supporting dependants or even booking a holiday becomes a gamble when income may stop within months. Temporary staff frequently miss out on entitlements such as sick pay, pension contributions and parental leave, and employers have little incentive to invest in training someone who may soon leave. Over time, this can trap people in a cycle of insecure jobs with limited prospects for promotion. The psychological toll should not be overlooked either, as persistent uncertainty is a well-known source of stress.

To sum up, short-term contracts can offer flexibility, variety and, for skilled professionals, higher earnings. For the majority of workers, however, these advantages come at the price of financial insecurity, reduced benefits and weaker career development, which is why such arrangements work best when they are genuinely chosen rather than imposed.

In many towns, the small shops are closing and large supermarkets and shopping centres are taking their place. In my opinion, this change has some advantages, but the disadvantages are more serious.

To begin with, there are some benefits of supermarkets. They are usually cheaper than small shops because they buy products in large quantity. This is important for families who have a low income. Also, supermarkets are very convenient, because customers can buy everything they need in one place, such as food, clothes and electronic, and they can park their car easily. Many of them are open for long hours, so people who works late can still do their shopping.

However, I think the disadvantages are more important. When small shops close, the owners lose their business and many local people lose their jobs. The money which people spend in supermarkets often goes to big companies in other cities, not to the local community. Moreover, the town centre become less attractive, because there are many empty shops and fewer people walking in the streets. Small shops also give a personal service. The shopkeeper knows his customers and can give them advices, but in a big supermarket nobody knows you. Finally, old people who cannot drive find it difficult to go to shopping centres outside the town.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres are cheap and convenient, but they damage local businesses and change the character of towns. For these reasons, I believe that the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and local governments should help small shops to survive.

Across many towns, independent shops are gradually disappearing as large supermarkets and out-of-town shopping centres take over. Although this development offers consumers some clear benefits, I believe the loss to local communities is greater.

It is true that large retailers bring certain advantages. Because they buy goods in enormous quantities, they can offer lower prices than small shops, which is especially important for households on tight budget. They also provide convenience: shoppers can buy groceries, clothing and household items under one roof, often late into the evening and with free parking. In addition, supermarkets tend to offer a much wider range of products, including foreign foods that small local stores would rarely stock.

Nevertheless, the disadvantages are more far-reaching. When independent businesses close, the effect goes beyond the owners themselves. High streets that were once busy become lined with empty premises, which makes town centres less attractive and can even encourage vandalism. More of the money spent also leaves the area, as profits go to national chains rather than circulating among local families. Moreover, small shops often play a social role that supermarkets cannot replace; a local grocer who greets customers by name offers a sense of connection that is particularly valuable for elderly people living alone. Finally, shopping centres built on the edge of town encourage car use, which increases traffic and puts residents without transport at a disadvantage.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres undoubtedly make shopping cheaper and more convenient. However, since they weaken local economies, damage town centres and reduce community life, I believe that on balance their disadvantages outweigh their advantages.

answers.text:
The decline of the independent high-street shop in the face of competition from supermarkets and shopping centres is a familiar story in many towns. While the change has undoubtedly benefited shoppers in certain respects, I would argue that, taken as a whole, its advantages are outweighed by its costs.

The case for large retailers rests largely on price and convenience. Economies of scale allow supermarkets to negotiate lower prices from suppliers and pass at least some of these savings on to customers, which matters considerably to families whose budgets are stretched. Their extended opening hours, extensive product ranges and ample parking also suit modern lifestyles, in which many people have little time to visit several separate shops. For consumers, then, the immediate benefits are tangible.

The disadvantages, however, are broader and longer-lasting. Independent shops are typically owned by local residents, so the money spent in them tends to circulate within the community, supporting other local businesses and jobs. When they are replaced by national chains, a greater share of that spending is channelled elsewhere. The physical fabric of towns suffers too: once enough shops close, footfall declines, remaining businesses struggle and high streets can enter a spiral of decline marked by vacant units. There is also a social dimension that is easily overlooked. Small shops often serve as informal meeting points where neighbours exchange news, and for older or less mobile residents, a daily visit to a nearby store may be an important source of human contact. Out-of-town shopping centres, by contrast, are designed around the car and can leave such people isolated.

In conclusion, supermarkets and shopping centres offer genuine savings and convenience, but these gains are largely private and short-term, whereas the erosion of local economies and community life affects entire towns. For this reason, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages.

answers.text:
The practice of companies paying popular social media personalities to advertise their goods has grown rapidly in recent years. Although this form of marketing has clear benefits for businesses, I believe that its negative effects on consumers are more significant.

From a commercial point of view, influencer marketing is highly attractive. It enables companies to reach specific groups of consumers, particularly young people who rarely watch television or read magazines. Because followers often feel a personal connection with the influencer, a recommendation from them can seem more trustworthy than a traditional advertisement. For smaller brands, it can also be more affordable than a national advertising campaign, allowing them to compete with larger rivals.

However, it is precisely this sense of trust that makes the practice problematic. Many followers cannot easily tell the difference between a genuine opinion and a paid promotion, especially when the commercial relationship is not clearly disclosed. As a result, consumers may be persuaded to buy products based on what they believe is honest advice, when in fact the influencer has been paid to praise them. This is particularly concerning because many social media users are teenagers, who are more vulnerable to pressure to follow trends. Influencers also tend to present an idealised lifestyle, which can encourage excessive spending and make young people feel dissatisfied with their own appearance or possessions. In some cases, products of poor quality or with unproven health benefits are promoted simply because the influencer was well paid to do so.

In conclusion, paying social media users to promote products is an efficient and relatively cheap marketing tool for companies. Nevertheless, because it often blurs the line between advertising and personal opinion and targets vulnerable young audiences, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, unless strict rules on transparency is enforced.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Influencer marketing, in which brands pay popular social media users to feature their products, has become one of the fastest-growing forms of advertising. While it offers undeniable advantages to businesses and, to a lesser extent, to consumers, I would argue that its disadvantages ultimately carry more weight.

The appeal for companies is easy to understand. Influencers command highly engaged audiences, often defined by specific interests such as fitness, gaming or cookery, so a brand can place its message directly in front of the people most likely to buy. This precision makes campaigns more cost-effective than broad television advertising, and it gives small and new businesses a realistic route to visibility. Consumers may benefit too, since a detailed video demonstration can reveal more about how a product performs than a polished thirty-second commercial.

Nevertheless, the model rests on a fundamental tension. Its effectiveness depends on audiences perceiving the influencer as an authentic, independent voice, yet the content is, by definition, paid for. When sponsorship is concealed or disclosed only in small print, followers are effectively misled into treating advertising as personal recommendation. The problem is compounded by the age profile of many audiences: children and teenagers are less equipped to recognise persuasive intent and more susceptible to the carefully curated lifestyles on display, which can fuel both overconsumption and insecurity about body image. Furthermore, because influencers are rewarded for promotion rather than expertise, products such as dubious supplements or risky financial schemes can reach large audiences with little scrutiny.

Admittedly, clearer labelling requirements could reduce some of these harms, but enforcing them across millions of posts remains extremely difficult.

In conclusion, paid promotion on social media is an efficient and accessible marketing channel, yet its reliance on blurring commerce and personal opinion, combined with its reach among young people, means that in my view the disadvantages outweigh the advantages.

In some cities, drivers have to pay money if they want to drive into the city centre during the busy times of the day. I think this policy has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that it reduce traffic. When people have to pay every day, many of them will decide to use the bus, the train or a bicycle instead of their car. As a result, the roads in the centre are less crowded and the journeys become faster for buses, taxis and delivery vans. The second advantage is about the environment. Less cars means less air pollution and less noise, so the city centre become a healthier and more pleasant place for people who live and work there. In addition, the government can use the money from the charge to improve public transport, for example by buying new buses.

However, this system also has some disadvantages. It is unfair for people with low income, because rich people can pay the fee easily but poor people cannot. Also, some people have no choice and they must use their car, for example workers who start very early in the morning when there is no buses. Shop owners in the centre are also worried that fewer customers will come to their shops.

In conclusion, charging drivers to enter the city centre can cause some problems, especially for poor people and small shops. However, I believe the benefits for traffic and the environment are more important, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. The government should use the money to make public transport cheaper and better for everyone.

answers.text:
Several major cities have introduced congestion charges, which require motorists to pay a fee for driving into the centre during peak hours. Although this measure can place a burden on some groups, I am convinced that its benefits outweigh its drawbacks.

The principal advantage is a reduction in traffic. Faced with a daily charge, many commuters switch to public transport, cycling or car-sharing, and the remaining traffic can move more freely. This benefits not only drivers but also buses and emergency vehicles, which are otherwise delayed by congestion. A second benefit is environmental. Fewer vehicles in central areas leads to cleaner air and less noise, improving the health and quality of life of residents and people who work there. In addition, the money raised can be invested directly in public transport, creating a positive cycle in which better services encourage even more people to leave their cars at home.

On the other hand, critics raise some valid points. The fee affects low-income drivers far more than wealthy ones, who may simply regard it as a minor expense. People who have little choice but to drive, such as those working night shifts or living in areas with poor transport links, may feel they are being punished. Some businesses in the centre also worry that the charge will discourage shoppers and push them towards out-of-town shopping centres.

However, these concerns can be addressed through careful design of the scheme. Discounts for residents, exemptions for disabled drivers and improvements to bus services before the charge is introduced can make the system considerably fairer.

In conclusion, although congestion charges may be unfair to certain groups and could affect some businesses, they are an effective way to cut traffic and pollution. On balance, therefore, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Charging motorists to enter city centres at peak times has been adopted by a number of cities seeking to tackle congestion and pollution. Although the policy raises legitimate questions of fairness, I believe that, when well designed, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

The rationale for such charges is that road space in a city centre is a scarce resource which, when provided free, is inevitably overused. By attaching a price to driving at the busiest times, a congestion charge encourages motorists to reconsider journeys that are not essential, to travel at quieter times or to switch to public transport. The result is faster, more reliable journeys for buses, deliveries and emergency services, whose efficiency is vital to the functioning of a city. The environmental gains are equally significant: reduced traffic means lower emissions and less noise in precisely the places where people are most concentrated. Moreover, the revenue generated can be ring-fenced for improving public transport, so that the alternatives to driving become steadily more attractive.

The main objection is that a flat fee is regressive. For a well-paid professional, the charge may be a trivial inconvenience, whereas for a low-paid worker who depends on a car, it can represent a substantial share of their daily earnings. Retailers in central districts also fear a loss of trade if shoppers choose to drive to suburban malls instead.

These concerns deserve serious attention, but they are arguments for refining the scheme rather than rejecting it. Exemptions for residents and disabled drivers, discounts for essential workers and investment in affordable public transport can all reduce the unequal impact, while a less congested, more pleasant centre may in fact attract more visitors on foot.

In conclusion, although congestion charges can bear more heavily on those with lower incomes, their capacity to reduce traffic, cut pollution and fund better transport makes them, on balance, a worthwhile policy whose benefits outweigh its costs.

Nowadays a lot of people prefer to spend their holidays in their own country instead of going abroad. This trend has several advantages, but there are also some disadvantages.

One advantage of domestic holidays is that they are usually cheaper. People do not need to buy expensive flight tickets, and they do not have to change money or pay for a visa. As a result, families with a limited budget can travel more often. Another advantage is that it is more easy and comfortable. Travellers speak the same language as local people, they understand the culture and they know what kind of food they will eat, so they feel more relax. Also, when people travel inside their own country, they help the local economy, because the money they spend goes to local hotels, restaurants and shops.

However, there are also some disadvantages. The main one is that people miss the chance to learn about other cultures. When you travel abroad, you can see different traditions, try new food and meet people from other countries, and this can open your mind. In addition, the weather in some countries are not very good, so people who want sunshine and beaches may be disappointed if they stay at home. Finally, popular places in their own country can become very crowded during the holidays season because everyone goes to the same places.

In conclusion, spending holidays in your own country is cheaper, easier and good for local economy. On the other hand, people cannot experience new cultures and sometimes the weather and crowds are a problem. I think both types of holiday are useful, and people should choose depend on their budget and interests.

In recent years, a growing number of people have chosen to spend their holidays exploring their own country rather than travelling overseas. This choice offers a number of practical and economic benefits, although it also means missing out on some valuable experiences.

The most obvious advantage of holidaying at home is cost. Without international flights, visas or currency exchange fees, a domestic trip is generally far more affordable, which allows families to take holidays more frequently. It is also less stressful, since travellers do not have to deal with unfamiliar languages, long security queues or complicated travel documents. Furthermore, domestic tourism supports the national economy, as money spent on hotels, restaurants and attractions stays within the country and helps to sustain jobs in rural and coastal areas. There is an environmental benefit too: travelling by train or car over shorter distances usually produces far less carbon than flying abroad.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. Perhaps the most significant is that people lose the opportunity to experience different cultures at first hand. Travelling abroad exposes people to new languages, customs and ways of thinking, which can broaden their outlook and make them more tolerant. Domestic holidays may also offer less variety; a person from a small country might feel they have already seen most of what it has to offer. In addition, when large numbers of people holiday at home at the same time, popular destinations can become overcrowded and prices for accommodation may rise sharply during peak season.

In conclusion, holidaying in one's own country is cheaper, easier and better for both the national economy and the environment. However, it cannot fully replace the cultural enrichment which comes from visiting other countries, so an occasional trip abroad still has an important value.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Choosing to explore one's own country instead of heading overseas has become an increasingly popular way to take a holiday. This preference brings clear financial, practical and environmental benefits, although it can also limit the broader horizons that international travel provides.

Chief among the advantages is affordability. Domestic trips avoid the expense of long-haul flights and foreign currency, and they can often be arranged at short notice, making regular breaks accessible to households that could not stretch to an annual trip abroad. They are also considerably less demanding: there are no language barriers, visa applications or unfamiliar healthcare systems to navigate, which is particularly reassuring for older travellers and families with young children. From a national perspective, domestic tourism keeps spending within the country, sustaining small hotels, guesthouses and restaurants in regions that may have few other sources of income. Finally, shorter journeys, especially by rail, generally have a far smaller carbon footprint than international flights.

Yet something is undeniably lost. Travelling abroad confronts people with different languages, values and ways of life, and this exposure can challenge assumptions and foster a more open-minded outlook in a way that familiar surroundings rarely do. Domestic holidays may also lack novelty for those who have grown up visiting the same resorts, and residents of smaller countries in particular may find the range of landscapes and climates limited. A further, more practical drawback is congestion: when large numbers of people holiday at home during the same school breaks, popular beauty spots can become overcrowded and local infrastructure stretched.

In conclusion, holidaying in one's own country is economical, convenient and comparatively sustainable, and it provides welcome support for local economies. Its main limitation is that it offers fewer opportunities for cultural discovery, which is why many people may still value an occasional journey further afield.

answers.text:
In a number of regions, extensive areas of farmland and open countryside are being converted into solar farms and wind energy sites. While this raises concerns about food production and the landscape, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that locations are chosen carefully.

The strongest argument in favour of these projects is the urgent need to reduce carbon emissions. Solar and wind power generate electricity without burning fossil fuels, so expanding them is one of the most effective ways for a country to tackle climate change and improve air quality. Large rural sites are often ideal for this purpose because they receive plenty of sunlight or strong winds and have space for installations that would be impossible in cities. Moreover, these projects can support rural economies. Farmers who lease part of their land to energy companies gain a stable income that does not depend on the weather or crop prices, which can allow them to keep farming the rest of their land.

Nevertheless, there are genuine disadvantages. Covering productive farmland with solar panels reduces the amount of land available for growing food, which could make a country more dependent on imports. Many residents also object to the visual impact of large turbines and rows of panels on landscapes they value, and in some areas this may harm tourism. There are environmental costs as well, since construction can disturb wildlife habitats, and turbines can pose a risk to birds.

However, many of these problems can be reduced. Energy projects can be located on poorer-quality land, and some farms successfully combine solar panels with sheep grazing beneath them.

In conclusion, although using countryside for renewable energy has some impact on agriculture, scenery and wildlife, the need to cut emissions and the economic benefits for rural communities is more pressing. Therefore, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
As countries race to decarbonise their energy systems, farmland and open countryside are increasingly being given over to solar arrays and wind turbines. This has provoked fierce local opposition in some areas, yet I believe that, if sited thoughtfully, such projects deliver benefits that outweigh their costs.

The central argument for these developments is environmental necessity. Replacing coal and gas with renewable electricity is essential if the worst effects of climate change are to be avoided, and generating that electricity at scale requires space that dense urban areas simply cannot provide. Rural sites offer open exposure to sun and wind, relatively low land costs and room for installations large enough to supply thousands of homes. Such projects can also strengthen the rural economy: rental payments from energy companies give farmers a reliable income that cushions them against poor harvests and volatile food prices, while local communities may receive funds for shared facilities.

The objections, however, are not trivial. Agricultural land is a finite resource, and converting large areas of fertile fields to energy generation could undermine a country's capacity to feed itself. Landscapes that have been valued for generations may be transformed by industrial-scale structures, affecting both residents' attachment to their surroundings and the tourism on which some rural areas depend. Poorly planned schemes can also fragment habitats and endanger bird populations.

Crucially, though, most of these drawbacks depend on where and how projects are built rather than on renewable energy itself. Prioritising lower-grade farmland, combining solar panels with grazing, and avoiding sensitive habitats and migration routes can substantially reduce the conflict between energy, food and nature.

In conclusion, the loss of some farmland and scenic value is a genuine cost, but it must be weighed against the far greater threat posed by climate change. With careful planning, the advantages of rural renewable energy projects clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

Nowadays, many young people continue to live with their parents after they finish their studies. This situation has some advantages and disadvantages for both the young adults and their parents.

For young adults, the biggest advantage is money. Rent is very expensive in most cities, so if they live at home they can save a big part of their salary. Later they can use this money to buy their own house or car. Also, they do not have to do all the housework alone, because the mother often cook and clean for the family. For parents, it can also be good. They can spend more time with their children and they do not feel lonely, especially if they are old. Moreover, the children can help them with shopping or with technology, for example using a smartphone.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Young adults who stay at home may not become independent. They do not learn how to pay bills, manage their own money or solve problems by themself. They also have less privacy, and sometimes they cannot invite friends to the house. For the parents, the problem is that they have to pay more for food and electricity, and they cannot enjoy their free time after retirement. In addition, there can be many arguments, because parents and children have different lifestyle and opinions.

In conclusion, living together helps young adults to save money and gives the parents company. But it can also stop young people from becoming independent and cause conflicts in the family. I think it is fine for a short time, but young people should moves out when they are ready.

answers.text:
It is increasingly common for young people to remain in the family home after completing their education, rather than moving into a place of their own. This arrangement has both benefits and drawbacks, not only for the young adults themselves but also for their parents.

For young adults, the most significant advantage is financial. With rents and property prices rising in many cities, living with parents allows them to save money for a deposit on a home or to pay off student loans more quickly. It can also provide emotional support during a stressful period, such as the search for a first job. Parents, too, can benefit. Many enjoy the continued companionship of their children, and as they grow older, having an adult son or daughter at home means there is someone to help with household tasks, shopping or unexpected health problems.

On the other hand, the arrangement has clear disadvantages. Young people who stay at home for too long may delay developing important life skills, such as budgeting, cooking and managing a household, and they may become overly dependent on their parents. A lack of privacy and personal space can also make it harder for them to build independent social lives. For parents, supporting an adult child can put pressure on their finances just when they are planning for retirement. Moreover, disagreements over household rules, chores or lifestyle are common when two adult generations share the same space, and these tensions can damage family relationships.

In conclusion, living together can offer young adults financial security and give parents company and practical help. However, it may also slow the development of independence and create financial and emotional strains on both sides. Ideally, such arrangement should be temporary and based on clear agreements about responsibilities.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In many societies, the age at which young people leave the family home is steadily rising, with growing numbers remaining with their parents well after they have completed their education. This trend carries a mixture of advantages and disadvantages for both generations, and its overall impact depends heavily on how the arrangement is managed.

For young adults, the benefits are largely economic. At a time when housing costs absorb an ever-larger proportion of starting salaries, living at home enables graduates to build savings, repay debts and accept lower-paid but career-enhancing positions that they could not otherwise afford. The family home can also serve as a safety net during an uncertain transition into working life. Parents may gain as well: the presence of an adult child can provide companionship, particularly for those who live alone, and practical assistance with everything from home repairs to navigating online services. In some cultures, multigenerational living is valued in its own right as a way of preserving close family ties.

The disadvantages, however, are equally real. Remaining under the parental roof can postpone the development of self-reliance, since many of the responsibilities that force young people to mature, such as paying rent and running a household, are absorbed by others. Limited privacy may also constrain their social lives. For parents, the arrangement can mean extra expense and a delayed opportunity to enjoy the freedom they may have anticipated once their children had grown up. Perhaps most significantly, adults with different routines and expectations sharing a home can generate friction, and unresolved tensions may strain relationships that would otherwise be harmonious.

In conclusion, continued co-residence offers young adults financial breathing space and parents companionship and support, but it risks delaying independence and generating conflict. The arrangement tends to work best when it is treated as a temporary stage, with clear expectations on both sides.

These days, a lot of people use smartwatches and apps on their mobile phones to check their health and fitness. I believe that this technology has more advantages than disadvantages.

The main advantage is that these devices motivate people to be more active. For example, a smartwatch can count how many steps you walk every day and remind you to move if you sit for a long time. When people see their progress on the screen, they feel happy and they want to do more exercise. Also, many apps help people to control what they eat and how many calories they take. Another advantage is that some smartwatches can check the heart rate and the sleep. If there is something unusual, the user can visit a doctor early before the problem become serious.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. Firstly, the information from these devices is not always correct, so people may worry about nothing or they may ignore a real problem. Secondly, some people become too obsess with the numbers. They check their phone all the time and feel stressed if they do not reach their target. Finally, these apps collect a lot of personal information about the users, and the companies can sell this informations to other companies without permission.

In conclusion, smartwatches and health apps have some problems, such as privacy and wrong information. However, they encourage people to live more healthy lifestyle and they can help to find health problems early. Therefore, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but people should use them careful and not trust them completely.

answers.text:
Wearable devices and smartphone applications that track steps, heart rate, sleep and diet have become part of everyday life for millions of people. Although these tools have certain drawbacks, I believe their advantages are greater.

Admittedly, there are some concerns. The data produced by consumer devices is not always accurate, and users may be falsely reassured or unnecessarily alarmed by the figures they see. Some people also become fixated on hitting daily targets, which can turn exercise from an enjoyable activity into a source of anxiety. Privacy is another issue, since these apps gather highly personal information about users' bodies and habits, and it is not always clear how technology companies store or share it.

Nevertheless, the benefits are more significant. The most important is that health tracking encourages people to take responsibility for their own wellbeing. Simple features, such as a daily step count or a reminder to stand up after an hour of sitting, can gradually change habits, and seeing progress over time is a powerful motivation to keep going. In addition, some devices can warn users about irregular heartbeats or poor sleep patterns, prompting them to seek medical advice before a condition becomes more serious. For people with long-term illnesses such as diabetes, apps can make it much easier to record information and share it with doctors, leading to better management of the condition.

Moreover, most of the disadvantages depend on how the technology is used. If people treat the data as a general guide rather than a medical diagnosis, and if governments introduces clear rules on data protection, the risks can be greatly reduced.

In conclusion, although health-monitoring technology raises questions about accuracy, obsession and privacy, its ability to motivate healthier lifestyles and detect potential problems early means that the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The use of smartwatches and mobile applications to record everything from daily steps to sleep quality and heart rhythm has become commonplace. While this constant self-monitoring has its downsides, I would argue that, for most users, the advantages outweigh them.

The chief benefit is behavioural. Many people know in principle that they should move more, sleep better and eat more sensibly, but struggle to translate that knowledge into action. By turning vague intentions into concrete, measurable goals and providing immediate feedback, fitness trackers make healthy behaviour visible and rewarding, and features such as streaks or friendly competitions can sustain motivation over months. Beyond motivation, some devices can flag potentially significant irregularities, such as an unusually high resting heart rate, prompting users to consult a doctor sooner than they otherwise would. For people managing chronic conditions, digital records can also give doctors a far richer picture than occasional clinic visits allow.

There are, however, legitimate reservations. Consumer devices are not medical instruments, and inaccurate readings can either create needless anxiety or offer false reassurance. For some individuals, the constant stream of data fosters an unhealthy preoccupation with numbers, turning exercise and even sleep into sources of pressure. Most troubling, perhaps, is the question of privacy: health data is extraordinarily sensitive, and users often have little understanding of how it may be stored, analysed or shared with third parties such as advertisers or insurers.

These concerns warrant stronger regulation and greater user awareness, but they do not negate the value of the technology. Treated as a guide rather than a diagnosis, and protected by robust data laws, health trackers can play a genuinely positive role.

In conclusion, despite issues of accuracy, obsession and data security, the capacity of smartwatches and apps to encourage healthier habits and support earlier medical attention means that their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.
