In many cities around the world, the government has put a lot of security cameras in public places like streets, stations and shopping centres. The aim is to reduce crime. In my opinion, this has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that cameras can stop people from committing crimes. If a thief knows that a camera is watching him, he will probably not steal anything because he is afraid to be caught. So the streets become safer. Secondly, when a crime happens, the police can watch the video and find the criminal more quickly. The recordings can also be used as evidence in court. Moreover, people feel more safe when they walk at night in areas with cameras, especially women and old people.

However, there are also some disadvantages. The most important one is privacy. Many people do not like that they are watched all the time when they are in public. They feel like the government is controlling them. Also, the information from cameras can be used in a wrong way, for example if someone share the videos on the internet. Another disadvantage is the cost. Installing and checking thousands of cameras is very expensive, and some people think that the money should spent on more police officers. In addition, criminals can simply move to other areas where there is not cameras.

In conclusion, security cameras have some problems such as privacy and cost. But I believe they help to reduce crime and make people feel safe, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. However, the government must make rules about how the videos are used.

answers.text:
In an effort to fight crime, many cities have installed extensive networks of surveillance cameras in streets, transport hubs and other public spaces. While this raises concerns about privacy and cost, I believe the advantages are greater.

The most important benefit of CCTV is its role in solving crimes. When an offence takes place in a monitored area, footage can help the police to identify suspects, trace their movements and provide strong evidence in court. This increases the chance that offenders are caught and punished, which in turn may discourage others. Cameras can also act as a deterrent in themselves; people planning to commit theft or vandalism are likely to think twice if they know they are being recorded. In addition, surveillance can help authorities respond quickly to emergencies, such as accidents or fights in crowded places, and it gives many members of the public a greater sense of security, particularly at night.

On the other hand, there are some drawbacks. The most frequently mentioned is the loss of privacy, as ordinary citizens are recorded constantly while going about their daily lives. There is a risk that footage could be misused, for example to monitor peaceful protesters or be leaked online. Critics also argue that cameras do not really reduce crime but simply move it to areas without surveillance. Finally, installing and monitoring thousands of cameras requires a considerable amount of public money that could be spent on other services.

Despite these concerns, I would argue that the problems can be managed through clear laws on who can access footage and how long it is kept.

In conclusion, although security cameras raise legitimate questions about privacy and value for money, their contribution to detecting and preventing crime makes them a worthwhile tool. Therefore, the advantages outweighs the disadvantages, as long as their use is properly regulated.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Surveillance cameras have become a familiar feature of streets, stations and squares in many cities, justified primarily as a means of reducing crime. Although their spread raises serious questions about privacy and civil liberties, I believe that, under proper regulation, their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

The strongest argument for public CCTV lies in its investigative value. Footage can establish a clear sequence of events, identify suspects and corroborate or challenge witness statements, often transforming cases that would otherwise remain unsolved. This is particularly important for crimes such as street robbery, where victims may have only a fleeting glimpse of the offender. Cameras may also exert a deterrent effect, especially in car parks and transport hubs, where opportunistic offences are common. Beyond crime, surveillance systems allow authorities to manage crowds at large events, locate missing people and coordinate rapid responses to accidents.

The disadvantages, nonetheless, deserve careful consideration. Blanket surveillance changes the nature of public space: people who know they are constantly observed may feel less free to gather, protest or simply behave spontaneously. The potential for misuse is considerable, whether through unauthorised access, the leaking of footage or, more worryingly, the combination of cameras with facial recognition to track individuals without their knowledge. Critics also point out that cameras are less effective against impulsive crime than their supporters claim, and that some offending is merely displaced to unmonitored streets, which raises doubts about whether the substantial public expenditure is justified.

These risks, however, point to the need for firm safeguards rather than the removal of cameras altogether. Strict limits on data retention, independent oversight and transparent rules on facial recognition can preserve most of the benefits while protecting civil liberties.

In conclusion, security cameras are not a complete solution to crime, and their misuse could threaten personal freedom. Nevertheless, their value in solving and deterring offences means that, carefully regulated, their advantages outweigh their disadvantages.

Nowadays, some countries invite skilled workers from other countries to come and live there because they do not have enough workers in some jobs. In my opinion, this policy has more advantages than disadvantages for the receiving country.

The first and most important advantage is that it solve the problem of labour shortages. For example, many countries do not have enough doctors, nurses or engineers, and training new people takes many years. When skilled workers come from abroad, hospitals and companies can continue to work well. Also, these workers pay taxes, which help the government to pay for public services like schools and pensions. This is very important in countries where the population is getting older and there is fewer young workers. In addition, people from different countries bring new ideas and cultures, which can make the society more interesting.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Some local workers may feel that the newcomers are taking their jobs or that they reduce the salaries. This can cause tension between local people and the new arrivals. Moreover, the new workers need houses, schools for their children and health services, so there can be more pressure on these services. Another problem is that the government may not train its own citizens because it is easier to bring workers from other country.

In conclusion, encouraging skilled workers from abroad can cause some problems such as tension and pressure on public services. However, I think the benefits for the economy and important services like health care is bigger. So the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, but the government should also invest in training local people.

Faced with shortages in key professions, a number of countries actively encourage qualified workers from overseas to settle permanently. Although this approach can create some social and economic challenges, I believe it brings greater benefits to the receiving country.

The most direct advantage is that skilled migrants fill gaps that cannot be filled quickly from within the domestic workforce. Training a doctor or an engineer can take many years, whereas recruiting experienced professionals from abroad allows hospitals, construction projects and technology firms to operate effectively in the meantime. This helps to maintain the quality of public services and prevents businesses from losing opportunities because they lack staff. Furthermore, many developed countries have ageing populations, and working-age migrants contribute taxes that help fund pensions and healthcare for older citizens. Skilled newcomers can also bring fresh ideas and international connections, which may stimulate innovation.

However, there are some potential drawbacks. If large numbers of people arrive in a short period, they can put pressure on housing, schools and transport, particularly in major cities where most newcomers tend to settle. There may also be concerns among local workers that competition from abroad will reduce wages or limit their own job opportunities, which can lead to social tension if it is not managed carefully. In addition, relying on foreign recruitment may reduce the incentive for governments and employers to invest in training their own citizens.

These disadvantages, though, can be managed through sensible planning. Governments can match recruitment to genuine shortages, invest in infrastructure where newcomers settle and continue funding domestic training programmes at the same time.

In conclusion, while attracting skilled workers from abroad can strain public services and cause some local resentment, its contribution to filling vital roles and supporting an ageing population make it highly beneficial. On balance, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

answers.text:
Many economies now rely on targeted immigration schemes to attract qualified professionals from abroad, particularly in sectors such as healthcare, engineering and technology. Although this strategy is not without complications, I would argue that, for the receiving country, its advantages clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

The most compelling benefit is the speed with which skills gaps can be closed. Domestic training pipelines take years to respond to changes in demand, and in the meantime shortages of nurses or software engineers can lengthen waiting lists, delay infrastructure projects and deter investment. Recruiting professionals who are already qualified allows these needs to be met almost immediately, and without the host country bearing the cost of their education. Skilled migrants also tend to be of working age and in well-paid employment, so they make a substantial contribution to public finances, which is increasingly valuable in societies where a shrinking workforce must support a growing number of retirees. Moreover, diverse teams often bring new perspectives, languages and international networks that strengthen innovation and trade.

The disadvantages are nonetheless significant. Rapid population growth in particular regions can outpace the supply of housing and school places, and if this pressure coincides with stagnant wages in some sectors, it can fuel resentment and social division. Employers may also come to regard overseas recruitment as a cheaper alternative to developing local talent, leaving domestic workers without opportunities to acquire in-demand skills. Finally, successful integration requires sustained investment in language support and the recognition of foreign qualifications, without which highly trained migrants may end up underemployed.

Crucially, these problems stem mainly from poor planning rather than from skilled migration itself, and they can be addressed through coordinated housing policy, parallel investment in domestic training and effective integration programmes.

In conclusion, attracting skilled workers from abroad carries social and practical challenges, but its contribution to essential services, public finances and economic dynamism means that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages for the receiving country.

In conclusion, investing in space research has benefits such as new technology and scientific knowledge, but it is also very expensive and some people believe the money should use for poor people. In my opinion, governments should continue space research but spend reasonable amount of money on it.

A number of governments are committing large budgets to space exploration and research. While these programmes can deliver significant scientific and economic benefits, they are also criticised for their high cost at a time when many problems on Earth remain unsolved.

One of the main advantages of space research is the technology it produces. Satellites, which were developed through space programmes, now support weather forecasting, global communications and navigation systems that people rely on every day. In addition, many innovations originally designed for space missions, such as improved materials and medical equipment, have later found uses in everyday life. Space research also expands scientific knowledge, helping us to understand the origins of the universe and to monitor changes in Earth's climate from above. Furthermore, ambitious space projects can inspire young people to pursue careers in science and engineering, which benefits the wider economy in the long term.

On the other hand, the most common criticism is the enormous expense involved. Critics argue that the money spent on launching rockets could instead be used to improve healthcare, education or housing, or to reduce poverty, which would have a more immediate impact on people's lives. There are also environmental concerns, since rocket launches produce emissions and the growing amount of debris orbiting the planet could damage working satellites. Finally, space missions involve considerable risks, and failures can waste vast sums of money in a matter of seconds.

In conclusion, government investment in space research brings valuable technological progress, scientific understanding and inspiration for future generations. However, its high cost and environmental impact means that governments need to balance this spending carefully against more urgent needs on Earth.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Space research has long been one of the most expensive and ambitious undertakings a government can pursue, and several countries are now expanding their programmes considerably. The merits of such investment are substantial, but so too are the objections, particularly regarding cost and priorities.

The case in favour rests first on the practical returns. Much of modern life depends on infrastructure that emerged from space programmes: satellites underpin weather forecasting, telecommunications, navigation and disaster monitoring, while technologies developed for spaceflight have been adapted for use in medicine and materials science. Space-based observation is also indispensable for understanding our own planet, providing long-term data on ice cover, sea levels and deforestation that would be impossible to gather from the ground. Beyond these tangible benefits, space exploration pushes the boundaries of human knowledge and, perhaps just as importantly, captures the public imagination, encouraging young people to pursue careers in science and engineering.

Against this, critics raise a powerful moral argument. When public resources are finite, allocating vast sums to exploring distant planets can appear difficult to justify while citizens lack adequate healthcare, housing or education. The benefits of space research are often long-term and uncertain, whereas the needs of the poor are immediate and pressing. There are environmental and practical concerns as well: each launch consumes enormous quantities of fuel, and the accumulation of debris in orbit increasingly threatens the satellites on which everyday services depend. Moreover, national prestige can sometimes drive spending more than genuine scientific value.

In conclusion, government investment in space research yields important technologies, scientific insight and inspiration, yet it competes with urgent social needs and carries environmental risks. The challenge for policymakers is therefore not whether to fund space programmes at all, but how to ensure that such spending remains proportionate and delivers clear public benefit.

Nowadays, many children's free time is filled with structured activities such as sports training, music lessons and language classes, leaving little opportunity for unstructured play. Although these activities offer real benefits, I believe that when they replace free play almost entirely, the disadvantages are greater.

There is no doubt that organised activities can be valuable. They allow children to develop specific talents, whether in football, swimming or playing the violin, under the guidance of qualified instructors. Regular practice also teaches perseverance and time management, and team sports in particular help children learn to cooperate and cope with both winning and losing. For working parents, clubs and lessons provide a safe and supervised environment, which is reassuring when children cannot be left alone at home.

However, free play offers benefits that structured activities cannot provide. When children invent their own games, they have to negotiate rules, solve disagreements and use their imagination without an adult telling them what to do. These experiences develop creativity, independence and social skills that are important throughout life. If every afternoon is scheduled, children lose these opportunities and may become dependent on adults to organise their entertainment. Moreover, a busy timetable of activities can cause stress and tiredness, especially when combined with homework, and some children feel pressured to perform well rather than simply enjoying themselves. There is also a financial aspect, as fees for lessons and equipment can be a heavy burden for many families.

In conclusion, organised activities help children to develop skills and discipline in a safe setting. Nevertheless, as free play is essential for creativity, independence and wellbeing, I believe the drawbacks of filling children's free time with structured activities outweighs the advantages, and a better balance between the two are needed.

In many families, children's leisure time is now carefully organised around sports clubs, music lessons and tutoring sessions, with unstructured play increasingly squeezed out. While organised activities undoubtedly have value, I would argue that when they come to dominate childhood, their disadvantages outweigh their advantages.

The benefits of structured activities are clear. Expert coaching allows children to acquire skills, from swimming to playing an instrument, that they would be unlikely to master alone, and the discipline of regular practice teaches persistence and the satisfaction of gradual improvement. Team sports and ensembles also foster cooperation and a sense of belonging, while giving children the experience of both success and disappointment in a supportive setting. For parents with demanding jobs, supervised activities offer the additional reassurance that their children are safe and productively occupied.

Free play, however, contributes to development in ways that adult-led activities cannot replicate. When children are left to their own devices, they must invent games, agree on rules and resolve conflicts among themselves, exercising creativity, negotiation and problem-solving in a genuinely independent way. Unstructured time also allows them to explore their own interests rather than those chosen for them, and simply to rest. A childhood filled with back-to-back commitments risks producing young people who are accomplished but anxious, accustomed to constant evaluation and uncomfortable with boredom, which is itself an important stimulus for imagination. The cost of multiple activities can also place considerable strain on family budgets and widen the gap between children from wealthier and poorer households.

In conclusion, organised activities provide valuable skills, discipline and safety, but they cannot substitute for the independence and creativity that free play nurtures. When structured activities largely replace unsupervised play, I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and families should deliberately protect time for children simply to play.

In some countries, important public services like water, electricity and trains are run by private companies and not by the government. There are some advantages of this system, but I believe the disadvantages are more.

On the one hand, private companies can be more efficient than government. They want to make profit, so they try to reduce waste and use their money carefully. Also, because of competition, companies must give a good service or customers will choose another company. For example, if there are different electricity companies, people can change to the one which is cheaper. In addition, private companies often invest in new technology, for example new trains, which can make the service better.

On the other hand, there are many disadvantages. The most important is that private companies care about profit more than people. They may increase the prices, and poor families will find it difficult to pay their bills for water and electricity, which is basic needs. Moreover, companies may not want to provide service in places where they cannot make money, such as small villages in the countryside. Another problem is that there is often no real competition, especially for water and railways, because only one company control the service in each area. So customers have no choice and must accept high prices and bad service.

In conclusion, private companies can bring efficiency and new technology to public services. However, I think these services are too important to be run only for profit. For this reason, the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, and the government should keep controlling of important services like water and electricity.

answers.text:
In a number of countries, essential services such as water, electricity and rail transport have been transferred from state control to private companies. Although privatisation can bring certain benefits, I believe that, for services of this kind, the disadvantages are more significant.

Supporters of privatisation argue that private firms are more efficient than state organisations. Because they need to make a profit, companies have a strong incentive to cut unnecessary costs, reduce bureaucracy and modernise their operations. Where there is genuine competition, as in some electricity markets, customers can switch providers, which encourages companies to keep prices competitive and improve customer service. Privatisation can also relieve governments of the huge cost of maintaining infrastructure, allowing public money to be spent elsewhere.

However, these advantages are often limited in practice. Water supply and railways are natural monopolies: it is not practical to build competing pipelines or rail lines, so customers in a particular area usually have only one provider. Without real competition, a private company may raise prices while failing to invest in maintenance, since its main responsibility is to its shareholders. Moreover, profit-driven companies may reduce services that are unprofitable, such as rural train routes, even though these are vital for the communities that depend on them. Because water and electricity are basic necessities, sharp price rises can push low-income households into serious hardship, and people cannot simply choose to stop using them.

For these reasons, even where private companies are involved, strong government regulation is essential to protect the public interest.

In conclusion, private ownership may improve efficiency in some cases, but for essential services that operate as monopolies and serve basic needs, the risks of higher prices, underinvestment and reduced access are too great. Therefore, I believe the disadvantages outweighs the advantages.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The transfer of utilities and railways from state ownership to private operators has been one of the most contested economic policies of recent decades. While private management can bring genuine improvements in efficiency, I would argue that, for services on which every citizen depends, the disadvantages ultimately prevail.

The principal argument for privatisation is that the discipline of the market drives better performance. State-run organisations are sometimes criticised for overstaffing, slow decision-making and political interference, whereas private firms, answerable to shareholders, have a clear incentive to control costs and innovate. Private capital can also fund investment in new trains, power stations or treatment plants without adding to public debt, and in sectors where competition is feasible, such as electricity retail, consumers may benefit from lower prices and more responsive service.

The weakness of this argument is that many essential services do not lend themselves to meaningful competition. A household cannot choose between rival water networks, and a commuter cannot select an alternative railway line; in such cases privatisation simply replaces a public monopoly with a private one. Once the pressure of competition is absent, the profit motive may encourage operators to raise charges, pay generous dividends and defer costly maintenance, leaving the public to deal with the consequences, from leaking pipes to unreliable trains. Accountability is also weakened: citizens can vote out a government that mismanages public services, but they have far less influence over a private company. Furthermore, because these services are necessities rather than optional purchases, price rises fall disproportionately on the poorest households.

Strict regulation can moderate some of these problems, but regulators often struggle to match the expertise and resources of the companies they oversee.

In conclusion, although private operators may deliver efficiency gains and fresh investment, the monopoly nature of many essential services, weaker accountability and the risk to vulnerable households mean that, in my view, the disadvantages of privatisation outweigh its advantages.

Nowadays, most people get their news from the internet instead of reading newspapers or watching television. This change has both advantages and disadvantages.

The main advantage of online news is that it is fast. When something important happen in the world, people can read about it on their phone in a few minutes, but newspapers have to wait until the next day. Another advantage is that most online news is free, so people do not need to buy a newspaper every day. Also, people can choose the topics they are interested in, for example sport, technology or business, and they can read news from many different countries. In addition, readers can write comments and share their opinion with other people.

However, online news also have some disadvantages. The biggest problem is fake news. Anyone can write something on the internet or on social media, and many people believe it without checking. This can cause confusion and even danger, for example when false information about health spreads quickly. Moreover, many websites use shocking titles to attract more clicks, so the news is not always serious or accurate. Another disadvantage is that social media shows people only the news which they already agree with, so they do not see other opinions.

In conclusion, getting news online is quick, cheap and convenient, and people have more choice than before. However, there is a big risk of false informations and one-sided news. I think people should read news from reliable websites and always check the facts before they believe or share something.

answers.text:
Over the last two decades, the internet has overtaken newspapers and television as the main source of news for many people. This shift has made information more accessible than ever before, but it has also created new problems regarding reliability and balance.

One clear advantage of online news is its speed. Breaking stories are reported within minutes and constantly updated, whereas printed newspapers can only report events the following day. Online news is also highly convenient and usually free, since readers can access it on their phones wherever they are. Another benefit is variety: people can compare coverage from many different outlets, including international sources, and focus on topics that interest them. Furthermore, the internet gives ordinary people a voice, as eyewitnesses can share photos and videos of events as they happen, sometimes before professional journalists arrive.

On the other hand, the move online has several drawbacks. The most serious is the spread of misinformation. Unlike established newspapers and broadcasters, which employ editors to check facts, many websites and social media accounts publish claims without any verification, and false stories can go viral before they are corrected. In addition, because many online outlets depend on advertising revenue, they are tempted to use sensational headlines to attract clicks, which can lower the quality of journalism. Algorithms on social media also tend to show users content that matches their existing views, so people may be exposed to only one side of an issue, which can increase division in society.

In conclusion, online news offers speed, convenience and a wide range of perspectives, but it also makes it harder to separate reliable reporting from rumours and can reinforce people's existing beliefs. For this reason, readers need to develop the skills to evaluate the sources they relies on.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The way people consume news has been transformed in a single generation, with websites, apps and social media now replacing the morning paper and the evening bulletin for a large share of the population. This transition has democratised access to information, yet it has also weakened some of the safeguards that traditional media provided.

The advantages are considerable. Online platforms deliver news almost instantaneously, allowing readers to follow developing stories in real time rather than waiting for the next edition or broadcast. Much of this content is free and available on a device most people carry at all times, which has made current affairs accessible to groups who might never have bought a newspaper. The sheer breadth of sources is also valuable: a reader can compare how a single event is covered by outlets in different countries, consult specialist analysis on niche subjects and even see footage captured by eyewitnesses on the ground. In this sense, the internet has diversified the range of voices that shape public debate.

However, the same openness brings serious drawbacks. Because anyone can publish, the traditional filters of editorial oversight and fact-checking are frequently absent, and misleading or entirely fabricated stories can circulate widely before they are challenged. The economic model of much online journalism compounds the problem: revenue depends on clicks, which rewards sensationalism over careful reporting. Perhaps most insidiously, the algorithms that curate news feeds tend to prioritise content that confirms users' existing views, gradually enclosing them in so-called echo chambers and contributing to a more polarised society. The shift has also undermined the finances of many local newspapers, leaving some communities with little independent coverage of local affairs.

In conclusion, online news offers unprecedented speed, accessibility and diversity, but these gains are accompanied by a decline in reliability and a tendency towards polarisation. Its value therefore depends heavily on readers' willingness to seek out trustworthy sources and a range of perspectives.

In many countries today, people use bank cards and mobile phone apps to pay for things more than cash. In my opinion, this change has more advantages than disadvantages.

The first advantage is that paying by card or phone is very quick and easy. You only need to touch the card on the machine and the payment is finish in a second. People do not need to carry a lot of coins and notes in their wallet, and they do not need to go to the bank to take out money. Secondly, it is safer. If a person lose his wallet with cash, the money is gone forever, but if he lose his card, he can call the bank and block it. Also, the apps show all the payments, so people can check how much money they spend every month and control their budget.

However, there are some disadvantages as well. Some old people do not know how to use smartphone apps and they prefer to pay with cash, so they may find it difficult in shops which only accept cards. In addition, some people spend more money when they pay by card, because they do not see the money leaving their hands. Another problem is that hackers can steal the information of bank accounts online. Finally, if there is a problem with the internet or electricity, people cannot pay at all.

In conclusion, using cards and mobile apps have some disadvantages, such as problems for elderly people and the risk of online crime. However, I believe that the advantages like speed, convenience and safety are more important, so the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

In many parts of the world, cash is gradually being replaced by debit cards, contactless payments and mobile phone apps. Although this trend creates difficulties for certain groups, I believe that its advantages are greater than its disadvantages.

The most obvious benefit of digital payments is convenience. Paying with a card or phone takes only a few seconds, there is no need to search for the correct change, and people can shop online or transfer money to friends instantly. This also benefits businesses, which save the time and expense of counting, storing and transporting cash. Secondly, electronic payment is generally safer. Carrying large amounts of cash makes people a target for theft, whereas a lost card can be cancelled immediately. In addition, every digital transaction is recorded, which makes it harder for criminals to avoid paying tax or to hide illegal earnings. Banking apps also allow users to monitor their spending in detail, which can help them manage their finances more responsibly.

Nevertheless, there are some drawbacks to a cashless society. Elderly people and those without bank accounts or smartphones may be excluded if shops and services stop accepting cash. It is often argued that people spend more when they pay digitally, since tapping a card feels less real than handing over notes. There are also concerns about privacy, as banks and technology companies can collect detailed information about where and how people spend their money, and about vulnerability to cyber-attacks or technical failures.

However, these problems can be reduced if governments ensure that cash remains available for those who need it and introduce strong rules on data protection.

In conclusion, although digital payments raise issues of exclusion, overspending and privacy, their speed, safety and transparency make them a positive development. Overall, the advantages clearly outweighs the disadvantages.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The steady decline of cash in favour of cards, contactless technology and mobile wallets has been one of the quieter revolutions in everyday life. Although this shift poses genuine risks for certain groups, I am convinced that its advantages outweigh its disadvantages, provided that access to cash is not abolished altogether.

For consumers, the appeal of digital payments lies chiefly in their convenience. Transactions are completed in seconds, purchases can be made online or across borders without exchanging currency, and money can be sent to friends or family at the touch of a button. Electronic payments also offer greater security for individuals: a stolen wallet full of notes is usually lost for good, whereas a card can be frozen instantly and fraudulent transactions are often refunded. At a wider level, a largely cashless economy is more transparent. Because every payment leaves a record, it becomes considerably harder to conceal income from tax authorities or to launder the proceeds of crime, which ultimately benefits honest taxpayers. Businesses, meanwhile, save on the costs of handling, securing and banking physical money.

The drawbacks, however, should not be underestimated. Those who are elderly, on low incomes or living in areas with poor connectivity may find themselves excluded from essential services if cash ceases to be accepted. Digital payments can also make spending feel less tangible, which may encourage some people to overspend or fall into debt. Furthermore, a society dependent on electronic systems is exposed to cyber-attacks and outages, and the detailed data generated by every transaction raises legitimate questions about surveillance and privacy.

These concerns, though serious, argue for safeguards rather than a rejection of digital payments. Guaranteeing that cash remains legal tender and widely accepted, while enforcing robust data-protection standards, would address the most significant risks.

In conclusion, the move away from cash brings efficiency, security and transparency that benefit individuals and society as a whole. As long as vulnerable groups are protected, the advantages of this trend clearly outweigh its disadvantages.

Mobile phones have become a constant presence in the lives of teenagers, and it is now common for students to be distracted by them even in the middle of a lesson. This habit creates difficulties for both learners and teachers, but I believe it can be managed through a combination of school policy and better classroom practice.

The most obvious problem is the damage to students' learning. Checking a notification may take only a few seconds, but each interruption breaks a student's concentration, and it can take several minutes to fully refocus on a difficult explanation. Over time, pupils who are frequently distracted tend to develop gaps in their understanding, which is often reflected in lower exam results. A second issue concerns the class as a whole. When teachers have to repeatedly ask students to put their phones away, valuable teaching time is lost and the atmosphere of the lesson can become tense. In addition, a student secretly watching videos can easily distract the classmates sitting around them.

There are, however, practical ways of tackling these problems. The most effective is probably a clear and consistently enforced policy, such as requiring students to hand in their phones at the start of the day or keep them switched off in lockers. Such rules only work if every teacher applies them, otherwise students quickly learn in which lessons they can ignore them. At the same time, schools could teach pupils about healthy technology habits, so that they understand why constant phone use harms their attention. Teachers can also reduce the temptation by designing more interactive lessons, since students who are actively involved are less likely to reach for their phones.

In conclusion, phone use during lessons weakens concentration and wastes valuable teaching time. Firm school rules, supported by education about digital habits and engaging teaching, offer the best chance of solving the problem.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In classrooms across the world, the smartphone has become a persistent rival for students' attention. While the device itself is not inherently harmful, its presence during lessons undermines both individual learning and the functioning of the class, and addressing this requires action from schools, teachers and families alike.

The most serious consequence is the erosion of sustained concentration. Learning complex material, whether an algebraic proof or the causes of a historical conflict, depends on following a line of reasoning without interruption. A single glance at a message may seem trivial, yet it fractures that reasoning, and a student who is interrupted repeatedly is left with a fragmented grasp of the topic that later surfaces as poor performance in assessments. Beyond the individual, phones damage the shared environment of the classroom. Teachers forced to police screen use lose time that should be spent teaching, and the constant tension between enforcement and instruction can sour relationships between staff and pupils. Moreover, distraction is contagious: one student scrolling through videos can draw the attention of an entire row.

The most direct remedy is an unambiguous, school-wide policy. Requiring phones to be stored in lockers or sealed pouches during the school day removes the temptation altogether, and applying the rule uniformly prevents the inconsistency that students are quick to exploit. However, restriction alone treats the symptom rather than the cause. Schools should also build digital literacy into the curriculum, helping young people understand how apps are designed to capture attention and how to regain control over their own habits. Parents have a complementary role in reinforcing these messages at home, while teachers can reduce the appeal of the phone by making lessons more participatory and less reliant on passive listening.

In short, mobile phones weaken concentration, waste teaching time and strain classroom relationships. A consistent ban, combined with education that equips students to manage technology themselves, offers the most durable solution.

In recent years, a lot of people have moved from the countryside to big cities because they want to find a job. Because of this, many cities become overcrowded. In this essay I will explain the problems which this causes and some measures to deal with them.

The main problem of overcrowding is housing. When too many people come to the city, there is not enough houses for everyone, so the rent becomes very expensive. Many poor people have to live in small rooms or in slums with bad conditions, where there is no clean water. Another problem is traffic. The roads are full of cars and buses, and people spend a long time to go to work every day. Also, the air pollution is increasing because of so many vehicles, and this is bad for people health.

There are several measures that government can take. First, they should build more cheap apartments for low-income workers, so they do not need to live in slums. Second, the public transport must be improved. If there are more metro lines and buses, less people will use their own cars and the traffic will be reduced. In addition, the government can create jobs in the rural areas, for example by building factories or supporting farmers. In this way, young people will not need to move to the city to find a work.

In conclusion, overcrowding in cities causes problems such as expensive housing, traffic jams and pollution. I believe that the government should build cheap housing, improve transport and develop the countryside, because this will make life better for everyone.

answers.text:
The steady movement of people from rural areas to cities in search of employment has left many urban centres struggling to cope with their growing populations. This essay will examine the main difficulties that overcrowding creates and suggest some measures that could ease them.

Perhaps the most serious problem is the shortage of affordable housing. As demand for accommodation rises faster than new homes can be built, rents increase sharply, and many newcomers on low wages are forced into cramped, poorly maintained buildings or informal settlements that lack basic services such as sanitation. Overcrowding also places enormous pressure on infrastructure. Roads become congested, public transport is packed at peak times and hospitals and schools are often unable to serve everyone, which lowers the quality of life for long-term residents as well as new arrivals.

To deal with these issues, governments need to act on two levels. Within cities, authorities should invest in large-scale social housing and expand public transport networks, for example by building new metro lines that connect affordable suburbs with business districts. This would allow people to live further from the centre without spending hours commuting. However, such measures only address the symptoms, therefore it is also important to reduce the pressure to migrate in the first place. Investing in rural areas, by improving roads, internet access and local industries, would give people realistic opportunities to earn a living without leaving their hometowns. Tax incentives could also encourage companies to relocate to smaller cities, which spreads economic growth more evenly.

In conclusion, rural-urban migration leads to housing shortages and overloaded public services in large cities. A combination of better urban planning and genuine investment in the countryside is the most effective way to tackle these problems.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Across much of the world, cities continue to swell as rural residents arrive in pursuit of work. Although this migration fuels economic growth, it frequently outpaces the capacity of urban areas to absorb newcomers, producing social and environmental strains that demand a coordinated policy response.

The most visible consequence is a crisis of housing. When population growth exceeds the rate of construction, prices rise beyond the reach of low-paid workers, who are pushed into overcrowded rented rooms or informal settlements on the urban fringe. These districts typically lack reliable water, sanitation and electricity, creating conditions in which disease spreads easily. A second set of problems stems from overstretched infrastructure. Transport networks designed for far smaller populations become gridlocked, lengthening commutes and worsening air quality, while schools and clinics struggle to meet demand. The result is a decline in living standards not only for migrants but for established residents too, which can in turn breed resentment between the two groups.

Tackling these difficulties requires measures both inside and outside the city. Within urban areas, governments should prioritise the construction of affordable housing and pair it with mass transit, so that new residential zones are connected to centres of employment rather than isolated from them. Upgrading informal settlements with basic services, rather than simply clearing them, is often a more humane and cost-effective approach. Equally important, however, is reducing the imbalance that drives migration in the first place. Investment in rural infrastructure, agricultural modernisation and regional industry can create viable livelihoods outside the major cities, while incentives for businesses to establish themselves in secondary towns would distribute economic opportunity more evenly.

In conclusion, rapid urban migration strains housing, transport and public services, lowering the quality of life for many residents. The most lasting solution lies in combining well-planned urban investment with a serious commitment to developing rural regions.

In many big cities, the price of houses and flats is very high, and workers like nurses and teachers cannot afford to live close to where they work. This situation causes several problems, and in this essay I will discuss them and suggest some solutions.

The first problem is that these workers have to travel very long distances every day. For example, a nurse who lives outside the city may need to spend two hours in a train to arrive to the hospital. This make them very tired and stressed, and a tired nurse or teacher cannot do their job well. Another problem is that many of them decide to leave their job or move to a cheaper city. As a result, hospitals and schools in the city do not have enough staffs, and people who live there receive worse service. For instance, classes become bigger and patients must wait longer for treatment.

There are some solutions to this problem. Firstly, the government can build special houses for essential workers with lower rent. This is already happening in some countries and it help workers to stay near their workplace. Secondly, employers such as hospitals could give their staff extra money for housing or for transport. Thirdly, the government should control the rent prices, so the landlords cannot increase them too much every year.

In conclusion, the high cost of housing in cities make it difficult for essential workers to live near their job, which cause tiredness and a shortage of staff. I think the best solution is to build affordable housing for these workers and also give them some financial support.

In many major cities, property prices and rents have risen so steeply that key workers such as nurses, teachers and police officers are being priced out of the areas they serve. This trend has serious consequences for both the workers themselves and the wider community, although there are several ways in which it could be addressed.

For individual workers, the main problem is the burden of long commutes. Many essential staff are forced to live in distant suburbs or neighbouring towns, which means spending several hours travelling each day, often on shifts that start early in the morning or finish late at night. This leads to exhaustion and stress, and it is not surprising that many eventually decide to leave the profession or relocate to cheaper regions. The consequences for the city are equally serious. Hospitals and schools struggle to recruit and keep staff, resulting in larger classes, longer waiting times and a greater dependence on expensive temporary workers.

One effective solution would be for local governments to build or subsidise housing reserved specifically for essential workers, offered at rents linked to their salaries rather than to the market. Public employers could also play a role, for example by converting unused land owned by hospitals into staff accommodation. In addition, a housing allowance for those working in high-cost areas would help to close the gap between wages and living expenses. In the longer term, governments need to increase the overall supply of affordable homes, since the underlying problem is that there are simply not enough housing for ordinary earners.

In conclusion, unaffordable housing leaves essential workers exhausted and cities short of vital staff. Dedicated affordable housing, targeted allowances and a broader increase in housing supply would together help to keep these workers close to where they are needed.

The soaring cost of urban housing has created a paradox in many cities: the people whose work keeps them functioning, including nurses, teachers and care staff, increasingly cannot afford to live in them. This essay argues that the problem damages both the wellbeing of these workers and the quality of public services, and that it calls for targeted housing policy alongside broader reform.

At a personal level, being priced out imposes a heavy daily toll. Essential workers displaced to distant towns face lengthy commutes that, combined with irregular shifts, leave little time for rest or family life. Chronic fatigue is not merely unpleasant; in professions where alertness matters, such as nursing, it can compromise the safety of those in their care. Unsurprisingly, many eventually conclude that the sacrifice is not worth it and either leave the profession or move to cheaper regions. For the city, the cumulative effect is a persistent shortage of skilled staff. Schools rely on a rotating cast of supply teachers, hospitals spend heavily on agency nurses, and residents experience longer waits and less continuity of care. Emergency services, too, become less resilient when those who staff them live an hour or more away.

The most direct response is to provide housing designated for key workers, with rents set as a proportion of income rather than market value. Public bodies are often well placed to do this, since hospitals, universities and councils frequently own land that could be developed for staff accommodation. Location-based salary supplements can offer further relief, although they risk being absorbed by rising rents if supply remains constrained. Ultimately, therefore, such measures must be accompanied by a sustained expansion of affordable housing, achieved through planning reform and public construction.

In conclusion, unaffordable housing exhausts essential workers and weakens the services cities depend on. Dedicated key-worker housing offers immediate relief, but lasting improvement depends on building enough homes for ordinary earners.

Every day, a huge amount of food is thrown away by families, restaurants and supermarkets. This is a serious problem because many people in the world do not have enough to eat. This essay will discuss the causes of food waste and what can be done to reduce it.

There are some reasons why people waste food. The first reason is that many families buy more food than they need. When they go shopping, they see special offers like buy one get one free, so they buy a lot and later the food go bad in the fridge. Another reason is that people are confused about the date on the food packet. They think the food is dangerous after the date, so they throw it even if it is still good to eat. In restaurants, the portions are often too big, and customers cannot finish their meal. Also, supermarkets throw away fruit and vegetables which do not look perfect, because customers do not want to buy them.

There are several ways to reduce this problem. Firstly, people should plan their meals before shopping and make a list, so they only buy what they really need. Secondly, the government could make the labels more clear and explain the difference between use by and best before. Thirdly, supermarkets and restaurants should give their extra food to charities or food banks instead to throw it away. Some countries already have laws about this and it is very useful.

In conclusion, food waste is caused by buying too much, confusion about dates and big portions in restaurants. If families, business and government all take action, the amount of food waste can be reduced a lot.

A significant proportion of the food produced around the world never reaches anyone's plate, being discarded instead by households, restaurants and retailers. This essay will outline the main reasons for this waste and suggest how it could be reduced.

At the household level, the key cause is poor planning combined with the relatively low cost of food in many countries. Shoppers often buy more than they need, particularly when tempted by multi-buy promotions, and perishable items such as bread and salad are then forgotten until they have spoiled. Confusion over date labels makes the situation worse, as many consumers treat a best-before date as a strict deadline and throw away food that is perfectly safe. In the commercial sector, the causes are somewhat different. Restaurants frequently serve portions that are larger than customers can eat, while supermarkets reject large quantities of fruit and vegetables for cosmetic reasons and discard stock once it passes its display date.

Reducing this waste requires action from several directions. Firstly, clearer labelling would make a considerable difference; if packaging only showed a use-by date where there is a genuine safety risk, consumers would throw away far less. Public campaigns that teaches simple habits, such as checking the fridge before shopping and freezing leftovers, could also change behaviour over time. For businesses, governments could introduce regulations requiring large supermarkets to donate unsold but edible food to charities rather than sending it to landfill. Restaurants, meanwhile, could offer smaller portions at lower prices and encourage diners to take leftovers home.

In conclusion, food waste results mainly from overbuying, misunderstanding of labels and commercial practices that put appearance and convenience before efficiency. A mixture of better information, changes in consumer habits and sensible regulation could reduce it substantially.

answers.text:
Despite widespread concern about food insecurity, vast quantities of edible food are discarded daily in homes, restaurants and supermarkets. The causes differ across these settings, but in each case waste stems from habits and systems that prioritise convenience over efficiency, and it can be reduced considerably through a mix of education, regulation and incentives.

In households, waste is largely a product of how people shop and store food. Relatively low prices in wealthier countries mean that discarding a half-used loaf carries little financial sting, while bulk promotions encourage people to buy more than they can realistically consume before it spoils. Misleading date labels compound the problem: many consumers fail to distinguish between a use-by date, which concerns safety, and a best-before date, which relates only to quality, and so throw away food that is still perfectly edible. The commercial sector has its own drivers. Supermarkets impose strict cosmetic standards that exclude misshapen produce before it even reaches the shelves, and they routinely overstock to avoid empty displays. Restaurants, for their part, often serve generous portions as a marker of value, much of which is left uneaten.

Tackling these causes calls for measures tailored to each. Simplifying date labelling, and removing best-before dates from items such as fresh fruit altogether, would prevent a great deal of unnecessary disposal at home, particularly if accompanied by public campaigns on meal planning and storage. For retailers, legislation obliging large stores to redistribute surplus edible food to charities has proved workable in several countries and could be adopted more widely. Supermarkets could also be encouraged to sell imperfect produce at a discount, and restaurants to offer flexible portion sizes.

In conclusion, food waste arises from overbuying, confusing labels and commercial practices that value appearance and abundance. Clearer information, redistribution laws and changes to retail and catering practice together offer a realistic path to reducing it.

In the last few years, extreme weather such as floods and heatwaves are happening more often in many countries. These events create a lot of difficulties for local communities. This essay will look at these problems and how communities can be more prepared.

The first problem is damage to homes and buildings. When there is a big flood, water enter into houses and destroys furniture and electrical things, and some families lose everything. Roads and bridges can also be broken, so people cannot go to work or school for many days. The second problem is health. During a heatwave, old people and small children can become very ill because of the high temperature, and some of them even die. After floods, the water is often dirty and it can spread diseases. In addition, farmers can lose their crops, and this make food more expensive for the whole community.

However, communities can prepare better for these events. One way is to build stronger infrastructure, for example flood walls and better drainage systems in the cities. Also, the local government should not allow people to build new houses in areas which flood very often. Another way is to give people information. If there is a good warning system on the phone and on television, people will have time to leave their homes before the flood arrive. For heatwaves, towns can open cool public buildings where old people can stay during the hottest part of day.

In conclusion, extreme weather causes damage to property, health problems and loss of crops. I think the best way to be prepare is to have strong infrastructure and a good warning system, so communities can protect theirselves.

answers.text:
As the climate changes, extreme weather events like floods, storms and heatwaves are occurring with increasing frequency in many regions. These events pose serious challenges for local communities, but careful planning can significantly reduce their impact.

The most immediate problem is the physical damage that such events cause. Floods can destroy homes, businesses and essential infrastructure within hours, leaving families homeless and cutting off access to hospitals, schools and workplaces. Rebuilding is often slow and expensive, and in poorer communities where few people have insurance, the financial losses can take years to recover from. Extreme heat creates a different but equally serious threat to public health. Elderly people, young children and those with existing medical conditions are especially vulnerable, and hospitals can quickly become overwhelmed during a prolonged heatwave. Furthermore, both floods and droughts can devastate local agriculture, which affects farmers' incomes and pushes up food prices for everyone.

Communities can prepare more effectively in several ways. First of all, investment in protective infrastructure, such as flood barriers, improved drainage and buildings designed to stay cool, would reduce the damage when disasters strike. Planning authorities should also stop approving new housing on floodplains, which only increase the number of people at risk. Secondly, early warning systems are essential. Sending alerts directly to mobile phones gives residents time to move valuables, evacuate or check on vulnerable neighbours. Finally, local councils could prepare detailed emergency plans, for example by identifying cooling centres for heatwaves and organising volunteers who know which residents live alone and might need help.

In conclusion, extreme weather threatens people's homes, health and livelihoods. By combining stronger infrastructure, sensible planning and effective warning systems, communities can become far more resilient to these growing risks.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Floods, storms and prolonged heatwaves, once regarded as rare events, are now a recurring feature of life in many parts of the world. Their consequences for local communities are wide-ranging, affecting property, health and livelihoods, but much of the harm can be mitigated if communities invest in preparation rather than simply reacting after disaster strikes.

The most tangible impact is the destruction of homes and infrastructure. A single severe flood can render entire streets uninhabitable, sever transport links and knock out power and water supplies, isolating residents from essential services. The costs of recovery fall disproportionately on low-income households, which are less likely to be insured and more likely to live in vulnerable locations. Heatwaves, though less visibly destructive, can be even more deadly. Prolonged high temperatures place severe strain on older people and those with chronic illnesses, particularly in densely built urban areas where heat is retained overnight. There are also slower economic consequences: repeated crop failures erode farmers' livelihoods, and small businesses forced to close again and again may never reopen.

Preparation must therefore operate on several levels. Physical adaptation is the foundation, from flood defences and permeable drainage to building codes that require better insulation and shading. Land-use planning matters just as much, since continuing to build on floodplains simply multiplies future losses. Infrastructure alone is insufficient, however, without effective communication. Reliable early warning systems, delivered through mobile networks and local media, give residents time to act, while clearly marked evacuation routes ensure that warnings translate into safety. Finally, strong community networks can make a decisive difference. Neighbourhood schemes that identify isolated or elderly residents, together with designated cooling centres, help ensure that the most vulnerable are not overlooked.

In conclusion, extreme weather damages property, endangers health and undermines local economies. Communities that combine resilient infrastructure, prudent planning and well-organised warning and support systems will be far better equipped to withstand these growing threats.

Nowadays, traffic congestion is becoming a big problem in many towns and cities around the world. This essay will discuss the problems that traffic jams cause and some solutions to solve them.

One of the main problem is that people waste a lot of time. Many workers spend one or two hours in their car every day, and this make them tired and stressed before they even start working. Also, when goods cannot be delivered on time, companies lose money, so it is bad for the economy too. Another serious problem is pollution. When many cars are stuck in traffic, their engines are still running and they produce a lot of smoke. This smoke is harmful for people who live near busy roads, especially children and old people, and it can cause breathing problems.

There are some ways to solve these problems. Firstly, the government should improve public transport. If buses and trains are cheap, fast and comfortable, many people will leave their cars at home. Secondly, cities can build more cycle lanes, so people can go to work by bicycle safely. This is also good for their health. Thirdly, some cities make drivers to pay money when they drive into the city centre at busy times. I think this is a good idea because it reduce the number of cars on the road. Finally, companies can let their employees to work from home some days of the week.

In conclusion, traffic congestion waste people's time, damages the economy and causes pollution. However, if governments and companies take the right actions, like better public transport and charges for drivers, this problem can be solved.

Traffic congestion has become a daily reality in many towns and cities, as the number of vehicles on the roads continues to grow faster than the capacity of the road network. This essay will discuss the main problems caused by congestion and propose some practical solutions.

Firstly, congestion has significant economic costs. Commuters lose hours each week sitting in traffic, which reduces the time they have for work, family and rest, and delayed delivery vehicles increase costs for businesses, which are eventually passed on to consumers. Secondly, and perhaps more seriously, heavy traffic damages the environment and public health. Vehicles moving slowly or idling in queues release large amounts of exhaust fumes, contributing to poor air quality in city centres and to respiratory illnesses such as asthma. The noise and stress associated with constant traffic also lowers the quality of life for people who live along busy roads.

There are several ways in which these problems could be tackled. The most effective long-term solution is to invest in reliable, affordable public transport, so that taking the bus or train becomes a more attractive option than driving. Cities which have developed efficient metro and tram systems generally have fewer cars on their streets. Alongside this, authorities could introduce congestion charges, which require drivers to pay to enter the busiest areas at peak times. This not only discourages unnecessary journeys but also raises money that can be reinvested in transport. Finally, encouraging cycling and walking through safe, separated lanes and pedestrian-friendly streets would provide a healthy alternative for shorter journeys.

In conclusion, traffic congestion wastes time and money and harms both the environment and people's health. A combination of better public transport, congestion charging and support for cycling offers the most realistic way to reduce it.

answers.text:
As car ownership has risen, the road networks of many towns and cities have become chronically congested, with rush-hour gridlock now an accepted part of urban life. This situation carries substantial economic, environmental and social costs, yet it is far from inevitable, and a number of well-tested measures can relieve it.

The economic burden of congestion is considerable. Time spent stationary in traffic is time lost to productive work or leisure, and unpredictable journey times make it harder for businesses to schedule deliveries and for employees to arrive punctually. These inefficiencies ripple through the economy, raising costs for firms and ultimately for consumers. The environmental and health consequences are equally serious. Stop-start driving is particularly inefficient, so congested streets generate disproportionate levels of exhaust emissions, degrading air quality and contributing to respiratory and heart disease. Residents of busy corridors also endure persistent noise, while heavy traffic discourages walking and cycling, reinforcing sedentary lifestyles.

Expanding road capacity might appear to be the obvious answer, but new roads tend to attract additional traffic and soon fill up again. A more effective strategy is to reduce demand for car travel. Frequent, affordable and reliable public transport is central to this, since people will only abandon their cars if a genuine alternative exists. Congestion charging, under which drivers pay to enter central zones at peak times, can then discourage non-essential journeys while generating revenue to fund transport improvements. Cities can further reshape travel habits by building safe, segregated cycle routes and by encouraging employers to adopt flexible hours and remote working, which spreads demand more evenly across the day.

In conclusion, congestion wastes time, burdens the economy and damages public health. Rather than building ever more roads, authorities should reduce reliance on cars through high-quality public transport, pricing mechanisms and support for active travel.

These days, many young people finish school or university but they cannot find a job easily. There are several reasons for this situation, and in this essay I will explain them and suggest what can be done to help.

The main reason is lack of experience. Most companies want to hire people who already have experience, but young graduates only have studied in the classroom. So it is like a circle: they cannot get experience without a job, and they cannot get a job without experience. Another reason is that what students learn at university is sometimes not useful for the job market. For example, many students study subjects like history or literature, but companies are looking for people with skills in technology or engineering. In addition, in some countries the economy is weak and there is not many jobs available for anyone, not only for young people.

There are some things that can help young people. Firstly, universities and colleges should work together with companies to give students internships during their study. In this way, students can get real experience and they will have more chance to get a job after graduate. Secondly, the government can give money to companies which employ young people, so that companies are more willing to hire them. Also, schools should give students better career advice, so they can choose a subject which have good job opportunities in the future.

In conclusion, young people find it difficult to get a job because they have no experience and their skills do not match what employers need. I believe that internships, government support and better advice can help them a lot to start their career.

In many countries, young people who have recently completed their education face considerable difficulty in finding employment. This essay will examine the main reasons for this and suggest some measures that could improve their prospects.

One major reason is the gap between the skills that young people acquire in education and those that employers actually require. Many school and university courses remains largely theoretical, so graduates may understand their subject well but lack practical abilities such as teamwork, communication or familiarity with workplace software. A related problem is the widespread demand for previous experience. Even entry-level positions often ask for one or two years of relevant work, which places young applicants in a frustrating situation where they cannot gain experience without first being employed. Finally, in periods of economic uncertainty, companies tend to reduce recruitment, and young people, who have the shortest work history, are usually the first to be affected.

To address these problems, educational institutions should work more closely with employers. Work placements and internships built into degree programmes would allow students to develop practical skills and graduate with genuine experience on their CV. Vocational courses and apprenticeships should also be given more status, since they prepare young people directly for specific careers. Governments, meanwhile, could offer financial incentives, such as reduced tax contributions, to companies that hire and train recent graduates, which would lower the risk of taking on inexperienced staff. In addition, better careers guidance in schools would help students to choose courses with realistic job prospects.

In conclusion, young people struggle to find work mainly because of a mismatch in skills, a lack of experience and weak economic conditions. Closer links between education and industry, combined with government incentives and better guidance, could make the transition from study to employment much smoother.

For many young people, the move from education into the workforce has become a prolonged and discouraging process, with months or even years passing before they secure stable employment. This difficulty has several interlocking causes, but it can be eased through closer cooperation between educators, employers and governments.

A fundamental cause is the mismatch between what education provides and what the labour market demands. Academic curricula often prioritise theoretical knowledge, leaving graduates ill-prepared for the practical and interpersonal demands of the workplace, while rapid technological change means that some skills are outdated almost as soon as they are taught. Compounding this is the so-called experience trap: employers, reluctant to invest in training, advertise even junior roles as requiring prior experience, which school leavers and graduates by definition do not possess. Structural factors play a part as well. In economies with sluggish growth, firms freeze recruitment, and because young people lack the seniority and networks of older workers, they bear a disproportionate share of the impact. The expansion of higher education has also intensified competition, as a degree no longer distinguishes an applicant in the way it once did.

Solutions should therefore target the transition itself. Embedding work placements and industry-led projects within courses would give students both relevant skills and demonstrable experience before they graduate. High-quality apprenticeships, which combine paid employment with structured training, offer an equally valuable route and deserve the same prestige as university study. Governments can reduce the risk employers perceive in hiring newcomers by subsidising wages or training costs for a limited period. Finally, careers guidance that draws on up-to-date labour market information would enable young people to make informed decisions about what to study.

In conclusion, youth unemployment stems from skills mismatches, the experience trap and wider economic weakness. By bridging the gap between education and work, societies can help young people establish themselves far more quickly.

Nowadays, many people spend most of their day sitting in front of a computer or watching TV, and they do not do much exercise. This lifestyle cause several problems, and in this essay I will discuss them and suggest how people can become more active.

The biggest problem is health. When people sit for many hours and do not move, they can easily put on weight, and this can lead to serious illnesses like heart disease and diabetes. Also, sitting too long is bad for the back and neck, especially for office workers who use computer all day. Another problem is mental health. Exercise helps people to feel relaxed and happy, so people who never do sport are more likely to feel stressed or depressed. Furthermore, when many people are ill, the country has to spend more money on hospitals, which is a problem for everyone.

There are some ways to encourage people to be more active. First, the government should build more parks, sports centres and cycle paths, and make them free or cheap, so everybody can use them. Second, companies can help their workers, for example by giving them a break every hour to walk around or by offering free gym membership. In addition, schools should have more PE lessons, because if children enjoy sport when they are young, they will continue it when they grow up. Finally, there should be advertisements on TV and social media to show people the benefit of exercise.

In conclusion, sitting too much can cause health problems for people and extra costs for the country. I think the government, companies and schools should all encourage people to do more physical activity and have more healthy lifestyle.

answers.text:
Modern lifestyles have become increasingly sedentary, with many people spending most of their working day at a desk and much of their free time in front of screens. This trend has serious consequences for individuals and society, although there are a number of ways to encourage people to move more.

The most significant problem is the impact on physical health. A lack of regular activity is closely linked to weight gain, which in turn raises the risk of conditions such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. Long periods of sitting can also cause back and joint pain, a common complaint among office workers. Physical inactivity affects mental wellbeing too, since exercise is known to reduce stress and improve mood, so people who rarely exercise may be more likely to experience anxiety or low energy. At a national level, these health problems place a heavy burden on healthcare systems, and they also reduce productivity when employees need time off due to illness.

Encouraging people to be more active requires making exercise easier and more appealing. Local authorities could invest in safe cycle lanes, well-maintained parks and affordable sports facilities, so that physical activity become part of everyday life rather than something requiring special effort. Employers also have a role to play, for instance by providing standing desks, encouraging walking meetings or subsidising gym membership. Schools are perhaps the most important place to start, because children who develop an enjoyment of sport are more likely to stay active as adults. Finally, public health campaigns could highlight that even small changes, such as taking the stairs or walking short distances, bring real benefits.

In conclusion, sedentary behaviour harms both physical and mental health and increases the pressure on public services. By making activity more accessible at home, at work and at school, governments and organisations can help people lead healthier lives.
