In recent years, people have become increasingly dependent on digital tools such as search engines and GPS applications to answer questions and find their way. This essay will explain why this shift has occurred and argue that, while it frees people from memorising facts, it can weaken their capacity for independent thought.

The main reason for this dependence is the sheer convenience of modern technology. With a smartphone in almost every pocket, any piece of information can be retrieved within seconds, so there seems little point in storing it in one's own memory. Why would a driver study a map when an app can calculate the fastest route and warn about traffic in real time? In addition, the amount of information people are expected to deal with has grown enormously, and handing routine facts over to devices allows them to cope with a demanding lifestyle. Many people no longer even know their close family members' phone numbers.

The effect on independent thinking is, in my view, largely negative. When answers are always available instantly, people have fewer reasons to work through a problem, evaluate evidence or remember what they have learnt. A student who immediately searches online for the solution to a maths question may get the correct answer but gains little understanding of the method behind it. Moreover, search engines rank results according to algorithms, so users often accept the first information they see without questioning its reliability. That said, technology can support critical thinking if it is used as a starting point for research rather than a substitute for it.

To conclude, people rely on technology because it is fast, convenient and helps them manage information overload. However, this habit can reduce people's ability to analyse and remember, and individuals should make conscious effort to think problems through before reaching for their phones.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Few people today would set off for an unfamiliar destination without a navigation app, and even fewer would try to recall an obscure fact when a search engine can supply it instantly. This growing reliance on technology stems largely from its convenience and ubiquity, and although it has clear benefits, I believe it risks eroding people's capacity to think independently.

The shift can be explained by several interrelated factors. The most obvious is accessibility: smartphones have placed vast quantities of information within constant reach, making the effort of memorisation seem unnecessary. At the same time, the pace of modern life encourages people to delegate routine mental tasks. A commuter juggling work messages and family arrangements has little incentive to learn a route by heart when an app will not only guide them but also adjust for traffic. Furthermore, these tools are generally accurate, so people have come to trust them more than their own, sometimes unreliable, recollection.

The consequences for independent thought are more troubling. Memory and reasoning are closely linked; people who store knowledge internally are better able to make connections, spot inconsistencies and form original judgements. When everything is looked up on demand, this internal framework is never built. Navigation offers a telling example: drivers who follow turn-by-turn instructions often develop little sense of how a city fits together and can become disoriented as soon as the signal drops. More broadly, search engines present information that has already been filtered and ranked, which can encourage passive acceptance rather than critical evaluation. Admittedly, technology can also stimulate thinking by exposing users to a wider range of sources, but this depends on people actively questioning what they find.

In conclusion, dependence on digital tools has arisen because they are fast, reliable and constantly available. While they undoubtedly save time, habitual reliance on them can weaken memory and discourage critical reasoning, so they are best treated as aids to thinking rather than replacements for it.

Nowadays artificial intelligence (AI) can make pictures, songs and even stories in few seconds. This essay will discuss how this change the way people value human creativity and whether we should limit AI in creative industries.

On the one hand, AI may reduce the value of human creativity for some people. When a computer can create a nice painting very quickly and cheap, some customers do not want to pay an artist for many hours of work. For example, a small company may use AI to design their logo instead of hiring a designer. As a result, people can think that creativity is not special anymore. On the other hand, I think many people will value human art even more because it is made by a real person with real feelings and experience. A song which is written by a singer about his own life have a meaning that a machine cannot copy.

In my opinion, there should be some limits on AI in creative industries. Firstly, AI programs learn from the works of human artists, and often these artists do not give permission or get any money. This is not fair and governments should make rules to protect them. Secondly, people should know if a book or a picture was made by AI, so companies must put a clear label on it. However, I do not think AI should be banned completely, because it can be a useful tool for artists to get new ideas.

In conclusion, AI can make some people think human creativity is less important, but others will value it more. I believe that there should be limits, such as protecting artists work and labelling AI products, but AI can still be used as a helpful tool.

answers.text:
The ability of artificial intelligence to generate artwork, music and fiction has raised important questions about the status of human creativity. In my view, AI is changing how creativity is valued in two opposite directions, and I believe some limits on its use in creative industries are necessary.

On one side, the availability of AI-generated content can make human creativity seem less valuable. Since an image or a piece of background music can now be produced in seconds at almost no cost, businesses may see little reason to commission professional illustrators or composers. When creative work becomes so easy to obtain, the public may start to regard it as a cheap product rather than the result of skill and effort. On the other side, this abundance could actually increase appreciation for genuinely human work. Many audiences value art because it reflects a person's emotions and experiences, and a novel inspired by the author's own struggles carries an authenticity that machine-generated text lacks. In the same way that handmade furniture is valued more highly than mass-produced items, human-created art may become a premium product.

As for regulation, I believe certain limits should be introduced. The most pressing issue is that AI systems are trained on huge collection of existing work, often without the consent of the original artists, who receive no payment. Laws should ensure that creators can decide whether their work is used and are compensated if it is. Furthermore, AI-generated content should be clearly labelled so that consumers know what they are buying. However, banning AI entirely from creative fields would be unrealistic and would deprive artists of a tool which can help with tasks such as editing or brainstorming.

In conclusion, AI may reduce the value people place on creativity in some areas while increasing it in others. Reasonable limits, particularly on training data and transparency, would protect artists without stopping innovation.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Now that algorithms can compose symphonies, write short stories and produce convincing portraits, the question of what makes human creativity valuable has become more pressing than ever. I would argue that AI is simultaneously cheapening some forms of creative work and deepening appreciation for others, and that carefully designed limits on its use are both justified and necessary.

The most immediate impact is economic. Commercial creativity, such as stock illustrations, advertising jingles or product descriptions, is increasingly treated as a commodity that AI can supply instantly and at negligible cost. In these areas, the perceived worth of human skill is clearly falling, and many freelance designers and writers have already seen demand for their services shrink. Yet this is only part of the picture. Art has never been valued solely for its surface qualities; audiences are also drawn to the intention, experience and vulnerability behind it. A song about loss means more when listeners know that its writer has actually grieved. Paradoxically, therefore, the flood of machine-generated content may make work that is demonstrably human rarer and more prized, much as handcrafted goods gained prestige after industrial production became widespread.

Regarding limits, a blanket ban would be neither practical nor desirable, since AI can be a genuinely useful instrument in the hands of artists. However, two forms of regulation seem essential. First, the data used to train these systems frequently consists of copyrighted work taken without permission, so creators should have the right to opt out and to receive fair payment when their work is used. Second, transparency is crucial: audiences and buyers deserve to know whether a piece was produced by a person or a program, which clear labelling requirements would guarantee.

In conclusion, AI is devaluing routine creative work while potentially elevating the status of authentic human expression. Rather than prohibiting the technology, societies should limit its use through fair rules on training data and mandatory disclosure, protecting artists while allowing innovation to continue.

First, the data used to train these systems frequently consists of copyrighted work taken without permission, so creators should have the right to opt out and to receive fair payment when their work is used. Second, transparency is crucial: audiences and buyers deserve to know whether a piece was produced by a person or a program, which clear labelling requirements would guarantee.
In conclusion,

AI is devaluing routine creative work while potentially elevating the status of authentic human expression. Rather than prohibiting the technology, societies should limit its use through fair rules on training data and mandatory disclosure, protecting artists while allowing innovation to continue.

In recent years, buying second-hand clothes has become more popular in many countries. This essay will explain the reasons for this trend and suggest some other ways that people can reduce the environmental damage caused by their clothes.

There are several reasons why people are interested in second-hand clothing. The first reason is money. Used clothes are much more cheaper than new ones, and many people, especially students, do not have a lot of money to spend. Secondly, people are more aware about environmental problems now. They know that fashion industry produces a lot of pollution and waste, so buying used items is a way to help the planet. Also, it is very easy to buy second-hand clothes today because there are many websites and apps where people can sell their old clothes. Some young people also think that vintage clothes look more unique and fashionable.

Apart from buying used clothes, there are other steps people can take. Firstly, they can buy less clothes and choose items with good quality that last for a long time. Cheap fast fashion clothes often break after few months and then they are thrown away. Secondly, people can repair their clothes instead of throwing them when there is a small hole. Thirdly, they can give their unwanted clothes to charity shops or recycle them, so they do not go to landfill. Finally, people can choose brands which use organic cotton or recycled materials.

In conclusion, second-hand clothes are popular because they are cheap, easy to buy and good for the environment. People can also help by buying fewer and better clothes, repairing them and recycling. If everyone do these things, the fashion industry will be less harmful.

Second-hand clothing, once associated mainly with people on low incomes, is now attracting a much wider range of buyers. This essay will discuss the reasons behind this change and outline further measures that consumers can take to make their clothing choices more sustainable.

One key reason for the growing popularity of used clothes is greater environmental awareness. Many consumers have learnt through the media that the fashion industry consumes enormous amounts of water and energy and generates vast quantities of textile waste. Buying pre-owned garments allows them to enjoy new outfits without adding to this demand. Financial factors also play a role, as rising living costs have encouraged people to look for affordable alternatives, and good-quality items can often be bought for a fraction of their original price. In addition, online resale platforms have made the process far more convenient. Instead of searching through crowded charity shops, shoppers can now browse thousands of items on their phone and have them delivered to their door.

There are, however, several other ways people can reduce the environmental impact of their wardrobes. The most effective is simply to buy fewer clothes and to choose durable ones. A well-made coat that lasts ten years is clearly less harmful than several cheap ones which wears out after a single season. People can also extend the life of their clothes by washing them less frequently and at lower temperatures, and by repairing minor damage rather than discarding the item. Finally, consumers can support brands that are transparent about their supply chains and use recycled or organic materials, which puts pressure on the wider industry to change its practices.

In conclusion, the rise of second-hand shopping reflects growing environmental concern, economic pressure and the convenience of online platforms. Alongside this, buying less, caring for clothes properly and choosing responsible brands can make a significant difference.

answers.text:
Charity shops and online resale platforms are enjoying a surge in popularity, as buyers who would once have insisted on new clothes increasingly choose pre-owned alternatives. This shift reflects a combination of ethical, economic and cultural factors, and while it is a positive development, it is only one of several ways in which consumers can make their clothing habits more sustainable.

Perhaps the most significant driver is a heightened awareness of the environmental cost of fashion. Widespread media coverage has exposed the industry's heavy use of water, its reliance on synthetic fibres and the mountains of discarded garments that end up in landfill, prompting many shoppers to reconsider their habits. Economic pressures reinforce this trend: with household budgets under strain, a designer jacket at a fraction of its retail price is an attractive proposition. Cultural attitudes have also shifted. Among younger consumers in particular, vintage clothing is seen not as a sign of hardship but as a way of expressing individuality, and resale apps have made browsing for such items as effortless as shopping on the high street.

Beyond buying second-hand, the single most effective step is to consume less. Choosing fewer, better-made garments and wearing them for longer reduces demand for new production far more than any recycling scheme. Caring for clothes properly also matters; washing at lower temperatures, air-drying rather than tumble-drying, and carrying out simple repairs can extend a garment's life considerably. When items are no longer wanted, they should be donated, swapped or sold rather than thrown away. Finally, consumers can use their purchasing power to reward manufacturers that are transparent about their supply chains and that use recycled or responsibly sourced materials.

In conclusion, the appeal of second-hand clothing stems from environmental concern, financial prudence and changing tastes. Its benefits can be multiplied if people also buy less, look after what they own and support genuinely responsible brands.

In many big cities, people live very close to each other but they do not know even the names of their neighbours. This essay will explain why this is happening and how cities can build a stronger community.

There are a few reasons for this problem. Firstly, people in cities are very busy with their work. They leave home early in the morning and come back late at night, so they have no time for talking with neighbours. Secondly, many people live in big apartment buildings where hundreds of families live, and it is difficult to know everybody. Also, people in cities often move house because of their job or rent, so they do not stay in one place for long time. Finally, technology is another reason. People spend their free time on their phones and social media instead of go outside and meet the people near them.

However, there are some ways to make a stronger community in cities. The local government can organise events like street festivals or sports competitions where neighbours can meet each other. For example, in some cities there are markets at weekends where people from the same area come together. Another idea is to build more parks and community centres, because these places give people chance to talk and make friends. Also, apartment buildings could create online groups for residents so they can share informations and help each other.

In conclusion, people in cities do not know their neighbours because they are busy, they move often and they use technology too much. I believe that events and public spaces can help to create stronger community, but people also need to make an effort themselves.

It is often said that city dwellers can live next door to someone for years without ever having a conversation with them. This essay will consider the main reasons for this lack of connection and suggest how urban communities could be strengthened.

The primary cause is the pace of urban life. Long working hours and lengthy commutes mean that many residents spend little time in their neighbourhood apart from sleeping there, leaving few opportunities for casual encounters. The design of modern housing makes the situation worse. In large apartment blocks, residents typically move directly from a car park or lift to their own front door, and there are rarely shared spaces where people might naturally stop and chat. Furthermore, city populations are highly mobile. Young professionals in particular tend to rent for a year or two before moving on, so there is little incentive to invest time in getting to know the people around them.

Despite these obstacles, a stronger sense of community can be encouraged. Urban planners have an important role to play by including communal areas such as small parks, playgrounds and shared gardens in new developments, since these places allow relationships to form gradually through repeated contact. Local councils could also support neighbourhood events, for instance by closing a street for an afternoon so that residents can hold a party or a market. On a smaller scale, digital tools can be helpful when they are used to connect people locally; neighbourhood messaging groups allow residents to lend tools, share recommendations and organise activities, which often leads to face-to-face friendship.

In conclusion, urban residents rarely know their neighbours because of busy lifestyles, isolating building design and frequent relocation. These problems can be reduced through better planning, local events and the sensible use of technology, although individuals also need to be willing to make first move.

answers.text:
Paradoxically, cities pack people together more densely than anywhere else, yet many urban residents could not name the person living on the other side of their wall. This anonymity has social, economic and architectural roots, but it is not inevitable, and there are practical ways in which a sense of community can be rebuilt.

One fundamental reason is the structure of urban working life. Long hours and extended commutes turn many homes into little more than places to sleep, so residents are seldom around at the times when neighbourly contact might occur. Transience compounds the problem. In cities where a large proportion of people rent, tenants may move every year or two, and there is little motivation to build relationships that seem likely to be short-lived. Architecture also plays a part: high-rise blocks with anonymous corridors and underground parking allow people to travel from their car to their flat without encountering anyone. Finally, online social networks now satisfy much of the need for connection that was once met locally, making it easy to feel sociable while remaining a stranger to one's neighbours.

Rebuilding community therefore requires action on several levels. Planners can design spaces that encourage chance encounters, such as courtyards, shared gardens and pedestrian-friendly streets lined with small shops and cafés, since relationships tend to grow out of repeated informal contact rather than organised gatherings. Local authorities can supplement this by funding regular events, from street parties to volunteering schemes, which give residents a shared purpose. Technology, too, can be turned to advantage; neighbourhood apps that allow people to borrow items or offer help frequently lead to offline friendships. Longer tenancy agreements would also help, giving renters the stability needed to put down roots.

In conclusion, city dwellers remain strangers because of demanding schedules, frequent relocation, isolating architecture and online distractions. Thoughtful urban design, community events and local digital networks, supported by more secure housing, can go a long way towards restoring neighbourly ties.

Nowadays more and more people decide to start their own business or work as freelancer instead of working for a company. In this essay I will explain the reasons for this choice and the qualities which a person need to be successful.

There are many reasons why people want to be self-employed. The biggest reason is freedom. When you work for yourself, you can decide your working hours and you do not have a boss who tells you what to do. For example, a graphic designer who is freelance can work from home and spend more time with his children. Another reason is money. In a company the salary is fixed, but if your own business is successful you can earn much more money. Also, some people are not happy with their job because they have a bad manager or boring tasks, so they decide to leave.

However, working for yourself is not easy and it needs some important qualities. First of all, a self-employed person must be very discipline. Nobody checks their work, so they must manage their time and meet deadlines without anybody help. Secondly, they need to be brave and take risk, because the income is not stable and in some months they can earn very little. Thirdly, good communication skills are important because they have to find customers and talk with them by themselves. Finally, they should be hard-working and ready to work long hours at the beginning.

In conclusion, people choose to work for themselves because they want freedom, more money and to escape from a bad job. To be successful, they need discipline, courage, communication skills and hard work.

An increasing number of people are leaving traditional employment to become freelancers, consultants or small business owners. This essay will outline the main motives behind this decision and discuss the personal qualities that are essential for success in self-employment.

The desire for independence is probably the most important motive. Employees often have little control over their schedules, the projects they work on or the way their performance is judged, whereas self-employed people can decide when, where and how they work. This flexibility is particularly attractive to parents with young children or people who want to combine work with travel. Financial ambition is another factor. While a salaried worker's income is usually limited by a fixed pay scale, a successful entrepreneur can benefit directly from their own effort and ideas. Some people also turn to self-employment out of frustration, for example after being overlooked for promotion or feeling that their skills are not valued.

Succeeding without an employer, however, demands a particular set of qualities. Self-discipline is the most crucial, since there is no manager to set deadlines or monitor progress, and it is easy to become distracted when working from home. Resilience is equally important, because income can be irregular and setbacks such as losing a major client are common, particularly in the first few years. In addition, independent workers need good interpersonal and marketing skills, as they are responsible for finding customers, negotiating prices and maintaining their reputation. Finally, they must be organised enough to handle practical matters such as taxes and invoices, which is often overlooked by people who is used to having an accounts department.

In conclusion, people choose self-employment mainly for independence, higher earning potential and escape from unsatisfying jobs. To succeed, they need self-discipline, resilience, strong communication skills and good organisation.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
For a growing share of the workforce, the security of a regular salary is no longer enough to outweigh the appeal of being one's own boss. People are drawn to self-employment for a mixture of personal and financial reasons, but turning that choice into a sustainable livelihood requires a demanding combination of character traits.

Autonomy lies at the heart of most decisions to go it alone. Working for an employer typically means accepting fixed hours, predetermined tasks and the judgement of a line manager, whereas independent workers can shape their own schedules and choose projects that genuinely interest them. For a parent who wants to be present at the school gate, or someone who does their best work late at night, this freedom can be transformative. There is also the prospect of greater reward: rather than seeing the benefits of their efforts absorbed by a company, the self-employed keep what they earn, and a thriving business may eventually generate far more than a salary ever would. Technology has made the leap less daunting, as online platforms allow even a single freelancer to reach clients around the world.

Yet freedom brings its own pressures, and certain qualities distinguish those who thrive from those who struggle. Self-motivation is paramount; without external deadlines or supervision, procrastination can quietly undermine a promising venture. Equally vital is resilience, since irregular income, demanding clients and unsuccessful pitches are an inevitable part of independent work. Successful freelancers also tend to be versatile, combining expertise in their field with the ability to market themselves, negotiate fees and manage finances. Finally, a degree of tolerance for risk is essential, as there is no guaranteed income at the end of each month.

In conclusion, people become self-employed chiefly to gain autonomy and to benefit directly from their own work. Achieving lasting success, however, depends on self-motivation, resilience, versatility and a willingness to live with uncertainty.

Advertisements are everywhere today, on television, on the internet and in the streets. Many of them try to make people believe that they need a product which they did not want before. This essay will explain how advertisers do this and whether it should be controlled.

Advertisers use different methods to persuade people. One common method is to use famous people like actors or footballers. When fans see their favourite star using a product, they want to buy it too because they want to be like him. Another method is to make people feel that their life is not good enough without the product. For example, a advert for a new phone shows happy young people with many friends, so the viewers think they will be more popular if they buy this phone. Also, advertisers use social media to collect information about users and show them ads which is based on their interests, so it is very hard to ignore them.

In my opinion, some control is necessary. Firstly, children are easily influenced by adverts and they often ask their parents to buy toys or unhealthy snacks. Governments should ban adverts for children in some times, for example during cartoons. Secondly, adverts should not give false information or promise things that the product can not do. However, I think adverts cannot be banned completely because companies need to tell people about their products and it help the economy.

In conclusion, advertisers create new wants by using celebrities, making people feel unhappy with their lives and targeting them online. I believe that governments should control adverts, especially for children, but not stop them totally.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Modern advertising frequently goes beyond informing consumers about products and instead convinces them that they need things they had never previously considered buying. This essay will explain the main techniques advertisers use to create such desires and argue that some regulation is justified.

One of the most effective strategies is to link a product with an attractive lifestyle or identity. Rather than focusing on what a car or a watch actually does, advertisements often show glamorous, successful people using it, suggesting that buyers will share that status. Advertisers also exploit people's insecurities. Beauty and fitness companies, for instance, may highlight minor imperfections that consumers had never worried about and then present their product as the solution. In addition, digital marketing has made persuasion more powerful than ever. By analysing people's browsing history, companies can target individuals with personalised adverts at exactly the moment they are most likely to make an impulse purchase, while social media influencers present sponsored products as if they were genuine personal recommendations.

I believe these practices should be controlled to some extent. The strongest case concerns children, who are less able to recognise persuasive intent, so advertising aimed at young audiences, particularly for unhealthy food and expensive toys, should be strictly limited. Transparency is also essential: influencers ought to be required to label paid content clearly, so that followers can distinguish advice from marketing. Furthermore, there should be clearer rules about how personal data can be used for targeting. That said, a total ban on persuasive advertising would be neither practical or desirable, as advertising funds much of the media and allows new businesses to reach customers.

In conclusion, advertisers create new wants by associating products with desirable lifestyles, exploiting insecurities and using personal data. Sensible regulation, especially to protect children and ensure transparency, would reduce the harmful effects without undermining legitimate marketing.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Much of modern advertising is not designed to meet existing demand but to manufacture it, persuading consumers that a product they had never heard of is suddenly indispensable. The techniques involved have become increasingly sophisticated, and in my view they warrant a degree of regulation, although not an outright ban.

At the core of most campaigns lies emotional association. Advertisers rarely sell objects on their practical merits; instead they sell the feelings and identities attached to them. A pair of trainers becomes a symbol of athletic success, while a luxury handbag is presented as evidence of sophistication. By repeatedly pairing a product with images of happiness, attractiveness or status, advertisers create a sense that ownership will deliver these qualities. A related tactic is the creation of dissatisfaction. Cosmetic and technology companies in particular are adept at convincing consumers that what they already own is inadequate, so that a perfectly functional phone begins to feel embarrassing the moment a new model is launched. Digital platforms have intensified these methods, allowing firms to target individuals with personalised messages and to reach them through influencers whose endorsements feel like the advice of a friend.

Some control over these practices seems reasonable. Children, who are especially susceptible to persuasion, deserve particular protection, and restrictions on advertising during children's programming or on apps aimed at them would be a sensible starting point. Clear disclosure rules for sponsored content would help adults recognise when they are being marketed to, and stricter limits on the collection of personal data would curb the most intrusive forms of targeting. However, advertising also finances free media and enables smaller companies to compete, so heavy-handed prohibition would do more harm than good.

In conclusion, advertisers generate new desires by attaching emotional meaning to products, fostering dissatisfaction and exploiting personal data. Targeted regulation, focusing on children, transparency and privacy, would limit manipulation while preserving the legitimate benefits of advertising.

Most people know that fruit, vegetables and whole grains are good for health, but many of them still eat a lot of junk food. This essay will explain why it is difficult to eat healthily and who should help people to improve their diet.

There are several reasons why people do not eat healthy food. The first reason is time. Many people work long hours and when they come home they are too tired for cooking, so they buy fast food or ready meals which is quick and easy. Secondly, unhealthy food is often cheaper than healthy food. For example, in many supermarket a burger costs less than a salad, so families with low income choose the cheaper option. Another reason is that junk food is very tasty and it is advertised everywhere, so it is difficult to resist it, especially for children.

In my opinion, both the government and individuals should be responsible for this problem. The government can make healthy food cheaper by reducing tax on fruits and vegetables and put higher tax on sugary drinks. They can also teach children about nutrition and cooking at school, so they will have good habits from young age. However, individuals and families also have responsibility, because nobody can force a person to eat well. Parents should cook healthy meals at home and give good example to their children.

In conclusion, people find it hard to eat healthy food because they are busy, healthy food is expensive and junk food is attractive. I believe the government should help by using taxes and education, but people must also take responsibility of their own diet.

answers.text:
Although most people are well aware that vegetables are healthier than crisps and fizzy drinks, poor diets remain common. This essay will examine why knowledge alone does not lead to healthy eating and argue that responsibility should be shared between governments, the food industry and individuals.

The gap between knowing and doing has several causes. Convenience is a major factor, as people with demanding jobs often lack the time or energy to prepare meals from fresh ingredients after a long day, and processed food offers a quick alternative. Cost also plays an important role. In many places, fresh produce is more expensive than heavily processed snacks, which makes healthy eating difficult for low-income households. Moreover, the modern food environment is designed to encourage overconsumption. Unhealthy products are heavily advertised, placed at eye level in supermarkets and made highly appealing through large amounts of sugar, salt and fat, so even people with good intentions find them hard to resist.

In my view, it would be unfair to place the entire burden on individuals when so many external factors shape their choices. Governments should take a leading role, for example by taxing sugary drinks, subsidising fruit and vegetables and requiring clear nutritional labelling. Schools can also contribute by providing nutritious lunches and teaching practical cooking skills. The food industry has a responsibility too, and manufacturers could be encouraged to reduce the sugar and salt content of their products. Nevertheless, individuals cannot be entirely excused, since they still make the final decision about what they buy, and parents shape children's eating habits from an early age.

In conclusion, people struggle to eat well because of busy lifestyles, the higher cost of healthy food and an environment full of tempting alternatives. Improving diets therefore requires a combined effort in which governments and the food industry makes healthy choices easier and individuals take responsibility for their own decisions.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
It is one of the curiosities of modern life that people can recite the benefits of vegetables and the dangers of sugar, yet still reach for a takeaway at the end of the day. The reasons lie less in ignorance than in the circumstances in which food choices are made, and for this reason I believe responsibility for improving diets must be shared, with governments playing the leading role.

Time pressure is a fundamental obstacle. For people working long hours or juggling several jobs, preparing a balanced meal from scratch can feel like an unrealistic demand, whereas ready meals and fast food require no effort at all. Price reinforces this pattern: calorie for calorie, processed food is often cheaper than fresh produce, so households on tight budgets may have little real choice. Perhaps most importantly, the food environment itself works against good intentions. Products high in sugar, salt and fat are engineered to be highly palatable, promoted relentlessly and positioned prominently in shops, which means that choosing the healthy option requires constant willpower. Knowledge, in other words, is rarely a match for convenience, cost and temptation combined.

Given these pressures, it would be unrealistic to expect individuals to solve the problem alone. Governments are best placed to reshape the environment in which choices are made, whether through taxes on sugary drinks, subsidies for fresh produce, restrictions on junk-food advertising or clear front-of-pack labelling. Food manufacturers should also be held accountable, for instance through targets to reduce harmful ingredients. Schools have a role in teaching cooking and providing nutritious meals, thereby shaping habits early. Individuals, of course, retain ultimate control over what they eat, but personal responsibility is far easier to exercise when the healthy choice is also the easy one.

In conclusion, poor diets persist because of time pressure, cost and a food environment designed to tempt. While individuals must play their part, governments, supported by industry and schools, should take the lead in making healthy eating affordable and convenient.

In many countries, the number of young voters in elections is lower than older voters. This essay will explain some reasons for this and the consequences it has for society.

There are several reasons why young people do not vote. Firstly, many young people are not interested in politics because they think it is boring and complicated. They do not understand the difference between the parties, so they do not know who to choose. Secondly, a lot of young people believe that their vote cannot change anything. They see that politicians make promises before elections but they do not keep them after, so they lose trust. Also, some young people are students who live far from their hometown, and it is not easy for them to register or go to the polling station on election day.

This situation has some serious consequences. The most important one is that politicians focus more on older people, because older people vote more. For example, government may spend more money on pensions and less on education or cheap housing for young families. As a result, young people problems are ignored and they feel even less connected to politics. Another consequence is that the democracy becomes weaker, because the government does not represent the whole population. In the future, if this young people never start voting, the problem will become more serious.

In conclusion, young people vote less because they are not interested, they do not trust politicians and voting is not convenient for them. This leads to policies which favour older people and a weaker democracy. I think schools should teach more about politics to encourage young people to vote.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Election results in many countries show that turnout among younger citizens is considerably lower than among older age groups. This essay will explore the reasons for this pattern and discuss its consequences for society as a whole.

One of the main reasons is a sense of disconnection from mainstream politics. Many young people feel that political parties are dominated by older politicians who neither understand nor prioritise their concerns, such as housing costs, job insecurity and climate change. As a result, they conclude that voting will make little difference. Another factor is a lack of political education. Unless they grow up in families that discuss current affairs, young adults may find the system confusing and feel unqualified to make a choice. Practical obstacles also play a role; students and young workers move house frequently, and if registration rules are complicated, they may simply not be registered in the right place when an election is called.

The consequences of low youth turnout are significant. Since politicians naturally pay attention to those who vote, policies tend to favour older voters, for example through generous pension increases, while issues affecting young people receive less attention and funding. This creates a vicious cycle, because young people then feel even more excluded from the political process and become less likely to participate in future. In the long term, this undermines the legitimacy of democratic institutions, as governments are elected by an increasingly unrepresentative section of the population. It may also encourage some young people to express their frustration through protest rather than through the ballot box.

In conclusion, young people vote less because they feel ignored, lack political knowledge and faces practical barriers. The result is a political system that neglects their interests, which in turn weakens democracy.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In many democracies, a striking generational divide exists at the ballot box, with people in their late teens and twenties voting at markedly lower rates than their parents and grandparents. This gap can be traced to disillusionment, limited political education and practical barriers, and its consequences extend well beyond young people themselves.

Perhaps the most significant factor is a perception that politics is not designed for them. Young voters frequently see parliaments dominated by older figures and debates that seem remote from their immediate concerns, such as unaffordable rents or insecure employment. When the connection between casting a vote and improving one's own life appears weak, abstaining can seem a rational response rather than mere apathy. This detachment is reinforced by inadequate civic education; many school leavers have little understanding of how government works or how party programmes differ, and uncertainty easily turns into disengagement. Practical obstacles add a further layer. Young adults change address frequently for study or work, and cumbersome registration procedures can mean that they are unable to vote even if they wish to.

The consequences for society are considerable. Politicians seeking re-election rationally direct their attention towards the groups most likely to turn out, which can result in policies that protect pensions and property values while underinvesting in education, affordable housing and long-term environmental measures. Such imbalances can deepen intergenerational inequality and, in turn, reinforce young people's belief that the system ignores them, creating a self-perpetuating cycle. More broadly, a government chosen by a narrowing slice of the electorate risks losing legitimacy, and frustration that finds no outlet at the ballot box may emerge instead as distrust or unrest.

In conclusion, low youth turnout stems from disillusionment, limited civic knowledge and practical hurdles. Its effects, from skewed policy priorities to weakened democratic legitimacy, make it a problem for the whole of society rather than for young people alone.

Today children usually have much more toys, clothes and electronic devices than children in the past. This essay will explain why this happen and how it affects their development.

There are several reasons for this change. Firstly, many families today are richer than before, so parents can afford to buy more things for their children. Secondly, most families have only one or two children, so parents and grandparents spend all their money on them. Also, toys are cheaper now because factories produce them in large numbers. Another reason is advertising. Children see adverts on television and YouTube and they ask their parents to buy the new toy. Some parents who work long hours also buy presents because they feel guilty that they do not spend enough time with their kids.

In my opinion, having too many possessions has more negative effects than positive effects on children. Children who get everything they want may not learn the value of money and they can become spoiled. For example, when a child has twenty toys, he often gets bored quickly and do not take care of them. Moreover, they have less chance to use their imagination, because in the past children made games with simple things like sticks and boxes. However, some toys, for example puzzles or building blocks, can help children to develop their skills and creativity.

In conclusion, children have more possessions today because families are richer, toys are cheap and advertising is powerful. Although some toys are educational, I believe that too many things can make children spoiled and less creative, so parents should buy less toys for them.

answers.text:
Compared with previous generations, many children today grow up surrounded by a large number of toys, gadgets and other possessions. This essay will examine the main causes of this change and argue that, although some possessions can be beneficial, having too many can hinder a child's development.

The most obvious explanation is rising prosperity. In many countries, households have more disposable income than they did several decades ago, and mass production has made toys and clothing far cheaper. At the same time, families have become smaller, so the attention and spending of parents, grandparents and other relatives are concentrated on fewer children. Commercial pressure also plays a major part. Children are exposed to constant advertising through television, online videos and games, and toy companies regularly release new versions of popular products, which creates a desire to keep up with friends. In addition, busy working parents sometimes use gifts to compensate for limited time spent together.

The effects of this abundance on development are mixed but mostly negative. On the positive side, educational toys, books and construction sets can stimulate curiosity and help children develop problem-solving and motor skills. However, when children have too many possessions, they tend to value each one less and may move quickly from one toy to other without engaging deeply with any of them. Many educators believe that a certain amount of boredom encourages creativity, and a child with only a few simple items is more likely to invent games and stories. Furthermore, receiving new things frequently may lead children to associate happiness with ownership, which can make it harder for them to learn patience and gratitude.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
A glance into many modern children's bedrooms reveals shelves crowded with toys, games and electronic devices on a scale that would have astonished earlier generations. This abundance is largely a product of economic and social change, and while it is not wholly harmful, I believe it often works against the qualities that children most need to develop.

Several forces lie behind this shift. Greater affluence and the global manufacturing of inexpensive goods mean that toys which were once special treats are now everyday purchases. Demographic change has amplified the effect: with fewer children per family, and often several grandparents eager to give presents, gifts that were once shared among siblings are now lavished on one or two children. Marketing, meanwhile, has become more direct and persistent. Children encounter advertising through online videos and games as well as television, and the constant release of new models and collectable ranges fuels a sense that what they have is never quite enough. Some parents, pressed for time, may also use gifts as a substitute for attention.

The developmental consequences depend partly on what children own, but quantity matters. Well-chosen toys such as building sets, art materials and books can foster creativity, concentration and fine motor skills. Yet when possessions are plentiful, each one tends to be valued less, and children may flit between them without the sustained engagement that deep play requires. A child with a cardboard box and a few figures is often forced to invent entire worlds, whereas one surrounded by ready-made entertainment has less need for imagination. There is also a risk that a steady stream of new items teaches children to seek satisfaction through acquisition, making patience, gratitude and the ability to cope with disappointment harder to learn.

In conclusion, children own more because of rising wealth, smaller families and relentless marketing. Although some possessions can enrich development, an excess tends to weaken imagination and encourage materialistic habits, so fewer, better-chosen items are generally preferable.

In some places, the number of crimes committed by teenagers is increasing and people are worried about this. This essay will discuss why some young people become criminals and what schools should do to prevent it.

There are many reasons why teenagers get involved in crime. One reason is family problems. If parents are divorced or they work all the time, children may not get enough attention and guidance, so they spend time on the streets with bad friends. Peer pressure is also a big reason. Teenagers want to be accepted by their group, so if their friends steal or fight, they do the same things to look cool. In addition, poverty can push young people to commit crime. For example, a teenager from a poor family may steal a phone because he cannot afford to buy one.

In my opinion, schools have a important role in preventing youth crime. Firstly, teachers spend many hours with students every day, so they can notice when a student has problems at home or behave badly. Schools should have counsellors who can talk with these students and helping them. Secondly, schools can offer after-school activities such as sports, music or drama clubs. These activities keep teenagers busy and give them something positive to do, so they have less time for getting in trouble. Finally, schools should teach students about the law and the results of committing a crime.

In conclusion, teenagers commit crimes because of family problems, peer pressure and poverty. Schools cannot solve this problem alone, but they can help a lot by supporting students, organising activities and teaching them about consequences.

Rising levels of teenage crime have become a concern in a number of communities. This essay will consider the main factors that lead some young people into criminal behaviour and argue that schools have an important, though limited, role in preventing it.

A difficult home environment is often at the root of the problem. Teenagers who lack supervision or who experience conflict and neglect at home may look for a sense of belonging elsewhere, sometimes in gangs that offer loyalty and status. Peer influence is closely connected to this. Adolescents are especially sensitive to the approval of their friends, and within certain groups, activities such as shoplifting or vandalism can be seen as a way of proving oneself. Economic disadvantage also plays a part, since young people growing up in deprived areas may have few legitimate opportunities and see crime as an easy way to obtain money or possessions.

Schools are well placed to address several of these factors. Because teachers see students daily, they are often the first adults to notice warning signs such as persistent absence, aggressive behaviour or sudden changes in friendship groups, and they can refer these students to counsellors or social services at an early stage. Schools can also provide constructive alternatives by running after-school clubs, sports teams and mentoring schemes, which give teenagers both supervision and a positive identity. Moreover, keeping students engaged in learning is itself a form of prevention, as those who are excluded or leave early are far more vulnerable to be drawn into crime. However, schools cannot be expected to solve the problem alone, and they need support from families and local authorities.

In conclusion, teenagers become involved in crime mainly because of family difficulties, peer pressure and poverty. Schools can play a valuable role through early intervention, extracurricular activities and keeping students in education, but prevention requires a wider community effort.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Teenage crime attracts considerable public attention, and in some areas it appears to be rising. Although there is no single explanation for why young people offend, the most common causes are social rather than individual, and schools, where adolescents spend much of their time, are in a strong position to help prevent it.

The family environment is frequently the starting point. Young people who grow up with little supervision, or amid conflict and instability, may lack both the guidance and the emotional security that discourage risky behaviour. In such circumstances, the pull of peers becomes especially powerful. Adolescence is a stage at which acceptance by one's group matters intensely, and where that group treats theft or violence as a badge of status, the pressure to participate can be difficult to resist. Poverty and a lack of opportunity compound these influences: in neighbourhoods where jobs are scarce and youth facilities have closed, crime may seem to offer money, excitement and respect that are unattainable by legitimate means.

Schools can respond to each of these pressures. With the most regular contact with young people of any institution, they are ideally placed to identify early warning signs, such as truancy, declining grades or abrupt changes in behaviour, and to connect vulnerable students with counselling before problems escalate. They can also offer the sense of belonging that some teenagers seek elsewhere, through sports teams, creative projects and mentoring by trusted adults. Perhaps most importantly, schools should work hard to keep struggling pupils in education rather than resorting quickly to exclusion, since those who drop out are left with time on their hands and diminished prospects. Nevertheless, schools cannot compensate entirely for problems at home, and their efforts are most effective when coordinated with families and local services.

In conclusion, youth crime is driven largely by family instability, peer pressure and lack of opportunity. Schools can make a significant contribution through early identification, positive activities and inclusive policies, but only as part of a broader, coordinated approach.

Nowadays many people only read news or watch programmes which agree with their own opinions. This essay will explain the reasons for this behaviour and the effects which it has on society.

There are several reasons why people do this. The first reason is that it is more comfortable. When people read something that agree with their ideas, they feel happy and confident, but when they read the opposite opinion they feel angry or uncomfortable. Secondly, social media and websites use algorithms which show users the same kind of news that they clicked before. For example, if someone like a political party and reads about it online, the website will show him more articles supporting this party. Also, many people are busy and they do not have time to search for different sources, so they just follow the news channel their family always watched.

This habit has several negative effects on society. Firstly, people become more extreme in their opinions because they never hear other sides of the argument. Secondly, society becomes divided into groups who do not understand each other and they argue a lot, especially on the internet. For instance, during elections, supporters of different parties often insult each other online instead of discussing. Moreover, it is easier for fake news to spread, because people believe any information that support their view without checking it.

In conclusion, people choose news which match their opinions because it feels comfortable and because of algorithms and lack of time. This makes society more divided and helps fake news to spread. I think people should try to read news from different sources to have more balanced view.

With a vast range of news sources now available, many people choose to consume only those that confirm their existing beliefs. This essay will explain why this tendency has become so common and discuss its effects on society, which I believe are largely harmful.

One key reason is psychological. People naturally prefer information that supports what they already think, because it makes them feel intelligent and secure, while opposing views can cause discomfort or even anger. The structure of the modern media landscape strengthens this tendency. Social media platforms and news apps use algorithms to recommend content similar to what users have previously clicked on, so a person who reads one article with a particular political slant will be shown many more like it. In addition, some news outlets deliberately target an audience with a clear political identity, since loyal viewers who share their outlook are commercially valuable.

The consequences for society are serious. First, when individuals are only exposed to one perspective, their opinions tend to become more extreme, as they rarely meet persuasive counter-arguments. This contributes to political polarisation, in which different groups not only disagree but regard each other with suspicion or hostility. Public debate suffers as a result, since it becomes difficult to reach compromise on important issues like climate policy when each side has different facts. Second, selective consumption helps misinformation spread more easily, because people are less likely to question a false story if it fits what they want to believe. Some argue that like-minded communities give people a sense of belonging, but this benefit hardly outweigh the damage to social cohesion.

In conclusion, people choose news that reflects their opinions because it is psychologically comforting and because algorithms and media companies encourage it. This leads to polarisation, weaker public debate and the rapid spread of misinformation.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The modern media landscape offers an almost unlimited choice of news sources, yet many people use this freedom to confine themselves to outlets that echo what they already believe. This behaviour has deep psychological roots and is reinforced by technology, and its effects on society are, in my view, predominantly damaging.

At the most basic level, people seek out confirming information because it is reassuring. Having one's views validated produces a sense of certainty and belonging, whereas encountering strong counter-arguments can be unsettling and may even feel like a personal attack. This natural bias is amplified by the design of digital platforms. Recommendation algorithms are optimised for engagement, and since users tend to click on content that aligns with their views, they are fed a steady diet of similar material until alternative perspectives effectively disappear from their screens. Commercial incentives play a role as well: news organisations have discovered that cultivating a loyal audience with a distinct ideological identity can be more profitable than attempting to appeal to everyone.

The social consequences are significant. When citizens inhabit separate informational worlds, they lose not only a shared set of opinions but also a shared set of facts, which makes productive debate extremely difficult. Views tend to harden, since they are rarely tested against opposing evidence, and people increasingly regard those who disagree not as fellow citizens with different priorities but as ignorant or malicious. This polarisation can paralyse decision-making on complex issues that require compromise. Furthermore, echo chambers provide fertile ground for misinformation, because claims that flatter a group's assumptions are shared eagerly and seldom checked.

In conclusion, selective news consumption stems from a desire for reassurance, reinforced by algorithms and commercial strategy. Its effects, including polarisation, the erosion of common ground and the spread of falsehoods, pose a real threat to healthy public discourse.

Many people like to learn about the history of their town or city. This essay will explain why people enjoy this and how local history can be more interesting for young generation.

There are some reasons why people are interested in local history. Firstly, it helps them to understand their identity. When people know how their town was built and what happened there in the past, they feel more proud and connected to their home. Secondly, local history is easier to imagine than world history because people can see the old buildings, bridges or monuments every day. For example, if there is an old castle in the city, people are curious to know who lived there. Also, some people learn about local history because their own family lived in the area for many years and they want to know about their grandparents life.

However, many young people think history is boring because they only read books and remember dates at school. There are some ways to change this. First, schools can organise trips to museums and historical places, so students can see things with their own eyes. Second, technology can be used, for example apps or videos which shows how the town looked hundred years ago. Young people love technology, so this will attract them. Another idea is to invite old people from the community to school to tell stories about the past, which is more interesting than a textbook.

In conclusion, people enjoy local history because it gives them identity and it is easy to connect with. To make it interesting for young people, schools should use trips, technology and stories from older people instead of only books.

answers.text:
Local history attracts a surprising amount of interest, with many people visiting museums, joining heritage walks or reading about the origins of their town. This essay will discuss the reasons for this interest and suggest ways to make the subject more engaging for younger generations.

One important reason is that local history provides a sense of identity and belonging. Knowing how a community developed, for example why a market town grew up beside a particular river or how local industries shaped the lives of previous residents, helps people feel rooted in the place where they live. Local history is also more tangible than national or global events. People pass historic buildings, statues and street names every day, and learning the stories behind them makes familiar surroundings more meaningful. In addition, many people have a personal connection to the past through their own families, and researching local records can reveal how their ancestors lived and worked.

Young people, however, often regard history as a dry subject, so it needs to be presented in more active ways. One effective approach is to take learning out of the classroom. Guided visits to historic sites, or projects in which students investigate the history of their own street, allow them to discover information for themselves rather than memorise facts. Technology can also help. Interactive apps could show teenagers how a square looked centuries ago, while local museums could use social media to share short and entertaining stories. Finally, involving older residents is valuable, as hearing first-hand accounts of how the town has changed make the past feel real and personal.

In conclusion, people enjoy local history because it strengthens their identity and connects them with familiar places and their own families. For young people, hands-on projects, digital tools and contact with older generations can transform it into a lively and relevant subject.

Local history is also immediate in a way that national history rarely is. The evidence is visible in everyday surroundings, from the architecture of the high street to the names of lanes and pubs, so each discovery transforms a familiar route into something richer. Finally, it often intersects with family history; parish records or old photographs may reveal where one's great-grandparents worked or worshipped, creating a direct emotional link with the past.

Engaging young people requires moving away from passive learning. Rather than being presented with dates and summaries, students could act as historians themselves, interviewing elderly residents, examining old maps or investigating the history of their own school. Such projects give them ownership of their findings and reveal that history is made up of real people's lives. Digital technology offers further possibilities: augmented reality apps can overlay historical images onto present-day streets, and short video formats allow students to share what they have uncovered in a style that appeals to their peers. Local museums, too, can attract younger audiences with interactive exhibitions rather than static displays.

In conclusion, local history resonates with people because it strengthens identity, gives meaning to familiar places and connects them with their ancestors. By encouraging active investigation and embracing digital media, schools and museums can make it equally compelling for the young.

Nowadays many tourists travel to famous places mainly because they want to take photos and post them on social media. This essay will explain why this is happening and how it change the experience of travelling.

There are several reasons for this trend. The main reason is the popularity of social media like Instagram and TikTok. People want to show to their friends and followers where they have been, and they feel happy when they get many likes and comments. Secondly, nowadays every person has a smartphone with a good camera, so taking photos is very easy and cheap. In the past, people used film cameras and they could only take few pictures. Also, some places become famous only because they look beautiful in photos, for example colourful streets or special cafés, so tourists go there to take the same picture which they saw online.

This trend changes travelling in several ways, mostly negative. Firstly, tourists spend a lot of time looking at their phone screens instead of enjoy the place. For example, some people visit a beautiful beach but they spend one hour to take selfies and do not relax. Secondly, famous photo spots become very crowded, and tourists have to wait in long queues only for one picture. This can also be a problem for local people who live there. On the other hand, photos can help people to remember their holiday and share their experience with family.

In conclusion, tourists take many photos for social media because it is popular and easy with smartphones. I think this makes travelling less enjoyable because people do not really experience the place, although photos can be a nice memory.

In recent years, many travellers seem more concerned with capturing images for social media than with exploring the places they visit. This essay will examine the causes of this development and discuss how it is changing the nature of travel.

The rise of image-based social media platforms is the most obvious cause. Sharing holiday photographs has become a way of presenting an attractive lifestyle to friends and followers, and the positive feedback in the form of likes and comments can be highly rewarding. Travel has therefore become, for some people, a means of building an online identity. At the same time, the tourism industry has adapted to this demand. Hotels, restaurants and even local councils create colourful murals, viewing platforms and other photogenic spots, knowing that shared images act as free advertising. Smartphones with high-quality cameras have also made it effortless to take hundreds of photographs in a single day.

This shift has altered the travel experience in significant ways. For many tourists, the focus has moved from experiencing a place to documenting it, so they may spend more time arranging the perfect shot than appreciating the atmosphere, talking to local people or learning about the history of a site. Travel itineraries are increasingly shaped by what looks impressive on a screen, which means that lesser-known but interesting places can be overlooked. Popular photo spots, meanwhile, become overcrowded, spoiling the visit for other travellers and creating problems for residents. Nevertheless, photography is not entirely negative; it can encourage people to notice details and helps them to preserve memories.

In conclusion, the desire to share images online, the tourism industry's response and easy access to cameras have made photography central to modern tourism. While it helps people record their journeys, it often turns travel into a performance rather than a genuine experience.

answers.text:
At many famous landmarks, it is now common to see visitors queuing not to enter a building or admire a view, but to reproduce a photograph they have already seen online. This trend reflects the central role of social media in modern life, and it is subtly changing what it means to travel.

The underlying cause is the way image-sharing platforms have turned travel into a form of self-presentation. A holiday was once a private experience, recounted afterwards to a few friends; today it can be broadcast in real time to hundreds of followers, and the approval this generates offers a powerful incentive to seek out striking backdrops. Influencers amplify the effect by popularising particular viewpoints, which then become obligatory stops for their audiences. The tourism industry has been quick to capitalise on this, designing hotels, cafés and attractions with photogenic features precisely because every shared image serves as free promotion. Ubiquitous smartphone cameras, of course, have removed any practical limit on how many pictures can be taken.

The consequences for the experience of travelling are considerable. When the primary goal is to capture an image, attention shifts from the place itself to how it will appear to others, and the unplanned encounters and quiet observation that once defined travel can be crowded out. Itineraries also become more uniform, as visitors converge on the same well-known spots while neighbourhoods without an obvious visual hook are ignored. For residents of popular destinations, this concentration brings congestion, while visitors may arrive only to find a place swamped by others with the same idea. That said, photography can still enrich travel when it encourages people to look closely and preserve meaningful memories rather than simply to accumulate evidence of having been somewhere.

In conclusion, photo-driven tourism has grown out of social media culture, industry marketing and constant access to cameras. While it need not be harmful, it risks turning travel from an act of discovery into a performance staged for an online audience.

In some countries, many people do not trust scientists and experts as much as before. This essay will discuss the reasons for this problem and how the trust can be built again.

There are several reasons why people lose trust in scientists. Firstly, the internet and social media spread a lot of false information. Anybody can post an article or video which says scientists are lying, and many people believe it because it looks convincing. Secondly, sometimes experts change their advice. For example, during a health crisis, experts may give one advice at the beginning and then different advice later, so people think that they do not know what they are doing. Another reason is that some people think scientists work for governments or big companies and they only say what these organisations want. This makes people suspicious about their research.

There are some ways to rebuild the trust. First of all, scientists should explain their work in simple language, so ordinary people can understand it. Many research is written with difficult words, so people cannot follow it. Secondly, scientists should be honest when they are not sure about something and explain that science changes when new evidence is found. Also, governments should make clear rules about who pays for research, so people know the scientists are independent. Finally, schools should teach students how to check information online and recognise fake news.

In conclusion, people trust scientists less because of fake news online, changing advice and the belief that experts are not independent. To rebuild trust, scientists must communicate more clearly and honestly, and people need better education about information.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Although science has brought enormous benefits to society, there are signs in some countries that the public is becoming more sceptical about the advice of scientists and other experts. This essay will explore the reasons behind this decline in trust and suggest how it might be restored.

A major reason is the changing way in which information is shared. Social media allows anyone to publish claims that contradict scientific evidence, and because such content is often emotional and simple, it can spread faster than careful explanations. When people see many confident voices questioning experts, it becomes harder for them to know who to believe. Another cause is the way scientific uncertainty is misunderstood. Science develops as new evidence emerges, so recommendations sometimes change, but members of the public may interpret this as inconsistency or even incompetence. Trust has also been damaged by a perception that experts are connected to political or commercial interests. When research is funded by large companies, some people suspect that conclusions are influenced by those who pay for them.

Rebuilding trust will require several steps. Firstly, scientists need to communicate more directly and accessibly, explaining not only what they have found but also how they reached their conclusions and what remains uncertain. Being open about the limits of knowledge can actually increase credibility, because it shows honesty. Secondly, greater transparency about funding and conflicts of interest would reassure people that research is independent. In addition, education system could place more emphasis on how science works, teaching students to evaluate evidence and identify unreliable sources, so that future citizens are better equipped to judge competing claims.

In conclusion, declining trust in experts stems from the spread of misinformation, misunderstanding of scientific uncertainty and suspicion of hidden interests. Clearer communication, transparency and better science education offers the most promising route to restoring confidence.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In several countries, the authority once enjoyed by scientists and other experts appears to be weakening, with some people openly dismissing expert advice on matters ranging from medicine to climate. This decline has multiple causes, some rooted in technology and others in the conduct of experts themselves, and restoring trust will require changes on both sides.

The transformation of the information environment is a central factor. Online platforms allow unverified claims to circulate as widely as peer-reviewed findings, and content that is dramatic or emotionally charged typically travels further than cautious, qualified explanations. In this crowded space, genuine expertise can appear to be merely one opinion among many. A second factor is a widespread misunderstanding of how science works. Scientific knowledge is provisional by nature, so advice is revised as evidence accumulates; however, to those who expect definitive answers, such revisions can look like confusion or deception. Finally, trust has been eroded by perceptions of bias. When experts are seen to be closely aligned with governments, or when research is funded by industries with a financial stake in the outcome, it is easy to suspect that conclusions have been shaped by interests rather than evidence.

Rebuilding confidence must therefore begin with openness. Scientists and public bodies should explain not only what they recommend but why, and be candid about uncertainty rather than projecting a false certainty that later has to be withdrawn. Full disclosure of funding sources would go some way towards addressing suspicions of hidden agendas. Experts also need to engage with communities directly, through local events and accessible media, rather than communicating solely through official statements. In the longer term, education has a vital role: teaching young people how evidence is gathered and assessed would equip them to distinguish credible research from persuasive misinformation.

In conclusion, trust in experts is being undermined by an unregulated information environment, misconceptions about scientific uncertainty and suspicions of bias. Greater transparency, honest communication and stronger scientific literacy offer the best prospect of restoring it.
