Today we have many machines and devices which make our daily tasks faster, for example washing machines, dishwashers and online shopping. However, many people say that they have less free time than before. This essay will explain why this happens and what can be done about it.

There are some reasons for this problem. The main reason is that technology makes people work more. Because of smartphones and emails, people can be contacted by their boss in any time, even in the evening or at the weekend, so work never finish. Secondly, people spend a lot of their free time on social media and watching videos, and they do not notice how many hours they lose. For example, someone may plan to check their phone for five minutes but then scroll for one hour. Also, life today is more competitive, so people try to do more activities, such as taking extra courses or working second job, to earn more money.

There are several things that can help people to have more free time. Firstly, companies should make rules that employees do not have to answer emails after working hours. Secondly, people should control how much time they spend on their phones, for example by turning off notifications or using apps which limits screen time. Finally, people should learn to say no to some activities and choose what is really important for them.

In conclusion, people feel they have less free time because technology connects them to work all the time and because they waste time on their phones. I think both employers and individuals needs to make changes to solve this problem.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Modern technology has dramatically reduced the time needed for many routine tasks, from washing clothes to paying bills. Paradoxically, however, many people complain that they have less leisure time than ever. This essay will explain the reasons for this contradiction and suggest ways of addressing it.

One important reason is that the time saved by technology is often filled with more work. Laptops and smartphones mean that employees can be reached at any hour, and many feel obliged to reply to messages in the evening or at weekends, so the boundary between work and home life has become blurred. In addition, expectations have risen along with efficiency. Because tasks can be completed more quickly, employers and individuals simply try to do more of them, and people end up busier rather than more relaxed. Technology also consumes free time directly. Social media and streaming services are designed to hold users' attention, and hours spent scrolling often feel neither restful nor satisfying, which increases the impression that there is never enough time.

Several measures could help to address this situation. At the workplace level, companies could introduce clear policies limiting contact outside working hours, and governments could consider a legal right to disconnect. More flexible working arrangements, such as compressed working weeks, might also give employees longer periods of genuine rest. On a personal level, individuals can take control of their digital habits by disabling non-essential notifications, setting limits on app usage and keeping certain times of the day free from screens. Finally, people may benefit from prioritising fewer activities rather than trying to fill every moment productively.

In conclusion, people have less free time despite technological progress because work has expanded into their personal lives, expectations have risen and digital entertainment absorb many hours. Workplace policies and more mindful use of technology could help them regain valuable leisure time.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Technology has spared people countless hours of domestic drudgery and administrative effort, yet complaints about a lack of time have never been more common. This apparent contradiction can be explained by the way the time saved is reabsorbed by work and digital distraction, and reclaiming leisure will require action from employers, governments and individuals alike.

The first explanation lies in the erosion of boundaries between work and private life. Devices that make it possible to work from anywhere also make it possible to be contacted everywhere, and in many workplaces an unspoken expectation has developed that emails will be answered promptly, whatever the hour. As a result, even time spent at home is frequently interrupted by professional demands. Secondly, efficiency tends to raise expectations rather than reduce effort: when a task can be completed in half the time, the typical response is to take on more tasks, not to rest. Finally, much of the time technology frees is quietly consumed by technology itself. Social media feeds and streaming platforms are deliberately designed to be absorbing, and hours spent on them rarely feel like genuine leisure, leaving people both occupied and unrefreshed.

Addressing the problem requires structural as well as personal change. Employers could make it clear that staff are not required to respond outside working hours, and legislation guaranteeing a right to disconnect would give such policies greater force. Shorter working weeks, where output can be maintained, would allow productivity gains to be shared with workers as additional free time rather than extra workload. Individuals, too, can reclaim hours by curbing their use of attention-grabbing apps, disabling notifications and deliberately protecting periods of the day for rest, hobbies or social contact.

In conclusion, people feel short of time because technology has extended the reach of work, raised expectations and created new distractions. Firmer boundaries set by employers and governments, combined with more deliberate personal habits, would allow the time saved by technology to become genuine free time.

In many countries, the number of people who live alone is growing quickly. This essay will explain the reasons for this trend and discuss its effects on society.

There are several reasons why more people live alone. Firstly, people today get married later than in the past, and some decide not to marry at all. Young adults want to focus on their career and enjoy their freedom, so they rent a small flat by themselves. Secondly, many people move to big cities for work, far away from their parents, so they have no choice except living alone. Also, there are more elderly people now because people live longer, and when their husband or wife die, they often continue to live alone in their house. Finally, some people simply prefer privacy and independence.

This trend has both positive and negative effects on society. On the positive side, people who live alone often spend more money on restaurants, entertainment and travel, which is good for the economy. However, there are more negative effects. First, it increase the demand for housing, because one person needs a whole apartment, so house prices become higher. Second, many people who live alone feel lonely, especially old people, and this can cause health problems. For example, an elderly woman who lives by herself may not talk with anyone for several days. As a result, government have to spend more money on social services.

In conclusion, more people live alone because they marry later, move to cities for work and live longer. I believe this trend has more negative effects than positive, because it makes housing more expensive and causes loneliness in the society.

Single-person households have become increasingly common in many parts of the world. This essay will examine the main reasons for this trend and consider its impact on society, which I believe is mixed but raises some serious concerns.

One of the most significant reasons is a change in social attitudes. In the past, young people usually stayed with their parents until they married, but today marriage often happens later or not at all, and living independently is seen as a normal stage of adult life. Economic growth has also made this possible, since many young professionals earn enough to rent their own apartment. Another factor is the ageing population. As life expectancy increases, more elderly people outlive their partners and continue living in the family home on their own. In addition, greater geographical mobility means that people frequently move to cities far from their relatives for work or study.

This trend has several effects on society. From an economic perspective, it has created new markets for smaller homes, single-portion meals and services aimed at individuals. However, it also puts considerable pressure on housing supply, because more homes are needed to accommodate the same number of people, which pushes up rents and property prices, particularly in large cities. A more worrying consequence is social isolation. Although many people living alone have active social lives, others, especially the elderly, can go days without meaningful contact, and loneliness can harm both physical and mental health. This may increase the demand on healthcare and social services. Finally, weaker family networks means that fewer people can rely on relatives for care and support.

In conclusion, more people live alone because of changing attitudes to marriage, increased wealth, longer lives and greater mobility. While this trend offers freedom and new business opportunities, it also contributes to housing shortages and social isolation.

answers.text:
Living alone, once associated mainly with widowhood or unusual circumstances, has become a mainstream choice in many societies. This shift reflects profound changes in values, economics and demography, and while it brings certain benefits, its wider effects on society are, on balance, a cause for concern.

Changing social norms are a key driver. Marriage now tends to occur later, if at all, and living independently is widely regarded as a desirable marker of adulthood rather than a temporary stage before settling down. Greater prosperity has enabled people to act on this preference, since many can afford a home of their own. Demographic trends reinforce the pattern: as life expectancy rises, a growing number of older people outlive their partners and choose to remain in familiar surroundings rather than move in with their children. Increased mobility plays a part as well, with people relocating for work to cities where they have no family ties.

The consequences are varied. Economically, single-person households have stimulated demand for compact apartments, convenience products and services tailored to individuals, and living alone allows people to pursue careers and interests with considerable freedom. However, because more dwellings are needed to house the same population, the trend places heavy strain on housing supply and contributes to rising rents in already crowded cities. It also has environmental implications, as people living alone typically consume more energy and space per person. Most significantly, it can foster isolation. Many who live alone lead rich social lives, but for others, particularly the elderly, solitude can turn into loneliness, with damaging effects on wellbeing. As traditional family networks thin out, the responsibility for care increasingly falls on public services.

In conclusion, the rise in solo living stems from evolving attitudes, economic independence, longer lifespans and mobility. Although it offers autonomy and new economic opportunities, its impact on housing, resources and social connection means that societies need to plan for its consequences.

Today we can find international brands and fast-food restaurants almost in every country. This essay will explain why this has happened and how it affects local businesses and culture.

There are several reasons for this situation. Firstly, globalisation made trade between countries much easier than before. Many governments have reduced taxes on foreign companies, so big companies can open branches in other countries without many problems. Secondly, these brands are very popular, especially among young people, because they see them in films, on television and on the internet. For example, many teenagers want to eat in famous burger restaurants or wear sports shoes from well-known brands because they think it is modern and cool. Also, these companies have a lot of money for advertising, so they can attract customers everywhere.

This trend has some negative effects on local businesses and culture. International chains are usually cheaper and more famous, so small local shops and restaurants lose their customers and some of them have to close. For example, a family café may not survive when a big coffee chain opens on the same street. In addition, traditional food and clothes become less popular, especially with young generation, and every city starts to look the same with the same shops. However, there are also some positive effects. International companies create jobs for local people and they sometimes bring new ideas and higher standards of service which local businesses can learn.

In conclusion, international brands are everywhere because of globalisation, their popularity and strong advertising. Although they create jobs, I think they have a bad influence on small local business and traditional culture, so governments should protect them.

Global brands and fast-food chains have spread to almost every corner of the world, from major capital cities to small towns. This essay will discuss the reasons for this expansion and examine its effects on local businesses and culture, which I believe are largely negative.

The main reason for this spread is economic globalisation. Over recent decades, many countries have opened their markets to foreign investment and reduced trade barriers, making it far easier for multinational companies to operate abroad. Improvements in transport and communication have also allowed these companies to manage supply chains across continents. Another important factor is the power of global media. Through films, television and social media, consumers around the world are exposed to the same brands, which become associated with a modern, attractive lifestyle. As a result, a well-known coffee chain or clothing label can have instant appeal in a new market even before it opens its first store.

The effect on local businesses is often damaging. Multinational companies benefit from enormous marketing budgets and economies of scale, allowing them to offer lower prices and more consistent quality than small independent firms. Family-run cafés, restaurants and shops may therefore struggle to compete and eventually close down. Culturally, the growing dominance of global chains can weaken local traditions. When young people prefer international fast food to traditional dishes, or when high streets in different countries fill with identical shops, the distinctive character of a place begins to disappear. On the other hand, global brands does provide employment and sometimes encourage local firms to raise their standards, and some chains adapt their menus to local tastes.

In conclusion, international brands have spread because of open markets, better logistics and the influence of global media. While they create jobs, they often put pressure on local businesses and contribute to a loss of cultural diversity.

answers.text:
From burger chains to coffee houses and sportswear labels, a handful of international brands have established a presence in almost every country on earth. Their spread is the product of economic liberalisation and global media, and its effects on local enterprises and cultural identity are, in my view, more harmful than beneficial, although not uniformly so.

The expansion has been driven above all by the opening of national markets. As governments have lowered trade barriers and actively courted foreign investment, multinational corporations have found it increasingly straightforward to establish outlets abroad, often through franchising arrangements that limit their financial risk. Advances in logistics mean that products can be sourced and distributed across continents with remarkable efficiency. Equally important is cultural reach. Films, television and social media have familiarised audiences everywhere with the same logos, and for many consumers, particularly the young, these brands carry an aura of modernity and cosmopolitan status long before a branch opens nearby.

For local businesses, the arrival of a global chain can be devastating. Such companies enjoy economies of scale, sophisticated marketing and the ability to absorb initial losses, advantages that independent restaurants and shops simply cannot match. Where these smaller enterprises close, profits that once circulated within the community are instead transferred abroad. The cultural consequences are subtler but equally significant. As international menus and products become the norm, traditional cuisine and crafts may come to seem old-fashioned, and town centres across the world grow increasingly indistinguishable. Nevertheless, the picture is not entirely bleak: multinationals provide employment and training, many adapt their offerings to local tastes, and competition can prompt local firms to differentiate themselves by emphasising authenticity.

In conclusion, global brands have proliferated because of open markets, efficient supply chains and the influence of global media. Although they bring jobs and some healthy competition, they frequently undermine independent businesses and erode the cultural distinctiveness that makes places unique.

Rich countries often give money to poor countries to help them. This essay will explain the reasons why they do this and which kind of help I think is the most effective in the long term.

There are several reasons for giving financial aid. The first reason is humanitarian. When there is a natural disaster like an earthquake or a flood, people in poor countries need food, water and medicine urgently, and rich countries want to help them because it is right thing to do. Secondly, wealthy countries also get benefits from giving aid. For example, they can build good relationship with the other country and later they can do business or trade with it. Also, some rich countries give aid because they want to have political influence in that region.

In my opinion, the most effective help in the long term is not only giving money but helping poor countries to develop themselves. Money can be spent quickly or can be stolen by corrupt officials, so the problem continue. Instead, rich countries should invest in education and training, so that people can get better jobs and earn their own money. For instance, building schools and training teachers will help a whole generation. Also, they can help to build infrastructure like roads, hospitals and clean water system, and share their technology with local farmers so they can grow more food.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid because they want to help people and also for their own economic and political benefits. I believe that education, infrastructure and technology is more useful than just money, because it helps poor countries to become independent in the future.

Wealthy nations commonly provide financial assistance to less developed countries. This essay will explore the motives behind such aid and argue that support which builds long-term capacity, particularly in education and infrastructure, is more effective than direct financial transfers.

Wealthy countries give aid for a combination of moral and practical reasons. The most obvious motive is humanitarian: when poorer nations are affected by famine, conflict or natural disasters, there is a strong ethical case for helping those in need, and public opinion in donor countries usually approves. However, aid is also a tool of foreign policy. By supporting a developing country, a donor can strengthen diplomatic ties and gain influence in a strategically important region. There are economic motives as well, since growth in poorer countries can create new markets for the donor's exports, and some aid is even tied to the purchase of goods or services from the donor nation. Finally, reducing poverty abroad may help to limit global problems such as the spread of disease.

As for long-term results, I believe aid which helps countries to become self-sufficient is the most valuable. Emergency funding is essential in a crisis, but continuous cash transfers can create dependency and are sometimes lost through corruption. By contrast, investment in education equips people with skills they can use for decades, and support for healthcare produces a healthier, more productive workforce. Projects such as roads, electricity networks and irrigation systems enable local businesses and farmers to increase their output and reach new markets. Such help works best when it is designed in partnership with local communities, so that projects meet genuine needs and is maintained after foreign experts leave.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid out of humanitarian concern as well as political and economic self-interest. In the long run, assistance that develops education, health and infrastructure is far more effective than simply providing money.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Financial aid from wealthy to poorer nations is a long-established feature of international relations, yet the reasons behind it are rarely purely altruistic, and the forms it takes vary greatly in their lasting impact. In my view, aid that strengthens a country's own capacity to generate wealth and provide services is by far the most effective over time.

The motives of donor countries are typically a blend of principle and self-interest. On a moral level, there is a widely shared sense that prosperous nations have an obligation to relieve suffering, particularly in the aftermath of disasters or during famines. At the same time, aid serves diplomatic ends. Supporting a developing country can secure its goodwill, strengthen alliances and extend a donor's influence in regions of strategic importance. Economic calculation also plays a role: a more prosperous partner becomes a larger market for exports and a more stable place to invest, and some aid is explicitly tied to contracts for the donor's own firms. Lastly, since epidemics and instability rarely respect borders, reducing poverty abroad can serve donors' own security.

When it comes to long-term effectiveness, the crucial distinction is between assistance that meets immediate needs and assistance that builds lasting capability. Emergency relief is indispensable in a crisis, but sustained cash transfers to governments risk fostering dependency and can be diverted by corruption. Investment in education, by contrast, pays dividends for generations, while support for primary healthcare raises productivity as well as wellbeing. Infrastructure such as reliable electricity, roads and irrigation enables farmers and entrepreneurs to expand, creating employment that no donation could sustain. These projects are most successful when shaped by local communities, which ensures that they reflect genuine priorities and continue once foreign involvement ends.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid out of a mixture of compassion, diplomacy and economic interest. The most effective long-term help is not money alone but investment in the education, health and infrastructure that allow poorer nations to prosper independently.

Nowadays many young people have problem to save money, even when they have a job. This essay will explain the reasons for this and suggest some ways to encourage them to save more.

There are several reasons why young people find it difficult to save. Firstly, the cost of living is very high today, especially in big cities. Rent, transport and food are expensive, so after paying all the bills, there is not much money left. Secondly, young people are influenced by social media and advertising. They see their friends or influencers buying new clothes, phones and going on holidays, and they want to do the same. Also, online shopping and credit cards make spending very easy, because you can buy something with one click and pay later. Another reason is that many young people did not learn how to manage money at school or at home.

There are some ways to encourage young people to save. Firstly, schools should teach financial education, for example how to make a budget and why saving is important. If students learn this early, they will have good habits in the future. Secondly, banks can offer special saving accounts for young people with higher interest, so saving becomes more attractive. There are also mobile apps which can save small amount of money automatically every time you spend. Finally, parents should give a good example and talk with their children about money.

In conclusion, young people find it hard to save because of high living costs, social pressure and easy spending. Financial education, special accounts and apps can help them to save more money for the future.

Many young adults today struggle to put money aside, even when they are in full-time employment. This essay will examine the main reasons for this difficulty and suggest measures that could encourage younger people to develop better saving habits.

The most significant factor is the high cost of living. In many cities, rents have risen much faster than wages, so a large proportion of a young person's income is spent on accommodation before other essential expenses such as transport and food are even considered. For those who are also repaying student loans, the money available for saving is even smaller. Consumer culture adds to the problem. Social media constantly exposes young people to images of fashionable products, restaurants and holidays, creating pressure to keep up with their peers. At the same time, contactless payments and 'buy now, pay later' services make spending so effortless that many people lose track of how much they have spent. Finally, a lack of financial education means that many young adults have never been taught how to budget effectively.

Several steps could help to change this situation. Schools could make personal finance a compulsory part of the curriculum, teaching students how to plan a budget, understand interest and avoid unnecessary debt. Banks and technology companies also have a role to play; apps that automatically round up purchases and transfer the difference into a savings account make saving almost effortless. Governments could offer incentives, such as tax-free savings accounts or bonuses for young people saving towards their first home, which would give them a clear goal to work towards. In addition, clearer regulation of short-term credit would reduce the temptation to overspend.

In conclusion, young people find saving difficult because of high living costs, social pressure and easy access to credit. Financial education, smart technology and government incentives could encourage them to builds more secure financial futures.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
For many young adults, building up savings now feels like an unattainable goal. The explanation lies partly in economic conditions beyond their control and partly in a consumer environment that makes spending effortless, but there are practical ways in which saving could be made both easier and more appealing.

Structural pressures are the most obvious obstacle. Housing costs in many cities have far outpaced wages, so rent alone can absorb a substantial share of a young worker's income, and entry-level jobs are increasingly insecure or poorly paid. Loan repayments for education leave even less room for anything else. These constraints are compounded by the culture in which young people live. Social media presents a constant stream of holidays, restaurants and new products, making modest living feel like missing out, while frictionless digital payments and instalment schemes disguise the true cost of purchases. Furthermore, many young adults leave school without ever having been taught to budget, so even those with some spare income may lack the habits needed to retain it.

Encouraging saving therefore requires a combination of education, design and incentives. Personal finance should be taught in schools as a practical skill, covering budgeting, interest and the dangers of high-cost credit, so that good habits are formed before the first salary arrives. Financial technology can also be harnessed for positive ends: automatic transfers on payday and apps that round up transactions into savings make putting money aside the default rather than an act of willpower. Governments could strengthen motivation by offering bonuses or tax advantages on savings for specific goals, such as a first home, and tighter regulation of instalment schemes would make the cost of borrowing more transparent.

In conclusion, young people struggle to save because of high living costs, insecure work and a culture that encourages consumption. By teaching financial skills early, designing tools that make saving automatic and offering meaningful incentives, society could help them build greater financial security.

Nowadays, a growing number of students decide to go to universities in foreign countries instead of studying in their home country. In my opinion, this is mainly a positive development, although there are some problems too.

The first reason why I think it is positive is that students can get a better education. Many universities in countries like the UK or Australia have modern facilities and experienced teachers, so students can learn things which is not available in their own country. For example, a student from a developing country who study engineering abroad can use advanced laboratories and learn the newest technology. When they return back home, they can use this knowledge to help the development of their country.

Secondly, living in another country helps young people to become more independent. They have to cook for themselves, manage their money and solve problems without the help of their parents. Also, they meet people from many different cultures, and this make them more open-minded. These skills are very useful when they start working, because many companies want employees who can work in international environment.

However, there are also some disadvantages. Studying abroad is very expensive, and some families have to borrow a lot of money for it. Moreover, some students do not come back after they graduate, so their home country lose talented people. This is a serious problem for poorer countries.

In conclusion, although studying abroad has some drawbacks such as the high cost and the loss of skilled people, I believe it is a positive development because it gives students a better education and helps them to grow as a person.

answers.text:
It has become increasingly common for young people to leave their home country in order to complete a degree abroad. While this trend brings certain risks, particularly for the countries that students leave behind, I believe that it is, on balance, a positive development.

The most obvious benefit is academic. Universities in popular destinations often offer research facilities, specialist courses and teaching methods that are simply not available in many students' home countries. A medical student from a country with few training hospitals, for instance, may gain far more practical experience at an overseas institution. Moreover, an internationally recognised degree can significantly improve a graduate's job prospects, both at home and abroad.

Beyond the classroom, studying overseas develops personal qualities that are difficult to acquire elsewhere. Students must adapt to an unfamiliar culture, communicate in a second language every day and cope without their families nearby. As a result, they tend to return more confident, adaptable and tolerant of different viewpoints. In a globalised economy, these are exactly the qualities that employers are looking for.

Admittedly, the trend has a downside. Many graduates choose to stay in the country where they studied, which means that their home countries lose the talent they invested in during school years. In addition, the high cost of tuition and accommodation means that this opportunity is mostly available for wealthier families, which may widen inequality. Nevertheless, these problems can be reduced through scholarships and incentives that encourage graduates to return.

In conclusion, although studying abroad can contribute to a loss of skilled workers and is not accessible to everyone, its benefits for individual students and, ultimately, for their societies are greater. I therefore regard it as a largely positive development.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
The number of students enrolling at universities outside their home countries has risen steadily in recent decades. Although this movement of young people is not without costs, I would argue that it is a predominantly positive development, both for the students themselves and for the wider world.

For individual students, the advantages are considerable. Studying abroad often provides access to specialised programmes, well-funded laboratories and academics at the forefront of their fields, resources that may be scarce at home. Equally valuable is the experience of living independently in an unfamiliar society. Navigating a new education system, managing a budget and building friendships across cultural and linguistic boundaries cultivate a degree of resilience that few domestic degrees can match.

The benefits also extend beyond the individual. International campuses bring together people who might otherwise never meet, and the professional networks formed there can later underpin cooperation between businesses, research institutions and even governments. When graduates return home, they frequently bring new expertise and fresh perspectives with them, which can stimulate innovation in sectors ranging from healthcare to engineering.

It would be naive, however, to ignore the drawbacks. The so-called brain drain is a genuine concern, as a proportion of graduates settle permanently abroad, depriving their home countries of skills that are badly needed. Furthermore, the considerable expense involved means that overseas study remains largely the preserve of affluent families. Yet these problems stem less from international study itself than from limited opportunities for graduates at home and insufficient financial support, both of which governments can address through targeted scholarships and incentives to return.

In conclusion, while the loss of talent and unequal access are legitimate concerns, the academic, personal and societal gains of studying abroad clearly outweigh them. This is, therefore, a trend to be welcomed rather than feared.

These days, many people use the internet to do almost all their daily tasks, for example paying bills, buying food and contacting government offices. I think this is a positive development for most people, but it can cause problems for some groups.

The main advantage of doing things online is that it save a lot of time. In the past, people had to wait in long queue at the bank or at a government office, and sometimes they needed to take a day off work. Now they can transfer money or renew a document in few minutes from their home. This is very convenient, especially for people who is busy with work and family.

Another benefit is that online services are available all the time. Shops and offices close in the evening, but websites and apps are open 24 hours. People who live in villages far from the city can also use the same services as people in the city, so they do not need to travel.

On the other hand, not everyone is comfortable with technology. Many elderly people do not know how to use smartphones, and they may feel left behind when banks close their branches. In addition, there is a risk of online fraud. Some people lose their money because criminals steal their passwords or send fake emails.

In conclusion, I believe that doing everyday tasks online is mostly a positive development because it is fast and convenient for most people. However, the government and companies should still keep some offices open for people who cannot use internet, and they should teach people how to stay safe online.

In many parts of the world, people now manage their finances, do their shopping and even apply for official documents without leaving home. In my view, this shift to online services is largely positive, although it must be managed carefully so that vulnerable groups are not excluded.

The clearest benefit is convenience. Tasks that once required a trip across town and a long wait in a queue can now be completed in minutes on a smartphone, at any time of day. For working parents or people with demanding jobs, this saves hours every month. It also benefits those living in rural areas, who previously had to travel long distances to reach a bank branch or a government office.

Online systems can also make services more efficient and transparent. When forms are submitted digitally, applications are processed faster and there are fewer opportunities for paperwork to be lost. In addition, digital records allow citizens to track the progress of a request, which reduce the frustration of not knowing what is happening. Governments and banks, meanwhile, can cut their running costs and, in theory, pass these savings on to the public.

Nevertheless, the move online has created real difficulties for some people. Older citizens and those on low incomes may lack the devices or skills needed to use digital services confidently, and as physical branches close, they risk being left without support. The growth of online fraud is another serious concern, since criminals increasingly target people who are unfamiliar with technology.

Overall, I believe the advantages of handling everyday tasks online outweigh the disadvantages, making this a positive development. However, it will only remain so if face-to-face options are kept for those who need them and people are taught how to protect themselves online.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Over the past two decades, the internet has quietly absorbed many of the routine chores of adult life. Bills are paid through banking apps, groceries arrive at the door and tax returns are filed on government portals. I consider this a broadly positive development, provided that it does not become compulsory for those unable to take part.

The most compelling argument in its favour is the time it returns to people. A task that might once have consumed an entire morning, involving a bus journey, a queue and a counter that closed at four o'clock, can now be completed during a lunch break. This flexibility is particularly valuable for shift workers, carers and residents of remote areas, for whom physical offices were always difficult to reach. In effect, digital services have removed a hidden tax on people's time.

There are systemic gains as well. Digital applications can be processed more quickly and consistently than paper ones, and the automatic record they create makes institutions more accountable. A citizen who can see exactly where a benefit claim has stalled is in a far stronger position than one waiting anxiously for a letter. Moreover, the savings from reduced administration can, at least in principle, be redirected towards improving the services themselves.

The danger lies in treating online access as universal when it is not. Many elderly people, as well as those who cannot afford reliable internet access, find digital systems bewildering, and the closure of branches can leave them dependent on relatives or simply unable to manage their own affairs. The rise of sophisticated online scams compounds this problem, as it is often the least confident users who are targeted.

In conclusion, the migration of everyday tasks online has made life markedly easier for the majority, and I therefore view it positively. Its benefits will only be fairly shared, however, if traditional channels remain available for those who still depend on them.

answers.text:
Recently, more people are using artificial intelligence programs to ask advice about their personal problems, like relationship problems or feeling sad. In my opinion, this is more a negative development than a positive one.

Some people think AI advice is useful. It is available at any time, even in the middle of the night, and it is free or very cheap. Also, some people feel shy to talk about their problems with friends or family, so they prefer to type their questions to a computer because nobody will judge them. For this people, AI can be a first step to understand their feelings.

However, I believe the disadvantages are more serious. Firstly, a computer program does not really understand human emotions. It gives answers based on data, but it does not know the person's full situation, their culture or their family history. Because of this, the advice can be too general or even wrong. For example, if someone has a serious problem in their marriage, a program cannot replace a trained counsellor who listen carefully and ask the right questions.

Secondly, people may become depend on AI and stop talking to real people. Friends and family give not only advice but also love and support, which a machine cannot give. If people share their problems only with a computer, they may feel more lonely in the long term. There is also a privacy problem, because personal information is saved by the companies who make these programs.

In conclusion, although AI can give quick and easy advice, I think this trend is negative because the advice is not always reliable and people can lose the real human connection that they need when they have difficulties.

answers.text:
Artificial intelligence chatbots are no longer used only for practical tasks; many people now turn to them for guidance on their relationships and emotional struggles. Although this can offer some short-term comfort, I believe it is, overall, a negative development.

It is easy to understand the appeal. AI programs are available around the clock, cost little or nothing and, crucially, do not judge. A person who feels embarrassed about a problem may find it easier to describe it to a machine than to a friend, and the response can help them organise their thoughts. For people who live in areas with few counsellors, a chatbot may be the only source of guidance available.

However, these advantages are outweighed by several serious concerns. The most important is that AI does not truly understand the people it is advising. It produces plausible answers based on patterns in data, but it cannot read body language, notice what is left unsaid or take full account of a person's history. As a result, its advice may sound convincing while being inappropriate, and in situations involving serious emotional distress this could be harmful.

A further problem is the effect on human relationships. Talking through a difficulty with a friend or relative is not only a way of finding a solution; it also strengthens the bond between them. If people increasingly confide in software instead, they may become more isolated, which is the opposite of what someone in a difficult situation need. There are also questions about how technology companies store and use such sensitive conversations.

In conclusion, while AI can be a convenient starting point for reflecting on personal issues, relying on it for emotional advice is a worrying trend. It should complement, rather than replace, support from people and qualified professionals.

while AI can be a convenient starting point for reflecting on personal issues, relying on it for emotional advice is a worrying trend. It should complement, rather than replace, support from people and qualified professionals.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
As conversational AI has become more sophisticated, a growing number of people are consulting it about matters that were once discussed only with close friends, family members or therapists. While I accept that such tools can play a modest supporting role, I regard the broader trend as a largely negative one.

The case in favour deserves to be taken seriously. Chatbots are instantly accessible, inexpensive and endlessly patient, and for someone too ashamed or anxious to confide in another person, the anonymity of a screen may lower the barrier to seeking help at all. Articulating a problem in writing can itself bring clarity, and a well-designed program may point users towards professional services they would not otherwise have considered.

Yet the limitations are fundamental rather than incidental. Personal difficulties are rarely what they first appear to be; a dispute with a partner may be rooted in years of unspoken resentment, and low mood may signal a condition requiring clinical attention. A skilled counsellor draws on tone, hesitation and context to uncover these layers, whereas an AI can only respond to the words it is given. Its answers therefore tend towards the generic, and because they are expressed fluently and confidently, users may place more trust in them than they merit.

Perhaps more troubling is what this habit may do to human connection. Seeking advice from a friend is an act of trust that deepens relationships, and receiving support reminds people that they are not alone. If individuals increasingly bring their most intimate concerns to software designed to keep them engaged, they risk becoming more isolated precisely when they most need others. Entrusting commercial platforms with such sensitive information raises additional concerns about privacy.

In conclusion, AI may usefully serve as a first step, but as a substitute for human insight and care it is inadequate. For that reason, the growing reliance on it for personal advice should be viewed with considerable caution.

In recent years, some governments have made laws to stop people using single-use plastic items like bags, straws and cups. In my opinion, this is a positive development, even though it can be inconvenient for some people at first.

The most important reason is that plastic is very harmful for the environment. Single-use items are used only for few minutes, but they stay in nature for hundreds of years. A lot of this plastic go into rivers and the sea, where fish and birds eat it and die. On many beaches, people can see bottles and bags everywhere, which is also bad for tourism. If these products are banned, the amount of rubbish will reduce a lot.

Another reason is that the ban changes people's habits. When shops stop giving free plastic bags, customers start to bring their own cloth bags. In my country, for example, after the government ban plastic bags, most people quickly got used to carry reusable bags, and now it is normal. So a law can teach people to think more about the environment in their daily life.

However, some people argue that the ban is not fair for small businesses, because paper or metal products is more expensive. Also, some disabled people need plastic straws to drink. These are real problems, but the government can help businesses with the cost and allow special exceptions.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that banning single-use plastic is a positive step, because it protects the environment and helps people to develop better habits. The small problems it cause are much less important than the benefits for nature.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
A number of countries have recently passed laws prohibiting single-use plastic items such as carrier bags, straws and disposable cups. Although these bans create some short-term difficulties, I firmly believe they are a positive development.

The main argument in favour is the scale of the environmental damage caused by disposable plastic. These products are typically used for a few minutes but can take centuries to break down, and a large proportion of them ends up in rivers and oceans rather than being recycled. Marine animals frequently become trapped in plastic waste or mistake it for food, and tiny plastic particles are now found in the food chain. Banning the most common items therefore tackles the problem at its source rather than relying on clean-up campaigns.

In addition, legislation is often more effective than voluntary change. For years, people have been encouraged to reuse bags and avoid plastic straws, yet many continued to use them simply out of habit. When a ban is introduced, alternatives quickly become the norm; customers remember to bring their own bags, and cafes switch to paper or reusable options. Such laws also send a clear message that protecting the environment is a shared responsibility.

Critics point out that substitutes can be more expensive and that some people, including certain disabled individuals, genuinely rely on plastic straws. These are valid concerns, but they can be addressed through sensible exemptions and temporary support for small businesses, rather than by abandoning the policy altogether.

In conclusion, while bans on single-use plastic cause some inconvenience, the long-term benefits for wildlife, oceans and human health are far greater. For this reason, I consider them a clearly positive development.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Governments in several countries have moved beyond encouraging responsible consumption and have begun to outlaw disposable plastic products altogether. Although such bans are sometimes dismissed as symbolic or inconvenient, I regard them as an unequivocally positive development.

The environmental rationale is difficult to dispute. Items such as straws and carrier bags serve their purpose for minutes yet persist in the environment for generations, and because they are light and cheap, they are among the items most likely to escape waste systems and end up in waterways. Once there, they entangle wildlife, break down into microplastics and ultimately return to humans through the food chain. Restricting their production addresses the problem at its origin, which is far more efficient than attempting to retrieve plastic once it has dispersed across coastlines and seabeds.

Equally significant is the effect such laws have on behaviour. Decades of public awareness campaigns achieved only modest results, largely because individual consumers had little incentive to abandon a convenient habit. A ban, by contrast, removes the choice and in doing so rapidly establishes a new social norm: carrying a reusable bag or cup soon feels unremarkable rather than virtuous. This shift can also stimulate innovation, as manufacturers compete to develop durable or biodegradable alternatives.

Opponents raise two legitimate objections. Replacement materials can be costlier for small retailers, and some people with disabilities depend on flexible plastic straws. Neither point, however, undermines the principle of a ban. Both can be accommodated through carefully designed exemptions and transitional support, and some substitutes carry their own environmental costs, which argues for promoting reuse rather than for retaining plastic.

In conclusion, laws against single-use plastics tackle a serious environmental threat directly and reshape everyday habits in a way that persuasion alone has failed to do. Provided they are implemented with appropriate flexibility, they deserve wholehearted support.

In many cities today, old factories and warehouses are being changed into expensive flats, shops and cafes. I think this is mostly a positive development, although it also has some negative effects on local people.

Firstly, redevelopment makes the city more beautiful and safer. Old industrial areas are often empty and dirty, and sometimes they become dangerous places at night. When these buildings are repaired and turned into apartments and cafes, the area become more lively and attractive. People start to walk there, go shopping and meet friends, so the whole neighbourhood improve.

Secondly, these projects are good for the economy. Building new apartments and shops create many jobs, both during the construction and after that, in the cafes and stores. The city government also receive more money from taxes, which it can spend on public services like schools and transport. In addition, using old buildings is better than building on green land outside the city.

On the other hand, there is a big problem, which is that the new apartments are very expensive. Local people who lived near the old factories often cannot afford the higher rent, so they have to move to another area. This is unfair, because they lived there for many years and they lose their community.

In conclusion, I believe that turning old industrial areas into apartments, shops and cafes is a positive development because it improves the city and the economy. However, the government should make sure that some cheaper homes are also built, so local people can stay in their area.

answers.text:
Across many cities, abandoned factories, docks and warehouses are being converted into luxury flats, boutiques and coffee shops. While such regeneration brings visible improvements, I believe that in its current form it is more of a negative development than a positive one, mainly because of its effect on existing residents.

Admittedly, there are clear benefits. Derelict industrial sites can be unsightly and even unsafe, and restoring them brings life back to neglected parts of a city. Converting existing buildings is also more sustainable than building on the countryside, and new businesses create jobs and generate tax revenue for local authorities. In some cases, historic industrial architecture is preserved that might otherwise have been demolished.

However, these benefits are not shared equally. As an area becomes fashionable, property prices and rents rise sharply, and long-term residents, who are often working-class families, are gradually priced out. The people who lived through the area's decline are therefore frequently unable to enjoy its revival. The small, affordable shops that served them are replaced by expensive cafes that cater mainly for newcomers and visitors.

Furthermore, this process can weaken the social fabric of a city. Established communities, with their networks of neighbours, schools and local organisations, are broken up when families are forced to move to cheaper districts further from the centre. Over time, cities risk becoming divided into wealthy inner areas and poorer outer suburbs, which increase inequality and commuting times for those with the lowest incomes.

In conclusion, although redeveloping old industrial areas improves the appearance and economy of cities, the displacement of local communities is too high a price to pay. Unless regeneration schemes include a significant share of affordable housing, I regard this trend as largely negative.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In cities around the world, the disused factories and warehouses of a former industrial age are being reborn as upmarket apartments, independent boutiques and artisan cafes. This transformation is often celebrated as urban renewal, and in many respects it is. On balance, however, I believe its benefits are real but narrowly distributed, which makes it, as currently practised, a largely negative development.

The case for regeneration is by no means weak. Vacant industrial land tends to attract crime and dereliction, and bringing it back into use can revitalise surrounding streets. Reusing existing structures is also considerably more sustainable than expanding into greenfield sites, and it can preserve architecture that gives a city its distinctive character. Local authorities, meanwhile, benefit from higher tax receipts and new employment.

The difficulty lies in who ultimately enjoys these gains. Once a former industrial district acquires a reputation as fashionable, land values rise and rents follow. Long-standing residents, frequently on modest incomes, find themselves unable to remain in neighbourhoods they have lived in for decades, and the hardware shops and inexpensive cafes they relied upon give way to businesses aimed at a more affluent clientele. What is presented as improvement for an area can thus amount to the replacement of one population by another.

The wider consequences are equally concerning. When displaced families relocate to peripheral suburbs, they lose not only their homes but also the informal support networks that sustain communities, while facing longer and more expensive journeys to work. Repeated across a city, this pattern produces a polarised urban landscape in which the centre becomes the preserve of the wealthy.

In conclusion, converting industrial land into expensive housing and leisure spaces undoubtedly revitalises the physical fabric of cities, but it too often does so at the expense of the people who already live there. Unless such projects are required to include genuinely affordable homes, the trend should be viewed as more harmful than beneficial.

Nowadays, in many cities people can rent electric scooters and bicycles by the hour using a phone app. Although this idea seems modern and useful, I believe it is more a negative development than a positive one.

It is true that these vehicles have some advantages. They are cheap and easy to use for short journeys, for example from the train station to the office. They also do not produce pollution like cars, so they can help to reduce traffic and make the air more cleaner.

However, the biggest problem is safety. Many riders of electric scooters go very fast and they do not wear a helmet. Some of them ride on the pavement, which is very dangerous for pedestrians, especially old people and children. In my city, I often see scooters that nearly hit people who are walking, and there has been many accidents. Also, some users do not know the traffic rules, because they only use the scooter one or two time.

Another problem is that these scooters and bikes are often left everywhere. Because users can leave them in any place, many of them block the pavement or the entrance of buildings. This is annoying for everyone and particularly difficult for people in wheelchair or with a pushchair. In some places scooters are even thrown into rivers, which make more pollution.

In conclusion, although hire scooters and bicycles are convenient and do not pollute the air, I think they are a negative development because they cause accidents and make the streets messy. The government should make strict rules, for example speed limits and special parking areas, otherwise the problems will continue.

answers.text:
Rentable electric scooters and bicycles, unlocked with a smartphone and paid for by the hour, have appeared on the streets of many cities in recent years. Despite some genuine problems, I believe this is a positive development for urban life.

The principal advantage is that these vehicles offer a practical alternative to cars for short trips. Many car journeys in cities cover only a few kilometres, which could easily be made by bike or scooter. Hire schemes make this option available to people who do not own a bicycle or have nowhere to store one. They are especially useful for the so-called last mile, the distance between a train station or bus stop and a person's final destination, and they can therefore encourage more people to use public transport.

Moreover, if these schemes replace even a small proportion of car journeys, the environmental benefits are significant. Fewer cars means less congestion, lower emissions and cleaner air, which improves public health. Cycling also provides exercise, and people who try a hire bike may decide to cycle more regularly.

Of course, the schemes have caused problems. Scooters are sometimes ridden dangerously on pavements, and vehicles are frequently left lying in the middle of footpaths, creating obstacles for pedestrians, particularly those with poor eyesight or limited mobility. However, these are problems of management rather than reasons to reject the idea. Cities can introduce designated parking zones, speed limits and fines for irresponsible users, as some have already done successfully.

In conclusion, although shared scooters and bicycles require careful regulation, they provide a cheap, flexible and environmentally friendly way of getting around cities. For these reasons, I consider their growing popularity to be a positive trend.

answers.text:
Dockless electric scooters and hire bicycles, located and unlocked through a smartphone, have become a familiar sight in many cities. Their arrival has provoked strong reactions, from enthusiasm about greener transport to irritation at cluttered pavements. Weighing these responses, I consider the trend a positive one, albeit one that demands firm regulation.

The strongest argument in their favour concerns the way people move through cities. A striking number of urban car journeys are short enough to be walked or cycled, yet habit and convenience keep drivers behind the wheel. Hire schemes lower the barriers to change: users need not buy, maintain or store a vehicle, and they can make a one-way trip without worrying about returning it. Crucially, scooters and bikes bridge the gap between public transport stops and people's homes or workplaces, making trains and buses a realistic option for those who previously found them impractical.

The potential environmental and social returns are considerable. Every car journey replaced reduces congestion and emissions, and cleaner streets benefit everyone, not only those who ride. For residents who cannot afford a car, affordable short-term hire also widens access to jobs and services across the city.

The drawbacks, nonetheless, are real and visible. Poorly parked scooters obstruct pavements, posing a particular hazard to blind and elderly pedestrians, and reckless riding has led to injuries. Yet these problems stem from the way schemes were initially introduced, often with minimal oversight, rather than from the vehicles themselves. Cities that have imposed designated parking bays, speed restrictions in pedestrian areas and penalties for operators have largely brought them under control.

In conclusion, shared scooters and bicycles offer a flexible, low-carbon complement to public transport. Provided that authorities regulate them rigorously, their spread should be welcomed as a positive development.

The potential environmental and social returns are considerable. Every car journey replaced reduces congestion and emissions, and cleaner streets benefit everyone, not only those who ride. For residents who cannot afford a car, affordable short-term hire also widens access to jobs and services across the city.

The drawbacks, nonetheless, are real and visible. Poorly parked scooters obstruct pavements, posing a particular hazard to blind and elderly pedestrians, and reckless riding has led to injuries. Yet these problems stem from the way schemes were initially introduced, often with minimal oversight, rather than from the vehicles themselves. Cities that have imposed designated parking bays, speed restrictions in pedestrian areas and penalties for operators have largely brought them under control.
In conclusion,

shared scooters and bicycles offer a flexible, low-carbon complement to public transport. Provided that authorities regulate them rigorously, their spread should be welcomed as a positive development.

Today, many companies use special software to check how hard their workers are working, for example by counting their keyboard use or taking screenshots of their computer. In my opinion, this is a negative development, although it has a few advantages for employers.

On the one hand, managers say that this software help them to make the company more efficient. They can see which employees are working hard and which are wasting time on social media. This information can be used to give rewards to good workers. Also, when people work from home, the manager cannot see them, so the software is the only way to check that they are doing their job.

On the other hand, I believe the disadvantages are much bigger. The first problem is that employees feel stressful when they know that a computer is watching them all the time. They may be afraid to take a short break or talk with colleagues, even though these things are normal and can help them to work better. As a result, their mental health can become worse.

The second problem is that the software does not measure real productivity. For instance, a designer who spend an hour thinking about a new idea may look lazy to the program, because he does not type anything. On the other hand, a worker who moves the mouse all day may look busy but produce nothing useful. So the company can make wrong decisions about their staff.

In conclusion, I think using software to monitor employees is a negative development because it creates stress and it cannot measure the quality of work properly. Companies should trust their staff more and judge them by the result of their work.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
With the growth of remote working, a rising number of employers have begun using software that records how long staff spend on particular tasks, which websites they visit and even how often they type. Although this technology may seem to offer greater efficiency, I believe it is essentially a negative development.

Supporters argue that monitoring tools give managers useful information. When teams work from home, it can be difficult to know whether tasks are being completed, and data on working patterns may help identify employees who are struggling or processes that waste time. Some also claim that such software is fair, since it judges everyone by the same objective standard.

However, the main weakness of this approach is that activity is not the same as productivity. Software can count keystrokes and log screen time, but it cannot measure the quality of a report, the value of a creative idea or the time an employee spends helping a colleague. As a result, workers may learn to appear busy rather than to work well, for example by keeping their mouse moving or avoiding tasks that involve thinking away from the computer.

Perhaps more importantly, constant surveillance damages trust between staff and management. Employees who feel watched every minute are likely to experience higher levels of stress, and many will feel that their employer does not respect them as professionals. This can lower morale and, ironically, lead to lower productivity and higher staff turnover. There is also a risk that personal data collected in this way are misused.

In conclusion, while monitoring software may give employers a sense of control, it measures the wrong things and undermines the trust on which good workplaces depend. For these reasons, I consider its increasing use to be a negative trend.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Software that logs keystrokes, captures screenshots and scores employees on their apparent activity has spread rapidly, particularly since remote work became widespread. Employers present it as a neutral tool for improving efficiency, but I would argue that its growing use is, on the whole, a negative development.

It is not difficult to see why managers find such tools attractive. Supervising a dispersed workforce is genuinely challenging, and aggregated data can reveal bottlenecks, uneven workloads or employees who may need additional support. In highly routine roles, such as processing claims or answering calls, some measurement of output is both reasonable and long established.

The central flaw, however, is that these programs mistake visible activity for valuable work. Much of what makes an employee effective, whether analysing a problem, mentoring a junior colleague or simply thinking before acting, leaves little digital trace. A system that rewards constant typing and penalises periods of inactivity therefore encourages staff to perform busyness rather than to achieve results, and may even discourage the reflective work on which innovation depends. In this sense, monitoring can distort the very productivity it claims to measure.

Equally damaging is its effect on the relationship between employer and employee. Continuous surveillance communicates distrust, and people who feel perpetually observed tend to become anxious, less willing to take initiative and more inclined to leave. Talented staff, who have the greatest choice of employers, are often the first to go. Furthermore, the detailed personal data such systems accumulate create obvious risks if they are stored carelessly or used for purposes employees never agreed to.

In conclusion, although monitoring software can offer useful insights in certain narrowly defined roles, its widespread use rests on a flawed understanding of what productive work looks like and erodes workplace trust. Organisations would be better served by judging employees on the outcomes they deliver.

Today, only a few huge technology companies control most of what people do on the internet, such as searching for information, shopping and using social media. Some people worry about this, but in my opinion it is mostly a positive development for ordinary users.

The main reason is that these big companies can offer very good services, and many of them are free. For example, anyone can use a search engine, send emails or watch videos without paying any money. Because these companies are so rich, they can invest a lot in new technology and make their products fast and easy to use. A small company would not have enough money to do this.

Another advantage is that it is easier for people to communicate when everyone use the same platforms. My family live in different countries, but we can talk every day using one messaging app. Also, small businesses can sell their products all over the world through a big online marketplace, which was impossible in the past.

However, there are some disadvantages. When a few company have so much power, they can collect a huge amount of information about their users and use it for advertising. Some people feel that their privacy is not protected. In addition, it is difficult for new companies to compete with them, so there are less choices for customers.

In conclusion, although there are some problems with privacy and competition, I believe that this situation is generally positive, because big technology companies give people free, useful services and connect people around the world. However, governments should make laws to protect users' personal data.

answers.text:
A handful of enormous technology firms now dominate internet search, social networking, online shopping and cloud computing. Although these companies provide popular and often free services, I believe that such a concentration of power is a negative development.

It is true that their size has brought some benefits. Large firms can afford to invest heavily in research, and this has produced fast, reliable services that billions of people use every day. Because so many people use the same platforms, communication across borders has also become much easier.

However, the main problem is the lack of competition. When one company controls most of a market, it can buy up or copy smaller rivals, which makes it very hard for new businesses to succeed. Without competition, there is less pressure to improve products or to treat customers and suppliers fairly. For example, independent sellers who depend on a single online marketplace may have to accept whatever fees and rules the platform decides to impose.

A second concern is the amount of personal data these companies hold. By tracking what users search for, buy and watch, they build detailed profiles that are used to target advertising and to keep people online for longer. Most users have little idea how this information is used, and there is always the risk that it is leaked or misused. Moreover, because these platforms decide what news and opinions people see, they have considerable influence over public debate, which is worrying when so few companies are involved.

In conclusion, while the dominance of a few technology giants has given people convenient services, it reduces competition, threatens privacy and concentrates too much influence in too few hands. Overall, therefore, I regard it as a negative development that governments needs to regulate more strongly.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Much of what people do online, from searching for information to shopping and keeping in touch with friends, now passes through the systems of a very small number of technology corporations. While this concentration has delivered undeniable conveniences, I believe its long-term consequences make it a predominantly negative development.

The benefits should be acknowledged. The scale of these firms allows them to offer sophisticated services free of charge, funded by advertising, and to invest in infrastructure and research that smaller companies could never afford. Their platforms have also created shared spaces in which people across the globe can communicate with ease.

The first cause for concern, however, is economic. Dominant platforms act simultaneously as marketplaces and competitors within those marketplaces, giving them both the ability and the incentive to favour their own products. Promising start-ups are frequently acquired before they can pose a threat, and the businesses that depend on these platforms for customers have little choice but to accept the terms imposed on them. Over time, reduced competition tends to mean slower innovation and fewer alternatives for consumers.

The second concern relates to personal and political freedom. These companies accumulate unprecedented quantities of data about individuals' habits, relationships and beliefs, and their business models depend on exploiting that information. At the same time, the algorithms that determine which content users encounter shape public opinion in ways that are neither transparent nor accountable to voters. When such influence is held by a handful of private organisations, a single policy change or failure can affect billions of people at once.

In conclusion, the dominance of a few technology giants has made the internet more convenient, but at the cost of competition, privacy and democratic accountability. It is, on balance, a negative development, and one that calls for more robust regulation.

Nowadays, in many countries people can talk to a doctor through a video call on their phone or computer, and they do not need to go to the clinic. I think this is a positive development, but it cannot replace normal visits completely.

The first advantage is that video consultations save time and money. Patients do not need to travel to the clinic or wait for a long time in the waiting room. This is very helpful for people who live in the countryside, where the nearest hospital can be far away. Also, working people do not have to take a whole day off for a short appointment, they can speak with the doctor during their lunch break.

Another advantage is that it reduce the spread of diseases. When sick people sit together in a waiting room, they can easily pass infections to each other. If patients with a cold or a flu stay at home and speak to the doctor online, other patients, specially old people and babies, are more safe.

However, video calls also have some limitation. A doctor cannot examine the patient's body properly through a screen, for example he cannot listen to the heart or check the blood pressure. So there is a risk that some serious illness is missed. In addition, some elderly people do not know how to use video call technology.

In conclusion, I believe that seeing a doctor by video call is a positive development because it is convenient and it can protect people from infections. However, it should be used only for simple problems, and patients should still visit the clinic when they need a physical examination.

answers.text:
In a growing number of countries, patients can now speak to a doctor over a video link rather than attending a clinic in person. In my opinion, this is a positive development, as long as it is used alongside traditional appointments rather than instead of them.

The greatest benefit is improved access to healthcare. For people living in remote areas, a visit to a clinic can involve hours of travel, and for elderly or disabled patients even a short journey may be exhausting. Video consultations allow these groups to receive advice quickly and from the comfort of their own home. They are also convenient for working people and parents, who no longer need to take time off work or arrange childcare for a routine appointment.

Remote consultations can also make health systems more efficient. Many appointments, such as renewing a prescription or discussing test results, do not require a physical examination, and handling them by video frees up clinic space for patients who really need to be seen in person. Furthermore, keeping people with infections out of crowded waiting rooms reduce the risk of illnesses spreading to other vulnerable patients.

Nevertheless, there are clear limitations. A doctor on a screen cannot carry out a full physical examination, and subtle signs of serious illness might be missed. In addition, not every patient has a reliable internet connection or the confidence to use the technology, so an over-reliance on video calls could disadvantage the very people who most need care.

In conclusion, video consultations make healthcare more accessible and efficient, and I therefore see them as a positive development. However, they should complement face-to-face appointments, and patients must always have the option of seeing a doctor in person.
