answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Consulting a doctor by video call, once a rarity, has become an established part of healthcare in many countries. I view this as a positive development, since it widens access to medical advice and relieves pressure on overstretched clinics, although it works best as a complement to, rather than a substitute for, face-to-face care.

The most important advantage is accessibility. For patients in rural areas, a routine appointment may involve a long journey and considerable expense, while for those with limited mobility or caring responsibilities, simply reaching a surgery can be a significant obstacle. A video consultation removes these barriers, and as a result people may be more willing to seek advice at an early stage rather than delaying until a problem becomes serious.

Remote appointments also allow health services to use their resources more intelligently. A substantial share of consultations, such as reviewing medication or discussing results, require conversation rather than physical contact. Handling these remotely shortens waiting times for patients who do need to be examined and reduces the number of potentially infectious people gathered in waiting rooms.

The limitations, however, should not be underestimated. Certain diagnoses depend on touch, sound and close observation, and a clinician relying on a camera may overlook important signs. There is also a danger that the convenience of video calls leads health providers to cut in-person services, disadvantaging older patients and households without dependable internet access. These risks do not negate the value of remote consultation, but they do mean that its use must be guided by clinical judgement rather than cost-saving alone.

In conclusion, video consultations represent a welcome advance: they bring medical advice within reach of people who previously struggled to obtain it and make better use of limited clinical time. Provided that in-person care remains readily available when needed, this development deserves to be embraced.

In many countries today, people wait until they are older before they have children. For example, many couples now have their first baby in their thirties instead of their twenties. In my opinion, this is generally a positive development.

The main reason is that older parents are usually more ready for the responsibility. When people are in their thirties, they have normally finished their education and have a stable job, so they have more money to take care of a child. They can pay for good food, clothes and education, and they does not need to depend on their own parents. In contrast, young couples often have financial problem and this can cause stress in the family.

Another reason is that older parents are more mature. They have more experience of life, and they already did many things they wanted to do, like travelling or building a career. Because of this, they are more patient and they can give more time and attention to their children. They also know better what kind of values they want to teach them.

However, having children later has some disadvantages. It can be more difficult for women to become pregnant when they are older, and parents may have less energy to play with young children. In addition, children may have less time with their grandparents, because the grandparents are also very old.

In conclusion, even though there are some problems, I believe having children later in life is a positive development. Parents who is older are usually more stable in money and more mature, and this is good for the children's future.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Across much of the world, the average age at which people become parents has been rising steadily. While there are understandable reasons for this, I believe that the trend is, on the whole, a negative development, both for families and for society.

It is true that delaying parenthood has some advantages. People who have children in their thirties or forties are often more financially secure and emotionally mature than younger parents. They may also have had time to complete their education and establish a career, which can reduce stress within the family.

However, there are significant biological disadvantages. It is widely recognised that fertility declines with age, so couples who wait may find it difficult to conceive and may need expensive medical treatment, which does not always succeed. As a result, some people who wanted children end up having fewer than they hoped, or none at all. Moreover, older parents may have less energy for the physical demands of raising young children.

The trend also has consequences across generations. When each generation has children later, grandparents are older when their grandchildren are born and may be less able to help with childcare or to enjoy an active role in their lives. At the same time, parents may find themselves caring for young children and elderly relatives simultaneously, which put considerable pressure on them. At a national level, later parenthood tends to contribute to lower birth rates, which creates an ageing population and places a heavier burden on the working-age population.

In conclusion, although older parents often enjoy greater stability, the difficulties with fertility, the strain on families and the long-term demographic effects make this trend largely negative. Governments could reduce it by offering better support to younger parents, such as affordable housing and childcare.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In many countries, the age at which people have their first child has risen considerably over the last few decades, as longer education, demanding careers and high housing costs encourage couples to postpone parenthood. Although this shift carries genuine risks, I believe it is, on balance, a positive development.

The principal benefit is that children are more likely to be born into stable circumstances. Parents who have completed their studies and established themselves professionally are generally better placed to provide secure housing, adequate income and a settled home life. Just as importantly, they tend to become parents through deliberate choice rather than circumstance, which often means they approach the role with greater commitment and emotional maturity.

Later parenthood has also changed opportunities for women in particular. When childbearing no longer coincides with the years in which careers are established, women are far better able to gain qualifications and seniority before taking time away from work. This not only benefits individual families financially but also allows economies to make fuller use of the skills of half their population.

That said, the drawbacks are not trivial. Fertility declines with age, and some couples who delay discover that conceiving is difficult or impossible, often after considerable emotional and financial strain. At a societal level, later parenthood tends to lower birth rates, compounding the challenges of an ageing population. Yet these concerns are arguably better addressed by making earlier parenthood more feasible, through affordable childcare and housing, than by regarding the choice to wait as a problem in itself.

In conclusion, while delaying parenthood can bring biological and demographic costs, the greater stability it affords children and the wider opportunities it creates for parents, especially mothers, outweigh them. I therefore regard this trend as largely positive.

In many countries, the difference between rich people and poor people is becoming bigger and bigger. In my opinion, this is a clearly negative development, because it causes many problems for poor people and also for the whole society.

Firstly, when the gap is big, poor people have less opportunities in their life. Rich families can pay for private schools, extra classes and good universities for their children, but poor families cannot afford this. As a result, children from poor family often get lower-paid jobs when they grow up, and they stay poor. This is not fair, because talented children should have the same chance to succeed.

Secondly, a big gap between rich and poor can cause social problems. When people see that some people have very expensive cars and houses but they cannot even pay their rent, they feel angry and unhappy. This can lead to more crime and less trust in the government. In some cities, rich and poor people live in completely different areas and they never meet each other, so the society become divided.

Some people say that inequality is not a problem because it motivate people to work harder and become rich. It is true that people need some rewards for hard work, but when the gap is too big, poor people feel that working hard is useless because they can never catch up.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that the growing gap between the richest and poorest people is a negative development. Governments should try to reduce it, for example by giving free education and making rich people pay more tax.

answers.text:
In many nations, the wealth and income of the richest citizens have grown far faster than those of the poorest, causing the gap between them to widen. I believe this is a highly negative development, as it limits opportunity and threatens social stability.

The first problem is that growing inequality reduces social mobility. Wealthy families can invest heavily in their children's education, health and connections, while low-income families often struggle to meet basic needs. As a result, a child's future increasingly depends on the family they are born into rather than on their talent or effort. This is not only unfair to individuals but also wasteful for society, since the abilities of many capable young people are never fully developed.

Secondly, a large gap between rich and poor can damage the cohesion of a society. When people feel that the economic system benefits only a small elite, they tend to lose trust in institutions and politicians. This frustration can fuel social unrest and support for extreme political movements. In addition, the wealthy are able to exert disproportionate influence over political decisions, for example through lobbying, which may lead to policies that further protect their interests.

Some argue that inequality is a natural result of a free economy and that it encourages people to work hard and take risks. There is some truth in this, as a certain degree of difference in income rewards effort and skill. However, when the gap becomes extreme, it no longer act as a motivation, because the poorest see no realistic way of improving their situation.

In conclusion, although some inequality is inevitable, a continually growing gap between the richest and the poorest is harmful. It restricts opportunities, weakens trust and concentrates power, and governments should therefore take steps to reduce it.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
In a large number of countries, the share of national wealth held by the most affluent has grown while the incomes of those at the bottom have stagnated. Some economists regard this as a tolerable by-product of growth, but I consider the widening gap to be an unmistakably negative development.

The most fundamental objection concerns opportunity. When wealth is heavily concentrated, advantage becomes self-perpetuating: affluent families can secure better schooling, healthcare and professional networks for their children, while those on low incomes struggle to meet everyday costs. Over successive generations, life chances come to depend increasingly on birth rather than merit, and a society squanders the potential of countless able people who never have the means to develop it.

A second objection is political. Extreme economic disparities tend to translate into disparities of influence, since those with vast resources can fund campaigns, shape public debate and lobby for favourable treatment. The result is a system that responds more readily to the concerns of the few than to those of the many. Unsurprisingly, citizens who perceive the system as rigged become disillusioned with mainstream institutions, and this erosion of trust can open the door to polarisation and instability.

Defenders of inequality argue that the prospect of great rewards drives enterprise and innovation. This argument has some force when applied to moderate differences in income, which do reflect variations in skill and effort. It becomes far less convincing, however, when the gap grows so wide that those at the bottom have no realistic prospect of advancement, for at that point inequality ceases to motivate and instead breeds resignation.

In conclusion, while a degree of inequality is an inevitable feature of any market economy, its continued growth undermines equal opportunity, distorts democratic politics and weakens social cohesion. It is therefore a development that governments should actively work to reverse.

These days, a lot of people post many details about their private life on social media, for example photos of their family, where they are on holiday and what they eat every day. In my opinion, this is a negative development, because it has more risks than benefits.

Of course, there are some good points. People can keep in touch with friends and relatives who live far away, and they can share happy moments like a wedding or the birth of a baby. Some people also say that sharing their problems online help them to get support from others.

However, the first big problem is privacy and safety. When people post their address, their school or the place where they are at the moment, criminals can use this informations. For example, if a family post photos from the beach, a thief can know that their house is empty. Also, pictures of children can be seen by strangers, which is dangerous.

The second problem is that sharing everything online can make people unhappy. Many users only post the best parts of their life, so other people compare themselves and feel that their own life is boring or not successful. Some people also become addicted to getting likes and comments, and they spend more time on their phone than with the real people around them. Another risk is that the things people post can stay on internet forever. A young person may share something embarrassing today, and many years later an employer can find it and decide not to give them a job.

In conclusion, although social media helps people to stay connected, I believe sharing private life publicly is negative because it is risky for safety and it can damage people's happiness and future.

answers.text:
It has become normal for people to post photographs of their homes, children, holidays and even personal struggles on social media for anyone to see. Although this trend certainly carries risks, I believe that overall it is a positive development.

The most obvious benefit is that it helps people maintain relationships. Families are now often spread across different cities or countries, and regular updates allow relatives to feel involved in each other's lives in a way that occasional phone calls cannot. A grandparent abroad, for instance, can watch a grandchild grow up through shared photos and videos.

More significantly, openness about private life can create support and reduce stigma. When people share their experiences of illness, unemployment or the challenges of parenting, others in similar situations realise they are not alone. Online communities built around such experiences offer practical advice and emotional encouragement, and public conversations about topics that were once considered taboo, such as mental health, have helped change attitudes in society.

That said, there are genuine dangers. Personal information can be misused by criminals, and posts made carelessly may harm a person's reputation or career years later. There is also a concern that constantly comparing oneself with the carefully edited lives of others can damage self-esteem. However, these problems largely depend on how people use social media, and they can be reduced if users learn to adjust their privacy settings and think carefully before posting.

In conclusion, while sharing personal details publicly requires caution, the ability to stay connected with loved ones and to find support from people with similar experiences makes this a mainly positive development in my view.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Social media has blurred the boundary between public and private life. Details that people once shared only with close friends, such as family celebrations, health scares and relationship breakdowns, are now routinely broadcast to hundreds or even thousands of followers. While this openness has some genuine merits, I believe that, taken as a whole, it is a negative development.

It would be unfair to dismiss the practice entirely. Sharing personal news allows people to sustain relationships across great distances, and candid accounts of difficult experiences can foster solidarity and help to dismantle stigma around issues that were long hidden. For some, a supportive online audience provides comfort that is not available in their immediate surroundings.

The difficulty is that most users greatly underestimate the permanence and reach of what they post. Content shared casually can be copied, archived and rediscovered long after it has lost its original context, sometimes resurfacing when its author applies for a job. Information that seems harmless in isolation, such as a child's school uniform or a holiday departure date, can, when pieced together, expose people to fraud, stalking or burglary. Children are particularly vulnerable, since parents frequently publish details of their lives before they are old enough to consent.

There is also a subtler psychological cost. When private experiences are presented to an audience, they tend to be curated for approval, and life becomes something to be performed rather than simply lived. Constant exposure to others' highlights encourages unfavourable comparison, while the pursuit of likes can make self-worth dependent on external validation.

In conclusion, although sharing personal lives online can strengthen connections and reduce isolation, the long-term risks to privacy, safety and wellbeing are, in my view, greater. It is therefore a trend that calls for far more caution than it currently receives.

In many countries where English is not the first language, more and more universities teach their courses in English. I believe this is a positive development, although it can be difficult for some students.

The first advantage is that English is the international language of science and business. Most important research papers, books and websites are written in English, so students who study in English can read them easily. Also, when they graduate, they can work for international companies or find a job in other countries, because their English level is high. This give them a big advantage in the job market.

Another advantage is that universities can attract students and teachers from other countries. For example, a university in Asia which teach in English can accept students from Europe, Africa and South America. This makes the university more international, and local students can learn about different cultures and make friends from around the world. The university also earn more money from international students.

In addition, if all courses are in English, the local language may become less important, especially in science subjects, and in the future there may be no modern textbooks in the local language at all.

In conclusion, I think teaching university courses in English is mostly a positive development because it helps students to find better jobs and make universities more international. But universities should give extra English classes to students who need it, so nobody is left behind.

answers.text:
Universities in many non-English-speaking countries are increasingly offering degree programmes taught entirely in English. Although this policy raises concerns about the quality of learning and the status of national languages, I consider it a positive development overall.

The main argument in its favour is that it prepares graduates for an international labour market. English is the dominant language of academic research, technology and global business, so students who have studied their subject in English are able to read the latest publications, attend international conferences and work confidently with colleagues from other countries. For a young engineer or economist, this can open up career opportunities that would otherwise be unavailable.

Teaching in English also allows universities to become more international. Courses in the local language are only accessible to local students, whereas English-medium programmes can attract applicants and academic staff from around the world. This diversity enriches the learning environment, as students are exposed to a wider range of perspectives, and it also bring valuable income from tuition fees.

Nevertheless, the trend is not without disadvantages. Students whose English is weak may understand only part of their lectures, and some lecturers may struggle to explain complex ideas in a second language, which could lower the standard of teaching. There is also a risk that the national language gradually loses its role in academic life, particularly in scientific fields. These problems, however, can be reduced by providing language support and by continuing to offer some courses in the local language.

In conclusion, while English-medium teaching presents certain challenges, it gives students valuable skills and helps universities compete globally. For these reasons, I regard it as a largely positive development.

The first problem, however, is educational. Learning a demanding subject is challenging enough in one's first language; doing so through a language in which one is less than fluent inevitably consumes cognitive effort that would otherwise go into understanding the material. Students may memorise terminology without grasping underlying concepts, while lecturers who are not fully confident in English may simplify their explanations or avoid spontaneous discussion. The result can be a degree that sounds international but conveys less knowledge.

A second concern is the long-term impact on national languages. When advanced study and research are conducted exclusively in English, the local language ceases to develop the vocabulary needed for specialised fields. Over time, it risks being confined to everyday use, and knowledge becomes less accessible to citizens who do not speak English well. This also tends to favour students from wealthier backgrounds, who are more likely to have received strong English tuition at school.

In conclusion, while proficiency in English is undeniably valuable, making it the sole medium of university teaching can undermine both learning and linguistic heritage. Strengthening English as a subject, while teaching most courses in the national language, would achieve the benefits without these costs.

Nowadays, many people decide to use their holidays for doing voluntary work in other countries, for example building schools, teaching children or protecting animals. In my opinion, this is a positive development for both the volunteers and the local communities.

Firstly, voluntary work can help poor communities. In many developing countries, there are not enough teachers, doctors or money for projects like building a clean water system. When volunteers come, they can give their time and skills for free. For instance, a group of volunteers can build a small school in a village in only few weeks, and many children can study there for years.

Secondly, volunteers themselves get a lot of benefits. They can learn about a new culture, a different way of life and maybe some words of the local language. This is much more interesting than lying on a beach in a hotel. Also, they learn to be grateful for what they have at home, and they can develop new skills such as teamwork and problem solving, which is useful for their future career.

However, some people say that volunteering holidays are not always helpful. Some volunteers have no experience, so the work they do is not very good quality. In addition, some companies charge volunteers a lot of money but only small part of it goes to the project.

In conclusion, I believe that doing voluntary work on holiday is mainly a positive development, because it helps communities in need and give volunteers an unforgettable experience. However, people should choose a good organisation and a project that match their skills.

answers.text:
Rather than spending their holidays relaxing on a beach, a growing number of people are choosing to volunteer on projects abroad, such as building homes, teaching English or supporting wildlife conservation. Despite some criticisms of this kind of travel, I believe it is a positive trend.

For communities that receive volunteers, the most direct benefit is practical help. Many projects in developing regions depend on outside labour and funding to succeed, and volunteers often contribute both. A conservation programme, for example, may rely on visitors to monitor endangered species, while the fees they pay help to cover the salaries of local staff. In this way, volunteering can support work that would not otherwise be possible.

The experience is also valuable for the volunteers themselves. Living and working alongside local people gives them a far deeper understanding of another culture than ordinary tourism provides. Many return home with a greater awareness of global issues such as poverty and environmental damage, and some go on to support charities or choose careers in development. The skills they gain, including adaptability and teamwork, are also highly valued by employers.

It is true that the industry has been criticised. Some projects accept volunteers with no relevant skills, for instance allowing untrained visitors to teach in schools for only a week or two, which can do more harm than good. There are also commercial agencies that charge high fees while giving little to the communities. However, these problems show the need for careful choice of project rather than a reason to reject volunteering altogether.

In conclusion, when volunteers choose responsible organisations and suitable projects, their work benefits both local communities and themselves. For this reason, I consider the rise of volunteer holidays to be a positive development.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Volunteer tourism, in which travellers spend their holidays working on community or conservation projects overseas, has grown into a substantial industry. The idea is admirable in principle, yet I would argue that, in the form it most commonly takes, it is a more negative development than its popularity suggests.

Its appeal is easy to understand. Volunteers hope to make a tangible difference, and some projects, particularly those involving skilled professionals such as doctors or engineers, undoubtedly do. Participants also gain an insight into unfamiliar cultures and global inequalities that conventional tourism rarely provides, which may shape their attitudes and choices for years afterwards.

The problem is that most short-term volunteers lack the skills the work requires. A teenager who spends two weeks teaching in a village school, with no training and no knowledge of the local language, is unlikely to contribute much to children's learning, and a steady stream of such visitors can disrupt continuity in the classroom. Similarly, construction projects carried out by inexperienced tourists may be of poor quality and may take paid work away from local builders who could have done the job better and more cheaply.

There are also ethical concerns. Because volunteering has become a profitable product, some agencies design projects around the wishes of paying customers rather than the needs of communities. In the worst cases, children in orphanages form attachments to a succession of visitors who then disappear, which can be emotionally harmful. Such arrangements risk treating poorer communities as a backdrop for the personal growth of wealthier travellers.

In conclusion, although volunteer holidays can broaden travellers' horizons and some skilled contributions are genuinely valuable, many schemes deliver little lasting benefit and occasionally cause harm. For this reason, I regard the trend as largely negative, and would suggest that donating to established local organisations is often a more effective way to help.

Because of the internet, many people can now work from home, and some of them decide to leave big cities and move to small towns or the countryside. I think this is a positive development for the people and also for the country.

The main benefit is for the people who move. Life in a big city is very expensive and stressful. Rent is high, the traffic is terrible and there is a lot of noise and pollution. In a small town, people can rent or buy a bigger house with a garden for less money, and they can enjoy fresh air and nature. This make their life healthier and more relaxing, especially for families with children.

Another benefit is for the small towns. In many countries, young people have left the countryside to find jobs in the city, so villages become empty and shops and schools close. When remote workers move there, they spend their money in local shops and cafes, and the town become more alive again. Also, big cities become less crowded, which help to reduce traffic and pollution.

However, this change can cause some problems. When many people from the city move to a village, the house prices goes up, and local young people cannot afford to buy a home. Also, the internet in the countryside is sometimes slow, and there are less hospitals and other services.

In conclusion, I believe that people moving from cities to the countryside because of remote work is a positive development. It gives people a better quality of life and brings new life to small towns. However, the government should improve internet and services in rural area.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
The rise of remote working has allowed many employees to leave expensive cities and settle in smaller towns and rural areas. In my view, this movement is a positive development, both for the individuals concerned and for the places they move to.

For the people who relocate, the improvement in quality of life can be considerable. City living often involves high housing costs, long commutes and limited green space. By moving to a smaller community, remote workers can usually afford more spacious homes, spend the time they once lost travelling with their families, and enjoy a calmer environment. Many report that this balance between work and personal life makes them healthier and more productive.

The trend can also help to revive rural areas. For decades, young people have moved away from the countryside in search of employment, leaving behind ageing populations and declining services. New residents who keep their city salaries bring spending power to local businesses, and their children help to keep village schools open. At the same time, a reduction in population pressure can ease congestion and housing shortages in overcrowded cities.

Admittedly, this migration creates some tensions. In popular areas, the arrival of wealthier newcomers has pushed up property prices, making it harder for local people to stay in the communities where they grew up. Rural infrastructure, such as broadband and public transport, may also struggle to cope with a growing population. However, these are problems that careful planning, such as building affordable homes for local residents and investing in digital connections, can address.

In conclusion, although the movement of remote workers to smaller towns needs to be managed carefully, it offers a better quality of life for many people and new energy for struggling rural communities. Overall, I see it as a positive trend.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Freed from the obligation to commute daily to an office, a significant number of professionals have left large cities for market towns, coastal villages and the countryside. Although this migration has created real difficulties in some places, I believe that its overall effect is positive.

The benefits for those who move are the most immediate. Residents of major cities frequently pay a large share of their income for cramped accommodation and spend hours each week travelling to work. Relocating allows them to exchange these costs for more space, cleaner air and closer contact with nature, while continuing to earn a city salary. For families in particular, this can mean more time together and a less pressured daily routine.

More significantly, the trend has the potential to reverse a long-standing imbalance between urban and rural areas. For generations, economic opportunity has been concentrated in a few large cities, drawing young people away from smaller communities and leaving them with shrinking populations and disappearing services. Remote workers bring income that circulates through local shops, cafes and tradespeople, and their presence can justify investment in schools, transport and broadband. Meanwhile, cities themselves may benefit from slightly reduced pressure on housing and transport.

The principal drawback is the effect on housing in desirable rural areas. When buyers with urban salaries compete for a limited supply of homes, prices can rise beyond the reach of local families, and young people may be forced to leave the very places that newcomers are moving into. This is a serious concern, but it reflects a failure of housing policy rather than a flaw in the trend itself, and it can be mitigated by building more homes and prioritising local buyers.

In conclusion, provided that its impact on local housing is managed responsibly, the movement of remote workers away from large cities improves individual wellbeing and helps to rebalance regional economies. I therefore consider it a positive development.

Today, many people prefer to buy almost everything online, such as clothes, electronic devices and even food, instead of going to the shops. In my opinion, this is a positive development, although it has some bad effects too.

The biggest advantage of online shopping is convenience. People can order things at any time of the day from their sofa, and the products are delivered to their door, sometimes on the next day. This is very useful for busy people, parents with small children and people who cannot walk easily. They do not need to drive to the city centre, look for a parking place and carry heavy bags.

Another advantage is that online shopping is often cheaper. Online stores do not need to pay rent for a big shop, so they can sell products for lower price. Customers can also compare the prices on different websites in a few minutes and choose the cheapest one. In addition, they can read reviews from other buyers, which help them to avoid buying bad products.

However, online shopping also causes some problems. Many small shops in town centres has closed because they cannot compete with big online companies, and some shop workers lost their jobs. Also, all the packaging and delivery vans create more rubbish and pollution. Sometimes the product looks different from the picture, and returning it take a lot of time.

In conclusion, I believe that buying things online is mainly a positive development, because it saves people time and money. However, people should also sometimes buy from local shops, so that town centres do not become empty.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Online shopping has grown so rapidly that many people now purchase the majority of their goods, from groceries to furniture, over the internet. Although this has made shopping more convenient, I believe that overall it is a negative development.

There is no doubt that buying online has clear advantages for consumers. It saves time, allows people to compare prices easily and gives access to a far wider range of products than any local shop could offer. For people with limited mobility or those living far from shopping centres, home delivery can be particularly valuable.

However, the decline of physical shops has serious consequences for local communities. As more spending moves online, independent retailers and even large chains are forced to close, leaving empty units in high streets and town centres. These places used to be not only somewhere to buy things but also social spaces where people met and interacted. When they decline, towns lose their character and jobs disappear, often in areas that already have limited employment opportunities.

In addition, the environmental cost of online shopping is often underestimated. Individual deliveries mean that large numbers of vans travel to people's homes every day, and each order usually comes with plastic and cardboard packaging. The ease of returning products also encourages people to order several items and send most of them back, which creates even more transport and waste. Furthermore, many warehouse and delivery workers face intense pressure and insecure contracts, which raise questions about the true cost of cheap and fast delivery.

In conclusion, while online shopping offers undeniable convenience for individuals, its effects on town centres, the environment and working conditions are harmful. For these reasons, I consider the shift towards buying most goods online to be a largely negative trend.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
For a large proportion of consumers, the weekly trip to the shops has been replaced by a few minutes on a smartphone, with purchases arriving at the door within a day or two. This shift has undoubtedly come at a cost to traditional retail, but I believe that, on balance, it is a positive development.

The most obvious gains accrue to consumers. Online retail offers a range of choice that no single shop could match, together with the ability to compare prices and read other customers' experiences before buying. The resulting transparency places downward pressure on prices, which is of real value to households on tight budgets. Home delivery, moreover, has been transformative for people who find conventional shopping difficult, including elderly and disabled people and those in rural areas without nearby stores.

The internet has also lowered the barriers to starting a business. Whereas opening a shop requires premises, stock and a location with sufficient passing trade, a craftsperson or small producer can now reach customers across the country, or even the world, through a website or online marketplace. In this sense, online shopping has broadened, rather than merely concentrated, commercial opportunity.

The losses, however, are real. High streets in many towns have been hollowed out as shops close, taking with them jobs and a sense of place, and the proliferation of delivery vans and packaging has a considerable environmental impact. Yet town centres were already under pressure before online retail became dominant, and those that have reinvented themselves around leisure, services and community events show that decline is not inevitable. Environmental harm, likewise, can be reduced through consolidated deliveries and recyclable packaging.

In conclusion, although the move to online shopping has contributed to the decline of traditional high streets, it has given consumers greater choice, lower prices and easier access, and has opened markets to small producers. Overall, therefore, I regard it as a positive change.

In some countries, public places like museums, libraries and parks now get a lot of their money from private companies. I think this is a positive development, because without this money many of these places could not survive.

The main reason is that governments often do not have enough money. They have to spend their budget on important things like hospitals, schools and the police, so culture and parks are not a priority. When a company give money, a museum can stay open, buy new exhibitions and keep its entrance free. A library can buy more books and computers, and a park can have new playgrounds and better cleaning.

Another reason is that both sides get benefits. The companies get good advertising, because people see their name and logo in the museum or the park, and they think the company is responsible and care about society. At the same time, the public can enjoy better facilities without paying more tax. So it is a win-win situation.

In conclusion, I believe it is a positive development that public facilities get money from private companies, because it helps them to provide better services for people. However, the government should make rules so that companies cannot control the content, and it should still give some money itself.

answers.text:
In many countries, museums, libraries and public parks are relying more and more on sponsorship and donations from private businesses to cover their costs. Although this extra funding brings short-term benefits, I believe that growing dependence on it is a negative development.

It is easy to see why such partnerships are attractive. Public budgets are under pressure, and cultural institutions and green spaces are often among the first areas to face cuts. Corporate money can pay for new exhibitions, longer opening hours or improved facilities, and companies gain a positive public image in return.

However, the first problem is that sponsorship can affect what these institutions do. A museum that depends on a particular company may be reluctant to host an exhibition that criticises that company's industry. Similarly, sponsors naturally prefer popular, eye-catching projects that attract publicity, so less glamorous work, such as preserving archives or running services in poorer neighbourhoods, may be neglected. Over time, decisions that should be made in the public interest become shaped by commercial priorities.

A second concern is instability. Private funding depends on a company's profits and marketing strategy, both of which can change quickly. If a sponsor withdraws during an economic downturn, a library or park that has come to rely on its money may be forced to reduce services suddenly. Moreover, heavy reliance on corporate support can give governments an excuse to reduce their own responsibility for funding facilities that all citizens is entitled to use.

In conclusion, while private contributions can be a useful addition to public funding, facilities that depend on them risk losing their independence and financial security. For these reasons, I regard this trend as mainly negative, and I believe governments should remain the main source of funding.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Faced with tight public budgets, many museums, libraries and parks have turned to corporate sponsors to fund everything from new galleries to playground equipment. Private support can be a welcome supplement, but when these institutions come to depend on it, I believe the development becomes a largely negative one.

The attraction of corporate money is understandable. Governments must balance cultural spending against the more pressing demands of healthcare, education and security, and in lean years it is often facilities such as libraries that suffer most. Sponsorship can keep doors open and admission free, and companies are often happy to fund projects that associate their brand with public benefit.

The difficulty is that funding is rarely neutral. Institutions that depend on a particular sponsor face a quiet but persistent pressure to avoid offending it, whether by declining an exhibition critical of its industry or by giving its logo prominence it has not earned. In some cases, sponsorship has been used by companies with poor environmental or ethical records to acquire respectability, a practice that implicates the institution in their public relations. Even without any direct interference, sponsors' preference for high-profile, marketable projects can divert resources from essential but unglamorous work, such as conservation or outreach to disadvantaged communities.

Dependence also creates fragility. Corporate budgets fluctuate with profits and marketing fashions, and a facility that has built its operations around a single donor can be left in crisis when that support is withdrawn. Perhaps most significantly, the availability of private money allows governments to retreat from funding institutions that exist precisely because they serve everyone, not just those who are commercially valuable.

In conclusion, private contributions have a legitimate role as an addition to public funding, but reliance on them compromises the independence and stability of institutions that belong to the public. The growing dependence described is therefore a trend that should be resisted rather than encouraged.

In some countries, people can now use an app on their mobile phone to report a crime and send videos to the police. In my opinion, this is a positive development, although it must be used carefully.

The first advantage is that reporting a crime become much easier and faster. In the past, people had to call the police or go to the police station, and many people did not want to do this because it take a lot of time. With an app, a person who sees a car accident or a theft in the street can send a report in only one minute. As a result, more crimes are reported and police can react more quickly.

The second advantage is that video evidence is very useful. Often, it is difficult for the police to know exactly what happened, because witnesses remember different things. A video clearly shows the person who commit the crime, his face and the time and place. This can help the police to catch criminals and to prove in court that they are guilty.

On the other hand, there are some problems. Some people may send false reports about neighbours they do not like, or they may film innocent people and put them in trouble. Also, if people try to film a dangerous situation, they can put themselves in danger. Moreover, the police may receive too many small reports and not have time for serious crimes.

In conclusion, I think crime reporting apps are a positive development because they make reporting easier and give the police good evidence. However, the police should check all reports carefully and tell people not to take risks for filming.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
Several countries have introduced mobile phone apps that allow citizens to report crimes and upload photographs or video evidence directly to the police. I believe this is a positive development, as it makes reporting easier and can improve the effectiveness of policing.

The main benefit is that it removes many of the barriers that discourage people from reporting crimes. Calling the police or visiting a station can be time-consuming and intimidating, so many minor offences, such as vandalism or dangerous driving, are simply never reported. An app allows a witness to submit a report within minutes, and even anonymously in some cases. This gives the police a more accurate picture of where and when crimes happen, which can help them decide where to send patrols.

Video evidence can also strengthen investigations. Eyewitness memories are often incomplete, particularly after a stressful event, whereas a recording captures details such as appearances, vehicle registration numbers and the order of events. This kind of evidence can help identify suspects more quickly and may also protect innocent people who have been wrongly accused.

Nevertheless, there are some risks to consider. Some users might submit false or malicious reports, and there are concerns about privacy when members of the public film others without permission. There is also a danger that people put themselves at risk by stopping to record a violent incident instead of moving to safety. However, these problems can be managed if the police verify all reports carefully and the app clearly advise users never to endanger themselves.

In conclusion, although crime-reporting apps must be carefully managed, they encourage more people to report offences and provide valuable evidence. For these reasons, I consider them a positive development in the fight against crime.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Police forces in a number of countries now allow members of the public to report offences through smartphone apps, attaching photographs or video footage as evidence. While such tools raise legitimate concerns about privacy and misuse, I consider them, on the whole, a positive development.

Their chief merit is that they make reporting crime far more accessible. Many offences go unreported not because witnesses are indifferent but because the process seems disproportionately burdensome: waiting on the phone, visiting a station or giving a lengthy statement for an incident that may appear minor. By reducing reporting to a few taps, apps capture offences that would otherwise disappear from official records, such as antisocial behaviour, fly-tipping or reckless driving. Better data, in turn, allows police to identify patterns and deploy their limited resources more intelligently.

Footage recorded at the scene can also be valuable evidence. Human memory is notoriously unreliable, especially under stress, while a timestamped video preserves details that witnesses may later forget or misremember. Such material can accelerate investigations and, just as importantly, can exonerate people who have been wrongly suspected.

The risks, however, deserve careful attention. An easy reporting channel may be exploited to harass neighbours or settle personal disputes, and the circulation of footage of identifiable individuals raises obvious privacy concerns. There is also a danger that the desire to record encourages bystanders to film incidents instead of seeking safety or offering help. These problems are serious but manageable: reports can be screened by trained staff, footage can be restricted to police use, and users can be clearly instructed to prioritise their own safety.

In conclusion, crime-reporting apps enable the public to contribute more effectively to their own security and supply the police with better intelligence. Provided that robust safeguards accompany them, they represent a welcome step forward.

In many countries today, children begin formal education at a younger age than before, sometimes when they are only three or four years old. I believe this is mostly a positive development for children and also for their parents.

Firstly, starting school early helps children to learn basic skills. At a young age, children's brains develop very quickly, so they can learn letters, numbers and even a foreign language more easily than older children. If they start school early, they will be more prepared when they go to primary school, and they can do better in their studies later.

Secondly, school gives young children the chance to make friends and learn how to behave with other people. At home, a child may only play with their parents or one brother or sister. At school, they must share toys, wait their turn and follow the rules of teacher. These social skills are very important for their future life. Also, early education is helpful for parents. Today, in many families both mother and father work full-time, so they need a safe place for their children during the day. When children go to school, parents can work without worry, and the family have more income.

However, some people think that young children need more time to play and they may feel stress if they study too much. This is true, so schools for small children should focus on games and activities, not on exams.

In conclusion, I think that children starting formal education earlier is a positive development, because it helps their learning and social skills, and it also support working parents.

answers.label: Band 7
answers.text:
In many parts of the world, children are now expected to begin formal schooling, with structured lessons in reading, writing and mathematics, at an increasingly early age. Although this is usually intended to give children a head start, I believe it is largely a negative development.

Supporters of early education argue that young children learn quickly and that starting sooner will lead to higher achievement later. It also meets the needs of working parents, who require reliable childcare, and can help children from disadvantaged backgrounds who may receive little educational support at home.

However, many young children are simply not ready for formal learning. At the age of three or four, most children learn best through play, exploration and conversation rather than by sitting at desks completing worksheets. When they are pushed to read and write before they are developmentally ready, some become frustrated and may begin to see learning as something difficult and unpleasant. This negative attitude can last for years and affect their motivation throughout school.

In addition, an early focus on academic skills can leave less time for developing other important abilities. Through unstructured play, children learn to solve problems, cooperate with others, manage their emotions and use their imagination. These qualities are essential for success in later life, yet they cannot be easily measured in tests, so they are often given lower priority in formal classrooms. Furthermore, children who spend long days in a structured environment from such a young age may experience stress and tiredness, which affect their wellbeing.

In conclusion, while early education can provide childcare and support for some families, introducing formal lessons too early may harm children's attitude to learning and limit their broader development. I therefore regard this trend as mainly negative, and I believe the early years should focus on play-based learning.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
Across many countries, the age at which children first enter a classroom and begin structured academic instruction has steadily fallen. This is generally justified as an investment in children's future achievement, but I would argue that, in most cases, it is a negative development.

The rationale for early schooling is not without merit. High-quality early education can narrow the gap between children from affluent and disadvantaged homes, since the latter may have fewer books and less adult conversation at home. For families in which both parents work, early school entry also provides dependable, affordable care.

Yet there is a crucial distinction between early education and early formal education. What benefits young children most is a rich environment of play, talk and exploration, in which language, curiosity and social skills develop naturally. Formal instruction, by contrast, demands sustained attention, fine motor control and the ability to sit still, capacities that many four-year-olds have not yet acquired. Children pushed into reading and arithmetic before they are ready may struggle, and early experiences of failure can shape a lasting belief that they are not good at learning.

There is also a question of opportunity cost. Every hour spent on phonics drills or worksheets is an hour not spent building with blocks, negotiating games with peers or inventing stories, activities through which children develop the creativity, resilience and self-regulation that underpin later success. Several countries with consistently strong educational outcomes do not begin formal schooling until around the age of six or seven, which suggests that an early start is by no means a prerequisite for high achievement.

In conclusion, while providing young children with stimulating care is highly desirable, subjecting them to formal academic instruction at an ever earlier age risks undermining both their wellbeing and their long-term enthusiasm for learning. This trend is therefore, on balance, a regrettable one.

Some governments are now testing a system where every adult get a regular amount of money, even if they do not have a job. In my opinion, this is a positive development, although there are some problems with the idea.

The most important advantage is that a basic income can reduce poverty. Many people today have jobs that pay very little or are not stable, so they worry about paying for rent and food. If everyone receive a fixed amount every month, nobody will be extremely poor. This can also reduce stress and make people more healthy and happy.

Another advantage is that basic income give people more freedom. For example, a person who wants to study a new skill or start a small business can do it without being afraid of losing all their money. Also, people who take care of their children or old parents at home can receive some money for their important work, which is usually unpaid.

On the other hand, many people think that basic income is too expensive for the government, and it may need to raise taxes. Some people also believe that if people get free money, they will become lazy and stop working. However, I think most people want to work because they want a better life, not only to survive.

In conclusion, I believe that experimenting with basic income is a positive development, because it can reduce poverty and give people more choices in their life. Of course, governments must test it carefully first to see if they can afford it.

answers.text:
In several countries, governments have begun trials in which every adult receives a fixed sum of money at regular intervals, regardless of whether they are employed. Although the aim of reducing poverty is admirable, I believe that this is essentially a negative development.

Supporters argue that a basic income would provide security in an economy where many jobs are low-paid, temporary or at risk from automation. It would also be simpler to administer than complex welfare systems, and it would recognise unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives.

However, the most serious problem is cost. Giving a meaningful amount of money to every adult, including those who are already wealthy, would require an enormous budget. To fund it, governments would probably have to raise taxes significantly or cut spending on other public services, such as healthcare and education, which the poorest people depend on most. In this sense, a universal payment may be a less efficient way of helping those in need than targeted support.

Another concern is the possible effect on work. While most people would continue working, some might reduce their hours or leave jobs that are unpleasant but necessary, such as cleaning or care work. If this happened on a large scale, it could cause labour shortages and slow economic growth, which in turn would make the scheme even harder to afford. Moreover, there is a risk that the payments push up prices, particularly rents, so that people is no better off in real terms.

In conclusion, although a basic income aims to give everyone financial security, its high cost and potential impact on employment and prices make it an unwise policy. I therefore regard governments' experiments with it as a negative development, and believe that resources would be better spent on improving existing welfare systems.

paragraphs.text: In several countries, governments have begun trials in which every adult receives a fixed sum of money at regular intervals, regardless of whether they are employed.
Although
the aim of reducing poverty is admirable,
I believe
that this is essentially a negative development.

Supporters argue that a basic income would provide security in an economy where many jobs are low-paid, temporary or at risk from automation. It would also be simpler to administer than complex welfare systems, and it would recognise unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives.
However,

the most serious problem is cost. Giving a meaningful amount of money to every adult, including those who are already wealthy, would require an enormous budget. To fund it, governments would probably have to raise taxes significantly or cut spending on other public services, such as healthcare and education, which the poorest people depend on most. In this sense, a universal payment may be a less efficient way of helping those in need than targeted support.
Another concern is the possible effect on work.
While

most people would continue working, some might reduce their hours or leave jobs that are unpleasant but necessary, such as cleaning or care work. If this happened on a large scale, it could cause labour shortages and slow economic growth, which in turn would make the scheme even harder to afford.
Moreover,
there is a risk that the payments push up prices, particularly rents, so that people is no better off in real terms.
In conclusion,

although a basic income aims to give everyone financial security, its high cost and potential impact on employment and prices make it an unwise policy. I therefore regard governments' experiments with it as a negative development, and believe that resources would be better spent on improving existing welfare systems.

answers.label: Band 8
answers.text:
A number of governments have launched trials in which adults receive a regular, unconditional payment, irrespective of whether they are in work. Whether a universal basic income would succeed as a permanent national policy remains highly uncertain, but I believe that the decision to test it is a clearly positive development.

The case for exploring the idea is compelling. Many welfare systems are complex, stigmatising and riddled with gaps, leaving people who are entitled to support unable to obtain it. Meanwhile, insecure employment and the prospect of automation have left many workers exposed to sudden losses of income. An unconditional payment could provide a stable foundation, allowing people to retrain, care for relatives or take the risk of starting a business without fear of destitution.

Equally, the objections to basic income are serious and deserve to be tested rather than assumed. Critics warn that it would be ruinously expensive, that it might discourage people from working and that landlords and retailers could simply absorb the extra money through higher prices. These are empirical questions, and debates about them have long been conducted largely on the basis of ideology. Carefully designed experiments can reveal how recipients actually behave, how much the policy would really cost and which groups benefit most.

It should be acknowledged that trials have limitations. Because they are small and temporary, participants may behave differently than they would under a permanent scheme, and a pilot in one region cannot fully reflect the economic effects of a national programme. Nevertheless, imperfect evidence is preferable to none, and gradual experimentation is far less risky than either adopting such a radical policy wholesale or rejecting it without investigation.

In conclusion, whatever the eventual verdict on basic income itself, governments that test it are approaching a difficult question in a responsible, evidence-based way. For that reason, I regard these experiments as a positive development.
